aardvark.context_blurb:
The aardvark is a shy night digger of the African savanna south of the Sahara. Its name is Afrikaans for "earth pig," and people also call it the antbear. Nearly every oddity of its body serves a single trade: breaking into the rock-hard nests of ants and termites and feasting on the insects inside.

At dusk it shuffles out of its den looking as if it were built from spare parts. The aardvark, Orycteropus afer, has a pig's snout, long ears like a rabbit's, a humped back, a heavy kangaroo-style tail and spade-clawed feet, and a big one weighs 60 to 80 kilograms.

Its front claws smash a mound open, and then the aardvark sends in a sticky tongue, thin as a snake and up to 30 centimeters long, that winds down the tunnels and gathers as many as 50,000 insects in a single night. It looks like an anteater, but the likeness is a coincidence. DNA places the aardvark in Afrotheria, an ancient African group whose living members include its closest cousins, the elephants and manatees, along with the little hyraxes. Biologists call this convergent evolution: the same ant-eating tools arose separately in families that are not related.

Its teeth are rootless columns of thousands of thin dentine tubes, which gave its order the name Tubulidentata, "tube-toothed," and they have no enamel at all, so they wear down on top and keep growing from below for life. The aardvark is also a tireless builder that digs a yard of tunnel in about five minutes and keeps carving fresh burrows it never revisits. Those empty burrows shelter warthogs, hyenas, mongooses, owls, pythons and wild dogs, and many of these animals would die in wildfire season without an aardvark hole to hide in, which is why biologists rank it a keystone species.

A strange plant depends on it too. The aardvark cucumber is the only cucumber that buries its fruit, ripening each melon about a foot underground. In a 2025 camera-trap study of seven mammal species, only the aardvark could find the buried melons and dig them up; it eats them for their water and later drops the seeds in its dung, replanting them with fertilizer.

aye-aye.context_blurb:
Found only in the rainforests of Madagascar, the big island off Africa's east coast, the aye-aye is a lemur that comes out at night. With shaggy dark fur, huge eyes, giant leathery ears and long bony fingers, it looks like no other primate on Earth. Nearly every strange part of its body is a tool for a single job: finding grubs hidden inside wood.

Creeping through the trees after dark with round yellow eyes, swiveling ears and a long, skinny middle finger for tapping bark, the aye-aye is the largest nocturnal primate in the world. Its body is about 15 inches long, and its bushy tail is longer still.

It hunts by rapping on the wood with that finger, as fast as eight taps a second, a habit called percussive foraging that no other primate shares, and it listens for the hollow echo that betrays a grub's tunnel under the bark. Inside each huge ear, tall ridges of bone act like a lens, focusing and funneling the faint echo toward the eardrum, along with the tiny sounds of larvae moving in the wood.

Once it hears a hollow, it gnaws through the bark with two long front teeth that, unlike any other primate's, keep growing throughout its life, which is why early naturalists mistook the aye-aye for a rodent. Then it fishes the grub out with its thin finger, doing the job a woodpecker does elsewhere with its beak, because Madagascar has no woodpeckers and the aye-aye evolved to fill that empty role.

That probing middle finger has a ball-and-socket joint at its knuckle, the only one of its kind in any primate hand, so the finger can rotate freely to hook a grub around the bends of a tunnel. Its fingers are so specialized that they are poor at gripping branches, and in 2019 Adam Hartstone-Rose and Edwin Dickinson found how it climbs anyway: a hidden sixth digit, a pseudothumb of bone and cartilage moved by three muscles and even marked with its own fingerprint.

babirusa.context_blurb:
The babirusa is a wild pig of the swampy rainforests of Sulawesi and a few nearby Indonesian islands. It is shy, mostly solitary and a quick runner for its size, and it wallows in mud and even swims between islands. The male's teeth make it one of the strangest-looking mammals alive.

The babirusa takes its name from the Indonesian words babi rusa, "pig-deer," because local people thought the male's curling tusks looked like a deer's antlers, and its nearly hairless gray body adds to the odd look.

The male's upper canines never leave his mouth the normal way: they grow straight up, punch through the skin on top of the snout and curve back over the face toward the forehead. He actually carries four tusks, because a lower pair of canines sweeps upward too, and in fights between males the lower tusks serve as weapons while the snout tusks act more like shields.

The upper tusks never stop growing, and food does nothing to grind them down, so on a rare old male an unworn tusk keeps arcing until it curls round and pierces his own skull. He grows his teeth through his face and, now and then, back into his own head.

binturong.context_blurb:
The binturong, often called the bearcat, is a shaggy, black, slow-moving mammal that lives high in the rainforest trees of South and Southeast Asia. It is neither bear nor cat but a viverrid, a cousin of the civets, and its genus name, Arctictis, is Greek for "bear-weasel." It eats mostly fruit and comes out mainly at night.

The surest way to recognize a binturong is with your nose: this black, cat-sized tree-dweller smells strongly of hot buttered popcorn.

In 2016 a team at Duke University traced the smell to a molecule called 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the very compound that gives hot popcorn and freshly cooked jasmine rice their scent, and found it in every sample of binturong urine they tested. When it leaves a tree, a binturong walks headfirst down the trunk, because its hind ankles can turn a full 180 degrees so the claws stay hooked into the bark, and its grasping tail serves as a fifth limb for balance.

That smell posed a puzzle, since popcorn gets the molecule from intense heat, as sugars and amino acids react in the pan. The lead scientist, Christine Drea, wondered how an animal could produce a cooking smell with no cooking at all, and her team believes microbes on its skin, in its fur or in its gut create the compound as the urine flows past.

capybara.context_blurb:
The capybara is a barrel-shaped grazer of the wetlands, rivers and flooded grasslands of South America. It is calm and social, living in family groups that share water holes with caimans, herons and even monkeys. Its body is built for a life spent half in the water and half grazing at the water's edge.

The capybara, Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, is the largest rodent alive, more than four feet long and usually 35 to 66 kilograms, roughly the weight of an adult man; the heaviest wild one on record, a female from Brazil, weighed 91 kilograms.

Like every rodent, it has front incisors that keep growing throughout its life, replacing exactly what the constant grinding of gritty grass wears away, and the word rodent itself comes from the Latin for "to gnaw." Eyes, ears and nostrils all ride high along the top of its head, the same layout a hippo uses, so it can sink until only that strip shows and still see, hear and breathe while hiding from a jaguar. It can even sleep in the water with just its nose poking out.

Grass is hard to digest, so bacteria in its enlarged hindgut break it down, and because the protein and B vitamins those bacteria make would otherwise pass out unabsorbed, the capybara eats its own soft morning droppings to run the food through a second time, the same trick rabbits use.

fossa.context_blurb:
Madagascar, the big island off Africa's east coast, has no lions, leopards or other big cats. Its top hunter is a sleek, reddish-brown carnivore with a cat-like face and a tail nearly as long as its body, which chases lemurs through the treetops. Only about 2,500 are thought to survive in the wild.

That hunter is the fossa, Madagascar's largest carnivore and apex predator, nicknamed the ghost of the forest because it can roam up to 16 miles a day.

A lemur fleeing up a tree usually gains time when a predator has to back down the trunk tail-first. The fossa's hyper-flexible ankles rotate almost 180 degrees, so it can grip the trunk from any angle and run straight down it head-first. Its long tail balances its leaps between trees.

For all its cougar-like looks, the fossa is not a cat. Its closest living relatives are the mongooses, and its whole family descends from a single mongoose-like ancestor that reached Madagascar about 21 million years ago. Its cat-like body evolved separately, a case of convergent evolution.

giant-panda.context_blurb:
The giant panda is a black-and-white bear of the cool, cloud-wrapped bamboo forests of central China, one of the most recognizable animals on Earth. It is a true bear, unlike the red panda, which belongs to a separate family, and it spends most of its day doing one thing: eating.

Sitting back for hours munching bamboo, with black patches around its eyes and round black ears, the giant panda is famous the world over.

To strip bamboo, a panda holds the stalk in a pincer grip, even though bears have no thumbs. Its "false thumb" is an enlarged wrist bone, the radial sesamoid, which works as a sixth digit to pinch the bamboo against its fingers. A mother may weigh 90 kilograms. Her newborn cub weighs only about 100 grams, the size of a stick of butter and about one nine-hundredth of her weight, one of the biggest mother-to-baby size gaps of any mammal.

About 99 percent of its diet is bamboo, a tough, watery, low-energy food. The panda kept a meat-eater's short, straight gut and digests only about 17 percent of what it eats, so it must eat for up to 14 hours a day, packing in 12 to 38 kilograms of bamboo.

Its genes record the switch. About 4.2 million years ago, as its ancestors turned to bamboo, the panda's gene for umami taste, the receptor that senses the savory flavor of meat, broke and has never worked since.

kangaroo-rat.context_blurb:
The kangaroo rat is a big-eyed rodent of the deserts of the American Southwest and Mexico, from the Mojave and Sonoran deserts to Death Valley. It comes out at night, bounding across the sand on its long back legs, and spends the hot days in a burrow it digs itself. Its whole body is tuned for a land where months pass without rain.

The kangaroo rat can live its entire life without a single drink: its remarkable kidneys waste almost no water, and its body wrings what it needs from a diet of dry seeds.

Nearly all of that water is made inside its own body: whenever an animal burns food for energy, the chemistry gives off water as a by-product, called metabolic water, and the kangaroo rat lives almost entirely on the water its body makes while burning dry seeds. Biologists named it Dipodomys, the two-footed mouse, because it hops like a tiny kangaroo. Its tail is longer than its whole body and works as a counterbalance, letting it make sharp, sudden turns in midair without tumbling.

Its sharpest moves are saved for snakes. A sidewinder rattlesnake buried in the sand strikes faster than a human eye can follow. A kangaroo rat that cannot leap clear twists in midair and drop-kicks the snake away with both hind feet, ninja-style, flinging it off before the fangs can inject venom, then lands back on its feet. High-speed cameras first caught the move.

lowland-streaked-tenrec.context_blurb:
In the rainforests of Madagascar, a little mammal roots through the leaf litter looking like a hedgehog dressed as a bumblebee. It belongs to an ancient family found only on that island, and it has a trick no other mammal is known to share.

The lowland streaked tenrec is hamster-sized and weighs only about 125 to 280 grams, with black quills banded in yellow, a yellow stripe running down its nose, and a taste for earthworms.

A mother calls to her young in the thick undergrowth by buzzing, without using her voice at all. In the middle of a tenrec's back sits a patch of 7 to 16 special quills in three rows, and the tenrec grinds them against each other to make its high-pitched clicks and buzzes. This is stridulation, the trick crickets and grasshoppers perform with their wings, and no other mammal is known to do it.

Roughly 30 million years ago a single ancestor reached Madagascar by rafting across the sea from Africa on floating vegetation. Its descendants became about 31 living kinds, shrew-like, hedgehog-like, mole-like and even otter-like, but the likeness is convergent evolution: the tenrecs' real cousins are elephants, aardvarks and sea cows.

maned-wolf.context_blurb:
The maned wolf is a long-legged, red-gold canid of the tall-grass savannas of central South America, such as Brazil's Cerrado. It is neither a true wolf nor a fox, and no other living animal shares its genus. It hunts alone around dusk and dawn, and it eats more fruit than any wolf should.

With a fox's face and long, slender black legs, the maned wolf stands up to 110 centimeters at the shoulder, the tallest of all wild canids, nicknamed the fox on stilts; its height lets it peer over the tall grass for prey and danger.

It is the sole survivor of an ancient branch of South American canids, the only large one to outlast the extinctions at the end of the Ice Age. Its closest known relative was the Falkland Islands wolf, now extinct, which shared an ancestor with it about 7 million years ago. In 2006, police at Rotterdam Zoo went hunting for someone smoking cannabis, but the smell came from the maned wolf's urine, which reeks of skunk and cannabis because of a long-lasting chemical, a pyrazine, that the wolf uses to mark its territory. Its nickname is the skunk wolf.

Unlike meat-loving wolves, it lives largely on fruit, especially the wolf apple, Solanum lycocarpum, and seeds that pass through the maned wolf's gut sprout over 40 percent of the time, against under 1 percent straight from the fruit, so the wolf sows the fruit it lives on. It often leaves its dung on leafcutter-ant nests, and the ants carry the seeds off to their refuse piles.

musk-ox.context_blurb:
Shaggy and about the size of a cow, the musk ox grazes the Arctic tundra. Despite its name it is not an ox but a closer relative of sheep and goats, a survivor from the Ice Age built to endure winters colder than forty below. Its long outer hair sweeps nearly to its hooves and hides one of the warmest fibers in the world.

Musk oxen overheat in a long run and cannot outrun wolves, so when a pack closes in, the adults wheel into a tight ring with their horns facing outward and the calves pressed against their mothers in the center. Against a single wolf, they form a line instead.

Under the outer coat lies a soft undercoat called qiviut, an Inuit word, shed all at once each spring; it is about eight times warmer than sheep's wool, finer than cashmere, and it will not shrink in water of any temperature. During the Ice Age its herds roamed Europe, Asia and North America alongside mammoths and sabre-toothed cats, and when the great die-offs took those animals, the musk ox endured, surviving as scattered herds in Greenland and the Canadian Arctic.

In the autumn rut, bulls charge each other at close to 35 miles an hour and smash foreheads up to 20 times, and what takes each blow is a solid horn boss about 4 inches thick, lying over 3 inches of skull bone right above the brain. On a calm day the crack carries a mile.

numbat.context_blurb:
The numbat is a small, striped, squirrel-sized marsupial found only in a few eucalyptus woodlands of Western Australia. It is one of the continent's rarest mammals, and nearly everything about it, from its tongue to its daily schedule, is built around one food: termites.

A numbat slurps up about 20,000 termites a day with a long, sticky, saliva-coated tongue that flicks out about 10 centimeters, nearly a third of its body length, deep into their narrow tunnels.

Nearly every other marsupial sleeps by day, but the numbat is fully active in daylight, because termites climb near the surface of their tunnels, within its reach, only during the day. Its whole schedule is set by its prey.

Unusually for a marsupial, the female numbat has no pouch: her four bean-sized young cling to exposed teats on a bare patch of belly, dangling in the open for months, sheltered only by crimped golden hair. When a fox or hawk hunts it, a numbat backs into a hollow log or burrow and jams the entrance shut with its thick, tough-skinned rump, using its hindquarters like a living door.

okapi.context_blurb:
The okapi is a shy, solitary forest animal of the dense rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is so secretive that Western science did not describe it until 1901, which makes it one of the last large land mammals to be discovered. It looks like a mix of several animals, but it belongs with only a single living relative.

The okapi wears a deep chocolate-brown coat, has big round ears, and its rump and legs are banded in black and white, as boldly striped as any zebra.

Despite its stripes, the okapi is no zebra: its only living relative is the giraffe, and the pair are the last members of the giraffe family, which split from a common ancestor about 11.5 million years ago. It is, in effect, a giraffe that stayed short and hid in the forest. Its blue-black tongue, about 30 centimeters long and reported up to 46, can grasp like a finger, and the okapi uses it to lick its eyes clean and even reach inside its ears, something almost no other mammal can do. The same tongue strips leaves from branches, just as a giraffe's does.

Local people had long known the animal. Sir Harry Johnston, following stories of a striped beast in the Congo, expected some kind of forest horse, but the tracks he examined were cloven, split into two toes, unlike the single hoof of a horse or zebra. A striped skin and a skull sent to London let the zoologist Ray Lankester declare it a new relative of the giraffe, named Okapia johnstoni.

pink-fairy-armadillo.context_blurb:
The pink fairy armadillo is the smallest armadillo in the world, a palm-sized burrower only about 9 to 11 centimeters long that lives in the dry, sandy country of central Argentina. It has a pale pink shell, huge front claws and a life spent almost entirely underground, so scientists still know little about it.

It was long believed to push through loose sand almost as fast as a fish swims through water, which earned it the nickname the sand-swimmer.

Its thin pink shell is mainly a radiator, not armor: a thick mesh of blood vessels runs under it, and by pushing blood in, the armadillo flushes deeper pink and sheds heat, while draining blood out turns the shell pale and holds its warmth.

Its rear end is capped by a flat, armored plate facing straight back, and as it digs forward, it uses this butt plate to press and pack the loose soil behind it, shoring up the tunnel and corking it shut, a feature that seems unique to this species.

proboscis-monkey.context_blurb:
The proboscis monkey is a big, orange-brown, potbellied monkey found only on the island of Borneo, in mangrove swamps and forests along muddy rivers. The species is named for one astonishing body part, and its whole life, from its voice to its belly, is shaped by a tough diet of leaves and a home full of rivers.

That part is the nose: an adult male grows the largest nose of any primate, a soft, dangling flap that can droop more than four inches (about 10 centimeters) down past his mouth. Females and youngsters keep small, neat, upturned noses.

The nose is not only for show. Where leaves block the view, the hollow space inside a male's huge nose works as a resonating chamber, making his honking call deeper and louder so it reaches listeners hidden in the trees. A bigger nose means a deeper, louder honk, so a female picking a big-nosed male is reading his fitness from the sound.

To cross rivers full of crocodiles, these monkeys drop off overhanging branches with a splash and paddle over with webbed hands and feet, and they can even swim underwater for up to 20 meters.

That famous paunch, as much as a quarter of the animal's weight, is a fermenting tank. Like a cow, the proboscis monkey has a stomach divided into several chambers and full of bacteria that ferment its tough diet of leaves, even breaking down the poisons in bitter mangrove leaves. Sweet ripe fruit is a danger, because its sugars ferment inside and can bloat the monkey badly, so it sticks mostly to young leaves and unripe fruit.

quokka.context_blurb:
The quokka is a cat-sized, furry marsupial from a few islands and patches of mainland in Western Australia that grazes at night and hides in thick scrub by day. On Rottnest Island, where there are few ground predators, quokkas are unusually tame, and tourists line up for selfies with their famously cheerful faces.

That grin is an accident of anatomy, not a mood: a quokka's short muzzle, round cheeks, big dark eyes and upturned mouth corners just happen to form the pattern people read as a smile. The quokka is not actually happy; reading a human feeling into an animal's face is a classic mistake.

Mothers carry their joeys in a belly pouch. If a predator such as a fox chases a mother, she relaxes the muscles of her pouch so the joey tumbles out, and the startled youngster thrashes and hisses on the ground, holding the hunter's attention while she gets away. The internet story that quokkas throw their babies is a myth; it is a release, not a toss.

In the long dry summer, a quokka gets nearly all the water it needs from the plants it eats, including juicy succulents that store water, so it can last about a month without a drink. Its tail does store fat, but that fat carries it through lean seasons for food, not through thirst.

red-panda.context_blurb:
High in the misty bamboo forests of the eastern Himalayas, from Nepal and Bhutan into southwest China, at about 2,000 to 4,300 meters, lives a tree-dwelling animal named for a giant cousin it barely resembles.

The red panda is a russet, cat-sized bamboo-eater, about 51 to 64 centimeters from nose to rump, with rich reddish-brown fur, a white-marked face and a long, bushy tail ringed in red and buff bands with a dark tip.

To hold a bamboo stalk it uses a false thumb: not a real finger but an enlarged wrist bone, the radial sesamoid, that sticks out from the side of the paw so the animal can pinch a stalk against its other digits. On freezing, windy nights it curls into a ball on a branch and wraps its long, bushy tail, almost as long as its body, around itself like a blanket, with its face and paws tucked under to hold in heat.

Bamboo makes up about 95 percent of its diet, yet the red panda's gut is short and simple, built for meat like its hunting ancestors'. The leaves rush through within two to four hours, hardly digested, so the red panda survives on sheer volume, eating about 1.5 kilograms of leaves or up to 4 kilograms of shoots a day, and by moving slowly to save energy.

The red panda sits alone in its own family, Ailuridae, neither bear nor raccoon, and its line parted from the giant panda's in the deep past. Yet both grip bamboo with the same false thumb, because each line evolved it separately and arrived at the same solution, which biologists call convergent evolution. A 9-million-year-old relative from Spain, Simocyon batalleri, already had the thumb but ate meat, so the thumb first evolved for gripping branches, not for eating bamboo.

saiga-antelope.context_blurb:
The saiga is a goat-sized antelope of the dry Central Asian steppes, in Kazakhstan, Russia, Mongolia and Uzbekistan. In the ice age it roamed from Britain to Alaska; today it is critically endangered. Huge herds still run across the grasslands on long migrations, and the saiga's strangest feature is built for exactly that life.

The saiga antelope is known at a glance by its oversized, bulbous nose that hangs down past its lips like a stubby trunk, and males alone carry horns: thick, heavily ridged and amber like old wax.

The nose is a piece of survival equipment. When a migrating herd kicks up choking clouds of dust, it works as an air filter: its winding inner chambers, lined with mucus glands, catch the grit before it can reach the lungs. In winter the same long, chambered passages warm and humidify the bitter air, so the saiga never breathes freezing air raw into its chest.

The saiga's worst enemy can live inside it. In May 2015 over two-thirds of all the saiga on Earth, about 200,000 animals, died across Kazakhstan in roughly three weeks, killed by a bacterium, Pasteurella multocida, that normally lives harmlessly in the saiga's own airways. An unusual spell of heat and humidity in the ten days before let the bacteria multiply and invade the bloodstream, causing a blood infection that shut down organs across whole herds.

slow-loris.context_blurb:
The slow loris is a small, shy primate of the rainforests of South and Southeast Asia, about the size of a small cat. It inches along slender branches at night, one grip at a time, and stares out of huge round eyes. Behind that cuddly look hides a weapon that makes it one of very few venomous mammals, and its fame in online pet videos has fed an illegal trade.

Of all the primates, monkeys, apes and humans included, the slow loris is the only one with a venomous bite, something rare even among mammals. It has no venom fangs; instead, when threatened, it raises its arms above its head and licks a gland on the inside of each elbow, the brachial gland, mixing that secretion with its saliva to make its bite toxic.

A flashlight makes a loris's eyes glow like coins because behind each retina lies a mirror-like layer, the tapetum lucidum, which bounces light back through the retina and gives the eye a second chance to catch faint light. That is the same eyeshine a cat shows in headlights.

The venom rots flesh and leaves wounds that will not heal, and on Java, Anna Nekaris's team found wild lorises with half their faces eaten away, bitten not by predators but by other slow lorises in fierce fights over territory and mates.

The main protein in loris elbow venom is shaped much like Fel d 1, the protein in cat dander that makes people allergic to cats, hinting that the loris may turn an allergen-like protein into a weapon. The link is still being researched and is not yet proven.

solenodon.context_blurb:
The solenodon is a rare, rat-sized mammal of the Caribbean, found only on Cuba and Hispaniola. It looks like an oversized shrew, about 28 to 32 centimeters from nose to rump, and it snuffles through leaf litter at night for worms and beetles. Introduced predators have pushed it toward extinction, though its family has survived for tens of millions of years.

Its eyes are tiny and almost useless, so a solenodon, with its long bare snout, finds its way through dark burrows by sending out high-pitched clicks and listening for the echoes.

Venomous mammals are rare, and the solenodon is one of them: toxic saliva flows into a bite through an open groove running down its second lower incisor, much as in some snakes, and its name means grooved tooth.

Its family split from all other living mammals about 73.6 million years ago, so its ancestors shared the world with the final non-bird dinosaurs and then survived the asteroid that ended the Age of Dinosaurs. Its body has barely changed since, which makes it a living fossil. At the base of its long, flexible snout sits a ball-and-socket joint, built like a human shoulder and found in no other mammal's face, which lets the snout swivel and probe deep into cracks and rotten logs for prey.

tarsier.context_blurb:
The tarsier is a tiny primate of the rainforests of Southeast Asian islands, including Borneo, the Philippines and Sulawesi. Small enough to sit in a child's palm, it clings upright to tree trunks with long fingers and leaps after prey at night. Nearly everything about it, from its eyes to its voice, is built for hunting in the dark.

The tarsier's eyeballs are enormous, each about 16 millimeters across and as big as or bigger than its whole brain, the largest eyes for body size of any mammal. Those giant eyes are locked in their sockets, so instead the tarsier turns its head about 180 degrees in either direction, the way an owl does, giving it a full circle of view without moving its body.

Almost every other primate eats plants, but the tarsier alone among primates lives on meat and nothing else: beetles, cicadas and grasshoppers, and even lizards, snakes, small birds and bats, with no fruit or leaves at all.

A Philippine tarsier sometimes opens its mouth wide as if screaming yet makes no sound we can hear, and in 2012 Marissa Ramsier's team, listening with bat detectors, found that it was calling in ultrasound near 70 kilohertz, far above the roughly 20 kilohertz limit of human hearing. It can hear up to about 91 kilohertz, so it can talk on a channel our ears cannot detect.

tasmanian-devil.context_blurb:
On the island of Tasmania, south of mainland Australia, a stocky black animal the size of a small dog hunts and scavenges by night. Its jaws are among the strongest of any mammal for their size, and its unearthly screams at feeding scuffles gave it its name. In recent decades a strange disease has pushed it toward collapse.

The Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii) is the largest meat-eating marsupial left in the world, a squat black hunter and scavenger that shrieks in the dark and raises its young in a pouch.

When a devil finally finds a wallaby carcass that foxes and birds have already picked over, it eats everything that is left, crunching up and swallowing bones, fur and even teeth. Small as it is, the devil makes a huge racket, with at least eleven distinct kinds of call, from soft clucks while feeding to screams in a fight.

A single litter holds 20 to 30 newborns, each the size of a grain of rice, but the mother's backward-opening pouch has only four teats, so the babies race to the pouch and only the first four to latch on survive.

Since 1996, Devil Facial Tumour Disease has killed roughly 80 percent of wild devils, and it is a transmissible cancer, one of only a handful ever found: living tumor cells pass directly from one devil to another through bites to the face during feeding scuffles and fights. No virus or bacterium is involved; the cancer itself is the infection.

antlion-the-larva-that-digs-a-sand-death.context_blurb:
The antlion is a winged insect, but it is famous for its larva: a stubby, spiny little hunter that lives in loose, dry sand on every continent except Antarctica. The larva can spend two or three years in the sand, building a trap and letting gravity do most of its hunting for it.

In dry sand under a porch or along a path, the antlion larva scoops out a neat funnel and buries itself in the bottom, leaving just its jaws exposed, so an ant that touches the crumbling rim slides straight down into them.

If a victim scrambles halfway back up the wall, the larva jerks its head and showers it with flung sand, setting off little avalanches that carry the ant back down into its jaws. The larva can walk only backward, and as it wanders in reverse looking for a place to dig, it leaves squiggly trails in the sand, which is why North Americans call it the doodlebug.

A larva may sit in its pit for years and never leave a dropping, because it has no anus; all the waste from years of hunting stays stored inside its body until it becomes an adult. At last it spins a silk cocoon in the sand, and out comes an adult with long, delicate, lacewing-like wings, so unlike its larva that people often mistake it for a damselfly or a dragonfly, and it no longer eats ants.

assassin-bug-the-ambush-hunter-that-wear.context_blurb:
Assassin bugs are a huge family of long-legged, hook-beaked true bugs found across the warm parts of the world. They are ambush hunters that stalk other insects, and some species have invented ghoulish tricks, both for getting close to their prey and for hiding from their own enemies.

An assassin bug never chews: it stabs its victim with a curved beak, injects saliva loaded with paralyzing toxins and digestive enzymes that turn the insides to liquid, and then drinks that soup back up through the same beak, like sipping a milkshake through a straw. Its saliva can dissolve prey much larger than the bug itself.

The nymph of Acanthaspis petax drains ants dry and then cements the empty bodies into a heap on its back with sticky threads from special hairs on its belly, wearing a dozen or more of its victims as a disguise. In Australia, the feather-legged assassin bug takes on jack jumper ants larger than itself by offering bait: a gland coats a feathery hind leg with an intoxicating ooze, and when an ant grabs the leg to taste it, the bug twists around and drives its beak into the soft joint at the ant's neck. Entomologists call this the "fatal attraction" strategy.

To test whether the corpse backpack really works, the researchers Jackson and Pollard offered jumping spiders both bare nymphs and ant-covered ones, and the spiders attacked the bare nymphs about ten times as often, even when the bugs were dead and motionless, so the disguise itself fools the spider's eyes.

atlas-moth-one-of-the-biggest-moths-with.context_blurb:
The atlas moth of the tropical forests of South and Southeast Asia ranks among the biggest moths in the world. People who glimpse one often take it for a bird. Its adult life is short and single-minded, and the tips of its wings carry a famous warning to anything that tries to eat it.

Its wings span about 25 to 30 centimeters, nearly a foot across, and by surface area it carries more wing than almost any other insect.

The curved tip of each forewing is patterned like a cobra's head, and when a bird attacks, the moth flaps and writhes so the two "snake heads" rear up at the predator; its Cantonese name means "snake's head moth." An adult lives only a week or two, because its mouthparts are a tiny, useless stub: it can never eat, and it survives on fat it stored as a caterpillar, living only to mate and lay eggs.

The large female barely moves, clinging near her cocoon and releasing a scent into the night, while the smaller male flies in from kilometers away, tracking her with huge, feathery antennae that pick up her chemical signal.

bolas-spider-the-spider-that-fishes-with.context_blurb:
The bolas spider is a small, night-hunting spider of the Americas, Africa and Australasia. Unlike most spiders, the female spins no web to trap insects. She hunts a single kind of prey, moths, with a single strange tool, working more like a fisherman than a trap-builder.

Hanging from a branch in the dark, the female lets down a silk line tipped with a sticky glue ball and swings it at passing moths like a bolas, the weighted throwing cords of South American cowboys, which is how she got her name. By day she sits perfectly still on a little pad of silk spun over a leaf, her waxy-white, lumpy body looking exactly like a fresh bird dropping, so birds pass her by.

She does not wait for luck: she gives off a chemical that copies the scent a female moth releases to attract mates, so male moths follow the fake trail straight to her swinging glue ball.

One North American species, Mastophora hutchinsoni, fakes the scent of one moth species early in the evening, then switches to a second species' scent after 11 p.m., matching whichever moths are flying at that hour, so the catch on her glue ball changes as the night goes on.

bullet-ant-the-worst-sting-on-the-schmid.context_blurb:
The bullet ant is a large black ant of the lowland rainforests of Central and South America. It nests at the base of trees and sends its workers up into the canopy to forage. It is famous worldwide for one thing, its sting, which entomologists rank at the very top of the pain scale, and researchers keep returning to the chemistry of its venom.

The entomologist Justin Schmidt, who let insects sting him so he could rank their pain on a four-point scale, gave the bullet ant a perfect 4, and in The Sting of the Wild, his 2016 book, he compared the pain to walking across flaming charcoal with a three-inch nail driven into your heel.

The burning, throbbing waves of pain can go on for up to a full day, which is why people in Venezuela call it hormiga veinticuatro, the 24-hour ant. Among the Satere-Mawe of the Brazilian Amazon, a boy proves he is ready for manhood by wearing a woven glove of leaves packed with dozens of the live ants, stingers turned inward, for about ten minutes, enduring the pain in silence about twenty times over his youth. The ants are first calmed in an herbal solution and then woven into the glove.

The agony comes from poneratoxin, a small protein in the venom that jams the sodium channels nerves use to fire, scrambling their signals, yet no human death from the sting has been recorded, and the toxin clears the body within about a day.

diving-bell-spider-the-spider-that-lives.context_blurb:
The diving bell spider is the one spider on Earth that lives out its entire life beneath the water. It lives among the plants of still ponds and weedy streams in Europe and parts of Asia, and it hunts, mates and raises its young below the surface, yet it breathes air like any land spider. Its secret is a home made of silk and air.

Underwater the spider shines like silver, because a film of air clings to the water-repelling hairs that cover its body. Its Latin name, Argyroneta, means roughly "silver spinner." It spins a silk dome among the water plants and fills it with air, a living diving bell. Breathing slowly uses up that air, and silk cannot make more. So the spider swims up to the surface, traps a fresh bubble against the dense hairs of its belly and legs, and carries it back down to top up the dome.

This spider breaks a spider rule as well. In almost all spiders the female is larger, but here the male is the bigger sex, about 15 millimeters to the female's 12. The likely reason is that males roam the pond, swimming about actively to hunt, and need extra strength to push through the water.

The bell is more than a tank: Seymour and Hetz showed that it works like a gill, because as the spider uses up oxygen, oxygen dissolved in the pond seeps in through the bubble's surface while carbon dioxide seeps out. A resting spider needs to surface only about once a day. The gill has a leak, though. As the oxygen is used, nitrogen makes up more and more of the bubble, and that nitrogen slowly seeps out into the water, so the dome keeps shrinking even while fresh oxygen flows in. A small bell loses half its volume in about 37 hours, which is why the spider cannot seal itself in for the winter.

giant-weta-the-heavyweight-insect-of-new.context_blurb:
Giant wetas, the genus Deinacrida, are huge, wingless, cricket-like insects found only in New Zealand, and several kinds now survive mainly on a few small islands. They belong to an ancient group that grew big in a land almost without mammals. Introduced rats and stoats have pushed several species to the edge.

A giant weta can be as long as an adult's finger, and a big female full of eggs can top 70 grams, heavier than a house sparrow, which makes it one of the heaviest insects alive. Cornered, it does not bite first. It stands up tall on its front legs, lifts its big spiny hind legs high and kicks them outward so the sharp spines threaten the attacker.

For ages New Zealand had no native land mammals except bats. With no mice scurrying across the forest floor at night, the giant weta grew large and took over their job of foraging in the dark, which earned it the nickname "the invertebrate mouse."

High in the mountains of the South Island, around 1,200 meters up, lives the scree weta, Deinacrida connectens. Once the air falls below about minus 5 degrees Celsius, its body freezes solid, and when it warms up it thaws and comes back to life. New Zealand's alpine wetas are by far the largest insects able to survive being frozen.

goliath-birdeater-the-biggest-spider-on-.context_blurb:
The Goliath birdeater, Theraphosa blondi, is a giant tarantula from the humid rainforests of South America's north, and the heaviest spider on Earth. Its hairy body is as big as a man's fist and its legs span a dinner plate. Despite its fearsome name, it is a burrow-dwelling ground hunter that seldom, if ever, catches birds.

A full-grown one tops out around 175 grams, about the weight of a young puppy, and although the giant huntsman spider has longer legs, no spider has more bulk.

It hunts at night on the forest floor, waiting and then pouncing. Most often it drags earthworms and toads back to its burrow, along with insects, frogs, lizards and the odd small snake or rodent. The "birdeater" name comes from a single 1705 engraving by Maria Sibylla Merian that showed a tarantula attacking a hummingbird.

Cornered, it rarely bites first, and its venom is only mild to humans anyway. Instead it turns around and rubs its back legs over its abdomen, flicking off a cloud of microscopic barbed hairs that itch fiercely in an attacker's eyes and skin.

It is also almost the only spider you can hear walking. One night in the Guyana rainforest, the entomologist Piotr Naskrecki heard a noise at his back and discovered a Goliath birdeater following close behind. Its hard-tipped feet and claws were clicking on the ground, a sound he compared to a horse's hooves.

honeypot-ant-living-storage-jars-for-the.context_blurb:
Honeypot ants live in hot, dry places such as the deserts of Australia, Mexico and the American Southwest, where food comes in short bursts and then disappears. Their answer is a living pantry: some workers do nothing but store food for everyone else.

Deep in their long underground nests, sister workers feed certain chosen ants nectar and sugary droplets again and again, far more than any normal ant could hold. The fed ant's abdomen stretches into a round, see-through globe about the size of a grape, full of honey, and these living storage jars are called repletes.

A replete grows far too heavy to walk. It hangs motionless, upside down, from the ceiling of an underground chamber, sometimes for months, one of a whole wall of living honey jars. When drought or winter leaves the surface bare, a hungry worker taps a replete gently with her antennae, and the replete brings up a drop of stored liquid from its crop into her mouth. The whole colony drinks from these jars until food returns.

In central Australia the Arrernte people call the honeypot ant yarumpa. During the dry season, Arrernte women and children follow the ants to their nests and dig down into the hard ground to get at the repletes. They eat the swollen amber abdomens as a sweet, a rare treat of sugar in the desert.

jewel-wasp-the-wasp-that-turns-a-cockroa.context_blurb:
Shimmering metallic green and about 22 millimeters long, the emerald jewel wasp lives in tropical Africa and Asia. The female hunts cockroaches much bigger than herself, and what she does to them sounds like science fiction: she turns each victim into a living nursery for a single young wasp.

She does not kill her huge victim; she makes it an obedient zombie, alive but docile, that will later walk to its own grave.

Her first sting hits the nerve cluster that works the roach's front legs, paralyzing them for a couple of minutes, just long enough to hold the roach still while she aims a second, carefully placed sting. Afterward she grabs what is left of one antenna and leads the roach to her burrow like a dog on a leash, the roach walking on its own legs the whole way.

The second sting goes directly into the cockroach's brain, and the venom switches off its escape reflex: the roach can still walk, turn upright and even swim, but the drive to run from danger is gone. Neuroscientists study the venom because it blocks one behavior with surgical precision while leaving others intact. In the burrow she fixes one egg to the roach's side and closes the entrance. About three days later the egg hatches, and the larva chews a hole into the still-living roach, crawls inside and eats its organs from within, while the roach never fights back.

lord-howe-tree-lobster-the-stick-insect-.context_blurb:
Lord Howe Island is a small, forested volcanic island in the Pacific between Australia and New Zealand. It was once home to a giant flightless stick insect, Dryococelus australis, until black rats from a shipwreck wiped it out around 1918. For more than 80 years it was thought gone forever.

The insect is glossy brown-black, up to about 18 centimeters long and nearly 25 grams in weight, and its heavy, armored bulk earned it the islanders' nickname, the tree lobster.

In 2001 climbers found a small colony still alive on Ball's Pyramid, a bare, sheer sea stack rising from the ocean about 20 kilometers from Lord Howe, and the find was hailed as the rarest insect in the world. Tree lobster pairs sleep coiled together through the day, and the male drapes three of his legs over the female beside him, a kind of pair bond almost never seen in insects.

Only about 24 had survived, and every one of them lived on a single spindly tea-tree bush, Melaleuca howeana, growing on a narrow ledge high on the rock: the entire species on one plant. Biologists have since bred the insects in captivity, with the hope of returning them to their home island.

new-zealand-glowworm-the-larva-that-fish.context_blurb:
The New Zealand glowworm, Arachnocampa luminosa, lives in damp caves and shady overhangs across New Zealand, hanging from the ceiling in a silk nest. It glows blue-green from the tail end of its body, and it fishes for its dinner with lines of sticky silk.

The glowworm is really no worm: it is the larva, or maggot, of a small fly called a fungus gnat, and it glows at its tail to lure flying insects into its sticky lines. In the Waitomo Caves, visitors drifting by boat through the dark look up at thousands of glowworm lights covering the ceiling, which look exactly like a starry night sky.

A hungry larva turns its glow brighter to lure more prey, then dims it once it is well fed; its light is true bioluminescence, made chemically at the end of its abdomen.

After 6 to 12 months as a hunting larva, it becomes an adult fly that lives only a few days, because it has no working mouth and cannot eat; it exists only to mate and lay eggs. The long life as a larva pays for that brief adult one.

ogre-faced-spider-the-net-caster-that-th.context_blurb:
Known as both the ogre-faced spider and the net-casting spider, this night hunter lives in warm forests on several continents. Rather than waiting in a web, it carries a small net of silk and throws it at its prey. Its genus name, Deinopis, means fearful appearance, after the enormous eyes that stare from its face.

Hanging head-down above a forest trail, the ogre-faced spider holds a small stretchy net between its four front legs, and when a beetle walks beneath, it flings the net down over the beetle the way a fisherman casts a net, then snaps it shut. The net is not sticky; its woolly silk tangles anything it touches, and it stretches to two or three times its size as it is thrown.

By day it hides in plain sight by stretching its thin body and legs out straight along a twig, so that it looks exactly like a stick and birds and lizards pass it by. No spider has bigger simple eyes than its two huge central ones, which gather light about 2,000 times more efficiently than ours, and they let it aim its net in almost total darkness. Each night it grows a fresh light-sensitive layer inside each eye, and it destroys that layer at dawn.

In 2020 Jay Stafstrom and Ronald Hoy at Cornell found that spiders with their eyes covered missed crawling prey yet still netted flying insects. The spiders have no ears, yet they hear the insects' wingbeats through sensors near the tips of their legs: when the scientists played low tones like buzzing wings, the spiders flipped backward and struck at the empty air.

orchid-mantis-the-flower-that-eats-the-p.context_blurb:
Pink and white and only a few centimeters long, the orchid mantis lives in the rainforests of Southeast Asia, shaped and colored so much like a flower that it fools the insects it hunts. For years naturalists thought its disguise was simply camouflage, until field experiments showed it was something stranger.

With its upper leg segments flattened into heart and petal shapes, the orchid mantis looks like a pink-and-white blossom, and bees fly straight at it, mistaking it for a flower.

A newly hatched orchid mantis is no flower at all: it is red-orange and black and disguises itself as an assassin bug, an insect that bites hard and tastes foul, so predators leave it alone until it molts into its pink form.

In 2014 James O'Hanlon set lone orchid mantises on plain green leaves near beds of wild flowers, and more pollinators flew to the mantises than to the real flowers, the first confirmed case of an animal using a flower disguise as a lure, not just a hiding place. Yet when O'Hanlon trimmed off the petal-shaped leg lobes, insects still flew in and were caught, so he now suspects the petals help hide the mantis from its own predators instead.

tarantula-hawk-the-wasp-that-hunts-taran.context_blurb:
The tarantula hawk (genus Pepsis) is a huge, blue-black wasp with rust-orange wings, found in dry parts of the Americas, especially the dry Southwest of the United States and Mexico. Its sting is one of the most painful of any insect, so almost nothing dares to eat it, and its life story is one of the eeriest in nature.

The wasp is named for its prey: a female hunts a live tarantula far bigger than herself and stings it, and her venom paralyzes the spider without killing it, because she needs it alive. She drags the paralyzed spider into a burrow, lays a single egg on it and seals it in, and the hatched grub feeds inside the living spider for around three weeks, leaving the vital organs until the very end, which keeps its meal alive and fresh.

The entomologist Justin Schmidt, who built a pain scale by letting insects sting him, rated the tarantula hawk at 4.0, second only to the bullet ant, and called the pain blinding and electric; his blunt advice to anyone stung was to lie down and scream. The mercy is that the agony fades in about five minutes.

The adult wasp never hunts for its own meals; it lives on flower nectar, sipping from milkweed, mesquite and soapberry blossoms, and fermented nectar can leave it flying tipsy. Only females hunt spiders, and only to feed their young.

trap-jaw-ant-jaws-that-snap-faster-than-.context_blurb:
Trap-jaw ants (genus Odontomachus) are ground-dwelling hunters of the leaf litter in warm forests around the world. A worker walks with its long, straight jaws cocked wide open like a mousetrap, and their snap is among the quickest motions any animal can make. The ant has also found a surprising second use for it.

The trap-jaw ant holds its huge mandibles open at a full 180 degrees and snaps them shut in about 0.13 milliseconds, at roughly 35 to 64 meters per second, over 60 at the top end. Cornered by a bigger predator, a trap-jaw ant points its jaws downward and snaps them against the ground, and the recoil catapults it backflipping about 8.3 centimeters into the air, over 20 times its body length, like a person leaping 44 feet.

Fine trigger hairs, sensitive to the lightest touch, line each open jaw on the inner side and connect straight to the nerves that release the catch, so the jaws fire the moment prey brushes them, with no aiming needed. No muscle could close the jaws that fast, so the ant works like a loaded crossbow: it locks the open jaws with an internal latch, stores up spring energy, and releases it all at once, accelerating the strike at about 100,000 times the force of gravity.

treehopper-the-insect-with-alien-headgea.context_blurb:
Treehoppers are tiny sap-sucking insects, relatives of cicadas, that cling to plant stems in fields and forests all over the world. They are famous for the bizarre helmets growing over their backs, shaped like thorns, antlers, horns or spikes, and a single tropical forest can hold dozens of species, each in its own costume.

That helmet is the pronotum, normally a small plate on top of an insect's thorax, which in treehoppers balloons into ornate shapes that give each species its own alien-looking headgear.

Many treehoppers are thorn mimics: lined up in a row along a stem, they look just like the plant's own spines, so a hunting bird looks right past them. Ants guard treehopper colonies like bodyguards, driving away ladybirds and other hunters, and in return the treehoppers give them honeydew, the sugary waste they release after drinking sap. This trade, good for both sides, is called mutualism.

When Cera Fisher studied how the helmet grows, she found hundreds of genes active in a pattern like the one that builds wings, not the thorax genes she had expected, which left her wondering how such a thing could ever evolve.

velvet-ant-the-cow-killer-that-is-really.context_blurb: The velvet ant, nicknamed the cow killer, is a brightly colored, fuzzy insect that walks across sunny ground in warm parts of North America. It is not actually an ant at all. The males have wings and look like typical wasps; the females are wingless and run across the ground, which is how the name got started. The velvet ant has one of the most painful stings of any insect in the United States, and it is also wrapped in several layers of defensive tricks on top of the sting.

velvet-worm-the-glue-cannon-hunter-of-th.context_blurb: Velvet worms are ancient, caterpillar-like animals that live in damp leaf litter in rainforests of the Southern Hemisphere, in places like South America, Australia, New Zealand, and southern Africa. They are not insects or worms; they are the only living members of their own branch of the tree of life, little changed from fossils more than 500 million years old. They are predators of small invertebrates, and they catch prey using a trick no other land animal has.

vinegaroon-the-whip-scorpion-that-sprays.context_blurb: The vinegaroon, also called a whip scorpion, is a nocturnal arachnid that lives in warm, dry regions from the American Southwest down into Mexico and parts of Asia. It looks like a scorpion crossed with a spider, with a long whip-like tail at the back instead of a stinger. Vinegaroons have no venom at all. Instead they defend themselves with a sharp-smelling chemical spray that scientists find useful partly because it comes out of the whip's base in a very precise, aimable jet.

zombie-ant-fungus-the-carpenter-ants-fat.context_blurb: The zombie-ant fungus is not actually an animal but a parasitic fungus of the genus Ophiocordyceps that infects carpenter ants in tropical rainforests, especially in Thailand and Brazil. The fungus takes over the ant's body in a very specific sequence of steps before killing it and bursting out to spread spores to the next victim. It is one of the most dramatic parasites known, and it has been featured in TV shows, video games, and medical research into fungal diseases.

armadillo-girdled-lizard-the-lizard-that.context_blurb:
The armadillo girdled lizard, Ouroborus cataphractus, is a small, armored lizard of the rocky deserts along South Africa's western coast. It hunts insects by day and shelters in cracks between the stones. Poaching for the pet trade has made it a protected species, and its armor and strange habits make it one of the most studied little reptiles of southern Africa.

Cornered by a mongoose on open rock, the lizard clamps its jaws onto its own tail and bends into a spiky loop, so its hard back and spined tail face outward on every side.

The point of the ring is its center, where the lizard tucks away its soft, unarmored belly, the one part a predator's teeth could pierce. Rows of thick, squarish, spiny scales cover its back and tail like a knight's suit of riveted plate armor, so teeth slide right off, and that armor plus the rolling-up trick explain why it is named after the armadillo. Unlike most lizards, it lays no eggs: after a pregnancy of six to eight months the female gives birth to live young, usually just one or two, and she is one of the few lizards that may care for her babies afterward.

It is also unusually social for a reptile, living in colonies of up to 30 to 60 lizards of all ages packed together in a single rock crevice. Most lizards live alone, so a crowded crack full of armored neighbors is a rare sight in the reptile world.

basilisk-the-lizard-that-runs-on-water.context_blurb:
The basilisk is a slim, bright-green, long-tailed lizard of the forest streams and rivers of Central and South America. When a predator surprises it near water, it pulls off one of the most famous escape tricks in nature. It eats both plants and small animals, lays its eggs on riverbanks, and can swim and dive if the trick fails.

Startled, it rears up on its hind legs and dashes across the surface of a stream without sinking, which looks so much like walking on water that people nicknamed it the Jesus Christ lizard, after the Bible scene of Jesus walking on the Sea of Galilee.

Water is always its escape route: a basilisk cornered on a branch will drop straight down from the tree into the stream below, then sprint or swim away and leave the land predator stranded.

Speed is everything, because its feet slap the water up to 20 times a second, so each foot is already lifting away before the water can close over it. Size matters too: a light young basilisk can sprint 10 to 20 meters across open water, but a heavy adult manages only a few meters before its weight breaks the surface and it sinks.

Could a person do the same? The biologists Glasheen and McMahon calculated that a human would have to slap the water faster than 30 meters per second, needing roughly 15 times the muscle power a person actually has, so no human ever will.

caecilian-the-legless-amphibian-whose-yo.context_blurb:
Caecilians are a little-known group of amphibians that burrow through warm, wet soil in the tropics of the Americas, Africa and Asia. They feed on worms and other small creatures, are rarely seen above ground, and look like nothing else in their class. Biologists have found one of their parenting habits especially startling: it sounds like a horror story, but it is really an act of care.

This legless, ringed, worm-shaped burrower is a caecilian, a true amphibian in the same class as frogs and salamanders, neither worm nor snake.

There are more than 220 species spread through the warm, wet tropics of several continents, but not one lives naturally in Australia. Nearly blind in the dark soil, it hunts with a chemical-sensing tentacle that sits in a groove between each eye and nostril and can be pushed out and pulled back, a sense organ unique among all vertebrates.

In the Kenyan caecilian Boulengerula taitanus, a mother's newly hatched young crawl over her and scrape at her with temporary hatchling teeth, peeling off and eating her fatty outer skin, which regrows in about three days, so they feed again and again and can gain up to ten times their weight in a week. Alexander Kupfer and his team first documented this skin-feeding, a form of maternal care, not cruelty.

Researchers in Brazil found in 2020 that Siphonops annulatus, the ringed caecilian, has tiny glands at the base of its teeth that release fluid carrying an enzyme also found in bee, wasp and snake venom, and if the finding is confirmed, caecilians may be the oldest land vertebrates with an oral venom system, older even than snakes. The finding is still under study.

darwins-frog-the-father-who-broods-young.context_blurb:
Darwin's frog is a small frog with a pointed, leaf-like snout that lives in the cool, mossy beech forests of southern Chile and Argentina. Charles Darwin first collected it on the voyage of the Beagle in the 1830s. Today it is critically endangered, and it is famous for two survival tricks.

When a bird or another predator comes too close, Darwin's frog plays dead: it flops onto its back and lies still, or hops into a stream and drifts belly-up without moving, a leaf-shaped frog posing as a dead leaf until the danger passes.

Its second trick is fatherhood. In almost every other backboned animal the mother does the caring, and in most frogs her work is over once the eggs are laid. In Darwin's frog the father waits until the eggs begin to twitch, then scoops them into his mouth and keeps them in his vocal sac, the balloon-like throat pouch he normally fills to call, where the tadpoles grow in safety.

draco-the-gliding-lizard-on-rib-wings.context_blurb:
Draco, the flying dragon, is a small lizard of the rainforest canopies of Southeast Asia and India. Resting on a tree trunk it is brown and almost invisible against the bark, and it rarely touches the ground. To cross between trees it does something no other lizard can: it glides on wings built from its own skeleton.

A bat's wing or a bird's is built from arm and hand bones, but the Draco's wing is skin stretched over five to seven hugely lengthened ribs, which special muscles swing outward like the sticks of a folding fan. After landing, it folds them flat against its sides again.

A male also carries a bright yellow throat flag, the dewlap, which he flicks out to warn rivals and court females. The flap is see-through, so he turns it to face the sun, and light shining through makes it glow against his camouflaged body. Dracos eat ants and termites and live their whole lives aloft, with one exception. A female climbs down to the forest floor to dig a hole, bury a clutch of about 2 to 5 eggs and fill it in, then returns to the trees.

In midair, Draco does something no other glider is known to do. It reaches forward and grips the front edge of each wing with its hands, holding the skin taut. Scientists call this a composite wing, built from two different body parts, and it leaves the legs free to climb the instant the lizard lands.

flying-snake-the-serpent-that-glides.context_blurb:
Flying snakes, the genus Chrysopelea, are slender green-and-black tree snakes of the rainforests of South and Southeast Asia. They have no wings, flaps or limbs, yet they sail between treetops through thin air. Biologists at Virginia Tech have filmed them in slow motion to learn how a snake turns a fall into a long, steered glide.

The flying snake turns its own body into a wing: it flattens itself into a ribbon and glides, moving through the air the way a water snake crosses a pond. High-speed cameras filmed one snake launching 239 times. In 177 of those launches, about three-quarters, it started the same way: it hung from the branch, lifted its head into a J shape, then sprang upward and outward like a released spring. Once airborne, it sucks in its belly and spreads its ribs, changing its round cross-section into a flattened, half-moon shape that is slightly hollow underneath, which catches the air and makes lift.

You might expect a glider to hold still, but the snake keeps rippling from side to side in a wide S the whole way down. That constant motion keeps it stable and stops it from tumbling and spinning out of control.

gaboon-viper-the-longest-fangs-of-any-sn.context_blurb:
The Gaboon viper, Bitis gabonica, is a thick, heavy snake of the leaf-littered floors of central African rainforests, and few snakes on Earth weigh more. It is slow, patient and almost invisible, and it rarely bites unless stepped on or handled. Its weapons put it in a record book of its own.

No snake has longer fangs: the Gaboon viper's reach about 5 centimeters, 2 inches. Fangs that long would stab through its own lower jaw if they stayed upright, so they are hinged, folding back flat against the roof of the mouth when the jaws close and swinging forward to strike.

It can lie fully in the open and still vanish. Its broad, flat, triangular head looks like a fallen leaf, right down to a vein-like line running along its middle, while the pale rectangles, dark hourglasses and fawn diamonds on its body melt into the leaf litter.

The Gaboon viper also carries enormous amounts of venom. Drop for drop, the inland taipan has the deadliest venom of any snake, yet one taipan bite holds just 44 to 110 milligrams. A single milking of a Gaboon viper has drained about 2,400 milligrams of dried venom, as much as dozens of taipan bites. It hunts by ambush, lying still under the leaves for hours until a rat, hare or bird walks right over it. Unlike most vipers, which bite and let go, it clamps down and holds the prey fast in its fangs until the venom finishes it.

hairy-frog-the-frog-that-breaks-its-own-.context_blurb:
The hairy frog, nicknamed the horror frog, is a plump frog of the rainforest streams of Cameroon, in central Africa. It looks harmless, but it carries a hidden weapon unlike any other animal's, and the "hair" that gives it its name is not hair at all.

When a predator grabs it, the hairy frog deliberately breaks the bones in its own toes and punches their sharp ends through the skin of its hind feet as claws. The frog wounds itself to arm itself, which has also earned it the nickname Wolverine frog. A cat's or an eagle's claw is a bone covered by a hard sheath of keratin, but the hairy frog's claws are bare bone: its own sharpened toe bones with no covering at all.

In the breeding season the male grows fringes of thin skin along his flanks and thighs. They are packed with tiny blood vessels and work like external gills, absorbing more oxygen from the water so that he can remain submerged longer while he guards his eggs.

Scientists have watched the claws pop out under X-ray machines. But one part of the trick remains a mystery: how a claw gets pulled back inside after the threat is over. Researchers can only guess that it slides back as the torn skin heals.

hellbender-the-giant-snot-otter-that-bre.context_blurb:
The hellbender, Cryptobranchus alleganiensis, is North America's biggest salamander, up to about two feet in length, with a wide, flattened head. It hides under big flat rocks in chilly, rushing Appalachian streams, where it ambushes crayfish. Pollution and damaged streambeds have put it in serious trouble.

Its baggy, wrinkled skin hangs in ruffled layers along each side, which earned it the folk name lasagna lizard, along with snot otter, devil dog and Allegheny alligator.

Those folds are how it breathes. The hellbender barely uses its lungs and takes almost all its oxygen from the water through its skin. Its loose, baggy wrinkles and side folds give that skin far more surface for oxygen to soak in.

The skin can absorb oxygen only from water that actually flows past it. So when a summer stream goes nearly slack, a hellbender rocks its body and ripples its folds to sweep fresh, oxygen-rich water across its skin.

hognose-snake-the-drama-queen-death-fake.context_blurb:
The eastern hognose snake is a stout, harmless snake of the fields, meadows and sandy grasslands of the eastern and central United States, named for its upturned snout. When threatened it puts on one of the most theatrical defensive shows of any North American animal, and its real weapon is the performance.

Cornered, it first thrashes about as though wounded, then rolls onto its back with its mouth open and its purple tongue hanging out and goes limp, often with a foul smell, pretending to be freshly dead and rotting so that predators lose interest. Its name comes from a hardened scale on its snout that curls upward like a little shovel, which it uses to dig toads out of sandy soil.

Its act is so committed that if you turn a "dead" hognose right side up, it promptly flops over onto its back again, as if a corpse could only lie belly-up.

To sell the death, it also smears foul musk and can even bleed from its mouth, so it looks and smells truly rotten.

Its diet is almost entirely toads, and toads fight back in two ways: they gulp air and swell into a hard balloon too big to swallow, and their skin oozes a heart-stopping poison. Enlarged adrenal glands help the hognose resist the poison. Enlarged teeth at the back of its mouth puncture the puffed-up toad and let the air out.

leatherback-turtle-the-warm-blooded-rept.context_blurb:
The leatherback is the giant of sea turtles, a dark, ridged swimmer that crosses whole oceans between tropical nesting beaches and cold feeding grounds. Its scientific name, Dermochelys coriacea, means leathery skin-turtle, and it breaks many of the rules we expect of a reptile.

The leatherback is the largest sea turtle alive, with a shell about 2 meters long, and a big adult can weigh 500 to 700 kilograms, as much as a small car, making it the heaviest reptile on Earth apart from crocodiles.

Alone among sea turtles, it has no hard, bony shell: its back is covered in tough rubbery leathery skin, which is just what its name means. Its food is almost entirely jellyfish, sometimes close to its own body weight in a day. Its throat is lined with hundreds of backward-pointing spines, made of the same keratin as fingernails, which grip the slippery prey so it cannot slide back out while the turtle spits out the seawater it swallowed.

Reptiles usually match the temperature of their surroundings, yet one leatherback taken from icy Atlantic water had a core running some 18 degrees C above the sea around it. Activity alone would warm a reptile by a degree or two. In 2006 a satellite tag on a leatherback released off the Cape Verde islands recorded a dive of about 1,280 meters, the deepest ever logged for any reptile and deeper than most whales ever go.

marine-iguana-the-only-sea-going-lizard.context_blurb:
The marine iguana lives only on Ecuador's Galapagos Islands, on shores of black volcanic lava. It is a stocky, dark lizard as big as a pet cat, and it does what no other lizard does: it feeds in the sea. Charles Darwin called these lizards imps of darkness, and nearly everything about their bodies has been reshaped by that ocean diet.

The marine iguana is the only lizard in the world that feeds in the ocean: it dives off the lava shores and grazes red and green algae from rocks under the waves. In a basking pile, the big, bright lizards fighting for the warmest rocks are the adult males, which weigh about twice as much as the females and grow bright breeding colors.

With every mouthful of algae it swallows seawater, and special glands linked to its nostrils concentrate the salt so it can sneeze it out in a forceful spray, which dries into a crusty white patch on its head. Most of its day is spent on shore, not in the water. A dive in the chilly Galapagos sea can drop its body temperature by about 10 C, so as soon as it hauls out it basks on hot black lava in the sun, warming back up to the 35 to 39 C it needs to digest and move well.

It can dive to 30 meters and stay under for as long as an hour, partly because underwater its heart slows to about 30 beats a minute, roughly half its rate of about 100 on land, saving both heat and oxygen.

When El Nino years wipe out its algae, a starving marine iguana does more than lose fat: Martin Wikelski, who followed about 6,000 of them, found that it shrinks its own skeleton, absorbing bone until it is up to 20 percent shorter, then grows back to full length when the food returns. Until then, no animal with a backbone was known to shrink its skeleton.

mata-mata-turtle-the-leaf-that-vacuums-u.context_blurb:
The mata mata, a strange turtle with a flat, triangular head, lives in the slow, murky streams of the Amazon and Orinoco basins in South America. It lies almost motionless on the leafy river bottom all day, waiting for fish to come close, and its whole body is built for that ambush.

Small fish swim fearlessly up to the mata mata because they mistake it for a fallen leaf or a lump of rotting bark: its knobbly shell is ridged like bark, and its flat triangular head trails ragged skin fringes like fallen leaves.

When a fish comes close, the mata mata throws its head forward and opens its mouth so fast that it creates a vacuum, sucking the fish in on a rush of water; then it spits out the water and swallows the fish whole. Its mouth is built for sucking, not chewing. To breathe, it never lifts its head: its long, thin snout works as a snorkel, and it simply pokes the tip up to the surface while its body stays hidden on the bottom.

In water too muddy to see through, researchers think the ragged flaps on its neck do a second job, sensing the tiny ripples a swimming fish makes so the turtle can time its strike.

olm-the-blind-cave-baby-dragon-that-live.context_blurb:
Deep in the limestone caves of southeastern Europe, mostly in Slovenia, black underground rivers hide a pale, finger-sized salamander called the olm. It is blind, it never fully grows up, and it may live a hundred years, a life so slow that scientists study it for clues about aging.

For centuries, when floods in the caves washed olms up into the daylight, local people believed they were baby dragons, the young of a great beast sleeping deep beneath the earth.

The olm's pinkish skin is so like a person's in tone that it earned a second name. Slovene speakers call the olm the 'human fish.' It keeps a baby's body for life. Amphibians usually begin life as gilled larvae in the water and reshape their bodies as adults. The olm never makes that change, and even at a hundred it still wears the feathery external gills that an adult frog loses, a trait called neoteny that it shares with the axolotl.

Its eyes are tiny, sunk beneath the skin and useless in the pitch dark. Besides smell and hearing, the olm finds its tiny prey by sensing the weak electric fields their bodies produce, using special sense organs called ampullary organs.

Its whole life runs on almost no energy. It eats rarely, and when scientists tracked tagged olms for years, most had moved less than 10 meters. One was found in exactly the same spot after 2,569 days, more than seven years without going anywhere. As the researcher Gergely Balazs put it, they are "hanging around, doing almost nothing," a thrifty way to live for an animal that can last a century.

purple-frog-the-pig-nosed-frog-that-surf.context_blurb:
The purple frog is a plump, glossy, dark-purple frog from the Western Ghats, a mountain range in southern India. Its body is swollen like a balloon, and its little pointed head looks too small for it. Western science formally described it only in 2003, because it spends nearly its whole life hidden deep in damp soil, and its family tree reaches back to the age of the dinosaurs.

An adult comes above ground for only about two weeks a year: with the first monsoon rains it climbs out to breed in short-lived streams, then vanishes back into the earth.

Its nickname, the pignose frog, comes from its small, pointed snout, shaped like a pig's, set on a tiny head with a pale-blue ring around each little eye. Its scientific name is Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis.

The purple frog does not hunt at the surface like most frogs. It eats termites and ants, catching them entirely underground with a long, fluted tongue that works with a special channel inside its mouth.

Its family has been evolving alone for an enormous stretch of time. Its closest living relatives are the little Sooglossid frogs of the Seychelles islands, far out in the Indian Ocean, and the two lines split about 100 million years ago, when the supercontinent Gondwana broke apart and India drifted away as an island continent of its own. That makes the purple frog a living fossil, the lonely survivor of a very old branch.

shingleback-skink-the-lizard-with-a-tail.context_blurb:
The shingleback skink (Tiliqua rugosa) is a short, slow, stocky lizard of the dry woodlands and scrub of southern Australia, armored in thick scales like the shingles of a pine cone. Australians also call it the sleepy lizard, bobtail or stumpy, and it is often seen basking by roadsides. Too slow to run from danger, it relies on bluff and trickery.

Its short, blunt tail looks so much like its own head that one of its names is the two-headed skink, and a predator often strikes the wrong end while the lizard escapes the other way. Unlike most lizards, the shingleback has lost the ability to shed its tail and regrow it, so that head-shaped decoy is a permanent, one-and-only piece of equipment it must protect.

When cornered, it turns to face the attacker, gapes to show the pink lining of its mouth and flashes a broad, bright-blue tongue while hissing, a bluff meant to scare off the hunter before any biting starts.

The shingleback is unusual in its family life, too. It is the only reptile known to be monogamous: a male and a female pair up and meet again at the same spot every spring, some couples for over 20 years, and one pair in a long-term study was still reuniting after 27 years. Instead of laying eggs, the mother gives birth to one to four live babies, usually two or three, and each one is huge for a newborn lizard, up to 220 millimeters long, nearly the length of a ruler.

spider-tailed-viper-the-tail-that-fishes.context_blurb:
The spider-tailed horned viper (Pseudocerastes urarachnoides) is a small, dust-colored viper of the stony mountains of western Iran, named as a species only in 2006. It hunts birds with one of the most astonishing lures in nature, and the trick depends on keeping every part of its body perfectly still except one.

The tip of its tail is shaped into a lifelike fake spider, a bulb-like body fringed with long, leg-like scales, and as the snake lies motionless it wiggles only that tip, so it looks like a spider scuttling over the rock.

When a bird swoops down to snatch the spider, the viper's real head, hidden among the rocks, whips around and strikes in about 0.2 seconds, a move researchers have caught on film. The lure mostly fools migrating birds passing through, especially shrikes and warblers, while local birds seem to have learned the trick and keep clear.

The first specimen, found dead on a road in western Iran in 1968 by two American travelers named Smith, puzzled scientists, who took its strange tail for a tumor, a deformity or a parasite clinging to an ordinary snake. Only in 2006 was the tail recognized as a true spider-mimic, and the snake as a new species.
