surinam-toad-babies-that-erupt-from-the-.context_blurb:
The Surinam toad (Pipa pipa) is a South American frog that spends its whole life underwater, in the warm, murky, slow rivers and swamps of the Amazon basin and the Guianas. It has no tongue and no teeth, it hunts by touch, and the way it raises its young is unlike anything else among amphibians.

The Surinam toad is almost completely flat, with a broad triangular head and mottled brown skin, so lying still on the muddy riverbed it looks just like a dead, rotting leaf on the bottom.

The tip of every front finger splits into a little star, earning it the nickname star-fingered toad, and these sensitive fingertips probe through leaf litter and murky water to feel out prey it cannot see and steer it to the mouth. With no tongue or teeth, it is a suction feeder: it suddenly expands its throat, inhaling a rush of water that vacuums the prey whole into its big mouth.

During mating the male presses the eggs onto the female's back, where her skin swells up around each one and seals it in its own pocket, turning her back into a honeycomb. The young skip the tadpole stage entirely, and after three to four months dozens of fully formed baby toads, each about 25 millimeters long, push out through her skin and swim away.

thorny-devil-drinking-through-skin-and-t.context_blurb:
The thorny devil (Moloch horridus) is a small lizard of the baking deserts of central and western Australia, covered head to tail in hard, cone-shaped spikes like a walking pincushion. For all its fierce looks it is slow and harmless, and it has evolved clever answers to two desert problems: finding water and escaping hunters.

The thorny devil never needs to bend down to drink: it drinks through its skin, where tiny grooves between the spines wick water up from a puddle or damp sand by capillary action and carry it across its body to its mouth. It eats nothing but ants, sitting beside an ant trail and picking them off singly with its sticky tongue, about one every second, perhaps 750 in a day. When a hunting hawk or goanna comes near, it tucks its real head down between its front legs and shows a knobby, spiny fake head on the back of its neck, a decoy that can heal if it is bitten.

When the only water is damp sand, it scoops that sand up over its back with its legs, pressing the wet grains against its skin so the grooves can draw out even more water. Crossing open ground in daylight, it walks with a slow, jerky gait, rocking back and forth and freezing, which probably makes it look like a leaf blown by the wind and confuses birds of prey watching from above.

Each of those skin channels is microscopic, about 200 micrometers wide and 100 micrometers tall, and together they form a network that runs all over the body to the corners of the mouth, pulling water uphill against gravity.

wallaces-flying-frog-the-frog-that-parac.context_blurb: Wallace's flying frog is a bright-green tree frog that lives in the rainforests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula. It was first described by the Victorian naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace during his years in the region in the 1850s. The frog spends almost all its time in the canopy, and when it needs to move between trees it does something no normal frog can do: it jumps and glides on a parachute built right into its own body.

why-the-ice-age-giants-died-overkill-vs-.context_blurb: At the end of the last ice age, between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most of the biggest land animals on every continent except Africa went extinct. Mammoths, giant sloths, saber-toothed cats, giant kangaroos, and many others disappeared in a wave that followed the arrival of modern humans and overlapped with sudden climate change. Scientists still argue about how much of the extinction was climate, how much was hunting pressure, and how much was both at once. The debate is one of the biggest in paleoecology.

archerfish.context_blurb:
The archerfish is a small, slim, silvery fish with bold black stripes, at home in mangrove creeks and brackish river mouths from Southeast Asia to northern Australia. It feeds on land insects perched far out of its reach, and it brings them down with one of the strangest weapons in the animal kingdom: water.

When a cricket, ant or spider sits on a leaf above the creek, the archerfish fires a precise jet of water from below the surface that knocks the insect off its perch and into the water, where the fish eats it.

Its aim is superb: an adult almost always hits on the very first shot, striking insects dead-on up to about 65 centimeters away, and its jet can reach prey as high as 3 meters.

The gun barrel is inside its mouth: the roof of its mouth has a deep channel, and the fish presses its tongue up against it, sealing the channel into a narrow tube, then snaps its gill covers shut to blast water through.

Water bends light at the surface, so from below a bug can appear as much as 25 degrees away from its real spot, yet the archerfish compensates for that bending and aims at the insect's real position. The fish's mouth muscles are too weak for such a hard hit, so the punch is built in flight: water fired last travels faster than water fired first, catching up and bunching the jet into one compact slug about six times more powerful than the muscles alone, the same physics an inkjet printer uses. Archerfish also learn by watching: in Stefan Schuster's 2006 study, fish that never fired during training matched the skill of the trained fish at hitting speeding targets as soon as they got a turn, having learned purely by observing the others.

box-jellyfish.context_blurb:
Box jellyfish live in warm coastal waters, especially off northern Australia and across the Indo-Pacific. They are pale and nearly invisible in the water, yet they swim with purpose, see with surprisingly complex eyes and carry one of the most dangerous stings of any animal on Earth, all without a brain.

The box jellyfish is named for its bell, a see-through cube with four flat sides instead of the rounded dome of an ordinary jellyfish, with a cluster of long tentacles trailing from each corner.

Unlike drifting jellyfish, it swims hard, squeezing its bell to jet along at about 1.5 meters per second, and it can whip around in a full 180-degree turn within a few pulses of its bell. Australia's deadliest box jellyfish, Chironex fleckeri, has 24 eyes, six apiece set in four tiny sensory clubs called rhopalia, yet it has no brain, only a ring of nerves around its bell.

Most of those eyes are simple patches that only sense light, but a few work like a camera, each with a lens, a cornea and a retina, able to form a picture, astonishing in an animal with no brain to make sense of it. Each tentacle carries hundreds of thousands of stinging capsules called nematocysts, tiny coiled harpoons that fire when they sense the chemicals on skin rather than at a mere bump, so they are not wasted on driftwood. Few animals carry deadlier venom than Chironex fleckeri: a serious sting can stop a person's heart, and untreated victims have died within two to five minutes, which is why swimmers on northern Australian beaches watch for it more carefully than for sharks.

Because the bell tumbles as it swims, each sensory club holds a heavy crystal called a statolith on a flexible stalk, and gravity pulls it straight down like a plumb bob, so the eyes stay pointed up and down no matter how the bell tilts.

coelacanth.context_blurb:
The coelacanth, Latimeria, is a large lobe-finned fish, deep blue in color, that lives in deep waters off eastern Africa and Indonesia. Its last fossils date to the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs, so scientists believed its whole group had vanished, until a live one turned up in 1938. It is closer kin to lungfish and to the ancestors of land animals than to a tuna or a trout.

In 1938 the young museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted a strange blue fish in a South African catch, with four thick, limb-like fins and a small extra tail, and it proved to be a coelacanth, the classic living fossil. J.L.B. Smith, the fish scientist who identified it, loved the fish so much that he titled his 1956 book Old Fourlegs, after its four leg-like fins.

Underwater film shows its four fleshy, muscle-tipped fins moving in the same alternating pattern a four-legged reptile uses when it walks, a hint of how life crawled onto land, though the coelacanth is not our direct ancestor. For sixty years that South African fish was the only kind known, until in 1997 the marine biologist Mark Erdmann, honeymooning in Indonesia with his wife Arnaz Mehta, spotted a second species laid out at a fish market in Sulawesi. It was later named Latimeria menadoensis.

Its skull has a true hinge running crosswise through the middle, something no other living animal has, and when it lunges, a special muscle swings the whole front of its head upward at that joint, opening its mouth extra wide and biting harder to swallow bigger prey. In 2021 scientists counted growth rings on coelacanth scales and found that a mother carries her young for about five years, the longest pregnancy of any animal known, before giving birth to 5 to 25 fully formed live pups. The same study found that coelacanths may live nearly a century and do not mature until about age 55.

cuttlefish.context_blurb:
The cuttlefish is a soft, flat-bodied cousin of the octopus and squid that lives in shallow seas from Europe to Australia. It has eight short arms, W-shaped pupils and a fin rippling along each side, and it is a master of disguise and one of the cleverest animals without a backbone.

It hunts by surprise, hovering over the sand with its arms spread to watch a shrimp. Then two long feeding tentacles, kept coiled out of sight, shoot out from between its arms and snatch the prey so fast the eye can barely follow. Its rich brown ink was a favorite drawing ink of Renaissance artists and mapmakers, and the color is named after the cuttlefish's Latin genus, Sepia, which is why we still call that dusty brown "sepia."

Those chalky white ovals clipped inside parakeet cages come from the cuttlefish too: each one is a cuttlebone, the animal's internal shell, sold for over a century so pet birds can sharpen their beaks on it and get calcium.

Unlike a snail's shell, the cuttlebone is not armor. It is a buoyancy tank divided into tiny chambers, which the cuttlefish fills with gas or liquid to rise or sink, so it can hover perfectly level like a submarine adjusting its ballast. Its color cells, the chromatophores, can flash new patterns in an instant. Yet its eyes hold just one kind of light-sensing cell, which by the usual rules makes the cuttlefish colorblind: the master of color probably cannot see its own displays the way we do. The broadclub cuttlefish of Indo-Pacific reefs uses its skin to hunt. Creeping toward a crab, it sends dark bands rolling down its head and arms over and over, a display called the passing cloud. A 2025 study at Bristol found that the rolling stripes swamp the crab's eyes with fake downward motion, which hides the fact that the hunter is creeping closer.

Every winter giant Australian cuttlefish crowd into South Australia's shallow bays to breed, and big guard males fight to keep the females. A small male cannot win a brawl, so he cheats: he turns his skin pale, tucks in his arms to copy a female's outline and hides his male display, then slips past the guard to reach the female.

How might a colorblind animal read color? In 2016 a father-and-son team, Alexander and Christopher Stubbs, proposed that the odd, off-center W-shaped pupil lets each color come into sharp focus at a slightly different depth, so the eye can tell which color it sees from how far it must refocus to make the image sharp. The idea is still being tested.

Cuttlefish, octopus and squid also edit the working copies of their genes on a vast scale, changing over 60 percent of those in the brain, where humans change fewer than 1 percent. In 2017 Joshua Rosenthal and Eli Eisenberg found the price. The editing machinery needs the DNA around each editing site to keep its exact shape, so those stretches of DNA have been frozen in place, and these animals gave up the normal pace of DNA evolution in exchange for flexible proteins.

electric-eel.context_blurb:
The electric eel is a long, dark, snake-shaped fish of the slow, muddy rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco in South America. It is famous for its shock, but it uses electricity for much more than killing: to find its way, to hunt hidden prey and to defend itself, sometimes in ways no one believed until recently.

Despite its name, it is not a true eel at all: it belongs to the knifefishes, the order Gymnotiformes, and its nearest relatives are other knifefish, not the marine eels it resembles. It is also an air-breather, rising to the surface about every two minutes to gulp air through its mouth, and an eel kept from the surface will drown.

Its body is mostly battery: its vital organs, heart and stomach included, are squeezed into the front fifth, and the electric organs fill the remaining 80 percent of its length. Those organs hold about 6,000 cells called electrocytes, lined up end to end like the batteries in a flashlight, one on top of the next, so their tiny voltages add up to one enormous jolt when they all fire together.

The eel has two settings: apart from its big killing blast, it sends out a weak, steady electric pulse all the time and senses how nearby objects disturb that faint field, like radar, so it can find its way and spot prey in dark, muddy water where its eyes are almost useless. Kenneth Catania of Vanderbilt University found the eel's boldest trick by accident, while moving eels with a net that had a metal rim. A cornered eel leaped up out of the water and jammed its chin onto the metal rim, shocking the threat directly instead of through the water.

Catania then measured those leaps. Underwater the eel's current spreads out in every direction, but out of the water it is forced through the target. So the higher the eel climbs up its target, the stronger the shock grows. He also found how the eel flushes out hidden prey. It fires a quick pair of high-voltage pulses about 2 milliseconds apart, which remotely sets off the prey's own muscles, so the fish twitches and gives itself away. When a big fish struggles too hard, the eel curls into a horseshoe with the prey trapped between its head and tail. Its positive pole is in its head and its negative pole in its tail, so bringing the two poles together more than doubles the voltage driven into the victim, whose muscles twitch until they lock in exhaustion.

Those discoveries settled an old argument. Back in 1800 the explorer Alexander von Humboldt wrote that eels had leaped from a pool to attack some 30 horses driven into it, stunning two that then drowned. For about 200 years scientists mocked the tale as nonsense, until Catania's studies of leaping eels showed that it could well be true. In 2019 a team led by C. David de Santana showed that the electric eel, long treated as one species, is really three. One of them, Electrophorus voltai, discharged 860 volts, the highest voltage ever measured from any animal, probably because the clear highland water it lives in carries current poorly. Fish have turned plain muscle into an electric organ on at least six separate occasions, a puzzle Darwin noticed. When scientists read the electric eel's genome in 2014, they found that each lineage had reused nearly the same set of genes to make that change.

giant-and-colossal-squid.context_blurb:
Giant and colossal squid are two different enormous squid of the deep open ocean, built for a world of darkness and crushing pressure. Live sightings are extremely rare, and most of what scientists know comes from specimens hauled up by fishing boats, washed ashore, or found inside the sperm whales that hunt them.

The colossal squid of the deep waters near Antarctica owns the biggest eye ever measured in any animal, about 27 centimeters across, as big as a basketball and two to three times wider than any other animal's eye.

A giant squid laid out on a dock may measure about 13 meters from tail fin to tentacle tip, but its body, the mantle, is only about 5 meters, and most of that length comes from its two long feeding tentacles, about 10 meters on their own. The colossal squid is armed differently: no other squid in its family has hooks on its arms, but it carries rows of sharp, swiveling hooks mixed among its suckers, with more hooks on its tentacle clubs. Its great enemy, the sperm whale, often surfaces covered with pale, plate-sized rings, the marks of giant squid suckers gripping the whale during battles far down in the dark.

In February 2007 the New Zealand fishing boat San Aspiring was hauling a longline from 1,500 meters down in the Ross Sea when it brought up a 495-kilogram colossal squid, the heaviest ever recorded. The squid had never been hooked itself: it had grabbed a toothfish caught on the line and refused to release it. It is now on display at Te Papa museum in Wellington.

Why such a giant eye? In 2012 Dan-Eric Nilsson's team showed that it is tuned to catch the faint light of plankton that a sperm whale sets glowing as it approaches, which lets the squid spot the whale about 120 meters away, in time to flee. A giant squid has no swim bladder, yet it hangs in the deep without sinking, because its flesh and body fluid are loaded with ammonium ions, which are lighter than seawater, so its body floats like a raft.

A fleeing squid squeezes its entire mantle at once in a single jet, and the signal races down a giant axon, a single nerve fiber up to a millimeter thick with no insulating sheath, whose sheer width speeds the impulse. It is so large that in 1952 Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley could slide electrodes inside it, work that later won them a Nobel Prize.

great-white-shark.context_blurb:
The great white shark is the biggest predatory fish alive, a powerful hunter of cool coastal seas from California to South Africa and Australia. It ambushes seals from below, carries a conveyor belt of teeth, keeps parts of its body warm and roams across whole oceans.

Its teeth work like a conveyor belt: when a front tooth snaps off, one from the row behind rolls forward to take its place, sometimes within 24 to 48 hours. At Seal Island in South Africa's False Bay, a great white lurks deep below a seal, then shoots upward with such force that its whole body may leave the water. Researchers named that vertical strike the Polaris breach, after a missile launched from submarines.

A great white carries about 300 teeth in up to seven rows, but most sit in reserve behind the working front row until they roll forward. Because it keeps shedding and replacing them, a shark can go through tens of thousands of teeth in a lifetime, which is why fossil shark teeth litter ancient seabeds. A great white almost never survives in captivity, and the record belongs to California's Monterey Bay Aquarium, which displayed a young one for 198 days in 2004 and 2005 before releasing it. Deep Blue, a female filmed off Mexico's Guadalupe Island in 2013, is roughly 6 meters, about 20 feet, long and is believed to be about half a century old. Divers swimming beside her look like small children.

Its upper teeth are broad, serrated triangles that slice through flesh and fat, while the narrower, pointed lower teeth grip and hold the catch. Unlike most fish, the great white is partly warm-blooded: a web of vessels, the rete mirabile or "wonderful net," keeps its muscle heat in the body instead of losing it at the gills. The extra warmth makes its swimming muscles work faster and keeps its brain and eyes sharp in cold water. Its coloring is camouflage, a dark gray back over a white belly. From below, the white belly blends with the bright surface, so a seal never sees the shark rising at over 40 kilometers per hour. Great whites die in tanks partly because they must swim constantly to push water over their gills to breathe. They also roam such distances that, penned in, they injure themselves against the walls and often refuse to eat.

A wounded seal leaks charged salts, called electrolytes, into the water, making an electric field up to three times stronger than a healthy animal's, so to the shark's electric sense an injured seal lights up. Temperature probes fed into the stomachs of great whites in water of only 13 to 16 degrees Celsius read about 25 to 27 degrees. That warmth is a family trait it shares with its fast relatives the salmon shark and the shortfin mako. Even so, the hunter often misses: long-term study at Seal Island found that only about 47 percent of breach attacks succeed. Great whites also live far longer than once thought, because in 2014 a Woods Hole team counted growth bands in their backbones, like tree rings, and found they can live more than 70 years. Their pups grow for about a year in the womb, where, unlike sand tiger embryos, they do not eat their siblings but swallow unfertilized eggs the mother supplies, along with a fatty "uterine milk," so several are born together.

Its ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores named after a 17th-century Italian anatomist, can sense electric fields as weak as about five billionths of a volt per centimeter. Satellite tags showed that great whites from California travel every year to an empty stretch of ocean midway between Baja and Hawaii, nicknamed the White Shark Cafe, and stay there for months. The great white is not a shrunken megalodon either. Carcharodon hubbelli, a 6.5-million-year-old in-between species from Peru whose teeth were only partway to growing serrations, shows that it evolved from a broad-toothed mako shark. Megalodon belongs to a separate family, and the likeness of their teeth is a case of convergent evolution, not close kinship.

hammerhead-shark.context_blurb:
Hammerhead sharks are a family of sharks of warm seas worldwide, named for the flattened, T-shaped head called the cephalofoil, Greek for "head wing." The hammer is not a club but a wide platform for sensors, and it changes how these sharks hunt, see, smell and swim.

On a reef, no diver mistakes the silhouette of a hammerhead shark: a head flattened sideways into a wide bar, with an eye at each tip. Most hammerheads measure between 5 and 10 feet, but the great hammerhead is the giant of the family, averaging about 15 feet, with the largest close to 20.

The underside of the hammer is studded with ampullae of Lorenzini, pores that sense the faint electric fields of living animals, so by sweeping its head low over the sand like a wide metal detector, a great hammerhead can find a stingray buried out of sight and dig it out. Stingrays are its favorite food, and the head is also a hammer. The shark knocks the ray down and then pins it flat against the sand with its own head before biting into its wings. One caught off Florida had 96 stingray spines lodged in and around its mouth.

With an eye at each end of the hammer, the shark can see almost all the way around itself. In the 2000s Michelle McComb swept small flashing lights around captured hammerheads and recorded each eye's electrical response, proving that it has a field of view of close to 360 degrees. Its nostrils sit out at the tips of the hammer too, and Kajiura's team found that this lets the shark smell in stereo: a scent reaches one nostril a split second before the other, telling it which way to turn toward the source. Scalloped hammerheads hunt alone in the open ocean at night, yet by day hundreds gather in slow-circling schools over underwater mountains called seamounts, such as the Alcyone seamount off Costa Rica's Cocos Island.

The great hammerhead's head covers roughly a fourth of its length, but the winghead shark's stretches nearly half its length, the widest head for its size in the family. Bonnetheads are small, shovel-headed hammerheads. In 2001 a captive female at a zoo in Omaha, Nebraska, who had not been near a male for three years, gave birth to a healthy pup. DNA tests ruled out stored sperm. Her egg had developed into a pup without any sperm, by fusing with a sister cell from its own division, the first confirmed virgin birth in any shark.

Scalloped hammerheads dive past 800 meters into near-freezing water to hunt, yet their muscles stay warm. When Mark Royer's tags followed them, one was filmed at 1,044 meters, and the trick became clear. The shark clamps its gill slits shut for the whole dive, holding its breath for about 17 minutes, so its gills cannot leak its body heat into the cold sea.

horseshoe-crab.context_blurb:
The horseshoe crab is a domed, armored sea creature with a long spiky tail, found along the Atlantic coast of the United States and the shores of East Asia. Every spring, crowds of them crawl out of the surf to bury their eggs in the sand. Its family has survived for some 450 million years, and modern medicine now leans on its strange blood.

Despite its name, it is no crab at all: it belongs to the chelicerates, the group that holds spiders and scorpions, which is why some people call it the sea spider.

Its body plan has barely changed in about 450 million years, so horseshoe crabs were crawling through the shallows over 200 million years before the first dinosaurs appeared, and they came through every one of the great mass extinctions. That is why it is often called a living fossil. Its long tail, the telson, is no stinger and carries no venom; when a wave flips the crab onto its back, it stabs the telson into the sand and uses it as a lever to heave itself right side up. It steers with the same tail when it swims.

Its blood is milky blue, because instead of our red, iron-based hemoglobin it carries oxygen with a copper-based protein called hemocyanin, and the copper turns blue when it meets the air. That blue blood also protects our medicines. Cells in it called amebocytes clot into a gel the instant they touch the toxins left by dead bacteria, so drug makers check every vaccine and injected drug with horseshoe crab blood before it reaches a patient. This check, the LAL test, was used on the COVID-19 vaccines too. The horseshoe crab also has ten eyes: a pair of big compound eyes on top of its shell, each with about 1,000 light-sensing units, several smaller simple eyes, a pair on its underside near the mouth, and light sensors along its tail.

On the high tides of May, near the full and new moons, the females crawl onto the sands of Delaware Bay and bury clusters of 3,000 to 5,000 green eggs each, millions in all. A threatened shorebird, the red knot, times its 9,000-mile journey to the Arctic so that it can stop at the bay, and after a fortnight of gorging on the fat-rich eggs its weight has nearly doubled, fuel for the rest of the flight.

mantis-shrimp.context_blurb:
Mantis shrimp are finger-length crustaceans of warm, shallow seas, many of them living in burrows they dig in the sand of coral reefs. They are not true shrimp but stomatopods, an ancient group of their own. They are famous for two things: arms that strike faster than almost anything in nature, and some of the strangest eyes on Earth.

On a coral reef, the mantis shrimp waits in its sandy burrow, its two thick, clubbed arms tucked beneath its head, ready to break open the shells of snails and crabs. Mantis shrimp come in two body plans, smashers and spearers: smashers such as the peacock mantis shrimp bludgeon hard-shelled prey with a blunt club, while spearers lurk in burrows and impale soft, fast prey such as fish with long, barbed arms.

A peacock mantis shrimp's club can crack ordinary aquarium glass with one blow, so keepers house it behind glass at least 8 to 10 millimeters thick. Its blow peaks at about 1,500 newtons, over 2,500 times the animal's own body weight.

Muscle alone is far too slow, so the shrimp loads a saddle-shaped spring, locks it with a latch and then releases the latch, releasing the spring's power in one burst, exactly the way a crossbow stores and releases its power. High-speed cameras show the club accelerating at thousands of times gravity's pull, 6,300 to 8,000 g, and reaching 14 to 23 meters per second, about 50 to 75 miles per hour, among the fastest strikes measured in any animal.

The strike is so quick that it rips the water apart, leaving a bubble of vapor behind the club. High-speed films of a single strike show two force spikes about 400 microseconds apart: the first is the club hitting the shell, and the second is the cavitation bubble collapsing, a second hammer blow that costs the shrimp nothing. As the bubble collapses, its tiny core flashes with light and heats to roughly 20,000 kelvin, hotter than the sun's surface, an effect called sonoluminescence, though that temperature is a debated estimate. Where a human eye has three kinds of color receptor, a mantis shrimp eye has twelve to sixteen, and it also senses ultraviolet and polarized light that we cannot see.

You might expect all those receptors to give finer color vision, but in 2014 Hanne Thoen trained mantis shrimp to choose between similar shades and found they did worse than people, because their receptors do not compare against one another the way our three do. Researchers think the eye instead scans the scene line by line, like a satellite's scanner or a barcode reader, recognizing each color almost instantly with little brain work. Its two eyes swivel independently on stalks, and each one is divided into three regions that look at the same point at once, so a single eye can judge depth by itself.

Mantis shrimp are the only animals known to detect circularly polarized light. Cell membranes in their eyes are rolled into tiny tubes that act as a living quarter-wave plate, the light-twisting part used in CD players and camera filters, and where a human-made plate works for a single color, the shrimp's works from near-ultraviolet to infrared. The smashers and spearers look like a pair that split from one ancestor at the same moment, but studies combining fossils and DNA show that spearing came first, and the crushing club arose far later, about 126 million years ago. Mantis shrimp themselves go back some 340 million years.

mudskipper.context_blurb:
When the tide drains out of tropical mangrove swamps and mudflats in Africa, Asia and parts of Australia, it leaves wide stretches of glistening mud. Most fish would be stranded. The mudskipper is just getting started: a bulgy-eyed fish that walks, leaps, fights and courts in the open air.

The mudskipper is a true fish, finger-length, yet it spends most of its life out of water, hauling itself over the mud instead of swimming.

To walk, it plants its two muscular pectoral fins like a pair of crutches and drags its body forward across the mud. When it needs speed, it changes gait. A sudden flex and push of its tail flings it through the air in a leap of up to about 61 centimeters, roughly two feet, and that skip is where the mudskipper gets its name.

Life in the air brings two problems: breathing and staying wet. Gills work poorly out of water. So, like a frog, the mudskipper absorbs air through its damp skin and through the moist lining inside its mouth and throat. Before a long trek across the mud, it fills its enlarged gill chambers with a mouthful of water and air, puffing out its cheeks like a scuba diver's tank, because if its gills dry out it can no longer take in oxygen. A male defends his patch of mud with a wild show: he rears up in push-ups, flares the fin on his back, beats his tail and leaps high. The display does double duty, warning rival males away while also showing off to impress females.

A mudskipper father's real masterpiece is underground. In tropical Asia, a male hollows out a burrow whose arched roof holds a pocket of air, then makes trip after trip to the surface to gulp air and carry it down; the biologist Karen Martin found that he may need about 100 mouthfuls to build that first air bubble for his eggs. For days he keeps the chamber stocked while he watches the tide. When the moment is right, he swallows the trapped air out of the chamber and lets the rising sea pour in, so the eggs can hatch and the larvae swim off to sea. Martin called him "really a very good papa."

nautilus.context_blurb:
The chambered nautilus is a shelled cousin of the octopus and squid that lives in the deep, warm waters of the western Pacific. While its relatives gave up their shells long ago, it still wears a coiled shell of sealed rooms, and in many ways it is a window onto the ancient seas.

Its lineage has kept a coiled outer shell for about 500 million years, swimming the oceans long before the dinosaurs, so biologists call the nautilus a living fossil. To flee a crab, it squeezes water out through a forward-pointing funnel, and the recoil shoots it backward, the same jet its squid and octopus relatives use.

Instead of eight arms covered in suckers, a nautilus has about 90 thin tentacles called cirri, and none has a single sucker: they hold prey simply because they are extremely sticky. It lives in the largest room of its shell, and by pumping gas and liquid in and out of the 30-odd sealed rooms behind it, it changes its density to rise or sink, a living submarine.

An octopus eye is a sealed ball with a lens, but the nautilus eye has no lens at all and is open to the ocean, so raw seawater flows right up against its retina. To empty a chamber, a living tube called the siphuncle draws salt from the liquid sealed in the chamber and passes it into the blood, and the water then follows the salt out on its own by osmosis, while gas seeps in to fill the space. That pump fails below about 240 meters, a puzzle, since nautiluses often hunt deeper.

Each chamber wall is ruled with about 30 fine growth lines, and Kahn and Pompea found that each line records one day, so a chamber holds about a lunar month of growth. The earliest nautiloids, 420 million years ago, show only about 9 lines per chamber, a month of about 9 days, from a time when the Moon orbited much closer and Earth spun faster.

ocean-sunfish-mola.context_blurb:
The ocean sunfish, or mola, is a huge, round fish of the open ocean and the heaviest bony fish in the world, weighing more than a ton. It drifts at the surface, dives deep after jellyfish and carries a heavy load of parasites, and its odd body looks as if half the fish is missing.

The ocean sunfish, Mola mola, resembles a huge head with fins and no body behind it: its body is flattened from side to side, tall fins rise above and below, and it ends abruptly in a blunt rear with no real tail.

Its stiff rudder, the clavus, is no shrunken tail: it forms where its top and bottom fins, the dorsal and anal fins, wrap around the rear of the body and meet.

It often basks sideways at the surface, and seabirds land on its upturned flank to pick parasites off its skin, while cleaner fish work on its underside.

Tagged sunfish dive up to 40 times daily to near 1,000 meters to hunt jellyfish in the cold dark, and each time they climb back to reheat their chilled bodies at the warm surface, like big solar panels. That habit has earned the mola the nickname the solar-powered fish.

octopus.context_blurb:
The octopus is a soft-bodied cephalopod found in every ocean, from tide pools to the deep sea. It has eight arms lined with suckers, three hearts and a mind spread through its whole body, and it solves puzzles, opens jars and changes its skin in a flash. It is among the clearest cases of intelligence that evolved far from our own branch of life.

An octopus has no bones at all, and the only hard part in its body is its beak, a parrot-like bite hidden at the center of its arms. When a predator closes in, it draws a big gulp of water into its mantle and blasts it out through a muscular tube called the siphon, rocketing backward like a jet. As it flees, it squirts dark ink into the same jet, making a smoke screen that hides it, and the ink also contains tyrosinase, which irritates a predator's eyes and garbles its sense of smell and taste.

With no skeleton, an octopus can squeeze through any gap its beak fits through, so a giant Pacific octopus weighing 50 pounds can slip through a hole the width of a two-inch coin. The beak works like bone and can crush crab and clam shells, but it is made of chitin, the same tough material that builds crab claws and insect shells. An octopus has three hearts: a pair push its blue blood, which carries oxygen with copper, through the gills to load it with oxygen, and the third pushes it on to the rest of the body.

Beneath its skin lie thousands of tiny color sacs called chromatophores, and while a chameleon shifts color slowly by moving pigment inside its cells, an octopus has muscles that yank its color sacs open in an instant, flashing a new pattern across its body. Below them sit iridophores that flash shimmering colors and leucophores that mirror the light around them. Every sucker is studded with chemical sensors, so when an octopus lays an arm on a shell or a bit of food, it can taste whatever it touches; a giant Pacific octopus has about 2,000 suckers, roughly 280 per arm.

An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, about as many as a dog, but roughly two-thirds of them live in its arms, where each arm has its own cluster acting as a mini-brain that can grab food or explore a hole without orders from the head. For all its skill at matching rocks, coral and sand, an octopus cannot tell colors apart: its eyes carry just a single visual pigment, so it is colorblind, and how it matches colors anyway is still a puzzle.

Bruce Robison and his colleagues at Monterey Bay sent a robot submersible to the same deep Pacific ledge again and again, and found the same female Graneledone boreopacifica curled over her eggs on every visit. She guarded her clutch of about 160 eggs for 53 months, some four and a half years, without ever eating, and died soon after they hatched. A mother octopus starves while guarding her eggs because her optic glands, small glands behind her eyes, release chemicals that switch off her appetite, and in experiments, mothers whose optic glands were cut out stopped starving and kept living. The earliest fossil relative of octopuses, Syllipsimopodi bideni, lived in Montana about 330 million years ago, long before any dinosaur, and it had ten arms, each with a double row of suckers, so the eight-armed plan came later, when a pair of arms was lost.

pistol-shrimp.context_blurb:
The pistol shrimp, or snapping shrimp, is a small crustacean of warm, shallow seas around the world. It has an ordinary pincer on one side and an enormous one on the other, and it uses the big claw as a gun that never touches its target. It also shares its home with a fish in one of the ocean's neatest partnerships.

When a pistol shrimp hunts, its giant claw, nearly half as long as its body, slams shut and fires a jet of water that stuns a passing fish from a distance; the claw itself never touches the prey. For all that power, a pistol shrimp is only 3 to 5 centimeters long, about the size of an adult's thumb, yet for its size it makes one of the loudest sounds of any animal.

In the Second World War, sonar operators on American submarines heard a loud crackle like frying bacon that jammed their sonar, made by colonies of snapping shrimp, and clever captains hid their subs inside the noisiest shrimp beds so the racket covered the sound of their own engines. The nearly blind shrimp shares its sandy burrow with a sharp-eyed goby that stands guard at the entrance, and the shrimp keeps one long antenna touching the goby, so when the fish flicks its tail and darts inside, the shrimp feels it and dives too.

The jet is so fast that the pressure behind it plunges and a vapor-filled cavitation bubble forms, and the real weapon is that bubble collapsing, which unleashes a shockwave that stuns or kills. If a pistol shrimp loses its snapping claw, the claws swap roles over the next molts: its small claw grows into the new weapon, while the stump regrows as a small claw.

In that instant the collapsing bubble also gives off a brief glimmer of light, too weak for our eyes, which researchers playfully named shrimpoluminescence, after sonoluminescence, the light from collapsing bubbles. The heat inside the bubble reaches at least 5,000 kelvin or so, nearly matching the Sun's surface at about 5,772 kelvin.

portuguese-man-o-war.context_blurb:
The Portuguese man o' war floats on warm seas, a glassy blue float trailing long stinging tentacles. It looks like a jellyfish but is something stranger, and its sting can paralyze fish and badly hurt a swimmer, though it is rarely deadly to people. Its scientific name is Physalia physalis.

A Portuguese man o' war is not a single animal but a colony of many bodies, called zooids, all identical clones fused so tightly that they work as one, which is why biologists call it they rather than it. It cannot swim: its blue-purple gas float rises up to about six inches above the water and the wind blows it like a sail, carrying it for miles.

The float measures barely a foot, but the stinging tentacles hanging below average about 10 meters and can stretch to 30 meters, roughly 100 feet, outstretching even a blue whale. Each kind of zooid has a single job, forming the float, stinging, digesting or reproducing, and they depend on one another so completely that any single zooid on its own would die.

The man o' war makes the gas for its float in special cells instead of gulping air, and that gas can be as much as 13 percent carbon monoxide, the toxic gas in car exhaust. The blue dragon, a grape-sized sea slug that floats upside down, eats men o' war unharmed and stores their most powerful stingers, unfired, in the tips of its feathery arms to fire as its own weapon, a trick called kleptocnidy.

The sails are built in two mirror-image versions, left-handed and right-handed, so men o' war tack off at about 45 degrees to either side of the wind, and a whole fleet never strands on the same beach at once. Part of the population always survives.

sea-cucumber.context_blurb:
The sea cucumber is a soft, sausage-shaped animal that lives on the seafloor in every ocean, from shallow reefs to the deep abyss. It looks like a fat, lazy worm, but it is an echinoderm, a relative of sea stars and sea urchins, and its quiet life hides some of the strangest tricks in the sea.

Inside that wormy body it keeps its family's hidden five-fold, wheel-like symmetry, the same plan a sea star wears on the outside, most easily seen in the ring of five tentacles around its mouth. Nicknamed the vacuum cleaner of the seafloor, it crawls along swallowing mud and sand, digests the tiny scraps of dead matter inside, and passes the cleaned sand out the other end. A single sea cucumber can clean more than 45 kilograms of seafloor sediment in a year.

When a crab or other predator grabs it, a sea cucumber can shoot its own guts out of its rear end, a trick called evisceration, startling the attacker or tangling it in sticky threads while the cucumber creeps away; over the following weeks it regrows the lost organs.

That rear end does more than you might guess. Lacking gills, a sea cucumber breathes through its anus, drawing seawater in through the rear opening into a branching respiratory tree just inside, pulling out the oxygen and pushing the water back out. No sea star or urchin breathes this way. A slender reef fish, the pearlfish, lives inside a living sea cucumber, and when it returns from its night hunt it finds the way by following the current the cucumber pushes out as it breathes, then waits for the opening to widen and slips in tail-first. Not every tenant is polite: some pearlfish nibble their host's reproductive organs from within.

A sea cucumber's body wall is made of catch collagen, a tissue its nerves can turn floppy or rigid in moments: one protein, tensilin, stiffens it, and another, softenin, relaxes it. So a sea cucumber can pour itself like liquid into a crack in the rock, then lock its body rigid so no hungry fish can pull it out.

sea-star.context_blurb:
Sea stars, often called starfish, live on the seabed in every ocean on Earth, from tide pools to the deep sea, in about 1,900 species. With no head, no brain and no blood, a sea star still walks, hunts, senses light and heals itself using some of the strangest equipment in the animal kingdom.

A sea star is not a fish at all but an echinoderm, a member of the spiny-skinned group that also includes sea urchins and sea cucumbers. It has no brain: instead of one command center it has a ring of nerves around its mouth and a nerve cord running down each arm, so every arm can act partly on its own.

It walks on hundreds of tiny suckered tube feet worked by its water vascular system, a plumbing loop that pumps seawater in and out of each foot to swell and shrink it like a little hydraulic piston, with no blood involved. All that water enters through a single intake on the sea star's top side, the madreporite, a small, pale, off-center button that works as a sieve, instead of soaking in through the skin.

Those tube feet are strong enough to open a clam. The sea star humps over its prey, grips both halves of the shell and pulls for hours. Once the shell gapes even a sliver, it shoves its own stomach out of its mouth, slides it into the shell and digests the clam outside its body, then slurps the soupy meal back in.

A sea star senses light with an eyespot at the end of every arm, so a five-armed star has five simple eyes, each made of about 80 to 200 tiny light-sensing units that tell light from dark rather than forming sharp images. That is how it creeps away from bright light toward shade.

A sea star can regrow a lost arm, and in a few bright tropical Linckia species a single arm broken off with no part of the central disc can rebuild a mouth and disc and grow into a whole new star. The lopsided stage, one long arm with four little ones sprouting, is nicknamed a comet because it looks like a shooting star, and the arm lives on stored nutrients until it can feed again.

seahorse.context_blurb:
The seahorse is a small fish of warm, shallow seas around the world, where it drifts upright among seagrass and coral. With a horse-shaped head, a curled tail and bony rings around its body, it hardly looks like a fish at all, and its way of life, from hunting to giving birth, is just as strange.

For all its odd looks, the seahorse is a true fish: it breathes with gills, steers with fins, floats with a swim bladder and has a bony skull, and instead of scales its skin is stretched over fused bony plates that form a suit of armor.

Its tail is prehensile: it coils around a blade of seagrass or a branch of coral and grips like a monkey's, anchoring the seahorse so storms and currents cannot sweep it away. Only its relatives the pipefish and pipehorses share that grip. With no teeth and no stomach, a seahorse hunts tiny copepods with its tube-shaped snout like an eyedropper, snapping its head up and sucking each victim in whole in a burst of suction, in just 2 to 4 thousandths of a second.

The dwarf seahorse of Florida, only about 2 centimeters long, is the slowest-moving fish ever recorded: its little back fin flutters 30 to 70 times a second, yet it travels only about 1.5 meters in an hour.

In seahorses the father gets pregnant: during courtship the female passes her eggs through a tube into a brood pouch on the male's belly, he fertilizes them inside and carries them, and when the time comes he pumps and squeezes the pouch to push out the fully formed young, from about 5 to 2,000 at once.

The pouch does more than shelter the eggs: its wall fills with tiny blood vessels like a placenta, feeding the embryos oxygen and rich nutrients such as fats and calcium. It also slowly shifts the saltiness of the pouch fluid to match the sea before the babies are born, work biologists used to credit only to mammal mothers.

whale-shark.context_blurb: The whale shark is the biggest fish in the ocean, a slow, spotted shark that can grow more than 40 feet long. It lives in warm seas around the world and is a specialist on some of the smallest food in the sea. Whale sharks gather in a few predictable places each year, which is where researchers and tourists go to see them. The entire body of this huge animal is built around that one specialized meal, and biologists are still learning where they go when they leave the known gathering sites.

beaver.context_blurb:
The beaver, a hefty rodent with a paddle of a tail, lives along the streams and rivers of North America and Eurasia. Few animals reshape their world as it does: it fells trees, dams streams into ponds and turns ponds into wet meadows. Its waterproof fur, scaly tail and strange teeth all serve that life between land and water.

Its front teeth are bright orange, because the outer enamel is packed with iron instead of the magnesium found in most animal teeth, which makes them harder and more resistant to acid and decay. Those teeth keep growing for life: new tooth forms at the root as fast as the tip wears away, so even an old beaver has a working set and must gnaw constantly. Its home, a dome of mud and sticks called a lodge, has its entrance underwater, so a beaver family gets in by diving while a fox or wolf on the bank cannot follow. The dam floods a safe moat all around the home.

The iron-hard enamel coats only the front face of each incisor, while the softer dentin behind it wears away faster, so every bite grinds the tooth back into a sharp chisel edge and the teeth sharpen themselves. Underwater a beaver keeps its eyes open behind a see-through third eyelid that slides across each eye like built-in swim goggles. Its broad, flat, scaly tail is a rudder for steering, and when danger appears, the beaver slaps it hard on the water with a loud crack that warns the whole colony.

In autumn it stocks an underwater larder of branches for winter, and before diving with a branch in its teeth it seals itself shut: valve-like muscles close its nostrils and ears, and its lips seal behind the jutting front teeth, so it can carry wood underwater for up to about 15 minutes without swallowing water.

Beavers also build big: in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, generations of beaver families raised a dam about 800 meters long, as long as eight football fields, and in 2007 the researcher Jean Thie spotted it in satellite images. It is the largest beaver dam known, and today conservationists use beavers as ecosystem engineers to restore damaged land.

camel.context_blurb:
The camel is a long-legged desert mammal of North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. People have ridden and loaded camels for thousands of years, but the animal's own biology is the real marvel. Nearly every part of its body solves a single problem: staying alive where water is scarce and the heat is fierce.

The one-humped dromedary is the hot-desert specialist, while the Bactrian camel, with two humps and a thick coat, belongs to the cold Gobi of Central Asia, where a single year swings from roughly -20°F to 120°F. On loose sand, each broad, two-toed foot spreads and flattens under the camel's weight and then pulls in as it lifts, working like a snowshoe that keeps it from sinking where a horse's narrow hooves would bog down.

Contrary to popular belief, the hump holds no water: it is a concentrated store of fat that the camel burns when food runs short, which is why a hungry camel's hump shrinks and flops to one side. Packing the fat into one hump, rather than under all its skin, also helps the rest of the body shed heat. A camel can even chew up a spiny cactus, because cone-shaped bumps of keratin lining its mouth turn the needles so they slide down its throat point-first. A vet described those bumps as feeling almost like plastic.

A badly dehydrated camel can drink well over 100 liters in about ten minutes, up to 145 liters at one go by the San Diego Zoo's count, replacing about a third of its body weight almost at once. Instead of sweating away precious water, a camel lets its body temperature swing, cooling to about 34 to 35°C overnight and climbing to 41 or 42°C by day, storing the heat in its body rather than spending water to shed it.

cheetah.context_blurb:
On the dry grasslands of Africa, with a last small population in Iran, lives a slender spotted cat built for one thing: the sprint. The cheetah lacks the bulk other big cats use to wrestle prey or climb, and nearly every part of it, inside and out, serves the chase.

No land animal is faster than the cheetah: from a standstill it can top 110 kilometers an hour, about 70 miles an hour, barely three seconds later, out-accelerating many sports cars. Small black spots cover its golden coat, and the pattern they make, together with the rings on its tail, is unique to each cheetah, like a human fingerprint, so researchers can tell individuals apart from photographs.

A cheetah cannot roar. It purrs, growls, hisses and stutters. A mother calling her cubs out of the tall grass uses a high, birdlike chirp. Other cats keep sharp claws tucked away until they strike, but a cheetah's claws are blunt and only partly retractable, poking out like a dog's so they dig into the dirt with every stride, the way spikes grip on a sprinter's shoes. Ridged paw pads add grip like tire tread.

The black 'tear marks' running from the inside of each eye down to the mouth soak up the sun's glare off its cheeks, like an athlete's eye-black, so it can keep prey in sharp focus on the bright plains. Its unusually flexible spine coils and springs open with every bound, flinging its hind feet out ahead of its front ones. At full gallop it is airborne twice per stride, once stretched out and once bunched up. When a gazelle jinks sideways, the cheetah swings its long tail as a counterweight to shift its balance, with the flattened, ringed tip working as a rudder, so it can take hairpin turns that would send other animals tumbling.

All that speed has a price. A sprint devours oxygen, so the cheetah gulps air through enlarged nostrils that open into roomy, air-filled sinuses, its breathing leaping from about 60 breaths a minute to around 150, fed by an oversized heart and lungs. Even so, top speed lasts only seconds. Its muscles burn fuel faster than oxygen arrives, lactic acid floods them, and the cat runs out of energy, which is why it must catch its prey within about 30 seconds or give up.

When five wild Botswana cheetahs wore GPS-and-motion collars, they did hit 93 kilometers an hour, but most hunts were run at a moderate pace and won by footwork: a firm grip, sharp maneuvering, and the muscle power to brake hard and turn. During the ice age, North America was home to a lean, spotted sprinter called Miracinonyx, long counted as an 'American cheetah.' Genetic and skeletal studies showed it was really a close relative of the cougar that evolved the same fast-chasing body independently, a textbook case of convergent evolution. In 1985 Stephen O'Brien's team grafted skin between fourteen unrelated cheetahs. A graft between unrelated lions is rejected as foreign, yet all fourteen healed in, as if they had passed between identical twins. A severe population bottleneck in the species' recent past left cheetahs so nearly identical at the genes the immune system uses to tell self from stranger that one cat's skin reads to another as its own. Wild-born cheetahs are just as uniform, so zoo breeding is not the cause.

echidna.context_blurb:
The echidna is a spiny, short-legged mammal of Australia and New Guinea that shuffles through the bush digging for ants and termites. It looks a little like a hedgehog, but it belongs to one of the oldest and strangest branches of the mammal family, and its snout carries a sense that almost no other land animal has.

Nearly every mammal gives birth to live young, but five living species, the monotremes, lay eggs instead. The platypus is one of them, and the other four are echidnas, the only other egg-laying mammals on Earth.

Its spines look like a porcupine's quills, but each one is a stiff, overgrown hair made of keratin, the same protein as your hair and fingernails. They grow up to about 12.7 centimeters long. The common short-beaked echidna lives across Australia, while three larger long-beaked echidnas survive only on the island of New Guinea, to Australia's north. A mother echidna produces just one leathery, grape-sized egg and carries it in a pouch-like fold of skin on her underside. After roughly ten days a tiny, pink, jellybean-shaped baby hatches out, and a baby echidna is called a puggle.

The echidna has no teeth. It tears open an ant or termite nest with its strong front claws. Then it flicks out a long, sticky tongue, up to about 18 centimeters long and coated with gluey mucus, to snatch up the insects as they pour out. It is far too slow to run from a dingo. Caught on soft ground, it digs straight down where it stands until only a shield of sharp spines is left showing.

Its snout hides a sixth sense. Like a shark or a ray, an echidna can feel the faint electric signals given off by the muscles of living prey. About 400 electroreceptors in its snout let it home in on ants and termites hidden in their nests, out of sight and smell.

elephant.context_blurb:
Elephants are the largest animals on land. There are three living species, the African savanna, the African forest and the Asian elephant, and all of them live in close family groups led by an older female. Their trunks, ears, feet and even their genes hold surprises that scientists are still uncovering.

The African elephant is the biggest land animal alive, and the record is a bull shot in Angola in 1955 that stood about 13 feet at the shoulder and weighed an estimated 10 tonnes or more. Mounted and nicknamed Henry, it still stands in the Smithsonian. Keeping such a huge body cool under the sun is hard work. When fanning its ears is not enough, an elephant sprays water or wet sand over itself, or plasters sticky mud over its hide and behind its ears to cool down and block the sun.

The trunk is a muscular hydrostat, like your tongue or an octopus's arm: it holds no bone at all, only muscle, tens of thousands of muscle units, which is why the same limb can be brutally strong and delicately precise. The huge, thin ears are radiators. Large blood vessels run just under the skin, and as the elephant fans its ears, the blood flowing through them cools by 3 to 5 degrees Celsius before it returns to the body. In about 20 minutes an elephant can cool its whole blood supply this way. You can even tell the species apart by the tip of the trunk, because an African elephant's ends in two finger-like lips and an Asian elephant's in just one.

Tusks are not horns but overgrown incisor teeth that never stop growing, adding about 6 to 7 inches a year, and the longest pair on record measured more than 11 feet. The tip of the trunk is laced with hair-thin muscle bundles, so with no bone or joint anywhere, the same trunk that shoves over a tree can curl around one blade of grass and pick it up. Memory matters as much as strength. Each herd is led by its matriarch, the oldest female, whose memory of distant water can save the family in a drought. In Kenya's Amboseli during the severe drought of 2009, families with older matriarchs lost far fewer calves than those with younger leaders.

Elephants drink by pulling several liters of water up into the trunk and then pouring it into the mouth. One study clocked the water rushing up inside the trunk at up to 330 miles per hour. They also talk in voices we cannot hear. In 1984 Katy Payne was visiting the elephants at a zoo when she sensed a pulsing in the air but could hear nothing: the elephants were calling in infrasound, rumbles of about 14 to 35 hertz, too low for human ears, which carry for miles. Elephants respond strikingly to their dead. In Kenya, Namibia and Tanzania, scientists have seen herds gather quietly around the body of an elephant they knew, touch it with their trunks, and return to the bones for years. Researchers describe this as observed behavior, not proof of human-style grief.

Elephants can also listen through the ground: their rumbles travel through the earth as seismic waves, and Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell's buried-speaker experiments at the Mushara waterhole showed that elephants pick up those vibrations with their feet. An alarm call played underground made a herd bunch together and freeze. Big bodies have trillions of cells and many chances for cancer, yet elephants rarely get it. Vincent Lynch found one reason: a broken, long-dead copy of a gene called LIF6, which the elephant line switched back on, so this reawakened "zombie" gene now makes a cell with damaged DNA destroy itself before it can become a tumor. An elephant appears to walk on five toes. CT scans made by John Hutchinson's team revealed a hidden extra support buried in the fat of the heel: a giant sesamoid bone that acts as a false sixth toe, propping up the foot like a stiletto heel. Museum preparers cut it off for centuries without realizing what it was.

giraffe.context_blurb:
The giraffe is a long-legged, long-necked plant-eater of the African savannas and woodlands, and the tallest living animal. Almost everything about its body, from its tongue to its heart to the skin on its legs, is shaped by the problem of being so tall.

Browsing at the crowns of acacia trees, where no other plant-eater can reach, the giraffe lifts its head as high as 5.5 meters, about 18 feet, and a big male is the tallest animal on Earth. A mother gives birth standing up, so her calf drops nearly 2 meters to the ground. The newborn is already about 1.8 meters tall, as tall as a grown man, and it can stand within about half an hour and run within an hour.

The giraffe's neck is about 2 meters long, yet it holds the same number of bones as yours, seven, and each of them is simply enormous, up to about 25 centimeters long. To pull down leaves, a giraffe snakes out its tongue, 45 to 50 centimeters long, and curls it around a twig like a hand to strip the leaves into its mouth.

The tongue is dark blue-black, and scientists think the dark pigment works as sunscreen, shielding it from sunburn as it hangs out in the blazing sun all day. Acacia branches bristle with thorns, but the giraffe's tongue is armored with tough bumps and coated in thick, sticky saliva, so it strips the leaves without getting hurt. Male giraffes settle rivalries by necking: they whip their necks around like sledgehammers and slam their heads into each other, with blows estimated at more than a ton of force.

Their duels are oddly honorable. Each giraffe swings as a lefty or a righty, and rivals respect each other's side. Researchers found that a giraffe will not strike a rival who has lost his balance. People assume such a tall animal needs a giant heart, but a 2016 study found the giraffe's heart is an ordinary 0.5 percent of its body mass. Its secret is the left chamber, walled with dense muscle 2 to 3.5 centimeters thick that generates the high pressure needed to push blood up the neck, and because that thick wall leaves only a small cavity, the heart makes up for it by beating fast.

Lowering its head to drink should send high-pressure blood surging into its brain. A sponge-like web of blood vessels where the neck meets the skull, the rete mirabile, soaks up the surge before it reaches the brain. When it swings its head back up, blood should pool in its legs, but tight, inelastic skin around the lower legs squeezes the veins like a compression stocking, so the giraffe does not faint.

Even the purpose of the famous neck is debated. Since Darwin's day it has been explained as a way to reach leaves no rival can. In 2022 a 17-million-year-old giraffe relative from China, Discokeryx, revived a rival idea: it had a helmet-like disc of bone on its head and the most reinforced head-and-neck joints known in any animal, built for ferocious head-butting duels. That fossil supports the idea that the neck was shaped as a weapon in battles over mates, though both pressures may have worked together.

gray-wolf.context_blurb:
The gray wolf is the largest wild member of the dog family, a hunter of forests, tundra and mountains across the northern half of the world. Wolves live and hunt as a team, run down prey bigger than themselves, and, as Yellowstone National Park has shown, can reshape a whole landscape.

A wolf pack is a family: a mother and father, the breeding pair, with the young they have raised over the last few years. A family spread over a huge territory needs a long-range voice. On the open Arctic tundra, with no trees to muffle it, one wolf's howl carries about 10 miles; in forest, about 6.

Wolves howl to gather the pack before and after a hunt, to find each other when a storm scatters them, and to warn neighboring packs off their territory. They hunt by endurance rather than speed; a fit deer wins a short dash. Trotting at about 5 miles an hour for hours, a wolf tracking prey can cover more than 50 miles in a day, and one was seen chasing a deer for 12 miles.

Seven or eight wolves facing a hundred elk cannot just charge in. Instead the pack works to cut one animal away from the group, testing many, since most hunts of big hoofed prey fail; an elk that stands its ground is often left alone, while one that runs or seems weak becomes the target. For decades people pictured an 'alpha wolf' that fought its way to the top. L. David Mech, the biologist whose 1970 book spread that idea, corrected himself in 1999: the alpha picture came from captive strangers thrown together, and in a wild pack the wolves the others follow are just the parents. The whole pack helps raise the pups: babysitters guard the den, and when the hunters return, the pups lick at their mouths and the adults regurgitate meat they swallowed at the kill for pups too small for raw meat.

When gray wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995 after about 70 years away, elk stopped lingering in the exposed valleys along the streams, and the willow and aspen they had chewed down began to grow tall again. Taller willows brought beavers back to build dams, a chain scientists call a trophic cascade. Researchers caution that the effect, though real, is sometimes overstated, since drought, bears and human hunters also thinned the elk.

hippopotamus.context_blurb:
The hippopotamus is a barrel-shaped giant of three tons or more that wallows in African waters from the Nile to the Zambezi. Its name means 'river horse,' but it is no horse. It spends its days in the water and comes out at dusk to graze.

The hippopotamus eats nothing but grass, yet it kills an estimated 500 or more people in Africa each year, more than lions or sharks do. It does not hunt people; its danger lies in its temper and its sheer bulk.

A hippo is too dense to float, so it cannot really swim; to cross deep water it strides along the river floor, kicking off the bed in a slow-motion underwater gallop with its toes barely touching down.

Scientists once grouped the hippo with pigs because of its molars, but blood-protein and DNA evidence showed that its closest living relatives are the whales and dolphins. The two lines probably split from a shared, water-loving ancestor about 55 million years ago. When a hippo flings its mouth open almost flat, nearly 150 degrees from jaw to jaw, it is not yawning but warning a rival. The gape shows off its real weapons: tusk-shaped canine teeth that keep growing all its life, reaching about 50 centimeters, kept sharp by grinding against the lower incisors.

honey-badger.context_blurb:
The honey badger, Mellivora capensis, is a stocky, low-slung, thickly muscled carnivore of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, more like an oversized weasel than a true badger. It weighs only about 9 to 16 kilograms, yet it has a reputation as one of the toughest animals alive.

Black with a pale back and no bigger than a small dog, the honey badger is listed by Guinness as the most fearless animal on Earth, because instead of fleeing lions or leopards it stands its ground and drives them off. It is also one of the best diggers among animals. With long, pick-like front claws, it can dig a fresh burrow into sun-baked ground in about 10 minutes. Its hide is part of its armor: the skin on its neck is about 6 millimeters thick, a quarter of an inch, and so tough and rubbery that bee stings, porcupine quills and even machete blows barely hurt it.

In the Kalahari, Colleen and Keith Begg, who spent years following wild honey badgers, saw a puff adder strike a hunting badger in the face. The badger went into convulsions and lay motionless for roughly two hours, then woke up, got up and went back to finish eating the snake that had bitten it. Part of its resistance is in its genes. Cobra venom works by grabbing a receptor on muscle cells. In the honey badger, a charged amino acid has been swapped into the receptor's binding site, so the venom cannot attach. Pigs and hedgehogs evolved almost the same change on their own.

kangaroo.context_blurb:
Kangaroos are the big hopping marsupials of Australia, the continent's main native grazers. The largest, the red kangaroo, is the biggest marsupial alive and can stand taller than a man. Everything about a kangaroo, from its springy legs to its strong tail and its tiny newborns, is built for life on dry, open plains.

The kangaroo is easy to spot: tall pointed ears, short little front legs, huge powerful hind legs, a heavy tail held out straight for balance, and a pouch on the mother's belly where a newborn the size of a jellybean rides. A sprinting red kangaroo can reach about 70 km/h, clearing more than 8 meters in a single bound and leaping as high as 3 meters.

High-speed film shows that a kangaroo hops at almost the same rhythm whether it is going slowly or fast; to pick up speed, it takes longer leaps, so going faster costs it almost no extra energy. Hopping only works at speed, so when a kangaroo moves slowly it walks on five legs, planting its tail on the ground, leaning on it and swinging both hind feet forward, and treadmill tests showed that the tail gives as much forward push as all four limbs together. Scientists call this pentapedal walking.

The tail can do this because it holds over 20 vertebrae linked by flexible joints, while each leg has only a few long bones, so it bends and pushes like a segmented limb, propping the kangaroo up while it grazes or fights. A red kangaroo's pregnancy lasts only about 33 days. Her blind, hairless joey, weighing under 2 grams, then crawls unaided up through her fur to the pouch in about three minutes, pulling itself along with its front legs.

In 1973, measuring the oxygen used by red kangaroos hopping on treadmills, Terry Dawson and Richard Taylor found that past a certain speed a kangaroo burns less oxygen the faster it hops, the opposite of every other running animal tested. Its huge leg tendons store the energy of each landing like springs and snap back to launch the next hop, doing more of the work as speed rises. A mother can also keep a spare embryo of 70 to 100 cells paused inside her for as long as 11 months while a joey nurses in the pouch, because the suckling of that pouch joey sends a hormonal signal that keeps the embryo on hold. If the joey dies, the signal stops and the embryo starts growing at once. Biologists call this embryonic diapause.

koala.context_blurb:
The koala is a small, grey, fuzzy-eared animal of the eucalyptus forests of eastern Australia that spends its life in the treetops. It lives on one of the toughest diets any mammal has chosen, and nearly everything about it, from its gut to its paws to its sleepy days, is shaped by that diet.

People call it the koala bear, but it is no bear: it is a marsupial that carries its baby in a pouch like a kangaroo, and its closest living relative is the wombat. Its diet is almost entirely eucalyptus leaves, from gum trees, which carry bitter oils and poisonous compounds that would harm most animals, but its specialized stomach and liver handle them safely.

Eucalyptus gives back so little energy that a koala passes as many as 20 hours a day sleeping and resting, to stretch the little fuel it gets. It rarely drinks, since the leaves supply almost all its water, and its name comes from the language of the Dharug people, in which koala is thought to mean no water.

At about six months old, a joey weaning onto gum leaves first eats pap, a soft, oily dropping from its mother that is packed with the live gut microbes it needs to digest eucalyptus.

A koala's fingertips carry loops and whorls so like a human's that even under a microscope they are hard to tell apart, and koalas evolved them for gripping branches and leaves, while their cousins the wombat and kangaroo have none. The same trait arose separately in koalas and in people, a case of convergent evolution.

naked-mole-rat.context_blurb:
Pink, wrinkled, almost hairless and almost blind, the naked mole-rat, a rodent about as big as a sausage, spends its whole life in tunnels beneath the dry plains of East Africa. It breaks so many mammal rules, in its family life, its pain, its breathing and its aging, that medical researchers study it closely.

It is the most extreme social mammal known: a colony works like an ant or termite nest, with a single breeding queen in charge, while the rest are sterile workers who dig, gather food and raise her pups. Every member must share the family smell, since a stranger is attacked on sight, so each mole-rat rolls and wallows in the colony's shared toilet chamber to pick up the colony scent. It digs with its front teeth, which sit outside its lips, and the lips seal shut behind the teeth so it can tunnel without swallowing dirt. Each front tooth can even move on its own, like chopsticks.

The queen wins her throne by fighting her sisters, and once she starts breeding, her lower-back vertebrae stretch and lengthen, so her body grows longer and can carry as many as 30 pups in a litter. Acid and chili-pepper juice that make other mammals flinch do nothing to it, because its pain nerves lack Substance P, a chemical that carries certain pain signals. Mice of its size are worn out by about two, but a naked mole-rat can live past 30 years, longer than any other rodent. It can barely make its own body heat, so when the burrow turns chilly the colony piles together into a tight, warm huddle and climbs to shallow, sun-warmed tunnels.

To chisel through soil packed as hard as concrete, it puts about a quarter of all its muscle into the muscles that snap its jaws shut. With no oxygen at all it can last about 18 minutes and then recover unharmed, and it survives at least five hours in air so poor in oxygen that a human would die within minutes. It is almost the only mammal whose body temperature drifts with its surroundings instead of staying steady, so in this one way it behaves more like a lizard than a rodent. A colony may dig up to 2.5 miles of tunnels, laid out like a house with separate rooms: a nursery, a food store and a designated toilet chamber.

When scientists used a harmless, modified virus to deliver the missing Substance P gene into just one hind foot, that foot alone could suddenly feel the chili-pepper burn, while the rest of the body still could not. Yet even with the gene restored, acid still caused it no pain at all, and no other animal is known to ignore acid so completely; its nerves are wired differently at a deeper level. Researchers who recorded thousands of its soft greeting chirps found that each colony speaks its own dialect, learned rather than inherited, and kept in line by the queen: pups raised in another colony take on its accent, and when a queen dies the accent falls apart until a new queen rules.

When oxygen runs out, it switches its cells from glucose to fructose, a fruit sugar, and burns it the way a plant does, keeping its brain alive. To get fructose into its brain it uses fructose pumps that, in every other mammal, exist only in the gut: it borrowed the tool from its intestines and installed it in the brain. For at least 18 years its yearly risk of dying does not rise with age, so it barely seems to grow old, a trait called negligible senescence. Its cells pump out a giant sugar molecule, hyaluronan, over five times larger than ours, which tells cells to stop crowding together and so blocks tumors from forming. Biologists long claimed it was a mammal immune to cancer, but in 2016 two old males living in zoos turned out to have tumors, a 22-year-old at Chicago's Brookfield Zoo and a 20-year-old at the National Zoo in Washington. Cancer is still astonishingly rare in these rodents, but never has become almost never.

pangolin.context_blurb:
Pangolins are shy, insect-eating mammals that live in Africa and across southern Asia. They are sometimes called scaly anteaters, but they belong to an order of mammals all their own. They have no teeth, eat almost nothing but ants and termites, and wear a coat unlike any other mammal's.

The pangolin is the only mammal covered in true scales, hard overlapping plates made of keratin, the stuff of your fingernails, which give it the look of a pine cone on legs. When a leopard closes in, a pangolin neither runs nor fights: it curls into a tight armored ball, wrapping its scaly back and tail around its soft belly and face, which is why its Malay name, penggulung, means the one who rolls up.

Its rolled-up armor is so tough that even a whole pride of lions, pawing and biting, cannot get through, and in the end the frustrated lions give up and stroll off, leaving the pangolin unharmed. Its three big, curved digging claws on each front paw are perfect for tearing into termite nests but useless for walking, so to spare them a pangolin often walks upright on its hind legs, holding its arms and tail up for balance.

With no teeth, it laps up insects with an extraordinarily long, sticky tongue that in a big pangolin can reach about 40 centimeters, sometimes longer than its own head and body. Before tearing open a nest of biting ants or termites, it uses strong muscles to seal its ears and nostrils closed, and it can then lap up as many as 20,000 insects in a day.

It cannot chew, so it swallows small stones that collect in a muscular stomach lined with keratin spines, where they churn and grind up the insects, just like a chicken's gizzard.
