marabou-stork.context_blurb:
The marabou stork is a huge, bald-headed scavenger of sub-Saharan Africa, often heavier than a small child. Its bare head, giant bill and dangling throat pouch have earned it a reputation as one of the ugliest birds alive, but each of those features does a job, and the marabou is a key member of Africa's clean-up crew.

Seen from behind, the marabou stork looks like a hunched mourner in a dark cloak, with black wings and back, spindly white legs and a few white wisps on its bald crown, which is why African guides call it the undertaker bird.

Its wings average about 2.6 meters across, wider than those of almost any other land bird, and rather than flapping it soars on thermals, rising columns of warm air that lift it higher without a single wingbeat, so it can travel huge distances without tiring, the way a vulture does. Like a vulture, it plunges its head deep into carcasses to get at the meat, and its bare pink head and neck stay far cleaner than feathers would, since feathers would soon be clotted with blood.

The long pink pouch hanging from its throat, up to about 46 centimeters, looks like a crop for storing food, but it is an air sac connected to the left nostril: the bird inflates it to croak in courtship and dominance displays, and it helps shed body heat.

oilbird.context_blurb:
The oilbird is a big, reddish-brown bird of northern South America and Trinidad that roosts in deep caves by the thousands. It is the only bird in the world that flies out at night to eat fruit, and it finds its way in the dark with a sense most people link with bats.

In pitch-black caves, the oilbird navigates by echolocation, firing fast clicks and listening for the echoes, like a bat, but its clicks are pitched low enough, about 2 kilohertz, that a person in the cave can hear them.

It eats nothing but oily palm and laurel fruits, and it takes each on the wing, hovering and twisting in midair to pluck the fruit off the branch, then swallowing it whole and dropping the seeds far across the forest. Its chicks gorge on oily fruit until they are up to a third heavier than their parents, and people once climbed into the caves and boiled the fat chicks down into oil for lamps and cooking, which is why its scientific name, Steatornis, means fat bird.

A single cave can hold 15,000 oilbirds all clicking at once, yet each bird finds its own echo, because neighbors click at slightly different pitches. The clicking switches on only when a cave grows too dark even for its sensitive eyes.

potoo.context_blurb:
Potoos are big-eyed, night-hunting birds of the tropical forests of the Americas, from Mexico south. After dark they sally from a perch to snatch flying insects, but by day they rely on one of the best disguises of any bird, and their haunting song has inspired folk tales.

By day the potoo perches bolt upright on a broken branch, points its bill at the sky and holds still for hours, so that it looks like nothing more than a dead, snapped-off stump of that same branch. Even its fluffy chicks can pass for clumps of fungus on the wood.

Its eyelids have two or three notched slits that stay open when its eyes are shut, so a potoo that seems asleep can still see light and movement and shift before a hawk can strike. The female builds no nest: she lays her single egg straight onto a bare dip in a branch or on top of a rotten stump, and a parent hides it by sitting over it like part of the wood.

After dark the common potoo sings a haunting phrase of as many as eight whistles that drop steadily in pitch and fade away into silence, like a distant human cry, which earned it names such as ghost bird and poor-me-one.

secretarybird.context_blurb:
The secretarybird is a tall bird of prey of the African savannas and grasslands south of the Sahara. It looks like an eagle's body set on a stork's legs, and although it flies well, it does nearly all its hunting on foot. Its fighting style is one of the strangest in the bird world, and it is now endangered as its grassland home shrinks.

The secretarybird (Sagittarius serpentarius) stands over four feet tall, about 1.3 meters, and instead of catching prey from the air like other raptors, it hunts on foot and kills snakes, even cobras, by stamping them to death.

Its killing kick is astonishingly quick: when Steve Portugal's team trained a captive secretarybird named Madeleine to attack a rubber snake on a force plate, each blow touched the target for only about 10 to 15 milliseconds, faster than a human blink. The strike is over before a snake can turn and bite back.

It is a tireless walker, striding up to about 30 kilometers (some 20 miles) a day through the grass at a steady 2.5 to 3 kilometers an hour, on the longest legs of any bird of prey.

Its name comes from its crest of more than 20 long black feathers sweeping back from the nape, which the French naturalist Buffon in 1780 said looked like the quill pens an old-time clerk would tuck behind his ear.

superb-bird-of-paradise.context_blurb:
The superb bird-of-paradise (Lophorina) is a small, jet-black bird of New Guinea's mountain forests. The male's courtship dance turns him into a shape that looks nothing like a bird at all. DNA work now splits the bird into at least two species, each with slightly different moves.

To court a female, the male superb bird-of-paradise snaps his black feather cape and his iridescent blue-green breast shield open into a perfect oval that looks like a bright smiley face floating in a void. As he bounces around her in tight loops, he keeps his electric-blue breast shield aimed squarely at the female, so she sees the whole floating face throughout the dance.

The cape is super-black, soaking up about 99.95 percent of the light that hits it head-on, while an ordinary black feather bounces back 3 to 5 percent, so the eye has nothing to judge the blue face against and the face seems to glow and float in empty space. It holds no special dark pigment; the darkness comes from structure, because the tiny barbules of each feather tilt upward into arrays with deep cavities, so light that enters bounces around inside and is trapped instead of reflecting back.

sword-billed-hummingbird.context_blurb:
The sword-billed hummingbird (Ensifera ensifera) lives in the foggy mountain forests of the Andes in Ecuador, Colombia and Peru. It weighs a mere 10 to 15 grams, yet it carries the most outrageous bill of any bird, and nearly everything about how it eats, rests and keeps clean is shaped around that bill.

It is the only bird whose bill outmeasures the rest of its body: the straight, sword-like bill runs 8 to 12 centimeters on a body of only about 13 to 14 centimeters, not counting the tail.

The bill is far too long to reach its own feathers, so instead of preening with its beak like other birds, it scratches its plumage clean with its feet. When it lands to rest, it tilts its heavy bill almost straight up at the sky, leaning its head back to balance the weight and ease the strain on its slim neck.

Dozens of hummingbird species compete for nectar in the Andes, but the sword-bill sidesteps the crowd by drinking from deep, tube-shaped flowers that no other bird can drain, such as the long trumpets of Passiflora mixta. Bird and flower are a matched pair.

toucan.context_blurb:
In the warm rainforests of Central and South America, flocks of toucans move through the canopy, each a black bird carrying a beak so big it looks like a cartoon. That bill is no clumsy ornament. Biologists have found that it is light, handy at mealtimes, and a tool for keeping the bird at the right temperature.

The toucan's brightly colored bill can be four times the size of its head and stretch almost the full length of the rest of the bird.

A toucan plucks fruit with the far end of its bill, well away from its mouth, so to eat it jerks its head back, flips the fruit into the air and catches it as it drops straight down its throat.

Such a beak should weigh the bird down, yet a toucan flies easily. The bill is built like a foam sandwich: a thin outer sheath of keratin, the stuff of fingernails, over an airy core of crisscrossing bony struts and closed, air-filled cells, so it weighs only a tiny fraction of the bird's body. It also works as a radiator the toucan can turn up or down. On hot days the bird sends more blood into its bill to shed heat, losing 30 to 60 percent of its body's heat there, and on cool nights it cuts the flow to hold its warmth in, a 'thermal window' that rivals an elephant's ears.

vulture.context_blurb: Vultures are a group of large scavenging birds that live on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They clean up carcasses that would otherwise rot and spread disease, and the ecosystem job they do is far bigger than most people realize until it stops. Vultures are extremely well equipped for a diet of dead flesh, with chemistry and anatomy tuned to a job no other large bird will take. Several vulture populations around the world have collapsed in the last few decades, and the knock-on effects have been severe.

albatross.context_blurb:
No bird owns the open sea like the wandering albatross, a giant white glider of the stormy Southern Ocean that rings Antarctica. It comes ashore only to breed on remote, windswept islands and spends the rest of its long life on the wing, crossing whole oceans while barely moving a feather. Its secrets lie in its wings, its senses and its unhurried family life.

Tip to tip, its wings span 11 or 12 feet, roughly 3.5 meters, the widest of any bird alive; the record holder measured 3.7 meters. Holding such wings out would exhaust ordinary flight muscles. The albatross does not have to, because a tendon in its shoulder locks each wing straight out like a latch, so the bird can glide for hours with no muscle effort at all.

Its fuel is the wind itself: friction slows the air just above the waves while the air a few dozen meters up races faster, so the albatross climbs into the fast upper air, swoops down into the slow air by the sea and climbs again, harvesting energy from the difference every time. Biologists call this dynamic soaring. With it, a foraging wandering albatross can cover about 950 km in a single day, averaging some 40 km an hour, and keep that pace for days while burning almost no energy. Its meals of squid and small fish come with mouthfuls of seawater, so a salt gland above each eye pulls out the extra salt and concentrates it into brine that drips from the bird's tube-shaped nostrils and down its beak. Those nostrils give albatrosses and their relatives the family nickname "tubenoses." Few birds live so long: a wandering albatross that reaches adulthood can survive 50 to 60 years in the wild, sometimes longer.

Satellite tags show how far all that gliding adds up: a GPS-tracked wandering albatross flew a full loop around Antarctica, about 11,600 km, in just 46 days without landing. Finding food in that emptiness is a puzzle, because squid and krill gather in patches far apart that no eye can spot from the air. When krill graze on tiny drifting plants, the plants give off a gas called dimethyl sulfide, the smell of the ocean, and the albatross catches that scent on the wind and zig-zags upwind toward it, tacking like a sailboat. When Gabrielle Nevitt's team GPS-tagged 19 wandering albatrosses in 2008, those upwind zig-zags led to over a third of daytime catches and nearly half at night, the first hard proof that these birds smell their way to dinner.

Family life runs just as slowly. A pair lays a single egg and incubates it for about 78 days, the longest of any bird, and then the fluffy chick sits on its grassy nest for around 278 days, nearly nine months, before its first flight. Because raising a chick takes so long, a pair breeds only every other year. Partners mate for life, yet between seasons they roam the ocean apart for months. When they meet again at the old nest, the two renew their bond with an elaborate greeting dance of sky-pointing, wing-spreading and loud clucking calls. A smaller Pacific cousin, the Laysan albatross, holds the age record: a female nicknamed Wisdom, banded on Midway Atoll in 1956, is the oldest wild bird known anywhere, more than seventy years old and still raising chicks. She has hatched an estimated thirty or more of them.

Even the albatross's fossil past held a surprise. Giant fossil seabirds from Antarctica with 21-foot wingspans were long filed as the biggest albatrosses that ever flew, since their legs and feet were near copies of an albatross's. Their jaws told the truth: they belonged to a separate lineage, the pelagornithids or "bony-toothed" birds, whose beaks bristled with spikes of bone that looked like teeth. Convergent evolution had shaped their legs alike. Real fossil albatrosses were modest; a 3-million-year-old skull from New Zealand belonged to a bird a little smaller than any albatross alive today.

arctic-tern.context_blurb:
The Arctic tern is a small, slender seabird of cold northern coasts. Each year it breeds in the far north, then flies all the way to Antarctica for the southern summer and back again, chasing the sun from one end of the planet to the other. For decades nobody knew the real length of that commute, until tiny tracking tags revealed it.

It is easy to recognize: a black cap pulled low over the head, white cheeks, a deeply forked tail like a swallow's, and a bill and feet of blood-red. No animal on Earth migrates farther, as a 2010 tracking study by Egevang and colleagues showed: every year the tern flies from its Arctic nesting grounds to Antarctica and back.

Living in summer at both ends of the world, the tern enjoys two summers a year and very likely sees more daylight than any other creature. It does not head straight south but follows a giant S-shaped path down the Atlantic, so its true yearly round trip averages about 70,900 km, roughly 44,000 miles. The birds in the study flew anywhere from 59,500 to 81,600 km in a year. Since a tern can live past 30, a lifetime of these trips adds up to about 2.4 million km, the same as flying to the Moon and back about three times.

That S-shaped path follows each ocean's prevailing winds: the tern swings counterclockwise around the great South Atlantic gyre, and on its way north it circles clockwise around the North Atlantic gyre, instead of fighting a straight crossing. To track a bird weighing roughly 100 grams without burdening it, the researchers fitted 11 terns from Greenland and Iceland with geolocators weighing just 1.4 grams each, attached to their leg bands.

bowerbird.context_blurb:
Bowerbirds are forest birds of Australia and New Guinea, and the males build one of the most elaborate courtship displays in the animal kingdom. On the forest floor each male raises a structure of twigs, a bower, and decorates it with carefully chosen objects to impress visiting females. Their arrangements show real attention to color, pattern and even perspective.

The satin bowerbird's bower, a pair of tidy twig walls side by side, is not a nest at all: the male builds it purely as a stage on which to court females, and he comes back to the same spot year after year. The glossy blue-black male is obsessed with blue, decorating his stage with blue clothes pegs, drinking straws, bottle tops and parrot feathers, a color that matches his own plumage and violet-blue eyes, and he will steal blue objects from as far as 12 kilometers away. A female tours several rival bowers and judges each male's strutting display, and after mating she builds a plain, saucer-shaped nest of sticks as high as 30 to 35 meters up a tree and raises the chicks entirely alone.

He even paints, mashing berries and spit into a purple paint and smearing it on the inside of the walls with a wad of bark held in his beak as a brush. Young males stay drab olive-green like the females for seven years, practicing on scrappy trial bowers, before they finally molt into glossy blue-black adult plumage.

In northern Australia, the male great bowerbird arranges pebbles, shells and bones on the court beyond his avenue in order of size, smallest near the spot where the female stands and largest at the far end, a forced-perspective trick that makes the court look smaller and so makes him look bigger. The golden bowerbird of northeastern Australia builds the tallest bowers of all, twin towers of sticks that a young male inherits and rebuilds on the same spot, and the oldest known bowers are over forty years old and more than 2 meters tall.

cassowary.context_blurb:
The cassowary, a towering bird that cannot fly, lives in the rainforests of northern Australia and New Guinea. It can be dangerous when cornered, yet it is also one of the forest's great gardeners, because a long list of rainforest trees depend on it to spread their seeds.

Standing up to about 2 meters tall, the southern cassowary has glossy black feathers, bright blue skin on its head and neck, red at the back of the neck, and a tall grayish helmet called a casque. Zookeepers who handle ostriches, emus and rheas fear it above all of them, and it is widely called the most dangerous bird in the world; a 2019 death in Florida was the first human fatality blamed on a cassowary in 93 years.

Cornered, it leaps and kicks both feet forward, and each foot's inner toe ends in a dagger-like claw about 12 centimeters, or 5 inches, long that can slash open internal organs.

Chicks trot behind their father, and they hatch striped brown and cream down the back and thighs like little watermelons, camouflage they lose at about three to six months as they turn plain brown.

Deep in the foliage it gives booming calls near 32 hertz, among the lowest sounds known from any bird and right at the bottom of human hearing, probably because such a deep note carries far through thick rainforest where higher calls fade. Its casque may help to send or pick up these calls, though what the helmet is really for is still debated.

emperor-penguin.context_blurb:
The emperor penguin is the giant of the penguin world, a flightless seabird that lives on the sea ice of Antarctica and raises its chick through the darkest, coldest winter on Earth. Its survival depends on fathers who fast for months, on huddles of thousands of birds, and on a body built for long, deep dives.

Standing about 1.15 meters, roughly 4 feet, and weighing up to about 45 kilograms, around 100 pounds, the emperor penguin is the biggest penguin alive. Its stiff wings are flippers for swimming, and it lives only in Antarctica, where it breeds in the coldest, darkest months of winter, when no other bird raises young.

In the black of winter the mother lays a single egg, passes it to the father, and walks for weeks back to the sea to feed. An egg that touches the ice can freeze in seconds. So the father balances it on the tops of his feet and covers it with a warm fold of belly skin called the brood pouch. For the 65 to 75 days until it hatches, he eats nothing at all, living on his stored fat.

Across the whole breeding cycle a father can go about 120 days without food and lose about 20 kilograms, dropping from around 38 to about 18. To survive temperatures near minus 40 degrees Celsius in howling wind, more than 4,000 fathers press together in a huddle. Birds on the edge would freeze, so the huddle keeps shuffling forward in slow waves every 30 to 60 seconds, which rotates each bird in turn through the warm center. Deep inside, the temperature can climb to about 37.5 degrees, close to human body heat. If the chick hatches before the mother returns, the starving father can still nourish it briefly with "crop milk," a protein-rich, curd-like food made in his throat. He can produce it for only about 3 to 7 days.

No other bird dives as deep as an emperor, and the deepest reliably measured dive reached 564 meters. Of more than 137,000 dives recorded, the only 12 that went past 500 meters were all made by one single penguin. On long dives the bird rations its oxygen by throttling its heart. A resting emperor's heart beats about 73 times a minute, but in one 18-minute dive it fell to just 3 beats a minute, one beat every 15 seconds.

Long before emperors, giant penguins ruled the same coasts. In rocks about 34 million years old on Seymour Island, off Antarctica, Carolina Acosta Hospitaleche studied the bones of Palaeeudyptes klekowskii, the "mega penguin," and in 2014 estimated that it stood up to 2 meters tall and weighed as much as 115 kilograms, nearly twice an emperor's weight.

hummingbird.context_blurb:
Hummingbirds are tiny, nectar-sipping birds found only in the Americas. About 360 species flash through the forests and gardens there, and every one of them lives at the extreme: the fastest wingbeats and the highest metabolism of any bird for its size, all built around a single skill, hovering at a flower.

The smallest of them all is the bee hummingbird of Cuba, which Cubans call the zunzuncito, the little buzzer: a male weighs about 1.6 grams, less than a penny, making it the smallest bird on Earth and the smallest warm-blooded animal of any kind. Some birds can hold still for a moment in a strong headwind, but no bird except the hummingbird can fly backward, reversing in midair with no wind at all.

The secret lies in the wingbeat: instead of pushing air down only on the downstroke, a hummingbird sweeps each wingtip through a figure-eight, like a swimmer's sculling hands, so it makes lift on the forward stroke and again on the way back. All this burns fuel at a furious pace. A hummingbird must feed at flowers every 10 to 15 minutes, and in a single day it eats about half its own body weight in sugar, so it would starve overnight if it simply slept. Its heart can beat over 1,200 times a minute, with rates near 1,260 recorded, and even at rest it breathes about 250 times a minute. The tiny bee hummingbird has tiny young, too. Her nest is a cup barely 2.5 centimeters wide, and in it she lays two eggs no bigger than a coffee bean apiece, the tiniest eggs laid by any bird.

Instead of sleeping normally, it slips into torpor, a nightly shutdown: its body cools, its heart, which raced past a thousand beats a minute by day, slows to a few dozen, and its energy use drops to about one twentieth. The ruby-throated hummingbird, a 3-gram bird that nests from the eastern United States up into Canada, winters in Central America, and twice a year it flies nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, up to 500 miles of sea, alone for 18 to 22 hours. To fuel the flight, it feeds for weeks beforehand until it has nearly doubled its body weight in fat.

For the backstroke to lift too, the wing must flip over between strokes, and the hummingbird does it at the shoulder, where the upper arm bone itself twists nearly 180 degrees. The male Anna's hummingbird puts on a courtship dive that, measured against his size, is the fastest of any backboned animal: he covers 385 of his own body lengths every second, while a diving peregrine falcon manages about 200. When he pulls out at the bottom, his body takes a jolt of nearly 10 g, ten times the pull of gravity, more than a fighter pilot can bear before blacking out.

Hummingbirds even burn sugar in their own way. The common ancestor of all living hummingbirds lost a muscle enzyme gene called FBP2 between about 48 and 30 million years ago, just when hovering and nectar feeding evolved. When Osipova and colleagues knocked the same gene out of bird cells, the cells burned sugar faster, built more mitochondria, their tiny power plants, and ran more efficiently. A loss, not a gain, helped unlock hovering.

Fossils add a twist. In 2004 Gerald Mayr studied a few small skeletons with long bills that had sat in a museum collection, and named the bird Eurotrochilus: a hummingbird already shaped for hovering and sipping nectar that lived some 30 million years ago in Europe, far from the Americas. Its name means the unexpected European hummingbird, and more fossils have since turned up in Germany, France and Poland.

kiwi.context_blurb:
The kiwi is a flightless, chicken-sized bird of New Zealand's forests and the country's national symbol. It comes out at night and snuffles through the leaf litter for food, and so much about it, from its feathers to its bones, is unlike other birds that it has been called an honorary mammal.

The kiwi's wings are so tiny they are hidden, and its body is covered in bristly, two-branched feathers that resemble a coat of rough brown fur. It is the only bird in the world with its nostrils at the very tip of its long beak, so it can sniff out worms and grubs underground as it probes the soil, snorting to blow the dirt out of them.

A female weighs about 1.7 kilograms, yet one produced an egg weighing 406 grams, close to one quarter of her weight and proportionally the largest egg of any bird, like a woman giving birth to a six-year-old child. The egg is about 65 percent yolk, while most birds' eggs hold only 35 to 40 percent, so the chick hatches fully feathered, opens its eyes and can feed itself within days, with almost no help from its parents. The kiwi also digs burrows like a badger and wears whiskers like a cat. Its body runs cool for a bird, about 38 C, a low, mammal-like temperature and the lowest of any bird, while most birds run at 39 to 42 C.

A flying bird anchors its wing muscles on a deep keel along its breastbone, but a kiwi has a flat breastbone, and its leg bones, instead of being hollow and full of air, are heavy and packed with solid marrow, like a mammal's. In 2014 ancient DNA showed that the kiwi's closest relative is not the giant moa it lived beside but Madagascar's extinct elephant bird, a 3-meter giant that lived 11,500 kilometers away across the ocean.

lyrebird.context_blurb:
The superb lyrebird is a big, brown, pheasant-sized songbird of the wet forests in Australia's southeast. It spends its life on the ground, scratching for food, and the male is one of the greatest mimics in nature, a star of countless wildlife films.

When a male courts, he flips his spectacular tail forward over his head into the shape of a lyre, a small ancient harp: two outer feathers curve in an S and frame twelve fine, silvery filaments. A kookaburra that hears its own laughing call coming from the bushes may answer back, fooled by a superb lyrebird that has copied its laugh so perfectly that the real bird thinks another kookaburra is calling. About 70 to 80 percent of a male's song is imitation, and he can copy more than 20 bird species well enough that the real birds answer.

Chook, a male lyrebird at Adelaide Zoo, lived for months beside the building site of the future panda house, and he wove the banging of hammers and the whine of power drills and saws into his song.

Viral clips show lyrebirds copying car alarms, chainsaws and camera shutters, but the researcher Hollis Taylor, after years of searching wild forests, says no known recording shows a wild lyrebird imitating man-made machine sounds: the famous clips come mainly from captive birds. Two of the three lyrebirds in David Attenborough's Life of Birds lived in a sanctuary or a zoo, and wild lyrebirds mostly copy forest sounds and other birds. The lyrebird's range comes from its voice box, the syrinx, the most complexly muscled of any songbird, whose two halves it controls separately, so a single bird can sing two separate melodies at the same time.

In the 1930s a farmer in the New England area of New South Wales kept a lyrebird that learned to copy his flute music. After the bird was set free and bred with wild lyrebirds, its descendants refined the melody and handed it down for generations, a documented case of a learned culture, though the exact origin story is still debated.

new-caledonian-crow.context_blurb:
The New Caledonian crow is a glossy black crow found only on the islands of New Caledonia in the southwest Pacific. It looks like any other crow, but it is one of the most skilled toolmakers in the animal world, and decades of experiments, many of them at Oxford, have pushed bird intelligence into territory once reserved for apes.

New Caledonia has no woodpeckers, so this crow has taken over their job of prying fat grubs out of dead wood, and since it has no drilling beak, it does the work with tools it makes itself and then wields, one of the only animals besides apes to make its own tools.

It snips a twig at a fork in a branch and trims the wood until a hook is left at the tip, the only animal besides humans known to manufacture hooked tools in the wild. It also cuts stepped strips from barbed pandanus leaves, and comparing designs across the island showed that the strips grew more refined over the generations, the new ones better than the old, a kind of cumulative culture found nowhere else outside the primates. Betty, a crow kept at Oxford, faced a food bucket at the bottom of a tube in 2002, and when her mate Abel flew off with the hooked wire, she took the straight wire left behind and bent it into a hook with her own beak.

She repeated the bending in nine later tests out of ten, and her feat was hailed as pure invention, but wild crows were later seen bending their tools the same way, so bending tools appears to be a natural crow move rather than a flash of genius. In a test of planning, wild crows got a short stick that could not reach a scrap of meat, while a longer stick sat locked in a box, and six of seven solved it on the first try: they used the short stick to fish out the long one, then used the long one on the meat. They also pass the test from Aesop's fable of the crow and the pitcher, dropping heavy, solid stones rather than floating or hollow ones to raise the water and reach a floating treat, showing an understanding of cause and effect about equal to that of a five-to-seven-year-old child.

ostrich.context_blurb:
The ostrich is the largest living bird, a flightless giant of the African savannas. A male can stand up to 9 feet tall and weigh around 300 pounds. It cannot fly a meter, but it can outrun nearly anything on the plains, and its eggs, eyes and feet all set records of their own.

The ostrich has big feathery wings, yet it can never fly, because its breastbone is flat, with no keel to anchor the powerful muscles that flight demands. It is the fastest running bird in the world, sprinting at around 43 miles per hour, about 70 kilometers per hour, in short bursts and cruising near 31 miles per hour over distance.

An ostrich egg is the largest of any living bird, about 1,500 grams and 6 inches long, as heavy as about two dozen chicken eggs. The shell is a mere 3.5 millimeters or so thick, yet its curved dome can bear about 220 kilograms pressing straight down, so a grown adult can stand on it without cracking it. Ostriches do not hide their heads in sand, whatever the old tale says; in danger an ostrich flattens itself to the ground, pressing its long neck and head down, so from a distance it looks like a low mound of earth.

The ostrich is the only bird with just two toes on each foot, a huge main toe and a smaller second toe that works as an outrigger for balance, a foot pared down for speed. No land animal has bigger eyes, almost 2 inches across, and each eyeball is bigger than its own brain.

Cornered by a lion or a hyena, an ostrich strikes forward with a foot armed with a knife-like claw, and the kick is said to be strong enough to kill a lion outright, a reputation that is often repeated but hard to verify.

owl.context_blurb:
Owls are mostly nocturnal birds of prey found on every continent except Antarctica, from the palm-sized elf owl to Blakiston's fish owl, with wings nearly six feet across. They hunt in near-total darkness with silent wings, huge eyes and astonishing ears, and each of those gifts rests on a special piece of anatomy.

With its round face and big forward-pointing eyes, the owl is the classic night raptor, dropping out of the darkness onto mice in the fields. An owl flies almost completely silently, so a mouse with excellent ears hears nothing until the talons close.

The secret lies in its feathers: a row of tiny comb-like serrations runs along the front edge of each wing feather, breaking up the turbulent air that would otherwise make a swooshing sound. A barn owl can place a sound up or down as well as left or right because its ear openings are offset: the left sits higher and points down, while the right sits lower and points up. Its flat, round face is a stiff dish of feathers that collects sound waves and funnels them to the ear openings, like a satellite dish. An owl's huge, tube-shaped eyes fill most of its skull and are locked in place by a ring of bone, so it cannot roll them and must turn its whole head to look around. It can turn its head some 270 degrees, three quarters of a full turn, though not the complete circle of the myth.

Silent wings bring a second advantage, as Krista Le Piane's study of 70 owl species showed: with almost no noise of its own, the owl's ears stay free to track the faint rustling of its prey. A barn owl can drop through a foot of snow onto a mouse it never saw, finding the exact spot by hearing alone. When scientists at Johns Hopkins injected dye into owls' arteries and scanned them as they turned their heads, they found blood pooling in reservoirs at the base of the skull, keeping the brain supplied during the twist. When an owl seizes prey, its outer toe swings back so that two talons point forward and two back, and a locking tendon ratchets the grip shut, holding it with almost no muscle effort.

A barn owl tells left from right by which ear a sound reaches first, by millionths of a second, but it tells up from down by comparing how loud the sound is in each ear: a sound from below is louder in the downward-pointing left ear. The owl's neck has 14 vertebrae, twice as many as ours, and the bony channels around its neck arteries are about ten times wider than the arteries themselves, giving the vessels room to twist.

Scientists still argue over what the velvety surface of owl feathers is for. Kroeger and Lilley's long-dominant view is that the velvet keeps air flowing smoothly across the wing. Christopher Clark, reviving an idea Graham proposed in 1934, notes that the velvet is densest exactly where feathers rub together, and he argues that it mainly muffles the noise of feathers scraping against each other. The debate is still open.

peregrine-falcon.context_blurb:
The peregrine falcon is a crow-sized bird of prey that nests on sea cliffs, tundra, desert canyons and city skyscrapers. It hunts other birds with a dive so fast that it holds the speed record for any animal. In the twentieth century a pesticide nearly wiped it out, and its comeback is one of the great recoveries in nature.

In its hunting dive, the peregrine falcon outpaces every other creature alive, plunging at more than 200 miles an hour, quicker than a cheetah or a racing car. It lives on every continent except Antarctica, which makes it the most widespread bird of prey in the world.

It hunts other birds, such as pigeons, ducks, gulls and songbirds, and makes its kill in mid-air, striking them out of the sky. In the last fifty years peregrines have moved into cities such as New York and Chicago, nesting on cathedrals, bridges and skyscraper ledges, drawn by the endless flocks of city pigeons, an easy food supply. A peregrine builds no nest at all: it scratches a shallow scrape into the gravel of a high ledge and lays its eggs right there.

In level flight a peregrine cruises at a modest 25 to 34 miles an hour, and barely 69 when chasing hard; it becomes the fastest animal alive only when it folds its wings and dives in a steep plunge called the stoop. After World War II, farmers sprayed the pesticide DDT, which built up in peregrines through the birds and mice they ate and thinned their eggshells until the eggs cracked under the parents, so by the 1960s not a single pair bred in the eastern United States.

Even in its fastest dive the falcon breathes easily, because a small cone of bone in each nostril spins the rushing air into a slowed spiral before it reaches the lungs; jet-engine designers have studied the shape. During the stoop, a see-through third eyelid sweeps across each eye, wiping it clear while the falcon keeps its target in focus. A trained falcon called Frightful, released from a small plane high in the sky in 1999 to dive after her falconer as he skydived, was clocked at 242 miles an hour, a record for any bird and more than three times her level chasing speed. Tom Cade of Cornell began a rescue in 1970, and his team reared young falcons from captive parents in towers, feeding them from hiding so that they would not grow tame, and by 1980 his released falcons were breeding in the wild. In 1999 the peregrine came off the United States endangered list. In a wind tunnel, a model of a diving falcon proved to be among the most streamlined shapes in nature, and at the spots on its back where the airflow would usually break away, small feathers pop up and keep the air flowing close, like the vortex generators on an aircraft wing.

In 2018 Mills, Hildenbrandt, Taylor and Hemelrijk ran physics simulations at Oxford showing that a stooping peregrine steers by proportional navigation, the homing rule used to guide heat-seeking missiles, turning harder the faster the line to its prey swings. Only at stoop speed can a falcon out-turn a dodging starling.

shoebill.context_blurb:
The shoebill is a huge, slate-grey wading bird of the papyrus swamps of central and eastern Africa, along the White Nile and in Sudan and South Sudan. Standing about five feet tall, it is one of the tallest wading birds in the world, famous for a golden-eyed stare, a bill like a giant wooden shoe and a sound unlike any song.

The shoebill is named for its enormous bill, about nine inches long and four inches wide, with the shape of a Dutch clog and a pointed hook on the end; its scientific name, Balaeniceps rex, means whale-head king. It fixes the water with a golden-eyed death stare, standing still for hours until a lungfish rises to breathe.

The moment a fish breaks the surface, the bird collapses onto it, hurling its whole five-foot body forward with its bill gaping and engulfing the fish along with water, mud and weeds in a couple of seconds. The hooked tip stabs slippery prey, and the razor-sharp edges of the bill let the shoebill decapitate a lungfish too big to gulp whole before swallowing it.

The shoebill has no true voice; instead it claps its huge upper and lower bill together in a loud, rapid, hollow clatter like machine-gun fire, males and females in different tones, to court mates and warn off rivals.

woodpecker.context_blurb: Woodpeckers are a group of birds found in forests on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They are specialized tree-poundingclimbers with chisel-like beaks, stiff tails, and feet built for gripping bark. Woodpeckers hammer into wood at speeds and forces that would knock out any other bird's brain, and the way they manage to not get hurt is one of the most carefully studied puzzles in avian biomechanics.

17-year-cicada.context_blurb:
In the eastern United States, the forest floor can lie quiet for seventeen years and then, in one summer, boil with insects. Periodical cicadas spend nearly their whole lives in the dark soil and surface by the billions at once, staking their survival on timing and sheer numbers.

The periodical cicada is unforgettable once seen: a glossy black body as long as your thumb, two bulging eyes as red as coals, and clear wings veined in bright orange. For about 99.5 percent of its life it is a pale nymph underground, feeding on the sap of tree roots for 13 or 17 years. Then a whole brood climbs out together in the same few days. Biologists call this survival trick, safety in overwhelming numbers, predator satiation.

The nymphs seem to count the years by sensing seasonal changes in the sap of the roots, then wait for one last cue: the soil about eight inches down warming to roughly 64°F. Out they come, and the males begin to sing. Each male snaps a stiff, ribbed membrane on either side of his body, the tymbal, so fast that the clicks blur together. His abdomen is hollow, and that empty chamber resonates like the body of a guitar, swelling the clicks into a roar of about 100 decibels, among the loudest calls of any insect. After all those years in the dark, an adult lives just four to six weeks above ground, long enough to sing, mate and lay eggs.

A cicada cannot sting, hide or outrun anything, so its defense is arithmetic. A single acre can hold more than 1.5 million of them. Birds and foxes gorge until they can eat no more, and still most of the brood survives to mate. Even the length of the wait may be a weapon, because 13 and 17 are prime numbers, divisible only by themselves and one. As the entomologists Monte Lloyd and Henry Dybas proposed in 1966, a predator whose numbers peak every two, three or four years will almost never peak in the same summer a prime-numbered brood appears, while a 12-year brood would meet all of those hunters at full strength. Stephen Jay Gould later made the idea famous, though it remains a leading hypothesis, not a proven fact.

army-ants.context_blurb:
Army ants live in the tropical forests of the Americas, Africa and Asia, and they never settle down. Instead of building a permanent nest, a whole colony marches through the forest in long columns, overwhelming prey far too big for any single ant. In Central and South American rainforests, Eciton burchellii sends out raids of hundreds of thousands of workers at once.

When the march halts for the night, the workers hook their feet together and become the nest themselves, a living shelter called a bivouac that walls in the queen and the young.

Remarkably, the workers that steer a raid are blind or nearly so, and they hold the swarm together by touch and by chemical scent trails, called pheromones, that they lay down with their own bodies. When a column meets a gap, such as a split between two leaves, ants hook together with the claws on their feet and span it with their bodies, a living bridge the raid pours straight across without slowing.

When Scott Powell and Nigel Franks set out planks full of holes of different sizes on a raiding trail, each worker picked a hole that matched its own body size and flattened into it, so ants carrying prey could run home at full speed over a road paved with their nestmates. Even a nest made only of ants has climate control: the colony opens and closes air passages through the cluster, holding its core near 28.5°C while the air outside heats and cools.

bombardier-beetle.context_blurb:
Barely half an inch long, the bombardier beetle is a ground beetle of fields and forests on every continent except Antarctica. It carries one of the most dramatic chemical weapons in the animal kingdom, blasted out of its hind end and aimed in almost any direction, and scientists still study the chemistry behind the blast.

Grab one and it fires back with a loud pop: a jet of scalding chemical spray, shot from its rear, that makes the attacker drop it at once. The jet comes out near 100°C, or 212°F, as hot as boiling water, enough to scald an attacker's mouth or feet.

The beetle stays safe from its own weapon by storing the two ingredients, hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone, in separate reservoirs and letting them meet only at the instant it fires. In a lab experiment, faint pops sounded from inside toads that had swallowed bombardier beetles, and 43 percent of the toads threw the beetle back up, after it had spent anywhere from 12 to 107 minutes inside; the slimy beetles scuttled away, and nearly all survived, one for at least 562 more days.

The ingredients meet in a reinforced chamber lined with the enzymes catalase and peroxidase, which make the reaction so fast and hot that it boils and blasts outward. High-speed photography showed that the spray is not a steady stream but a pulse jet of about 70 tiny explosions fired at roughly 500 a second, and the pulsing protects the beetle, since each blast escapes before the next builds up, so the chamber never overloads.

dragonfly.context_blurb:
Dragonflies are long-bodied, four-winged hunters that patrol ponds and streams on every continent except Antarctica. Nearly their whole lives are spent hunting, first underwater and then in the air, and every part of their bodies is built for catching other insects. They have ruled the air over fresh water for hundreds of millions of years.

The dragonfly is the acrobat of the pond: it can stop dead in midair and hover, then dart sideways, backward or straight up, tricks most insects cannot manage. Its head is almost all eye. The two glossy domes wrap so far around that a dragonfly sees nearly a full circle at once, everything except the patch straight behind its head.

It is also one of the deadliest hunters alive: high-speed films show that a dragonfly catches its prey on about 90 to 95 percent of its tries, close to 19 of every 20 attempts, a better record than any lion or shark. It cruises at around 30 miles per hour, yet it beats its wings only about 30 times a second, where a honeybee manages roughly 200. The secret is in the wiring, because in most insects the wings beat in unison, but each of a dragonfly's four wings is worked by its own set of muscles and moves independently, which lets it hover, fly straight backward and turn on a dime.

A dragonfly does not chase its prey the way a hawk or a dog does. It aims at the empty sky ahead, because it has already worked out where the prey will be and flies to meet it at that point. A winged adult lives just a few weeks, but by then the insect can be years old, because it spent nearly all that time underwater as a fierce hunting nymph. The nymph is a stocky brown creature that creeps along the pond floor and breathes through gills. It hunts with a hinged lower jaw called the mask: when a tadpole, mosquito larva or small fish comes near, the mask shoots out almost too fast to see, grabs the prey, and folds back under the head. When the nymph is ready to change, it climbs out of the water onto a reed, its skin splits down the back, and the winged adult pulls itself free, leaving an empty husk called an exuvia clinging to the reed.

About 300 million years ago, in the Carboniferous period, a giant cousin named Meganeura soared on wings roughly 75 centimeters wide, as broad as a hawk's. Textbooks explain its size by the air of the time, which held about 30 to 35 percent oxygen, roughly a third, against about a fifth today, so an insect breathing through tubes could power a giant body. Some living dragonflies are champions of distance. The small globe skimmer rides the monsoon winds over the Indian Ocean from India to East Africa and back, with no land below, and its round trip of about 11,000 miles, flown in relay by parents, children and grandchildren, is the longest migration of any insect. And its hunting brain is astonishingly simple. Just sixteen nerve cells, eight pairs running from the brain to the wing muscles, carry the direction of the prey, tracking a target all the way around the dragonfly with an error of only about one degree.

That tidy oxygen story has a problem. Edouard Harlé first proposed it in 1911, but the biggest insect ever known, Meganeuropsis, had wings nearly 71 centimeters across. Meganeuropsis lived later, in the Permian period, after oxygen levels had already fallen. Some scientists now suspect other reasons for the giants, such as a sky with no birds or pterosaurs yet to hunt them.

dung-beetle.context_blurb:
Dung beetles are stout, glossy beetles that live on droppings. They are found on every continent except Antarctica, and by burying dung they recycle nutrients across grasslands and farms. Many kinds roll their prize away as a ball, and scientists keep discovering how a beetle pushing a ball backward knows where it is going.

On the African savanna a fresh heap of droppings soon draws a dung beetle, which shapes some of the dung into a tidy sphere and rolls it off to bury in the ground, a store of food for itself and its young. In many species the mother shapes a special brood ball like a pear, lays one egg in the slim end and buries the ball deep. Then, unlike most insects, she stays down in the burrow, tending and guarding the ball while her young grow up, a kind of parental care that is rare among insects.

The ancient Egyptians watched this daily labor along the Nile and saw something cosmic in it. To them it was the sacred scarab, and they pictured the god Khepri rolling the sun across the sky each day, just as the beetle rolls its ball, so the scarab became a symbol of the rising sun and of rebirth.

A roller must flee in a straight line before rivals steal its prize. Before setting off, the beetle climbs on top of its ball and turns a full circle in a little dance, storing a snapshot of the sky in its brain to fix a straight bearing. By day it steers by the sun and by night by the moon. On moonless nights it still rolls straight, guided by the faint glowing band of the Milky Way, and Marie Dacke's team proved it in a planetarium, making the dung beetle the first animal known to navigate by the galaxy.

Some dung beetles are astonishingly strong. A male Onthophagus taurus can pull 1,141 times its own weight, making it the strongest insect for its size, comparable to a person hauling six double-decker buses. That strength did not evolve for moving dung but for fighting: horned males brace and shove head-to-head against rivals in the breeding tunnel, and the strongest wins the female.

firefly.context_blurb:
Fireflies, also called lightning bugs, light up warm summer nights on every continent except Antarctica. Their glow is a language, a chemical marvel and, for some fireflies, a deadly trap. Each species blinks its own code, and biologists study firefly light both for its evolutionary story and for its uses in medicine.

Despite both nicknames, a firefly is neither a fly nor a true bug: it is a beetle, one of about 2,000 species in the family Lampyridae.

A firefly's light is "cold light." An old light bulb wastes about 90 percent of its energy as heat, but nearly all of a firefly's energy leaves as light and only a tiny amount as heat. Each species has its own flash code of single, double or multiple pulses. A male patrols in the dark flashing his code, a female of his kind flashes back, and the two keep up this conversation of flash patterns until they find each other, sometimes for more than an hour.

The light is made in the firefly's lower belly, where a molecule called luciferin combines with oxygen and the energy molecule ATP, a reaction sped along by an enzyme called luciferase. On certain June nights, crowds gather in the Great Smoky Mountains to watch Photinus carolinus, the one North American firefly whose males blink together in perfect unison: bursts of 5 to 8 flashes, then about eight seconds of shared darkness. Whole hillsides seem to switch on and off at once.

Some fireflies use light as bait. A predatory Photuris female, nicknamed the femme fatale, copies the answering flash of a Photinus female. When the fooled Photinus male lands beside her, she seizes him and devours him. She gains more than a meal: Photinus males carry defensive steroids called lucibufagins that Photuris cannot make, and eating them gives her toxic chemicals that protect her from birds and spiders.

hercules-beetle.context_blurb:
The Hercules beetle is a giant rhinoceros beetle of the tropical forests from Central America to South America, reaching almost seven inches and ranking among the biggest beetles in the world. Much of that length is horn, and only the males carry it.

A male has two horns that close like a giant pincer. The smaller one juts up from his head, and the much bigger one grows from his back, arching forward above the wing covers. Two males wrestle on a branch over a female. Each tries to catch the other between his horns, then uses the long horn as a lever to pry his rival loose and hurl him off the branch.

The hard wing covers change color with the weather: olive-green or yellow when the air is dry, darkening toward black as the humidity rises.

The adult is only the short last chapter of its life. Before that, it lives for as long as two years as a plump white grub curled in a C, chewing through rotting logs. The grub can reach about 11 centimeters and more than 100 grams, heavier than the horned adult it becomes. The adult then lives only three to six months, sipping sap and fruit.

honeybee.context_blurb:
Honeybees live in colonies of tens of thousands, with a single queen, a few hundred males and a vast crowd of female workers, in a hollow tree or a hive box. Kept by people for thousands of years and vital for pollinating crops, they are among the most studied insects on Earth, above all for the dance they use to share directions.

Nearly all the bees in a hive are workers, females unable to produce eggs, and they do almost every job: gathering nectar and pollen, building wax comb, feeding the larvae and guarding the entrance.

A forager who finds rich flowers flies home. There she dances on the comb in the dark, tracing a figure eight again and again, a straight run with her body shaking and then a turn back to where she began, while the others press close to follow her: this is the waggle dance. Meanwhile the queen does one job at a staggering pace, laying about 2,000 eggs a day, more than her own body weight, each egg only half as big as a rice grain.

Karl von Frisch, an Austrian biologist, worked out the code in the 1940s. The angle of the straight run tells the other bees which way to fly, judged by the sun's position: a run pointing straight up means fly toward the sun, and a run 45 degrees to the left means fly 45 degrees left of it. The length of the waggle tells them how far away the flowers are, a short waggle for nearby food and a long one for a longer flight. Every larva starts out the same, yet one becomes a queen, because the workers feed the chosen larva royal jelly all through her growth, while worker larvae are cut off after three days. Workers make the wax for the comb themselves. It oozes as pale flakes from eight wax glands beneath her abdomen, and she chews it soft and shapes it, but only when the hive is warm, around 95 degrees Fahrenheit, 35 Celsius. Defending the hive costs a worker her life. Her stinger is barbed like a fishhook, so it lodges in the victim, and when she pulls away it tears free, ripping out part of her abdomen. A wasp's smooth stinger slides out, so a wasp can sting again.

She dances in total darkness on a vertical comb, so she uses gravity in place of the sun, treating straight up as the sun's direction. When von Frisch argued in 1927 that the dance was a real coded language, many scientists laughed. He settled it by reading a dance and watching the recruits: bees that had only watched it flew straight to a feeding spot none of them had ever visited. He later shared the 1973 Nobel Prize. Wax is costly, about 8 pounds of honey eaten for every pound of wax made, so the colony builds its cells as hexagons, the shape that holds the most honey with the least wax and stays strong. A meadow also looks different to a bee, because its eyes see ultraviolet light, invisible to us, which reveals glowing bull's-eyes and stripes on many flowers that guide it to the nectar.

Honeybees have an odd family system too. A female hatches from a fertilized egg, with 32 chromosomes from both parents, but a drone grows from an egg that was never fertilized and carries only his mother's 16, so a drone has no father at all. The dance itself was once fiercely disputed: in 1967 Adrian Wenner argued that bees find food by smell and that the dance means nothing. In 1989 Axel Michelsen's team built a robot bee of brass and beeswax with a razor-blade wing buzzing about 280 times a second, programmed it to dance, and it sent real bees to a spot that only it had named, proving that the dance itself carries the location.

leafcutter-ants.context_blurb:
Leafcutter ants live in the tropical forests of Central and South America, in underground nests that can house millions of workers. Their marching columns, each ant holding up a scrap of green leaf, are one of the great sights of the rainforest, and they hide one of the oldest farms on Earth.

A green ribbon flowing along a forest path, made of thousands of small ants each holding a bit of leaf aloft like a sail, is the classic sight of leafcutter ants hauling leaves home, each piece far heavier than the ant itself. They do not eat the leaves: underground they chew them into mulch and grow a fungus on it, and the fungus is what they eat. A colony of Atta, one of the biggest leafcutters, can strip every leaf off a full-grown citrus tree in a single night, leaving the whole tree bare by morning.

Workers come in very different sizes, and each size has a set task: huge, armored majors guard the entrance, middle-sized workers cut the leaves, and the tiniest, called minims, with heads less than a millimeter wide, care for the fungus garden deep in the nest, tending and weeding it. Minims also ride on top of the leaves the bigger workers carry, acting as bodyguards that chase off parasitic phorid flies trying to lay eggs on the carrier's head.

A parasite mould, Escovopsis, constantly attacks the garden, and the ants fight it with antibiotic-making bacteria that they carry on their own bodies in tiny pits in their skin; some colonies carry so many they look dusted with powdered sugar. People invented farming about twelve thousand years ago, but leafcutter ants began farming fungus roughly fifty million years ago, and they had fully tamed their crop about 15 million years ago.

monarch-butterfly.context_blurb:
The monarch is a big orange-and-black butterfly found across North America, from Canada through the United States to Mexico. It is famous for one of the greatest migrations on Earth, a journey shared by several generations between mountain forests in central Mexico and summer meadows far to the north. Its other secret is poison, borrowed from the one plant it eats.

A monarch caterpillar, striped black, yellow and white, eats only milkweed and refuses every other leaf, even if it means starving, so the female lays her eggs right on milkweed plants. Milkweed's bitter chemicals stay in the monarch's body, and its loud orange-and-black wings are a warning to birds that says, do not eat me: the butterfly is loaded with heart poison and tastes foul. Biologists call such warning colors aposematism.

A typical adult monarch survives just four weeks or so, far too short to fly the thousands of miles from central Mexico to Canada. Instead the spring migration is a relay run by three or four generations, each living only weeks: a butterfly flies partway, breeds and dies, and its young carry on north. The last brood of each summer, the super generation, is different: instead of dying in a month, it lives about eight months, long enough to fly south and wait out the winter. Some call it the Methuselah generation.

Every autumn the super generation flies as far as 3,000 miles south and settles in the very same oyamel fir groves on Mexico's mountains that its great-great-grandparents left the spring before, though not one of the new arrivals has seen them. The caterpillar does not break down milkweed's heart poison, called cardenolide; it stores it in its body and keeps it right through metamorphosis, so both caterpillar and butterfly stay poisonous for life. A young blue jay that swallows a monarch throws it up minutes later, sickened by the poison, and from then on it refuses to touch a monarch again: one bad meal teaches it to avoid the orange-and-black pattern for good.

A migrating monarch steers by the sun, correcting for its motion across the sky with a body clock, and that clock sits not in the brain but in its antennae: remove them and the butterfly loses its bearings. On overcast days it switches to a second compass: in 2014 Patrick Guerra, Robert Gegear and Steven Reppert put monarchs in a flight simulator, flipped the tilt of the magnetic field around them, and watched them turn north, proving that they read Earth's magnetic field. Those magnetic sensors also sit in the antennae and work only in ultraviolet and blue light.

The winter hideout stayed a mystery until January 9, 1975, when the volunteer Ken Brugger called the researchers Fred and Norah Urquhart with the news: he had found millions of monarchs clustered in evergreens beside a mountain clearing. At those Mexican colonies, the black-backed oriole cuts monarchs open and picks out only the least poisonous parts, but the black-headed grosbeak swallows them whole because it is genetically immune to cardenolides. Together the two birds kill about 15,000 monarchs a day. The viceroy, a butterfly dressed in the monarch's colors, and was long called a harmless faker, but a 1991 test by David Ritland and Lincoln Brower showed that the viceroy is just as foul-tasting as the monarch, so the two share one warning uniform. Its caterpillar feeds on willow and poplar, whose bitter salicylic acid, the aspirin family, helps make it taste bad.

Milkweed's poison blocks the sodium-potassium pump, a protein every animal cell depends on, and the monarch's pump resists it thanks to just three tiny changes in that one protein's shape. In 2019 Noah Whiteman's lab put the same three changes into fruit flies, and the flies became about a thousand times more resistant to the poison, as tough as a monarch.

peacock-spider.context_blurb:
Peacock spiders are tiny jumping spiders of Australia, and the males put on one of the most dazzling courtship shows in the animal world. Their small size kept them hidden from science for a long time, but their colorful dances have made them internet stars, and scientists have studied every move.

To court a female, the male peacock spider raises his back end straight up and spreads a fan of flaps in brilliant colors, normally tucked against his body, waving it at her like a peacock fanning its tail. Both males and females are only about 5 millimeters long, roughly as big as a grain of rice, which is why they went unnoticed for so long.

The stakes are high: if his dance fails to impress her, the female may pounce on him, kill him and eat him, sometimes even after mating. As he dances, he also drums the ground with his abdomen, sending vibrations that travel through the ground and reach her through her legs. Scientists have named the three kinds rumble-rumps, crunch-rolls and grind-revs.

Part of his fan is ultra-black, reflecting as little as 0.35 percent of light, yet it contains no black pigment at all: tiny lens-like bumps on the cuticle, about 6 micrometers tall, trap the light. His shimmering blues contain no blue pigment or dye either: microscopic nanostructures on his scales bend and reflect just the right wavelength of light, the same physics that makes a soap bubble shimmer.

praying-mantis.context_blurb:
Praying mantises are long, slender predatory insects found across much of the world, especially in the tropics. They hunt by ambush, and they are named for the way they hold their folded front legs, as if in prayer. Their eyes, their reflexes and their courtship have all become textbook examples.

The slender green insect waiting motionless on a stem with its spiky front legs folded up before it is a praying mantis, named for that posture, which is really a cocked spring ready to snap.

When prey drifts close, its spike-lined forelegs snap forward and shut like a spring-loaded trap in as little as 50 to 70 milliseconds, faster than a person can blink. To judge whether prey is within reach, the mantis uses true 3D depth perception, stereo vision found in no other insect.

The biggest mantises have killed and eaten frogs, lizards, small fish, mice and small birds, and on a single remarkable occasion, a small bat. In the field, the orchid mantis of Southeast Asia, pink and white with petal-shaped legs, draws in more insects than the real flowers growing nearby, as James O'Hanlon's study showed. The old story says a female always bites her mate's head off, but most matings end with the male alive, and experiments show she eats him mainly when she is hungry: well-fed females ate none of their mates, while starved females did.

Vivek Nityananda's team at Newcastle University glued tiny blue-and-green 3D glasses onto mantises with beeswax and showed them a 3D movie of prey, and the mantises lunged to grab prey that was not really there, proving they see in 3D. Many mantises have a single ear on the underside of the chest that hears bat ultrasound, and when it picks up a hunting bat in flight, the mantis spirals down in a steep power dive, escaping about 80 percent of the time.

tardigrade.context_blurb:
Tardigrades are eight-legged animals too small to see without a microscope, and they live almost everywhere on Earth, from the moss in your yard to Himalayan mountaintops, the deep sea and Antarctica. They are famous as the toughest animals known, surviving drying, freezing, boiling, radiation and even open space, and scientists are still working out how they do it.

In 1773 the German naturalist Goeze named it the little water bear for the way it lumbers along on its eight stumpy legs like a bear, and it is still called the water bear, or sometimes the moss piglet. Most tardigrades are about half a millimeter long, tinier than a single grain of sand, and the whole body is built from only about 1,000 cells.

The best place to hunt for them is moss: soak a clump, wring it out and examine the water with a microscope, and a single square meter of moss can hold over 2 million tardigrades. Each of its eight legs ends in a tight cluster of tiny claws, usually four to eight on each foot, for gripping and clambering through the tangled jungle of moss strands. To feed, it pierces a moss cell or a rotifer, an even smaller animal, with a pair of needle-like stylets made of the hard mineral aragonite and then sucks the juices out of it.

When its moss dries out, a tardigrade draws its legs inside and dries into a shriveled barrel called a tun, its metabolism almost stopped. Two tuns and an egg in Antarctic moss frozen since 1983 were thawed in 2014 and came back to life after more than thirty years, and one of the revived animals even laid 19 eggs. Dried into a tun, a tardigrade has survived being heated to about 149 degrees Celsius and chilled to about minus 272, just one degree above absolute zero, the coldest anything can ever be.

Just 5 to 10 gray of radiation kills a person, but a tardigrade survives about 5,000 gray, thanks partly to a protein called Dsup, for damage suppressor, which wraps itself around the DNA as a shield and absorbs the harm. Added to human cells in the lab, Dsup made them about 40 percent more resistant to X-rays. A 2007 European space test named TARDIS left dried tardigrades exposed on the exterior of a satellite for ten days of raw vacuum and cosmic rays, and most survived, revived and went on to have healthy babies. That made the tardigrade the first animal ever shown to survive open space.

Many other drying survivors, such as brine shrimp, rely on a sugar called trehalose, but a tardigrade makes almost none; instead it floods its cells with its own floppy CAHS proteins, which set into glass as the water drains away, locking membranes and enzymes in place. When Thomas Boothby's team silenced those proteins, the tardigrades could no longer survive drying.

Tardigrades have lived since before the dinosaurs, yet only three unmistakable fossil tardigrades have ever been found, every one sealed in amber, which is fossilized tree resin. The two oldest, Milnesium swolenskyi and Beorn leggi, lie in Cretaceous amber 72 to 90 million years old. The third, described in 2021 from 16-million-year-old Dominican amber, is only half a millimeter long and sat unnoticed beside three trapped ants for months.

axolotl.context_blurb:
The axolotl is a soft, pale-pink salamander with black eyes and a frilly crown, found in the wild only in the old lake canals of Mexico City. Millions live in laboratories and home aquariums around the world, because the axolotl does two things almost no other animal can: it keeps a baby-like body all its life, and it rebuilds lost body parts.

Its frilly crown is made of six feathery branches fanning out behind its head, and they are external gills: oxygen passes straight from the water into the blood flowing through them. Its famous grin says nothing about its mood; the smile is simply the fixed, upturned shape of its mouth.

The axolotl never grows up in the usual way: it keeps its feathery gills, soft body and tail fin for life, yet it becomes fully mature and breeds while still in that larval form, a condition biologists call neoteny. It is also a champion of regrowth: if a tankmate bites off a leg, a complete new leg grows back within weeks, with bone, muscle, nerves, blood vessels and even the pigment pattern, and no scar. Yet in the wild it is critically endangered: pollution and sewage cut the population by 99 percent between 1998 and 2014, and perhaps 50 to 1,000 survive, all in the canals of Xochimilco, the last scrap of the great lakes that once surrounded Mexico City.

Legs are only the start, because the axolotl can also regrow its tail, its jaw, sections of its spinal cord, portions of its brain and even parts of its heart. The secret lies in how a wound heals: a human cut closes with a patch of collagen that toughens into scar tissue, but an axolotl stump clears away the debris and then switches its cells back into embryo-style growth, rebuilding the part perfectly. Its immune system is unusually tolerant, too: scientists have grafted eyes and even pieces of brain from one axolotl onto another, and the foreign organs settled in and worked normally, with no rejection. Its baby form can even be undone: given thyroid hormone, an axolotl loses its gills, its tail fin shrinks, and it crawls onto land as a gill-less salamander that looks almost exactly like its cousin the tiger salamander.

In a 1968 experiment reported in the journal Science, researchers grafted a second head onto an axolotl, and the extra head not only survived but grew and behaved like a normal head, snapping at and eating prey on its own. Regrowth depends on the immune system: in 2013 Godwin, Pinto and Rosenthal wiped out an axolotl's macrophages, a type of immune cell, before amputating a limb, and the stump healed like a mammal's wound, sealed for good under thick collagen scar tissue, so no leg ever grew back, even after the macrophages returned.

When scientists read its genome in 2018, it was the largest ever assembled, about 32 billion letters, more than ten times the human genome, and it held a shock: Pax3, a gene every other backboned animal was thought to need, is missing, and its close cousin gene Pax7 has taken over the job.

chameleon.context_blurb:
Chameleons are slow, mostly tree-dwelling lizards of Africa, Madagascar, southern Europe and parts of Asia. They are famous for turret eyes that move on their own, a tongue fired like a projectile, and skin that changes color. Modern research has shown that each of these tricks works differently from the old textbook story.

Perched motionless, a chameleon catches an insect with its tongue, which rockets out about 2.5 times the length of its body and hits the bug in roughly 20 milliseconds, a fraction of a blink.

Its two eyes sit in cone-shaped turrets and swivel independently, so it can watch a hawk overhead with one eye and a beetle behind it with the other, scanning almost a full circle without turning its head while its brain handles two separate pictures. The moment it spots prey, both eyes swing forward and lock onto the same target, sizing up the distance to within a few millimeters, because once the tongue fires there is no correcting its aim. Its famous color change is mostly not camouflage: a chameleon changes color mainly to signal its mood and intentions and to warm up or cool down, so a calm chameleon and an angry one are literally different colors.

About half of the roughly 200 chameleon species live only on Madagascar, the big island off Africa's east coast. There lives the nano-chameleon, Brookesia nana, whose male has a body just 13.5 millimeters long, about 22 with the tail, small enough to perch on a fingertip and possibly the smallest reptile on Earth. Male Jackson's chameleons of the East African mountains carry three forward-pointing horns like a tiny Triceratops, and rival males lock horns and try to push each other off the branch.

In 2015 Swiss researchers studying panther chameleons found that the skin holds a grid of tiny guanine crystals, and tightening or loosening that grid changes which colors of light bounce back, blue when packed tight and yellow or red when spread apart, a structural color rather than pigment. The club-shaped tongue tip is coated in mucus about 400 times more viscous than human saliva, and the quicker the tongue whips home, the stronger that grip becomes, letting a chameleon haul in surprisingly heavy prey. Per kilogram of muscle its tongue launch delivers about 14,000 watts, more than any reptile, bird or mammal, and among all backboned animals only salamanders beat it.

The launch works even when its body has cooled to 3.5°C, because the tongue is a spring: a slow accelerator muscle first stretches a sleeve of coiled collagen sheaths around a stiff bone in the tongue, and the loaded sheaths then slide off its tip and recoil all at once like a drawn bow. In tests, cold cut the power of the launch only slightly, while the muscle-powered pull back weakened sharply. A chameleon can also judge range with only one eye, the only vertebrate known to do so, by focusing that eye on the prey and treating the focus setting as a measure of distance, helped by a lens and cornea that enlarge the image so tiny focus changes show up clearly.

glass-frog.context_blurb:
Glass frogs are small, lime-green tree frogs of the cloud forests and rainforests of Central and South America, about 160 species in all. They spend their nights on leaves above rushing streams, and their bodies are partly see-through, a disguise scientists have only recently begun to understand.

Flip a glass frog onto its back and you can see straight through the skin of its belly to the organs inside. Most of them sit still, but one never stops moving: through that clear skin you can watch its heart beat as it pumps blood, along with the liver and looping intestines.

Glass frogs lay their eggs on the underside of leaves that hang over streams, so the hatching tadpoles drop straight into the water. It is the male that guards the eggs, standing watch for days and driving off egg-eating wasps, sometimes over several clutches at once.

By day a sleeping glass frog is two to three times more transparent than an active one. In 2022 scientists filming resting frogs discovered how: the frog hides nearly 90 percent of its red blood cells, which would give away its red tint, crammed inside its liver, whose mirror-like lining conceals them. At night it releases them again, and somehow the packed blood never forms a deadly clot.

goliath-frog.context_blurb:
The goliath frog, Conraua goliath, is the biggest frog on Earth. It lives only along fast, rocky rainforest streams in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, where the adults perch on boulders amid the white water. Hunting and habitat loss have put it in serious trouble.

It can grow to about 34 centimeters long and 3.3 kilograms, roughly the size and weight of a house cat.

Most male frogs call by puffing up a vocal sac on the throat, but the goliath frog has none and cannot croak. To attract a female, the male simply opens his mouth and gives a whistle. In 2019 scientists found these frogs doing something never seen before in any frog or toad of Africa. They build nests, clearing little ponds along the riverbank and dragging rocks around the edges to wall them off, then guarding the eggs inside.

Those rocks can weigh more than half the frog's own weight, up to about 2 kilograms. The scientists who study it think that all this heavy hauling of nest stones may be what drove the goliath frog to grow so far beyond every other frog.

king-cobra.context_blurb:
The king cobra is a long, slender, hooded snake that lives in the steamy jungles of India and across Southeast Asia. Its scientific name, Ophiophagus hannah, begins with a Greek word meaning snake-eater, and it lives up to it. Yet this fearsome hunter is also a surprisingly devoted mother.

A big king cobra can reach about 18 feet, roughly the height of a tall adult giraffe, which makes it the longest venomous snake in the world. When cornered, it rears up as much as a third of its body, spreads its hood and keeps gliding forward, tall enough to look a grown person in the eye.

It rarely bothers with rats or birds; instead it hunts other snakes, even deadly ones such as the banded krait, a striped snake with a lethal nerve venom, tracking them down, biting them and swallowing them whole. Its stretchy jaws let it gulp down prey longer than itself, and it will overpower and eat a big reticulated python, one of the longest snakes in the world, as well as Indian cobras and even other king cobras. A single bite delivers so much nerve venom that it could kill about 20 people, or even a full-grown elephant, and without treatment a bitten person can die in as little as 30 minutes. Almost every snake lays its eggs and leaves, but the female king cobra is the only snake that builds a nest: she scrapes dry leaves into a mound, lays her eggs inside and guards them fiercely for two to three months until they hatch.

A cornered king cobra does not hiss thinly like other snakes: its warning sounds like a dog growling, because it uses only deep frequencies, below 2,500 hertz with a main tone near 600. In the dark its eyes are nearly useless, so it hunts by scent, flicking its tongue and pressing the scent molecules into the Jacobson's organ, two small pockets above its tongue. Because each tip of the forked tongue feeds its own sensor, the cobra smells in stereo: it can tell which side a scent is stronger on, and follows a trail like a bloodhound.

The longest king cobra ever measured, 18 feet 8 inches, came from Port Dickson in Malaya and lived at the London Zoo, but at the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 keepers put it down so that it could not escape into the city if bombs struck the zoo.
