komodo-dragon.context_blurb:
The Komodo dragon is a giant monitor lizard that lives wild only on a few dry islands of Indonesia: Komodo, Rinca, Padar and Flores. It is the top predator of those islands, killing deer, wild boar and even water buffalo, and scientists are still uncovering the secrets of its bite, its armor and its family history.

The Komodo dragon is the largest lizard alive: males grow to about 3 meters, some 10 feet, and the heaviest one ever weighed reached 166 kilograms, or 366 pounds. It cannot chase prey far, so it lies hidden beside a game trail as still as a log, then bursts from cover and lunges at a passing deer's legs, belly or throat.

Because it may go weeks between kills, a dragon gorges when it finally eats, swallowing as much as 80 percent of its body weight at one sitting. As it patrols, its forked yellow tongue darts in and out. The two tips carry scent separately to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of its mouth, which gives it a three-dimensional sense of where a smell comes from, and it can find a rotting carcass up to 2.5 miles, about 4 kilometers, away.

Its mouth holds about 60 curved teeth with saw-like edges, like a shark's, and the backward-curving serrations hook into flesh so prey cannot tear free, opening deep wounds. Worn teeth are replaced throughout its life. For decades, textbooks blamed its deadly bite on filthy saliva full of bacteria, but in 2009 Bryan Fry's team at the University of Queensland found venom glands in its lower jaw, whose toxins stop blood from clotting and make the victim's blood pressure crash. A later study found its mouth bacteria are no more dangerous than any other meat-eater's. So after a bite the dragon need not chase: it lets a big animal such as a water buffalo stagger off, then follows at a leisurely pace for hours or even days until blood loss brings it down.

In 2006 a Chester Zoo dragon in England named Flora, who had never been kept with a male, laid 11 eggs that hatched into healthy babies, through parthenogenesis, a virgin birth from unfertilized eggs.

Every hatchling of such a virgin birth is male, because the Komodo's sex chromosomes work the reverse of ours: females are WZ and males ZZ, and when an unfertilized egg doubles its chromosomes, only the ZZ pairing survives. That means a lone female washed onto an empty island could found a whole population by herself: she could produce sons by parthenogenesis and then breed with them.

In 2019, CT scans by the paleontologist Jessica Maisano revealed thousands of tiny bones called osteoderms just beneath a Komodo's skin, in four shapes, forming a full-body suit of chain-mail armor that covers everything but the nostrils, the eyes and the pineal third eye. Babies hatch with no armor; it grows in as they mature and mainly shields adults from other dragons' bites. A 2024 study found that the deep orange stripe along each tooth's tip and serrated edge is a coating of iron, concentrated on the cutting parts, which hardens the fine serrations and keeps them razor-sharp. Many reptiles carry a trace of iron in their enamel, but only the Komodo lines its cutting edges with it, and meat-eating dinosaurs such as T. rex may have kept their teeth sharp the same way.

Textbooks once said the Komodo dragon swelled into a giant on its islands from a small, stranded ancestor. In 2009 Scott Hocknull described Komodo dragon fossils from eastern Australia, between 300,000 and 4 million years old, showing that the species first evolved on mainland Australia and only later spread west into Indonesia, about a million years ago. It vanished from Australia about 50,000 years ago along with that continent's other giant beasts, so today's dragons are the last survivors of an Australian dynasty that also produced the even larger extinct monitor Megalania.

poison-dart-frog.context_blurb:
Poison dart frogs are tiny, jewel-bright frogs of tropical America. Their colors are warnings: some carry enough poison to kill people. Yet the poison is not made by the frog itself, and their family life is as surprising as their chemistry.

On the rainforest floor from Central America south through the Amazon, fingernail-sized frogs in reds, blues, yellows and greens bright enough to glow are poison dart frogs, about 200 species in all. After the eggs hatch, the tadpoles cling to the slime on a parent's back, and the adult climbs a tree to drop each one into a little pool of rain caught in the cup of a bromeliad.

The blazing colors are aposematic, an honest signal to every predator that the frog is deadly and must not be eaten, and the more toxic the frog, the brighter its colors tend to be. The golden poison frog of Colombia's Choco rainforest, no longer than a paper clip, carries about a milligram of toxin on its skin, enough to kill between 10 and 20 people, or some 20,000 mice.

The frog does not make its poison: it gathers it from the poisonous ants, mites and small beetles in its wild diet, so a captive dart frog fed harmless fruit flies never becomes poisonous at all. Indigenous hunters once wiped blowgun darts along a living frog's back to coat the tips, which gave the frogs their name, but only a few species, all in the genus Phyllobates, were ever used, not the famous jewel-colored Dendrobates. The mother strawberry poison frog of Central America carries each tadpole to its own pool in a bromeliad leaf and returns week after week to feed it her own unfertilized eggs, the only food the tadpoles will accept.

The golden poison frog's batrachotoxin jams open the sodium gates in nerve and muscle cells so they can never reset, and as the cells fire nonstop, the victim's muscles freeze and the heart stops. The dyeing poison frog's bold pattern warns predators up close, but from a distance the same markings blur together and blend into the background, giving it warning colors and camouflage at once.

saltwater-crocodile.context_blurb:
From the river mouths of northern Australia and India east through Southeast Asia to the islands of the western Pacific, one reptile rules the brackish water and even the open sea. The saltwater crocodile is an ancient design with record-breaking power, and it crosses wide stretches of water between islands.

The saltwater crocodile is the largest reptile alive: a big male reaches about 20 feet from snout to tail and can weigh around a ton. Nearly every other crocodile lives in fresh water. The saltie, as it is nicknamed, thrives at sea and in the salty water where rivers meet the ocean, and it turns up far out at sea, hundreds of miles from the nearest river.

It hunts by ambush, floating like a log with only its eyes showing until a buffalo or other big animal wades too close, then bursting upward to seize it. The crocodile drags a victim too heavy to wrestle on the bank into deep water and holds it under until it drowns. Its teeth are made to grip, not chew, so a carcass larger than one gulp is a problem. It solves this by clamping onto a limb and spinning its whole body over and over until the piece twists free, a move called the death roll.

That grip comes with record force. Gregory Erickson measured it in Australia's wild salties with a cushioned bite gauge between their jaws. The biggest clamped down with some 3,700 pounds of force on every square inch, the strongest bite measured in any living animal, enough to crush bone or a turtle's shell in one bite. When Erickson's team tested all 23 kinds of crocodilian, from little caimans to the largest crocodiles, the saltwater crocodile topped the list, beating even the mighty American alligator, which managed about 2,980 pounds. It does not even need to see its prey. Thousands of tiny black domes freckle its jaws and skin, pressure sensors so delicate they can feel the ripple a single drop of water makes, so the crocodile can strike at a fish or bird moving in pitch-black water.

Out at sea, salt is the danger, and there is no fresh water to drink. Special glands on its tongue pump the extra salt back out, and they work nearly three times as hard when the crocodile is in the sea as in a river. Satellite tags revealed how it travels so far. Tracked crocodiles moved with the current on 96 percent of their long journeys and almost never fought against it, riding the tides like surfers; one male traveled 590 kilometers in 25 days after leaving the Kennedy River. Steve Irwin, famous worldwide as the Crocodile Hunter, helped tag the animals for that research, and the discovery appeared in print only after he died suddenly in 2006.

Crocodiles are often called living fossils, because their basic body plan is more than 200 million years old. But the shape and the species keep different clocks. Jamie Oaks used DNA to map how the true crocodiles are related, and found that the whole genus Crocodylus, the saltie's own group, arose and spread only about 13.6 to 8.3 million years ago, from an ancestor in the tropical Indo-Pacific. The saltwater crocodile is a young species wearing an ancient design.

sea-turtle.context_blurb:
Sea turtles are big, long-lived reptiles that roam the world's warm oceans. There are seven living species, and all of them are threatened or endangered. Adults spend nearly their whole lives at sea, crossing whole oceans, and only the females ever return to land, to lay eggs on the same beaches where their own lives began.

A sea turtle is an air-breathing reptile built for the open ocean, with lungs, legs shaped into broad flippers and a low, streamlined shell for gliding; it sleeps and feeds underwater and rises to the surface to breathe. Only nesting females come ashore, digging a pit in the sand at night and laying about a hundred round eggs.

What happens next in the sand decides each baby's sex: not chromosomes, as in mammals, but how warm the nest stays during the two months the eggs lie buried, with warmer nests making females and cooler nests making males, and an even split near 29 degrees Celsius (about 84 Fahrenheit).

A hatchling finds the sea by racing toward the lowest, brightest stretch of sky, where moonlight and starlight glint off the water and the beach slopes down. That is why beachfront lights can lure hatchlings the wrong way, inland. Decades later, a grown female crosses whole oceans to lay her eggs on the very beach where she herself hatched, a homecoming called natal homing. She finds it by magnetism: as a hatchling she imprinted on her home beach's own magnetic signature, the angle and strength of Earth's field there, and years later she reads that field like a map and compass to steer home.

The green sea turtle is the only plant-eater among the seven species, grazing seagrass and algae, and that diet tints its body fat green, which, rather than its brownish shell, is what gave the turtle its name. Heat now threatens it. On Raine Island, a speck of sand on the Great Barrier Reef where more green turtles nest than anywhere else, the beaches have grown so hot that over 99 percent of the young turtles scientists studied had hatched female, leaving almost no males for the future.

The leatherback is the largest turtle alive, up to about 2 meters long and outweighing a grizzly bear at more than 640 kilograms, and in place of a hard shell it has a leathery, ridged back, which gives it its name. It lives mostly on jellyfish, and a floating plastic bag looks so much like a jellyfish that leatherbacks swallow them by mistake, one reason they are endangered. A jellyfish is slippery and mostly water, but the leatherback's throat is lined with hundreds of spines that point backward, so a meal can only go down. An adult can eat up to about 73 percent of its body weight in jellyfish a day.

One leatherback carrying a depth logger in the Caribbean plunged past 1,344 meters into black, freezing water, the deepest dive ever recorded for any reptile, deeper than a nuclear submarine can go. Its core stays up to 18 degrees Celsius warmer than the sea because its constantly working swimming muscles make heat, and countercurrent exchangers in its flippers, where warm blood flowing out runs beside cold blood flowing in and hands over its heat, stop that warmth from leaking away. A thick layer of insulating fat helps too, so a turtle that nests in the tropics can hunt jellyfish off Canada, in water close to freezing.

The biggest sea turtle of all time, Archelon, swam over what are now the Dakotas some 80 to 74 million years ago; the biggest one found, nicknamed Brigitta, was about 4.6 meters long and weighed over 2,200 kilograms. Like a leatherback it had a leathery, ridged back, but it belonged to the Protostegidae, an early branch that split away before today's sea turtles arose, so the leathery shell evolved twice, by convergent evolution.

tuatara.context_blurb:
Off the coast of New Zealand, on a handful of small islands, lives a reptile shaped like a lizard: the tuatara. It looks like a lizard but is not one: it is the last survivor of an ancient order of reptiles that otherwise died out long ago. Everything about it, from its slow growth to its long life and its strange third eye, is unusual among reptiles.

Its Māori name means peaks on the back, for the spiny crest down its spine, largest in males, and a male facing a rival flares that crest and darkens as he puffs up his body.

Its relatives once shared the world with the dinosaurs across almost every continent, but only the tuatara survives, the sole member of an order that flourished 200 million years ago and split off before lizards and snakes existed, which is why it is called a living fossil. On top of a hatchling's head sits a pale patch covering a working third eye, the parietal eye, complete with its own lens and retina, which scales slowly grow over as the animal matures. Unlike most reptiles, the tuatara likes the cold: its preferred body temperature of about 16 to 21 degrees Celsius is the lowest of any reptile, it stays active down to 5 degrees, and it can die of overheating above about 28.

That third eye cannot form pictures, but researchers think it works as a sun-compass, reading daylight to keep the tuatara's daily rhythms and its body heat in step with the seasons. Tuatara grow slowly for their first 35 years and can live past 100, and Henry, a captive male at the Southland Museum, was still fathering offspring at age 111.

wood-frog.context_blurb: The wood frog is a small, dark-masked frog that lives in forests across much of Canada and the northern United States, farther north than any other North American amphibian. It survives winters that would kill every other North American frog by doing something to its own body that biologists find hard to believe the first time they read about it. The wood frog is one of the clearest living examples of how an animal can survive conditions that would otherwise be lethal.

dire-wolf.context_blurb:
The dire wolf was a big, heavily built hunter of ice-age America, ranging across North America and into South America until it died out about 10,000 years ago. Thousands of its skeletons have come out of the La Brea tar pits of Los Angeles, and ancient DNA has shown that it was no ordinary wolf.

The largest dire wolves averaged about 68 kilograms, around 150 pounds, while a big male gray wolf weighs about 43. Its powerful jaws were made for crushing, and it specialized in giant ice-age plant-eaters such as camels, ground sloths, western horses and ancient bison. When those big animals died out at the end of the ice age, the dire wolf vanished with them, while smaller, more adaptable gray wolves survived.

For over a century scientists treated it as simply a larger cousin of the gray wolf. Then in 2021 a team led by the biologist Angela Perri recovered ancient DNA from dire wolf bones and found it was no close relative of wolves at all, so distinct that it was moved into a genus of its own, Aenocyon dirus. At La Brea, sticky asphalt seeped up and held fast any animal that stepped in. When a big plant-eater got stuck, its cries drew predators and scavengers, and the dire wolves that came for an easy meal got stuck as well, again and again over thousands of years.

The DNA showed that the dire wolf line had branched off on its own about 5.7 million years ago. After so long apart it could not interbreed with gray wolves, and its genes show no mixing. Its closest living relatives turned out to be African jackals; its wolf-like look evolved separately, a case of convergent evolution. Between 5 and 17 percent of La Brea dire wolf specimens have cracked or broken teeth, while among modern wolves and lions the figure is 0.5 to 2.7 in every hundred. That damage points to bone crunching during hard, competitive feeding on big carcasses.

There were really two kinds of dire wolf, split by the Rocky Mountains, and Björn Kurtén named them in 1984. The eastern form, about 68 kilograms, had long legs like a modern wolf's, built for the chase. The western form, the one dug up by the thousand at La Brea, averaged about 60 kilograms and stood on shorter, stockier legs, its hind limbs about 8 percent shorter than a Yukon wolf's, which made it the weaker runner of the two. A 2019 study has since questioned whether the two are truly separate subspecies.

giant-ground-sloth.context_blurb:
Giant ground sloths were huge relatives of today's tree sloths that walked the Americas during the ice age. The biggest, Megatherium of South America, was the size of an elephant and survived until about 12,000 years ago. Unlike its small modern cousins it lived on the ground, and its bones and footprints are still revealing surprises.

Megatherium stretched about 6 meters long and weighed around 4,000 kilograms, the size of a bull elephant, yet its closest living relatives are the cat-sized tree sloths that hang in South American rainforests. Those tree sloths move so little that green algae grows in their grooved hair, tinting them green and hiding them among the leaves.

To reach high leaves, Megatherium rose up onto its hind legs and tail, braced like a tripod against a tree trunk, standing about 3.5 meters tall and pulling branches down with its forelimbs. Its front claws were about 30 centimeters long, too long for it to plant its feet flat. Like a modern anteater, it walked on the outer edges of its feet with the claws curled inward.

Those claws were also weapons: a single swipe could kill an attacker, so even sabre-toothed cats and dire wolves rarely challenged a full-grown adult. Under its shaggy fur, the skin was studded with thousands of tiny bones, from lentil-sized to about 2 centimeters, forming a chain-mail mesh that armored it against a predator's bite. At White Sands in New Mexico, fossil footprints at least 11,700 years old show a person stepping inside a giant sloth's own tracks, stalking it across an ancient mudflat.

For a century, scientists sorting sloths by their skeletons thought today's two-toed and three-toed sloths were close cousins. In 2019, ancient DNA and fossil proteins showed otherwise: the three-toed sloth sits among the relatives of Megatherium, while the two-toed sloth groups with another ground sloth, Mylodon. So each of the two took up its slow life hanging in the trees independently, descended from a different giant ground sloth. Richard Fariña and Ernesto Blanco noticed that Megatherium's elbow lever, the spot where the triceps muscle anchors, is short, built for speed rather than force, as in meat-eaters. They proposed that it may have been a part-time predator or scavenger that drove its claws in like daggers, though chemical evidence from its bones points to a plant diet, and the idea remains debated.

glyptodon.context_blurb:
Glyptodon was a giant armored relative of the armadillo that grazed the grasslands of South America during the last ice age. Picture an armadillo blown up as big as a small car, its whole back hidden under one huge bony dome. Glyptodons died out along with most of the other big American animals, and DNA has since revealed where they belong.

The glyptodon grew to about 3 meters long, and the biggest species reached around 2 tonnes, as big as a Volkswagen Beetle. For all its armor and the helmet of fused bone on its head, it was a plant-eater, with a broad muzzle for grazing low grasses and plants along forest edges.

A modern armadillo can roll into a ball because its shell is made of flexible bands. Glyptodon could not: its dome was about 1,800 bony plates fused solid into a single rigid shell and locked onto its hip bones. At the Pay Paso 1 site in Uruguay, human spear points lie beside glyptodon fossils. Researchers think early South Americans may have sheltered under the huge empty shells in bad weather, like ready-made domed tents.

Doedicurus, a close cousin, carried a spiked club of bone at the end of its tail that could deliver about 60 kilonewtons of force, far more than the roughly 4 needed to snap a human thigh bone. Some glyptodont shells carry dents that match the size and shape of such a club, evidence that these living tanks clubbed each other, probably in fights over mates or territory. Micro-CT scans show why a single plate, about 2.5 centimeters thick, could take a blow: each is built like a sandwich, with dense outer layers of bone wrapped around a porous inner lattice that absorbs the impact and stops cracks from spreading. Armor engineers now copy the design.

In 2016 Delsuc, Poinar and their colleagues read the mitochondrial DNA of Doedicurus and found that glyptodonts sit deep inside the armadillo family tree. Their common ancestor with modern armadillos weighed only about 6 kilograms, so the glyptodon line multiplied its body mass more than 300 times over, reaching about 2,000 kilograms.

irish-elk-giant-deer.context_blurb:
The Irish elk, better called the giant deer, roamed Ice Age Europe and northern Asia, from Ireland east into Siberia, and it survived until roughly 7,700 years ago. Irish peat bogs have yielded so many of its skeletons that it was named for that island. Its stags carried the most extravagant headgear of any deer, and those antlers sit at the heart of the debate over why it vanished.

Standing some 2 meters tall at the withers and weighing as much as 700 kilograms, a giant deer stag matched a modern Alaskan moose in size. Yet its popular name is wrong twice over: it lived far beyond Ireland, and it was no elk, because DNA from ancient bones shows that its closest living relative is the fallow deer. The stag's antlers were the largest of any animal known, broad flat palms reaching about 3.6 meters from tip to tip, a span equal to the length of a family car, and 4.26 meters in the biggest specimen.

Every year the stag grew that entire rack anew from bare stubs, some 40 kilograms of bone, and then shed it, only to build it all again the next spring. Rival stags sometimes locked the lower parts of their antlers to push and shove, but the great palms were mainly for show, to win mates, an extreme case of sexual selection, much as in red deer today.

Rebuilding the rack took more calcium and phosphate than any spring grass or leaves could supply. Models suggest the stag drew up to 80 percent of that calcium out of his own bones, about twice the drain a moose faces, so a stag that could not refill on rich grazing risked brittle bones.

Many people once blamed the antlers, claiming the rack grew so heavy that it doomed the stags. In a famous 1974 paper, Stephen Jay Gould showed that the antlers were just the size expected for so big a deer, and an advantage in display rather than a fatal handicap. The evidence now points to a climate that changed and a habitat that vanished: as the Ice Age forests and mineral-rich plants disappeared, the deer could no longer eat enough to rebuild bone and antler every year. Human hunting may have dealt the final blow to herds already under stress.

The rack also cost raw energy: a 1999 simulation by Moen, Pastor and Cohen estimated that growing it took about three-quarters as much energy as the stag needed to build all his summer reserves of fat and muscle, against about half for a living moose. A 2008 model by O'Driscoll Worman and Kimbrell argued that the antler story is largely wrong: antler size can shrink easily over generations, and losing big-antlered males barely slows a herd's growth. In their model the females took the real hit, because as the Ice Age growing season shortened, the cost of carrying and nursing fast-growing young could have cut each mother's output of young by up to half. The debate is still open.

mastodon.context_blurb:
The mastodon was an elephant relative that roamed the forests of North and Central America during the Ice Age and died out around 10,000 years ago. It looked like a woolly mammoth, but it belonged to a different family, and its teeth tell the whole story of how differently it lived.

The mastodon was a mammoth look-alike, huge, shaggy and tusked, but stockier and shorter in the leg, and its brow sat low and flat, without the high dome of a mammoth's head. A single molar gives it away: a mastodon's molar is studded with rows of large, blunt cones, while a mammoth's molars are flat, with washboard ridges for grinding grass.

Those cones were built for crushing woody food: the mastodon was a forest browser that ate twigs, leaves and branches, while the mammoth grazed on open grassland. While the mammoth roamed the open, windy grass steppe, the mastodon made its home in spruce and pine forests and boggy swamps, so the two giants could share a continent without competing.

Early Americans who dug up its giant bones at places like Big Bone Lick, Kentucky, first took it for an elephant, later for a mammoth, and for years simply labeled it the American incognitum, Latin for the unknown one, until Cuvier showed in 1806 that it was a separate species that had died out. Georges Cuvier, the French anatomist, named the animal from the Greek words for nipple and tooth, because the rounded cones on its molars reminded him of nipples: mastodon means nipple-tooth.

A tusk adds a new layer every year, like a tree, and the oxygen and strontium sealed in each layer record where the animal drank that season. In 2022 scientists read the tusk of the Buesching bull from Indiana. As a youngster he wandered with no seasonal pattern. From the year he matured, he made a repeated spring journey of about 157 kilometers to one fixed mating ground in northeast Indiana, then returned to his home range. It was the first seasonal migration ever traced this way in an extinct animal.

short-faced-bear.context_blurb:
In ice-age North America lived the giant short-faced bear, Arctodus simus, a long-legged, blunt-muzzled bear that vanished with most of the continent's great beasts at the end of the last ice age. No bear yet found stood taller, and much of what people once believed about it has been overturned.

On its hind legs Arctodus reached about 11 or 12 feet, high enough to peer down over a basketball hoop's rim, which hangs at 10 feet.

People once imagined it as a racing super-predator that chased saber-tooths off their kills, and older chemical studies read it as a pure meat-eater. In 2010 Borja Figueirido's team studied its teeth and argued instead that it was a giant opportunistic omnivore: the teeth show wear from eating plants and lack the meat-slicing shape of a true super-predator. What Arctodus ate is still debated. It was not even the heaviest bear. That record belongs to Arctotherium angustidens, a South American cousin of the short-faced bears, known from a skeleton about a million years old found during hospital construction in La Plata, Argentina, and estimated at about 1,588 kilograms, roughly double a large Arctodus.

Even its name may be a mistake. Arctodus looks stubby-faced because of a deep snout and short nasal bones. But when Figueirido measured the skull, the face proved no shorter than other bears' at all, just taller and wider, so it only looked short.

smilodon-saber-toothed-cat.context_blurb:
Smilodon was a stocky, lion-sized predator of the Americas during the ice age, famous for two long, curved upper fangs. People call it the saber-toothed tiger, but that name is wrong. Thousands of its skeletons, pulled from one famous site in Los Angeles, have taught scientists how it hunted, fought and healed, though some questions are still argued over.

The saber-toothed cat is properly called Smilodon, and it was neither a tiger nor a close cousin of any living big cat: its branch, the Machairodontinae, split from the ancestors of today's cats about 20 million years ago. At Los Angeles' La Brea Tar Pits, natural asphalt seeped up for thousands of years and trapped plant-eaters, and the predators that came to eat them were caught in turn, building up the greatest saber-tooth fossil bed on Earth.

The biggest species, Smilodon populator of South America, could top 470 kilograms, one of the largest cats ever, and it hunted the heaviest plant-eaters around, including giant Megatherium ground sloths. North America's Smilodon fatalis weighed about 160 to 280 kilograms.

Its fangs, about seven inches long, were slender and snapped easily if twisted sideways, so Smilodon had to pin its prey still before driving them into soft flesh.

Computer modeling by McHenry and colleagues in 2007 showed that its bite was only about a third as strong as a lion's, but its jaw could swing open to about 120 degrees, well past a right angle, where a lion manages only about 65. The real killing power came from its massive neck and forelimbs. Many La Brea skeletons show serious injuries that healed, including one cat crippled in the hip from a young age, and some researchers argue that Smilodon may have lived in groups that shared food with the injured, though that idea is still debated.

terror-bird.context_blurb:
Terror birds, or phorusrhacids, were huge flightless predatory birds of South America, the top land hunters of their continent for millions of years after the dinosaurs and on into the ice age. Their fossils turn up across the pampas of Argentina and beyond, and each new find shows more of how a bird could rule as a giant predator.

A terror bird stood as tall as 3 meters (nearly 10 feet), with powerful running legs and a massive hooked beak, and it was the top land predator of South America at a time when the continent had almost no big hunting mammals. Built to chase prey across the open pampas on foot, it had long, muscular legs but tiny, nearly useless wings. Its weapon was a huge, hatchet-shaped beak with a hooked tip, and rather than grabbing and shaking prey like a lion or a wolf, it drove the beak straight down, the way you would swing a pickaxe, to break the neck or skull.

The largest bird skull known, a 71-centimeter (28-inch) skull of the terror bird Kelenken with a hooked beak about 46 centimeters long, was dug up in Patagonia in 2006 by Guillermo Aguirre-Zabala, a high-school student.

Computer stress tests on a fossil skull explain the pickaxe style: its bones were fused rigid, strong against a hard downward blow but weak against twisting a victim from side to side, which could have snapped it. Llallawavis scagliai, a terror bird from Argentina described in 2015 and about 95 percent complete, even preserved its inner ear, and CT scans showed hearing tuned unusually low for a bird, to deep sounds that travel far. It could probably hear prey moving out of sight and answer with deep, booming calls of its own.

In 2024 a single 12-million-year-old shin bone from Colombia's Tatacoa Desert revealed what may be the largest terror bird ever, yet it is scarred with bite marks that match Purussaurus, a giant caiman about 10 meters long, longer than a school bus. Even the age's ultimate land hunter could be dragged down at the water's edge.

woolly-mammoth.context_blurb: The woolly mammoth was a huge, shaggy elephant-cousin that lived across the cold grasslands of Eurasia and North America during the ice age. Mammoths were close relatives of today's Asian elephant, with long curved tusks and a dense double coat for the deep cold. Most of them went extinct around the end of the last ice age, though a tiny isolated population survived on a remote Arctic island until a few thousand years ago. Frozen specimens have given paleontologists an unusually complete picture of the animal.

woolly-rhino.context_blurb: The woolly rhino was a shaggy, cold-adapted rhinoceros that lived across the cold grasslands of Eurasia during the ice age and died out around 10,000 years ago. It shared its range with mammoths and giant deer. Mummified and frozen specimens found in Siberia and Poland have given scientists a very detailed picture of its coat, its horn, and its diet, which was unusually specialized for a rhino. Ancient cave paintings in France and Spain show that early humans knew it well.

armor.context_blurb:
Teeth and claws are half of nature's arms race; armor is the other half. Plates, scales and shells grown on an animal's own body turn aside bites and blows, and armor has evolved again and again in very different creatures. It is never free: it is heavy, costly to grow and stiff, so every armored animal strikes its own bargain.

The pangolin, a shy ant-eater of Africa and Asia, is the only mammal scaled from head to tail, and its scales are keratin, the same protein as your fingernails. The tortoise keeps it simple. Caught by a jackal in open country, it tucks head, legs and tail inside and waits. It needs no burrow or rock, because its fortress rides on its back.

A lion pawing at a pangolin finds only a tight ball, with no gap to slip a claw under a scale, and the animal's name records the move: 'pangolin' comes from the Malay pengguling, 'one who rolls up.'

A hermit crab moves into a bigger borrowed shell when it outgrows the old one; a turtle never can. A turtle's shell is its own ribcage and backbone, fused and flattened into a dome, so leaving it would be like stepping out of your skeleton. Most armadillos escape by bolting underground. The three-banded armadillo instead snaps itself into a sealed ball, the plates of its head and tail fitting together to close the gap. A rolled-up pangolin has an edge as well: its order is named Pholidota, 'clad in scales,' and the scales are sharp. When a curled pangolin twists and heaves, its scales double as slashing blades. On bare South African rock, the armadillo girdled lizard cannot outrun a mongoose, so it bites its own tail and bends into a hoop. The mongoose, looking for a soft belly, meets only a ring of sharp, spiky scales.

Armor grew grandest in South America. Some ten thousand years ago, car-sized glyptodons, extinct relatives of the armadillo weighing as much as two tons, roamed there alongside the first people to arrive. Hundreds of bony plates called osteoderms were fused across a glyptodon's back into a single solid dome, with none of the sliding bands that let a living armadillo bend. The turtle paid a stranger price for its shell. Every other animal with a backbone carries its shoulder blades outside its ribs. Because a turtle's ribs became its shell, its shoulder blades ended up inside the ribcage.

Paleontologists long argued over which half of the shell came first, the domed top or the flat plate beneath. Odontochelys, 'toothed turtle with a half-shell,' settled it in 2008. This 220-million-year-old turtle still had teeth, which every living turtle has traded for a horny beak. Over its back it had only broadened ribs where the dome should be, yet its belly was fully armored with a bony plastron. The plate under the belly evolved first, and the carapace over the back came later. The fossil looks like a modern turtle embryo caught halfway through building its shell.

chemical-weapons.context_blurb:
Many animals defend themselves not with teeth or speed but with chemistry. Their weapons range from foul smells to scalding sprays, sticky slimes and bitter blood, and they reach an attacker as sprays, oozes, ejected threads and even flung guts. How an animal makes, stores and fires its chemicals without harming itself is often the most surprising part of the story.

The bombardier beetle, a small dark beetle that hides under logs, answers an attack by aiming the tip of its abdomen at the attacker and firing a scalding spray, mixed only at that moment from two chemicals it keeps apart inside its body. A cornered skunk first warns, stamping its front feet, raising its tail and hissing, and only then fires its musk, a reeking spray of sulfur compounds called thiols that sears a predator's eyes and nose.

The beetle's two harmless liquids, hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide, wait in separate tanks until it is bitten. Then it squirts them, along with powerful enzymes, into a tough little reaction chamber at its rear, where the reaction flash-heats the fluid to near 100°C and blasts it out at the attacker. A skunk aims just as well, because each of the two musk glands under its tail ends in its own nozzle that the skunk can point, landing the spray on target from about 3 meters away, while the smell drifts as far as 1.5 kilometers.

Inside the beetle's chamber, the pressure spikes so hard that it slams shut the valves leading back to the storage tanks, protecting its own organs, and the blast vents outward. A hagfish, an eel-shaped, jawless creature of the deep sea, escapes a shark's bite by releasing tiny bundles of mucus and tightly wound protein threads that burst open in seawater, filling the shark's mouth almost instantly with nearly a liter of gill-clogging slime. That slime is 99.996 percent seawater, held together by tens of thousands of silky threads. A cornered sea cucumber, a soft, sausage-shaped cousin of sea stars, can tear open its own rear end and fling out its toxic, coated guts at the attacker, then regrow the lost organs over days to weeks. Some sea cucumbers have a second weapon, Cuvierian tubules, milky threads that stay soft while they shoot out and stretch about twentyfold, until on contact a stiffening protein called tensilin locks their collagen rigid and the predator is trapped. A ladybug's red-and-black shell advertises that it tastes foul, and when poked it bleeds on purpose from its leg joints, oozing its own bitter yellow blood, laced with an alkaloid called coccinelline.

In 1990 Thomas Eisner's team at Cornell filmed firing bombardier beetles with a high-speed camera and found that the spray comes out not in a steady stream but in rapid bursts, roughly 500 pulses every second. The whip scorpion, or vinegaroon, sprays acetic acid, the acid that gives vinegar its sour taste, from a pore at the base of its whip-like tail, at about 84 percent strength, the most concentrated acetic acid known in nature. Its long tail is a feeler, not a stinger. Skeptics claimed the bombardier beetle's weapon was far too complex to have evolved step by step, but Metrius contractus, the most primitive living bombardier beetle, has the same two-chamber glands and hot quinone chemistry and simply lets a bubbling foam well up and coat its own body, a stage that came before the explosive jet. It shows how the weapon could have built up in useful steps.

ditching-a-body-part-autotomy.context_blurb:
When a predator gets a grip, some animals simply let go of the part it holds: a lizard its tail, a crab its claw, a sea cucumber its insides. Biologists call this autotomy, meaning 'self-cutting,' a clean, deliberate break that buys an escape and is often followed by regrowth.

The green anole is a bright green lizard of the southern United States. When a bird snatches one by the tail, the tail comes away in the beak and the lizard sprints off without bleeding. Its tail is made with a weak seam where it is meant to break, so it snaps free in an instant. The sea cucumber, a soft, slow, sausage-shaped reef animal, can neither swim nor bite. When a fish seizes it, the cucumber squeezes hard and fires its own guts out of its back end at the attacker. The sticky organs distract the fish, and the cucumber regrows them later; the move is called evisceration.

When a fox catches a leopard gecko, the dropped tail thrashes, lunges and flips on its own, leaping up to 3 centimeters high for as long as 30 minutes, while the gecko escapes. Crabs and lobsters shed whole legs or claws at a ready-made break point, the basi-ischium. A crab's body fluid is not held in neat vessels, so an open stump could drain it. Instead, a membrane at the break seals the wound the instant the claw comes away. A soft, folded limb bud then waits at the stump until the crab next molts out of its old shell, and only then unfolds and hardens into a working claw.

Regrowth is rarely a perfect copy. A skink's regrown tail has no chain of little vertebrae, only one stiff rod of cartilage with no breaking points, so if the new tail is grabbed it can only break off closer to the body, above the rod. Lizards save the trick for a last resort, because the tail is costly to lose. In many skinks and geckos it is the main store of fat, the lizard's energy reserve. A tailless lizard is also slower and often loses fights and territory to rivals. Still, the escape is so useful that evolution invented autotomy independently at least nine times, in groups as unrelated as lizards, sea cucumbers, crabs and worms.

faking-it-mimicry.context_blurb:
Mimicry is the art of looking, sounding or acting like something else. A harmless animal may copy a dangerous one to scare off predators, dangerous animals may copy each other, and a hunter may fake a friendly signal to lure its prey. Biologists have found it everywhere, from snakes and butterflies to fireflies and octopuses.

The scarlet kingsnake of the American South is harmless, but its red, yellow and black bands copy the coral snake, a deadly snake of the same region, so predators leave it alone. Mimicry can work the other way, too. The alligator snapping turtle lies still on a river bottom with its mouth open and wiggles a pink, worm-shaped part of its own tongue, and when a fish darts in for the "worm," the jaws slam shut. This is aggressive mimicry, a fake friendly signal that draws prey close.

A copycat is safe only where the real danger lives. A scarlet kingsnake in a Florida county with coral snakes is left alone, because predators there have learned to fear the pattern from the real thing, but in a county with no coral snakes, birds eat it. This is Batesian mimicry, a harmless faker borrowing a dangerous model's warning. Stinging wasps and bees play a different game. Dozens of species that really can sting share almost identical yellow-and-black stripes, so a predator has to learn that warning only once, and every species benefits. Biologists call that Müllerian mimicry.

On sandy Indo-Pacific seafloors, the mimic octopus, Thaumoctopus mimicus, impersonates other animals on demand. It spreads its arms out in a spiky fan to pose as a venomous lionfish, hides six arms and holds the rest out straight to look like a banded sea snake, or flattens all eight behind it to glide like a flatfish. There is evidence that it picks each disguise to suit the particular predator it is facing at that moment. Fireflies have a darker trick. A male Photinus firefly blinks his species' code over a summer meadow, and a female of his kind flashes the right answer back. But a female Photuris, a firefly of a different genus, can fake the answering flash code of other species, up to three of them, luring the males in and then eating them.

Photuris gets more than a meal: Photinus males carry bitter steroids called lucibufagins that she cannot make herself, and after she eats them she tastes foul too, so jumping spiders spit her out. Textbooks long called the viceroy butterfly a tasty cheat copying the toxic monarch. In 1991 Ritland and Brower tested the taste directly, offering red-winged blackbirds butterfly bodies with the wings removed. The viceroy turned out to be just as distasteful as the monarch, so the pair is a Müllerian partnership, not a cheat and its model.

Mimicry can even outlive its model. Coral snakes had vanished from the North Carolina Sandhills by about 1960. Yet when Akcali and Pfennig measured museum kingsnakes from the decades that followed, the red and black bands had come to match the lost coral snake's exact proportions more and more closely. They call it evolutionary momentum: a predator that mistook a real coral snake for a harmless one died, while wrongly avoiding a kingsnake cost almost nothing, so the disguise kept sharpening. One butterfly species, Heliconius numata, comes in as many as seven forms, each a copy of a different poisonous butterfly, and every form is inherited cleanly. Joron and colleagues showed why: all the pattern genes sit together in a supergene, one block of chromosome held together by an inversion, which stops the genes from shuffling and passes each disguise on as a single unit.

playing-dead-tonic-immobility.context_blurb:
Many animals answer a deadly threat by going limp and faking death, a defense biologists call tonic immobility, or thanatosis. It is more than lying still: the animal's body chemistry, smell and even heartbeat change, often enough that a predator loses interest and lets go.

The classic death-faker is the Virginia opossum of North America, a slow, cat-sized animal that, when cornered, collapses with its eyes glazed open and its tongue lolling out, which is where the phrase playing possum comes from. Faking death turns up across a huge range of animals, from beetles, spiders and crickets to ducks, frogs, lizards, snakes and even sharks and seahorses.

As a fainting opossum lies limp, glands under its tail ooze a foul green fluid while it drools, wets itself and soils the ground, so it reeks like a body that has been rotting for days, and many predators, which avoid spoiled meat, drop it.

The faint is real: when scientists wired up opossums, the heart rate dropped almost by half, about 46 percent, breathing slowed by about 31 percent and the body cooled slightly. Sharks flipped upside down fall into the same limp trance, and off Mexico an orca group called Moctezuma's pod uses it against young great white sharks: the orcas flip a shark over and, while it lies paralyzed, rip out its rich, oily liver and eat it.

safety-in-numbers.context_blurb:
For a small animal, open water or open grassland is a dangerous place to be alone. Sardines, starlings, herring and meerkats all live in crowds, and a crowd defends itself in clever ways: by overloading a hunter's eyes, by sharing the work of keeping watch, and by moving as one.

When a tuna charges a tight, flashing school of sardines, so many fish twist and dart at once that its eyes are swamped and it struggles to pick out and follow any one fish; biologists call this the confusion effect.

Dolphins turn the trick around: a superpod of common dolphins herds the sardines up to the surface into a packed, churning sphere called a bait ball, so the school's own instinct to crowd together becomes its trap. In the Kalahari Desert, a meerkat family posts one sentinel on a lookout mound, and it gives one alarm bark for a hawk in the sky and a different bark for a snake on the ground, so the others know which way to run without ever looking up. The calls even tell the mob how urgent the danger is.

Inside a bait ball, each sardine wriggles toward the crowded middle. In 1971 the British biologist W. D. Hamilton called a group formed this way a selfish herd: it holds together not through teamwork but because each animal edges inward to put its neighbors between itself and danger, and the safest spot is the middle.

Starlings swirl over Rome on winter evenings in clouds of thousands, a murmuration, folding away like one body when a peregrine falcon dives. In 2008 Andrea Cavagna's team filmed flocks of up to 4,000 starlings from several angles and reconstructed each flock in three dimensions, and found that every bird keeps track of a fixed number of neighbors, about seven, rather than all the birds within a set distance. Counting neighbors instead of measuring distance keeps the flock from tearing apart.

Herring keep their places in the school even in pitch-black water because each fish feels its neighbors through its lateral line, a line of pressure sensors running down each side, packed with clusters of hair cells that read the tiny wakes a nearby fish makes when it speeds up or turns.

spines-and-quills.context_blurb:
Spines, quills and prickles are one of nature's favorite defenses: make yourself painful to bite, and most predators give up. Porcupines, hedgehogs, pufferfish, lionfish, sea urchins and starfish all carry sharp weapons, but each group arms and uses them in its own way, and some add venom or poison to the points.

A slow, chunky pufferfish cannot outswim a hunter, so it gulps water into a stretchy stomach sac and swells to as much as three times its normal size, becoming a spiny ball far too big to swallow. A hedgehog has spines only on its back and sides, so when a fox catches it in the open it curls into a tight ball, pulling the spiny skin over its soft, unprotected belly.

Porcupines cannot shoot their quills; that old story is a myth. The barbed quills are only loosely rooted, so they come away the instant a predator touches them and stay stuck in whatever brushed against them. The African crested porcupine, a giant among porcupines, never has to face an attacker: it charges backward and rams its quill-covered rump into the predator, and its quills have been found driven more than six inches into a lion's snout.

Each quill is a stiff, hollow, modified hair whose tip carries microscopic barbs pointing backward, which slide in easily but catch in the flesh, and the victim's own muscle movements work the quill deeper. A ring-shaped muscle that runs around a hedgehog's body, the orbicularis, draws the spiny skin shut over the belly like the string of a purse and holds it there with very little effort, so the hedgehog can stay balled up for hours and simply wait a predator out. The porcupinefish keeps its spines, which are modified scales, lying flat until danger comes; when it gulps water and swells, they stand straight out, turning it into a bristling ball. The lionfish drifts in the open, striped boldly in red, white and black, because its up to 18 venomous spines make it dangerous, and the stripes are warning coloration, telling predators that the sting is not worth the meal.

Easy to push in yet hard to pull out, the barbed porcupine quill solves a problem engineers had chased for centuries, and it has inspired improved hypodermic needles and surgical staples that hold tissue. Many pufferfish also carry tetrodotoxin, a poison made by marine bacteria that climbs the food chain; puffers raised on toxin-free food are harmless. There is no antidote: tetrodotoxin plugs the sodium channels that nerves and muscles use to fire, so the nerves fall silent, the breathing muscles go limp and the victim suffocates while fully awake. The crown-of-thorns starfish, a coral-eater of Indo-Pacific reefs, is covered in venomous spines 2 to 3 centimeters long but has no way to inject; instead, the venom-coated skin of a spine tears away and stays in the wound when it pierces an attacker. The flower urchin's pretty pink-and-white flowers are really venomous pincers, tiny jaws that snap shut on a threat and inject a paralyzing nerve poison, and they can break off and keep injecting for hours.

DNA shows that the two porcupine families invented their quills separately: the tree-climbing New World porcupines of the Americas are closest kin to guinea pigs, capybaras and other South American rodents, not to the Old World porcupines of Africa and Asia, and the two lines split some 30 to 40 million years ago. Their hardware differs to match: New World quills are round and barbed, while many Old World porcupines grow longer, grooved, mostly barbless quills and hollow tail quills that rattle a warning.

vanishing-camouflage-and-active-color-ch.context_blurb: Camouflage lets an animal disappear into its background. It can be as simple as a fixed color pattern that matches a specific environment, or as sophisticated as a cephalopod's skin changing pattern, color, and texture in a fraction of a second. Both kinds matter here, from the quiet static camouflage of a stick insect or a stonefish to the active, changing camouflage of octopuses and flatfish, and the sensory machinery each kind depends on.

wearing-a-warning-aposematism.context_blurb: Some animals do the opposite of camouflage: instead of hiding, they wear bright, bold colors that advertise the fact that they taste bad, sting, or are toxic. Biologists call this aposematism, and the strategy only works when predators learn to associate the signal with a bad experience. Poison dart frogs, monarch butterflies, skunks, and coral snakes all use some version of warning signaling, and the signal has to be loud, consistent, and backed up by a real cost to the attacker.

all-in-vs-none-parental-investment.context_blurb:
Every animal parent faces the same budget problem: a lifetime holds only so much food, energy and time. Some species pour almost everything into a few young and guard them fiercely. Others scatter vast numbers of eggs and leave them to luck. From the frozen Antarctic to tropical reefs, the oceans show both bets at their most extreme.

The emperor penguin sits at the all-in end. In the dark Antarctic winter the female lays a single egg and leaves for the sea. Her mate keeps the egg balanced on his feet beneath a warm fold of belly skin, holding it near 38°C while blizzards howl and the air falls to -40°C. The female sea turtle makes the opposite bet. She crawls up a beach at night, digs a pit, lays roughly 80 to 120 eggs, buries them, and then hauls herself back into the surf for good, never meeting her young. Weeks later the hatchlings dig themselves out and race for the waves with no parent in sight.

A giant Pacific octopus mother hangs tens of thousands of eggs from the roof of her den, then spends roughly six months blowing fresh water over them and grooming them clean without eating a single meal, living off her own body fat until she dies soon after they hatch. The ocean sunfish, Mola mola, goes to the other extreme: a female can release up to 300 million eggs at once, more than any other known animal with a backbone, each about a millimeter across, and she gives them no care at all. Nearly all are eaten. Some fish take a guarding middle path. A cichlid mother in Africa's great lakes carries her eggs, and later her fry, in her mouth for up to two weeks without eating, and when a predator glides near, the whole cloud of babies darts back into her mouth.

The penguin father's sacrifice can be weighed. Through the winter he fasts about 120 days in all, huddled on the ice, and loses about 20 kilograms, shrinking from roughly 38 to 18. What keeps the egg alive is his brood patch, a bare, blood-rich patch of skin on his belly held at about 36 to 37°C, nearly 80 degrees warmer than the air, and the males crowd together in dense huddles, shuffling so each takes a turn out of the wind. When the mother returns fat with fish, the pair must pass the egg from his feet to hers in seconds, because if it sits bare on the ice longer than about two minutes, the embryo freezes and dies. Fathers carry the load among some reef fish too. In cardinalfish, small big-eyed fish of tropical reefs, the male holds the whole egg mass in his mouth for two weeks or longer, unable to feed, and every two or three minutes he gapes in a yawn that churns the eggs and bathes them in fresh, oxygen-rich water. The sea turtle's gamble pays only in bulk, since only about 1 hatchling in 1,000 lives to become an adult. That is why she lays thousands of eggs over her life.

Biologists call the two broad strategies few-and-tended and many-and-abandoned; the sea turtle shares the abandoning extreme with the sunfish, while the octopus, the penguin and the mouth-brooding fish are all tenders. Neither camp is the better answer; each solves the same problem a different way. Even the octopus mother's death turned out to be part of her strategy. In 1977 the biologist Jerome Wodinsky removed both optic glands, a pair of organs behind the eyes, from brooding octopus mothers, and they left the eggs, began to feed and survived for months beyond the usual end, proving that her death is a self-destruct program switched on by hormones, not exhaustion or old age.

eggs-vs-live-birth.context_blurb:
Animals produce their young in two main ways: they lay eggs, or they give birth to live young. Birds, frogs, insects and most fish and reptiles lay eggs, and most mammals carry their babies inside. But the line is messy. A few mammals lay eggs, some snakes and sharks give live birth, and in one fish the father does the birthing.

Almost every mammal grows its babies inside the mother, but the platypus and the four kinds of echidna, the monotremes, still lay eggs, a habit kept from their reptile-like ancestors. Birds have no exceptions at all: every bird, from a hummingbird to an ostrich, lays eggs, and not one species gives live birth. The leading explanation is flight, because carrying growing babies inside for weeks would make a flying animal too heavy, so a bird lays its egg and lets it finish developing outside.

A platypus mother lays one to three soft-shelled eggs, each about the size of a marble, curls around them in her burrow to keep them warm, and roughly ten days later each one hatches into a tiny puggle. What proves a monotreme is a mammal comes next: the mother nurses her babies with milk, the defining mammal trait. She has no nipples, so the milk oozes from patches of skin and the baby laps it up.

In seahorses the roles flip: the female puts her eggs into a pouch on the male's belly, and he carries them, feeds them through a network of blood vessels and then gives birth to the young himself, a true male pregnancy. Snakes are split as well. Pythons and boa constrictors look alike, but a female python produces eggs and wraps her coils around them. A female boa is a live-bearer instead: she carries her young for four to five months and then gives birth to a wriggling litter of ten to sixty-five live snakelets.

A seahorse birth is hard work, because the father's pouch squeezes again and again for hours, firing out young in bursts, up to about 2,000 of them in a single birth. Some sharks and skates lay eggs instead of bearing live young, sealing each embryo in a tough leathery case with four curly horns at its corners. Beachcombers who find these dried cases on the sand call them mermaid's purses.

Live birth can carry a species into the cold: the European adder, Vipera berus, keeps its young inside her and warms them by basking, which lets it range up to 69 degrees north, inside the Arctic Circle, farther north than any other snake. Live birth can also be brutal. A pregnant sand tiger shark starts with up to 50 embryos in her two wombs. In each womb the largest embryo grows teeth first and then eats its smaller siblings, so only one pup is born from each side, about 3 feet long.

Eggs had their own great breakthrough. A frog's jelly eggs shrivel in dry air, which keeps frogs tied to water. The first reptiles evolved the amniotic egg, sealed in a shell around four inner membranes and carrying its own supplies, and that invention gave rise to all of today's reptiles, birds and mammals. What happens inside an egg can be strange too. An American alligator egg has no sex chromosomes; the warmth of the nest decides. Females hatch from both cool and hot nests, and males only from a narrow middle band, roughly 32.5 to 33.5 degrees Celsius, so a warming climate can tip a whole population toward one sex.

Live birth is ancient. A 248-million-year-old fossil of Chaohusaurus, among the earliest sea reptiles shaped like fish, was caught in the middle of giving birth, with three young at different stages. Ocean reptiles today deliver tail-first, so a newborn cannot drown before it is fully out. But these babies were emerging head-first, the pattern of land animals, so Motani and his colleagues argued that these reptiles inherited live birth from ancestors on land and carried it into the sea.

insect-super-societies-eusociality.context_blurb:
Some insects live in societies so tightly organized that the whole colony works like one giant body. Honeybees, ants, termites and some wasps share the same plan: one mother lays the eggs, while thousands or millions of workers who never breed raise her young, gather food and defend the nest. Biologists call this eusociality, and at least one mammal lives the same way.

In a hive of some 50,000 honeybees, nearly all are female workers who never lay eggs, and each is the queen's own daughter, so the hive is one huge family serving one mother.

A queen takes just one mating flight, early in her life, and keeps millions of sperm stored in a pouch in her body for years. She then decides the sex of each egg: a fertilized egg becomes a female, a worker or a new queen, while one she deliberately leaves unfertilized hatches into a male drone. Biologists call this system haplodiploidy. Each summer she lays a few thousand such eggs, and the drones that hatch, males with huge eyes and no sting, do no work in the hive at all: their only job is mating with a queen. In autumn the workers shove them out to die. A leafcutter ant colony of the genus Atta, in the tropical forests of Central and South America, can hold about five million workers, all of them daughters of one queen, and she can live over a decade, laying eggs the whole time.

Atta workers are built in a range of sizes, and each size has its own job: big-jawed majors guard the nest, while the tiniest, the minims, spend their lives deep underground tending a garden of fungus. The ants cut leaves not to eat them but to feed that fungus, which they then eat, and their division of labor makes the colony work like one superorganism. Eciton army ants of the American tropics have no fixed home; the colony roams the jungle as a hunting swarm, and each night the workers hook their legs together and link their own bodies into a living wall, the bivouac, with the queen and larvae sheltered inside. Eciton soldiers carry huge, curved, saber-like jaws built purely for fighting, so a soldier cannot even feed itself, and ordinary workers must feed it mouth to mouth.

Deep in a red-earth mound on the African savanna lies a Macrotermes termite queen whose belly has swollen to about 11 centimeters long, too huge for her to move, and, tended by her workers, she lays about 30,000 eggs a day for years. Biologists call that swelling physogastry.

Why would a worker give up breeding to raise her mother's young? W. D. Hamilton's classic answer pointed to haplodiploidy: because males come from unfertilized eggs, two full sisters share on average about three-quarters of their genes, more than the half a mother shares with her own young, so a worker may pass on more of her genes by raising sisters. It was a leading idea, not settled fact. Termites broke the story, because they live the same way without haplodiploidy, and Jacobus Boomsma proposed a theory that covers every case: each origin of these societies began with a founding mother who mated with just one male for her entire life. Under strict lifelong monogamy, a female is exactly as related to her full siblings as to her own young, so staying home to raise siblings costs her nothing in genes. Boomsma found that all eight separate origins of eusociality among bees, ants and wasps trace to such a mother.

The naked mole-rat, a hairless, wrinkled rodent of the Horn of Africa, runs its burrow like a hive, with one breeding queen and dozens of sterile workers, and it can live about 30 years, roughly ten times as long as a house mouse. When a queen dies, breeding-age females fight, sometimes to the death, for her place, and once the winner starts having pups her backbone lengthens, the vertebrae of her lower back growing about 32 percent longer so she can carry more young. Oxygen runs low in its stuffy tunnels, and with none at all a naked mole-rat can last about 18 minutes, because when normal glucose burning jams, its cells switch to fructose, a sugar they can burn without oxygen, much as plants do.

metamorphosis.context_blurb:
Many animals do not simply grow bigger. They rebuild themselves from one body into a completely different one, a change called metamorphosis: a crawling eater becomes a flier, and a gilled swimmer becomes a hopper with lungs. Insects and frogs do it in different ways, and the most extreme versions melt the young body down and build the adult from the pieces.

A caterpillar is the young of a butterfly: it does little but eat leaves and grow, then seals itself into a hard case, where its body breaks down and is rebuilt as a winged butterfly. In a spring pond, a tadpole swims with a finned tail and takes oxygen from the water through gills, then over a few weeks it grows legs, soaks up its own tail, becoming a frog with lungs that leaps on land.

A butterfly caterpillar wraps itself in nothing: its last skin turns into a hard, smooth case hanging from a little silk pad, often flecked with metallic gold or silver, and the case is called a chrysalis, from chrysos, the Ancient Greek word for gold. A moth caterpillar takes an extra step, first wrapping itself in silk it spins, so the cocoon belongs to moths and the bare chrysalis to butterflies. The periodical cicada of the eastern United States spends 13 or 17 years underground as a nymph, sucking sap from tree roots, then climbs out, molts one last time and lives just four to six weeks as a winged adult. A newly hatched butterfly's wings are small, damp and crumpled, and it inflates them by pumping its blood, called hemolymph, into the wing veins until they stretch to full size and stiffen.

Inside the chrysalis, enzymes released by the caterpillar digest most of its tissues, so a chrysalis opened at the right moment would ooze a thick yellowish soup, not a tiny folded butterfly. A young grasshopper skips the pupa entirely: it hatches looking like a small, wingless version of the adults, a young form called a nymph, and simply molts into bigger bodies, sprouting wings bit by bit, a pattern called incomplete metamorphosis. A dragonfly nymph hunts underwater for months or years, shooting out a hinged lower jaw to grab tadpoles and small fish, and when it is ready it climbs out of the pond, its skin splits down the back, and the winged adult pulls free.

How is a butterfly rebuilt from soup? Small groups of cells called imaginal discs come through the breakdown intact, one for each adult part such as the wings, legs, eyes and antennae, all set aside back in the egg, and they use the soup as raw material. In a fruit fly, the wing's disc starts with about 50 cells when the larva seals itself in, and by the time the adult emerges it has multiplied to about 50,000. A frog's change is run by thyroid hormone, which sets off a planned self-destruction of the tail's cells, recycling the whole tail within days, and which also grows the hind legs, builds lungs and turns a plant-eater's gut into a meat-eater's.

Martha Weiss and Doug Blackiston gave tobacco hornworm caterpillars a mild shock whenever they smelled ethyl acetate, and after the caterpillars dissolved and rebuilt as adult moths, the moths kept steering clear of that smell, so some memory survives the soup. The axolotl never makes the change at all: because its thyroid signal never fires, it breeds while keeping its gills and tail fin for life, a condition called neoteny, and an injection of thyroxine will finally make it transform. At every caterpillar molt, juvenile hormone in the blood acts as a brake: while it is present, the trigger for each molt just builds a bigger caterpillar, and only once it fades in the final caterpillar stage can the body build a pupa. Carroll Williams called it the status quo hormone, and his golden oil, an extract rich in it from Cecropia silkmoths, could make a pupa form a second pupa instead of an adult.

pouches-and-tiny-newborns-marsupials.context_blurb:
Marsupials are mammals that give birth to tiny, barely formed young and finish raising them outside the body, usually in a pouch. They live mostly in Australia and the Americas, and every step of their strange parenting, from birth to weaning, works differently from ours.

Opossums, wombats, koalas, kangaroos and Tasmanian devils all belong to the marsupials, the pouched mammals, unlike placental mammals such as mice and monkeys, which carry their babies to full term inside the womb. After only about 33 days inside its mother, a red kangaroo is born blind, hairless and about the size of a jellybean, roughly 2 centimeters long and under a gram.

Born near the base of the tail, the newborn gets no help from its mother: it hauls itself up through her fur on tiny clawed forelimbs, the only well-developed part of its body. The climb takes about three minutes, and with no working eyes the newborn steers by a keen sense of smell and of direction. A Virginia opossum, the only marsupial living wild in North America, gives birth to more than twenty babies at once, but she has only about 13 teats, so only the newborns that reach a teat live. Her pregnancy lasts just 12 or 13 days.

Once a joey latches on, the teat's tip balloons into a bulb within the joey's mouth, locking the pair together for months so firmly that the joey stays put even when its mother bounds at full speed. A red kangaroo's pouch opens forward, yet her joey never falls out mid-leap, because a strong sphincter muscle lets her cinch the opening shut like a drawstring bag. A wombat's pouch opens backward, toward her hind legs, so when she digs her burrow and throws dirt back under her belly, she does not bury her baby.

A red kangaroo can keep a fertilized embryo of about 100 cells paused inside her, and what holds it on pause is the suckling of the joey that already fills her pouch; when the pouch empties, the embryo starts to grow. A mother red kangaroo often feeds a big joey at foot and a tiny newborn in the pouch at once, making two different milks from two teats at the same time: fat-rich milk for the older joey and low-fat, immune-rich milk for the newborn. At five to six months, a koala joey eats pap, a soft dropping from its mother's gut, not for calories but for the live gut bacteria that let it digest tough, toxic eucalyptus. A kangaroo mother carries two separate uteruses because, in the marsupial embryo, the ureters, the tubes draining the kidneys down to the bladder, pass between the paired reproductive tracts as they form and keep them from fusing into the single system of placental mammals.

showing-off-to-win-a-mate-sexual-selecti.context_blurb:
Many of the showiest things in nature exist to win a mate: a peacock's fan, a bowerbird's decorated stage, a spider's rainbow dance. Biologists call this sexual selection. Usually the males perform and the females choose, and over many generations that choosing reshapes the males, sometimes into something that looks almost ruinous.

The famous fan is not a peacock's tail at all but his train: about 140 to 170 long feathers that grow just above his short true tail, each ending in an eyespot of blue, copper, green and bronze, together about 1.5 meters long. A male satin bowerbird of eastern Australia builds an avenue of twigs, two woven walls side by side, and heaps the ground before it with blue: parrot feathers, berries, flowers, even bottle caps and clothes pegs. Unusually, the female judges his architecture and decorating, not his own plumage.

When the peacock raises and quivers his train, he is not challenging rivals but advertising, and then he waits while the peahen looks him over and makes up her mind, because in peafowl the female does the choosing. The train is heavy, drags at him in flight and catches a predator's eye, and that burden is the point: only a truly fit male can survive while hauling it around, so the ornament is an honest signal because it is costly. The male peacock spider of Australia, about 5 millimeters across, raises a rainbow fan on his abdomen and waves his third pair of legs like flags, and his colors come not from pigment but from light-bending nanostructures in his scales, the same physics that makes a soap bubble shimmer.

At Whipsnade, Marion Petrie snipped eyespots off some males' trains, and even though the trains still glittered, the peahens lost interest in those males and picked rivals whose eyespots were whole, proof that females read the eyespots themselves. The satin bowerbird even paints, chewing berries or charcoal into colored pulp and daubing it onto his twig walls, sometimes holding a wad of bark in his beak as a crude brush, a rare case of a bird using a tool to decorate. Because blue things are scarce on the forest floor, males raid the bowers of absent rivals and steal their prize blue objects. Gerald Borgia found that older, more experienced males build neater bowers and pile up more blue loot, partly by out-thieving their rivals. Before he dances, a male superb bird-of-paradise clears a patch of forest floor into a clean stage; then he flicks up a jet-black cape into an oval framing two bright blue eyespots that look like a grinning face, and if his moves are not flawless, the female walks away.

In a 1994 breeding study, Petrie found that chicks fathered by the peacocks with the most elaborate trains grew bigger and survived better than chicks of plainer fathers, so the fan really does advertise good genes. The great bowerbird covers his display court with pale stones, bones and shells, arranged from small at the front, where the female stands to watch, to large at the back. That size gradient is forced perspective, the stage designer's trick, an illusion that changes how the scene looks, and Laura Kelley and John Endler showed that the males who build the strongest illusion win the most mates. A peacock spider also courts on a second channel, drumming vibrations through the ground that the female feels through her legs, and the stakes are high, because a female he fails to impress may eat him. The bird-of-paradise's cape is among the blackest feathers known, soaking up as much as 99.95 percent of the light that hits it with no extra pigment: its tiny barbules are tilted and curved into deep cups, so light bounces among them until almost none escapes. Beside that super-black, the blue looks even brighter.

Why female choice runs to such extremes is an old fight. Amos Zahavi's handicap principle holds that an ornament must be costly so that a weak male cannot fake it, an idea Alan Grafen showed could work in 1990. Ronald Fisher's rival runaway idea says no honesty is needed: choosy mothers bear both showy sons and choosy daughters, so the taste and the trait reinforce each other and balloon together. Modern work suggests the two explanations need not exclude each other.

switching-sex.context_blurb:
For many animals, male and female are not fixed for life. Some reef fish change sex partway through life, in one direction or the other, as their social group changes, and some snails and worms are both sexes at once. Each strategy is a different answer to the problem of passing on genes, and each is a wonder of animal biology on its own terms.

A clownfish family lives inside one stinging sea anemone in a strict order of size: the biggest fish is the female and lays the eggs, the second-biggest is the breeding male, and the smaller ones do not breed at all. Common earthworms swap sperm belly-to-belly on damp nights, and each one drives about 30 of its 40 tiny bristles into its partner to keep the slippery pair from sliding apart.

When the female clownfish dies, her partner changes sex and becomes the new egg-laying female, a one-way switch that cannot be undone; this male-first pattern is called protandry, and clownfish are the classic example. The whole rank then moves up: the largest remaining non-breeder, the role little Nemo plays in Finding Nemo, grows into the new breeding male and mates with her. The film's tidy father-and-son ending is not how a real clownfish family works.

The California sheephead, a wrasse of the Pacific kelp forests, works the other way: every fish is born a pink female, and between the ages of four and six, or when the harem's male dies, the dominant female turns into the male, growing a black head and tail with a red band around the middle. This female-first switch is called protogyny, and it can be finished in as little as five days to two weeks. Each garden snail is male and female at once, and just before mating each one fires a sharp chalky love dart into its mate, whose chemical coating boosts the shooter's chances of fathering the partner's eggs.

In the common clownfish, the change begins in the brain, not the gonads: a brain region called the preoptic area grows to female size within about six months while the gonads are still male, and some fish stay that way for over three years. As the biologist Justin Rhodes put it, such a fish has a female brain and male gonads. The Caribbean bluehead wrasse starts life drab yellow-brown and female; when the dominant fish becomes a terminal-phase male, it turns green, gains black-and-white bands and grows a bright blue head, which gives the species its name. When the male is removed, a female starts acting male within hours and completes the change in about eight days.
