virgin-birth-parthenogenesis.context_blurb: In a handful of animal species, females can produce offspring without any input from a male. Biologists call this parthenogenesis. It is common among some lizards, insects, and crustaceans, and it has been documented in a few surprising places, including sharks, snakes, and birds in captivity. The interesting questions are how parthenogenesis works at the genetic level, what triggers it in species that can do both options, and the specific trade-offs that come with reproducing without a partner.

ankylosaurus.context_blurb:
Ankylosaurus, a plant-eater of western North America, lived about 68 to 66 million years ago, among the last of the armored dinosaurs. It shared its world with huge meat-eaters such as T. rex, and nearly every part of its body was a defense, built to survive in a land of giant predators.

Low, wide and four-legged, Ankylosaurus was the classic armored tank of the dinosaur world, plated in bone from head to tail as it grazed. From nose to tail it measured 6 to 8 meters, about a school bus, and it weighed perhaps 5 to 8 tonnes, roughly as much as an elephant, body and armor together.

Bony plates grew right in its skin, from pebble-sized knobs to tiles longer than a foot. It even had bony eyelids, plates of bone that could close over its eyes, a feature found in almost no other known dinosaur. Yet the underside went bare: its belly carried no armor, so the animal hugged the ground to keep that soft spot from a predator's jaws, and its species name, magniventris, means "great belly."

Its tail ended in a bony club as big as a beach ball; one measured 60 centimeters long and 49 wide. To swing that club, the last seven tail bones were welded together into one rigid handle, with knobs of armor fused over the tip. Its wide skull ended in a broad, flat beak shaped like a shovel, which cropped low ferns and shrubs without choosing the best leaves, a style called non-selective low browsing.

Chewing was not its strength. Its teeth were tiny, just a few millimeters tall, and its jaws too weak to grind, so paleontologists infer that microbes in a huge, chambered gut fermented the plants it swallowed nearly whole, the way modern plant-eating lizards digest their food. Its head held another secret. In its relative Euoplocephalus, the nasal passage looped and twisted for about 80 centimeters inside the snout, working as a heat exchanger that recovered up to 84 percent of each breath's heat and cooled the blood flowing to the small brain.

A popular claim says the club could shatter a T. rex leg, and when the scientists Arbour and Snively modeled the impacts, they found the blow was real but rare: only adults with the biggest knobs, wider than about half a meter, struck with around ten times the force bone can withstand, while average and small clubs fell short.

archaeopteryx.context_blurb:
Archaeopteryx is a crow-sized feathered animal from the Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago, when southern Germany was a scatter of low tropical islands. Its fossils come from the fine limestone of Solnhofen, which preserves even single feathers. Since 1861 it has stood among the most famous fossils ever found, a creature caught between two worlds.

The first skeleton, lifted from the quarry in 1861, wore a full coat of real feathers that no earlier reptile had ever carried, and its name means "ancient wing." Germans called it the Urvogel, the "primeval bird," yet its jaws were lined with small, sharp teeth, a holdover from its reptile ancestors that no living bird keeps.

Each wing ended not in a smooth feathered tip but in three clawed fingers, claws that may have grasped prey or gripped branches. With feathers on one side of the ledger and teeth, finger claws and a long bony tail on the other, Archaeopteryx became the textbook transitional fossil linking meat-eating dinosaurs and birds, evidence that birds descend from dinosaurs related to the raptors.

The Solnhofen mud preserved a feather vane, the flat part along the shaft, so crisply that scientists could see it already had the shape of a modern bird's flight feather 150 million years ago. Better still, the two sides of that vane were lopsided, narrow on one edge and wide on the other, the uneven shape that helps a flying bird's feather grip the air, while flightless birds such as ostriches grow feathers with equal sides. Even so, Archaeopteryx lacked the deep, keeled breastbone that anchors a modern bird's big flight muscles, so scientists still argue whether it flapped weakly or mostly glided.

A 14th skeleton, the Chicago specimen described in 2025, preserved long tertial feathers along the upper arm for the first time, and they sealed the gap that its unusually long upper-arm bone opens between wing and body, so air could not leak through and the wing worked as one smooth surface. Its close feathered relatives had wing feathers that stopped at the elbow, a big reason they could not fly. Its bones tell a slower story: when scientists cut thin slices and counted the growth rings, they found Archaeopteryx grew about three times slower than a living bird its size, pausing each year like a small dinosaur rather than shooting up in weeks.

argentinosaurus.context_blurb:
Argentinosaurus was a long-necked, plant-eating titanosaur that roamed Patagonia, in the far south of Argentina, some 95 million years ago. It ranks among the largest animals ever to walk on land. Only a few of its bones have been found, so much of what we know about it comes from careful measuring and clever reasoning.

The discovery began in 1987, when the farmer Guillermo Heredia spotted a huge object on his land near Plaza Huincul, decided it was a petrified log and phoned the local museum; the "log" was a gigantic bone. Estimates make it 30 to 35 meters long, with a mass between 65 and 80 tons, heavier than a dozen African elephants put together and nearly as long as a basketball court.

No complete skeleton exists, only about seven back vertebrae, some ribs, a shinbone and a hip bone, so its length and weight come from scaling up the whole animal from that handful of its own bones, and honest paleontologists flag the uncertainty. Yet every Argentinosaurus started small, hatching from an egg somewhere between a cantaloupe and a basketball in size, and over decades it grew about 100 times longer to reach adult size.

Its back and neck bones were lightened inside by a complex pattern of air-filled chambers, the same trick modern birds use, so the giant could carry its bulk without a crushingly heavy skeleton. When a team led by Bill Sellers built a computer model of its muscles and bones and let software hunt for the most efficient way to move, the best it found was a slow walk, topping out near 2 meters per second, about 5 miles an hour, never a run or a gallop. They concluded that such a body is close to the limit of what a land animal can manage.

A rival giant, Patagotitan, was named from the same Patagonian badlands in 2017. Which titan is bigger depends on which back vertebrae researchers choose to measure: in 2017 Carballido and colleagues used the cross-section of the front back vertebrae to rank Patagotitan about 10 percent larger, while in 2019 Gregory Paul argued Argentinosaurus was still bigger because its backbone column was much longer. Several later studies favor Argentinosaurus again, so the crown keeps changing hands.

spinosaurus.context_blurb:
Spinosaurus was a giant meat-eating dinosaur of the rivers of North Africa, around 95 to 100 million years ago, where the Sahara Desert lies today. For most of the twentieth century it was known from a single partial skeleton that was destroyed in World War II. New fossils from Morocco show it was built unlike any other big predator, for a life tied to water.

Spinosaurus is the longest predatory dinosaur known, about 14 to 15 meters long (46 to 48 feet), a little longer than T. rex, which lived some 30 million years later in North America. Ernst Stromer, the German paleontologist who described it in 1915, found its most striking feature was a tall, skin-covered sail rising from its back, unlike anything carried by any other big predator. The sail was held up by bony spines up to about 1.8 meters (6 feet) tall, each a thin blade growing from a single vertebra and over ten times as tall as its vertebra was wide.

Unlike T. rex with its short, bone-crushing skull, Spinosaurus had a long, narrow, crocodile-like snout lined with straight, cone-shaped teeth with few or no serrations, built to grip slippery fish like fishhooks rather than saw through flesh. Its nostrils were set high up and well back from the tip of its snout, so like a crocodile it could keep most of its head underwater and still breathe. Its back legs were stubby, roughly a quarter of its whole body length, awkward on land but fitting for an animal that hunted in water.

Cristiano Dal Sasso noticed tiny pits clustered at the tip of its snout, the same pits that hold pressure sensors in living crocodiles, and they would have let Spinosaurus feel the ripples of prey moving in murky water. In 2020 Nizar Ibrahim's team, with Stephanie Pierce and George Lauder of Harvard, had a robot swish a flat plastic model of its paddle-shaped tail through a water tank, and it performed nearly as well as a crocodile's or a newt's tail, giving about eight times the forward thrust of land dinosaurs' tails.

How it hunted is still argued. Ibrahim's team sees its swimming tail and its heavy, dense bones, which would work like ballast, as evidence that it dove and chased fish underwater. Looking at the same bones, David Hone and Thomas Holtz argue instead that it waded in the shallows like a giant heron and snatched fish from the surface. Donald Henderson's 2018 buoyancy model found that it would float high and even tip sideways, making long underwater chases unlikely. Same fossils, opposite conclusions: the question is still open.

stegosaurus.context_blurb:
Stegosaurus was a big plant-eating dinosaur that roamed the floodplains of western North America in the Late Jurassic, some 150 million years back. With its double row of tall back plates and its spiked tail, it is one of the most recognizable dinosaurs of all, and paleontologists still argue over how it used its odd equipment.

Stegosaurus was about 6.5 to 7 meters long and weighed some 3.5 tonnes, with a double row of tall, pointed bony plates along its back and four sharp spikes at the end of its tail. There was no grass and no flowering plant anywhere yet, so Stegosaurus browsed within about a meter of the ground on ferns, mosses and other soft plants that grew low. Its brain weighed only about 80 grams, about the size of a walnut, in a braincase no bigger than a dog's. Its four tail spikes, each 60 to 90 centimeters long, are called the thagomizer, a name from a 1982 Far Side cartoon by Gary Larson that paleontologists such as Kenneth Carpenter later took up in earnest.

The spikes were real weapons: an Allosaurus tail bone from the American West has a round hole punched through it that a Stegosaurus spike fits exactly, and its edges are healed and remodeled, so the Allosaurus survived the stab. Nearly one in ten Stegosaurus skeletons shows battle damage on its tail spikes. The plates were far too thin to be armor, left the sides and belly bare and were laced with blood vessels, so most scientists now think they served for display and for heat control, soaking up sun or shedding heat. Museums once mounted the 17 to 22 plates in matching pairs, but skeletons found with their plates still in place show two rows that alternated, each plate offset from its neighbor on the other side.

The plates left the throat bare, exactly where a low-slung hunter would aim, but a mosaic of small bony studs called gular ossicles, set into the skin there, guarded it.

How hard it could bite is still debated. In 2010 Miriam Reichel's computer model found a feeble bite, able to snip only branches about a centimeter thick. But Stephan Lautenschlager's 2016 digital model of the whole skull of Sophie, a famous fossil, put its bite in the same range as a sheep's or a cow's, so it could have browsed tougher plants. Both models still stand.

triceratops.context_blurb:
Triceratops was a huge horned plant-eater of western North America in the final years of the dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. It lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex and is one of the most familiar dinosaurs of all, with its great bony frill and horned face, and its fossils still hold surprises.

Triceratops means three-horned face: it had one stubby horn on the snout and a pair of long brow horns, with a great shield of bone, the frill, spreading behind the skull. It was built like a giant rhinoceros, 26 to 30 feet long on stout, low legs, and the biggest weighed 6 to 10 tons.

It cropped tough leaves with its hooked, parrot-like beak and ground them down with dental batteries, some 36 to 40 columns of 3 to 5 stacked teeth each, up to 800 teeth at once, with fresh ones always rising to replace worn ones. Triceratops lived right up to 66 million years ago, among the very last dinosaurs, and its world ended in the extinction that followed when a city-sized asteroid struck what is now Mexico, at Chicxulub.

Its skull, about 8 feet long, was the largest of any land animal ever, nearly a third of its whole body length. Triceratops skulls carry far more healed frill wounds than the skulls of its one-horned cousin Centrosaurus, a sign that Triceratops locked horns and jousted with rivals of its own kind.

In 2015 Erickson and colleagues mapped five tissues in a Triceratops tooth, one more than in a horse's, including a soft dentine full of blood vessels that wore away about 1.6 times faster than its neighbor, carving a groove that kept the tooth self-sharpening. The groove works like the fuller ground into a sword blade. A growth series of skulls, from a 38-centimeter hatchling to 2-meter adults, showed that a young Triceratops had brow horns that curved backward toward the frill and only turned to point forward once it was fully grown.

tyrannosaurus-rex.context_blurb: Tyrannosaurus rex was a huge meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America at the very end of the age of the dinosaurs, about 68 to 66 million years ago. It is the most famous dinosaur in the world. Modern paleontology has reshaped the picture of T. rex considerably in the last few decades, from its bite force to its posture to the small size of its arms to whether it had feathers. Look closely at the specific details that current evidence actually supports.

velociraptor.context_blurb: Velociraptor was a small, feathered meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now Mongolia and northern China about 75 to 71 million years ago. The real Velociraptor was closer in size to a large turkey than to the people-sized predators in Jurassic Park. It had a long stiff tail, a brain unusually large for its body size, and a long curved claw on each foot that paleontologists have been studying with CT scans and physics models to work out how it was actually used.

basking-shark-cetorhinus-maximus.context_blurb:
The basking shark, Cetorhinus maximus, is a huge, slow shark of cool oceans around the world, the second-largest fish alive after the whale shark. It gathers in large numbers at a few predictable spots off Britain, Ireland and the northeastern United States, cruising near the surface with its vast mouth agape.

Though it can top 33 feet and weigh several tons, it eats only tiny drifting plankton, such as the shrimp-like copepods it strains from the sea. A diver who meets one has nothing to fear, because this gaping giant is completely harmless to people, a gentle filter-feeder with no interest in anything bigger than plankton.

Unlike the whale shark and the megamouth, which pump and gulp water across their filters, the basking shark just keeps cruising at about 2 knots, mouth agape, and lets its own forward motion ram the water through its gills; that way a five-meter shark can filter 500 tons of water in an hour. Inside, dark, comb-like gill rakers on the gill arches catch the copepods while the water flows out through the gills; the shark's real teeth are tiny, only 5 to 6 millimeters, and useless for feeding.

The Zuiyo-maru, a Japanese trawler working off New Zealand in 1977, netted a rotting carcass with a small head, a long neck and four flippers, and the crew took it for a plesiosaur, but tests on tissue they saved showed it was a decayed basking shark. A rotting basking shark loses its lower jaw, gills and fins first, leaving what looks like a small head on a long neck, so dead ones are often mistaken for sea monsters.

Off County Clare in Ireland, drone and underwater footage from 2016 to 2021 showed groups of 6 to 23 mature sharks, males and females in equal numbers, circling in a stacked ring, rolling belly-up and brushing fins, and David Sims called it slow-motion speed dating, the first courtship ever recorded for the species, where each shark can look over many potential partners at the same time.

Naturalists once believed basking sharks hibernated on the seabed through the lean winter, but David Sims worked out that filtering pays off whenever plankton is thicker than about half a gram per cubic meter, so the shark keeps feeding year-round on any patch rich enough and simply abandons thin water, where pushing its huge open mouth along would burn more energy than it gains.

cookiecutter-shark-isistius-brasiliensis.context_blurb:
The cookiecutter shark, Isistius brasiliensis, is a cigar-shaped little shark of the warm oceans that lives in the deep. For decades biologists found tidy round holes, like scoops from a melon baller, in whales, dolphins, tuna and even great whites, and no one knew what was making them.

Once scientists finally caught the culprit, its size was the shock: a female grows to only about 56 centimeters and a male about 42, barely half a meter, yet it bites the biggest and fiercest animals in the sea. The shark clamps its thick lips onto a giant's side, sinks in its lower teeth and spins its whole body before letting go. It leaves behind a near-perfect round crater about 5 centimeters wide and 7 deep, as if a cookie cutter had been pressed into dough.

The shark also glows. Its belly gives off a green light, the strongest glow known in any shark. A cookiecutter hauled onto a fishing boat at night soon goes still, yet its belly keeps shining green for as long as three hours.

That glow is camouflage. A hunter in the deep looks upward, where the faint light from the surface turns any swimmer above into a dark shape. The shark's lit belly matches that dim light from above and wipes out its own silhouette, a trick called counter-illumination. One part of the underside stays dark: a band beneath the throat. Seen from below against the glowing belly, that dark collar looks like the outline of a small fish, so big predators swim close to grab it, and the little shark bites them instead. It may be the only known lure made from a missing glow.

The lower teeth lock together into one connected row, like a saw blade, and when the row wears down, the whole set comes loose at once. The shark swallows the old set whole, recycling its calcium; one shark went through 15 full sets, over 400 teeth, while growing from 14 to 50 centimeters. The lips make a seal like a gasket, and then the shark pulls back its tongue, working it like the plunger of a syringe to suck the space inside its mouth empty, so the low pressure locks it on like a suction cup.

For all its fame as a whale biter, big animals are not its main food. In 2021 a team led by Carlisle worked out its diet from chemical tracers in its body, including isotopes, fats and scraps of DNA. Roughly 55 percent of the diet turned out to be small fish and squid of the middle depths, about 39 percent more midwater prey that migrates up and down, and only about 5 percent the big surface animals. Those famous flesh plugs are a side dish: tiny midwater fish and squid are what the cookiecutter mostly lives on.

frilled-shark-chlamydoselachus-anguineus.context_blurb:
The frilled shark is a long, dark, eel-shaped shark of the deep Atlantic and Pacific, usually found more than 500 meters down and nearly 2 meters long. It is called a living fossil, but recent research has shown that one of its most "ancient" features is not ancient at all.

Its family has a fossil record reaching back about 95 million years, so frilled sharks were already swimming when Tyrannosaurus rex walked the land. With its slender body and its mouth right at the tip of its snout, it looks less like a shark than a giant snake or eel, which earned it the nickname lizard shark.

Most sharks have five gill slits on each side, but the frilled shark has six pairs, ruffled and red, and the first pair wraps around its throat like a collar, giving it its name. Its jaws carry about 300 tiny teeth in some 25 rows. Each tooth is shaped like a trident with three points that curve backward, so a struggling squid only drives itself deeper onto them. Squid make up about 60 percent of its diet.

Because its jaws sit at the front, it cannot roll under prey as other sharks do. Instead it braces its tail, bends its body back like a spring and lunges like a striking snake, swallowing prey whole up to about half its own body length. One 1.6-meter shark held a whole catshark weighing 590 grams. It also bears live young, and its embryos grow only about 10 to 17 millimeters a month in the chilly, hungry depths. So a pregnancy may last an estimated 3.5 years, one of the longest of any backboned animal, though some studies suggest it may be shorter.

Its long jaws attach directly to the skull behind the eyes, which gives a huge gape but little leverage and only a weak bite. So the frilled shark lunges like a snake and gulps soft, slippery prey such as squid down whole instead of slicing or crushing it.

In 2020 Lopez-Romero and colleagues watched the mouth form in embryos. The jaws begin underneath, in the usual shark position, and shift forward only late in development. So the authors concluded that the front-set mouth is a later specialization, not a relic of an ancient body plan.

goblin-shark-mitsukurina-owstoni.context_blurb:
The goblin shark, Mitsukurina owstoni, is a pinkish shark of the deep sea, found in warm waters around the world but best known from Japan. It has a flattened, sword-like snout, small eyes, flabby muscles and the most astonishing jaws of any living shark, which shoot out of its face to grab prey.

Japanese fishermen named it tenguzame, the tengu shark, after the tengu, a goblin of Japanese folklore with a red face and a long nose, and English-speaking scientists translated that straight into goblin shark. A young one looks ghostly white. Its adult pink is real: its skin is so thin and pale that red blood vessels show through it, and the color deepens with age.

In the dark water far below the surface, jelly-filled pores called ampullae of Lorenzini dot its flattened snout and sense the weak electrical signals that hidden animals give off.

The shark is a slow ambush hunter. Its huge, oil-filled liver, which can make up a quarter of its weight, makes it almost weightless in the water, so it can hover and drift silently toward prey. Sharks have no swim bladder. Then its whole mouth catapults forward and snaps back. In 2016 Nakaya's team analyzed film of wild goblin sharks shot by Japan's broadcaster NHK and measured the jaws moving as fast as 3.1 meters each second, faster than any other shark's jaws.

Those jaws shoot out about 9 percent of the shark's body length, sprung by paired elastic ligaments where the jaws hinge, so they can push out between about 2 and 9 times farther than an ordinary shark's. It is the only living member of a family of sharks about 125 million years old. Early scientists mistook it for Scapanorhynchus, a shark known only from ancient fossils. It carries two kinds of teeth: long, narrow front fangs that spear soft, slippery fish and squid, and small, flattened rear teeth near the jaw corners for crushing hard-shelled prey such as crabs.

Scientists expected those fast jaws to work like a vacuum gun, sucking prey in. Nakaya's study showed otherwise: the shark opens its mouth all the way with its gill slits still open, and only afterward fires its jaws, so the pressure in its mouth pushes water out rather than drawing prey in. It is a ram feeder, overtaking its prey by rushing its mouth over it.

greenland-shark-somniosus-microcephalus.context_blurb:
The Greenland shark, Somniosus microcephalus, is a sluggish giant of the deep, near-freezing waters of the North Atlantic and the Arctic Ocean. It lives on an astonishingly slow timescale, and it may be the longest-lived backboned animal on Earth.

In the black water off Greenland and Iceland lives the Greenland shark, which reaches about 6.4 meters, 21 feet, and more than 1,000 kilograms, and cruises 100 to 1,200 meters down in water from just below freezing to about 7 degrees Celsius.

Nearly every Greenland shark carries a small pinkish-white parasite, the copepod Ommatokoita elongata, anchored to the cornea of each eye, where it feeds for years and scars the eye until the shark is nearly blind. Its flesh is loaded with urea and a chemical called TMAO, which work as antifreeze in the frigid water. In raw meat, though, the same chemicals act as a poison, and sled dogs that eat it can become unable to stand.

Blindness hardly matters half a mile down, where no sunlight reaches. There it hunts mostly by smell, a sense that is extremely keen, helped by electric-sensing pores on its snout. It scavenges almost anything that sinks: polar bears, reindeer, moose and even a horse, probably animals that had already died, have turned up in its stomach. No fish its size swims more slowly; it creeps at about a foot per second, yet fresh seals turn up in its stomach too. Scientists think it sneaks up on seals while they sleep in the water, where they doze to hide from polar bears.

Urea on its own is dangerous, because it slips between the folds of proteins and pries them apart. TMAO prevents that, holding the proteins folded and also bracing them against the crushing pressure of the deep, so the deeper the shark lives, the more TMAO it carries.

How old do these sharks get? In 2016 Nielsen's team used the carbon-14 that atomic bomb tests of the 1950s and 1960s spread through the ocean. That spike showed up in the eye-lens cores of only the smallest sharks, meaning the giants were already alive before the tests. The largest, about 5 meters long, was estimated at roughly 392 years old, give or take 120, and the sharks seem to mature only at about 150.

sawfish-pristidae.context_blurb:
Sawfish are big, flat-bodied fish of warm, shallow coasts, river mouths and estuaries around the world, with strongholds in northern Australia and the southern United States. Out in front of the face each one carries a rostrum, a long, flat snout-blade studded along both edges with tooth-like points. Today sawfish are among the most endangered animals in the sea.

For all its shark-like look, a sawfish is really a ray, a member of the flattened, bottom-dwelling group, and the giveaway is its gill slits, which open on its belly, just as a ray's do. The largetooth sawfish, the biggest of them, can grow to about 7 meters (23 feet), roughly the length of a school bus.

The rostrum carries 14 to 37 tooth-like points on each side, depending on the species. When a sawfish charges into a school of mullet, it swipes its saw from side to side, slashing through the fish, and mullet have been filmed fleeing in panic from a hunting sawfish.

In 2012 the Australian biologist Barbara Wueringer showed that the saw is a sense organ as well as a weapon: thousands of tiny pores on the blade pick up the faint electric fields that all living animals give off, so a sawfish can find hidden fish in muddy water and strike exactly where they are. Her films of captive sawfish showed that one sideways blow can slice a small fish in two, and when a swipe only wounds its prey, the sawfish pins the injured fish against the seabed with its saw until it can turn its underslung mouth and eat.

Andrew Fields ran DNA tests on 190 smalltooth sawfish caught wild in Florida waters, and seven pups had no father's genes at all: virgin births, the first wild case ever proven in a shark or ray. Some 3 percent of that estuary's young had no father, and scientists suspect this kind of birth kicks in when mates grow scarce, exactly the plight of a species sliding toward extinction.

A sawfish's saw-teeth grow all its life and are never replaced, so they keep a chemical diary: barium runs high in fresh water and strontium high in seawater, and the balance of the two laid down in a growing tooth records how salty the water was. Reading a single museum saw from base to tip lets scientists replay every trip that fish made between rivers and the sea.

The toothed saw evolved more than once. Onchopristis, a saw-snout 3 to 4 meters long from about 125 to 94 million years ago, was not a true sawfish but a sawskate that grew its saw on a separate branch, a case of convergent evolution nicknamed pristification. Its remains have turned up in the jaw and gut region of the giant predatory dinosaur Spinosaurus, so this ancient saw-bearer ended up as dinosaur food.

thresher-shark-alopias.context_blurb:
Thresher sharks are slim sharks of temperate and tropical oceans around the world, best known for a huge, curved upper tail fin that trails behind them like a scythe. They hunt schools of small fish with a weapon almost no other predator uses, and high-speed filming off the Philippines finally showed how it works.

The upper lobe of a thresher's tail can be as long as the shark's entire body, sweeping back in a long sickle-shaped arc unlike any other shark's tail. The thresher kills with its tail: rather than biting first, it whips that giant upper lobe overhead like a bullwhip to stun and kill fish, something researchers call extraordinarily rare among animals.

It charges a ball of sardines and pulls its broad side fins in sharply as brakes, which tips its back end up and lets it fling its tail forward over its head like a trebuchet. Slowed-down film of threshers hunting sardines off the Philippines showed that a single overhead tail-slap can kill several fish at once, an average of 3.6 sardines per successful strike and once 7 in a single blow. For all that power, threshers are shy with people, and the International Shark Attack File records no unprovoked or fatal attack by a thresher on a person.

The tail-tip moves so fast that it makes the water boil, a process called cavitation, and high-speed film caught bubble plumes streaming off it, much as a mantis shrimp's punch does. The researchers think the shockwave may be strong enough to stun small prey.

Of the three thresher species, only the common thresher runs warm: its red swimming muscle sits deep by the spine, wrapped in heat-trapping nets of blood vessels called retia mirabilia, and stays a few degrees above the sea, while the bigeye and pelagic threshers stay at water temperature.

About 15 million years ago, threshers as big as a great white lived in the seas off what is now Maryland, known only from teeth in the Calvert Cliffs, and when one was named Alopias palatasi in 2023, its teeth stunned scientists by being serrated like a steak knife, unheard of in a thresher. Nearly every other thresher tooth ever found, living or fossil, has a smooth edge.

wobbegong-orectolobidae-carpet-sharks.context_blurb: The wobbegong is a group of flat, patterned carpet sharks that live mostly on the reefs around Australia and the Indo-Pacific. They are camouflaged so well against the coral and sand that divers often swim right over one without seeing it. The wobbegong has a wide, fringe-edged mouth and acts as an ambush hunter rather than a chaser. Its body plan is unlike almost any other shark's, and the fringed camouflage keeps appearing in textbooks on how a predator can hide in plain sight.

beaks-for-every-meal.context_blurb:
A bird has no hands and no teeth, so its beak does nearly every job: tearing, drilling, sipping, scooping, straining and cracking. Across the bird world, almost every kind of meal has carved its own beak shape, and on the Galápagos Islands scientists have even watched beaks change from one generation to the next.

The bald eagle, a fish hunter with a snow-white head, pins its catch under its talons and tears the flesh with a downward-curving hook, the bill shape of a meat-eater. A woodpecker props itself on its stiff tail and goes after hidden grubs and beetle larvae with a hard, straight bill that works like a chisel, punching through solid wood. A hummingbird hovers before a deep, tube-shaped flower and reaches down for the nectar at the bottom with a slender, needle-like bill.

The brown pelican plunges beak-first into the sea, and its stretchy throat pouch scoops up about 3 gallons, some 11 liters, of water and fish, more than the bird itself weighs, then drains the water before the bird swallows. The roseate spoonbill sweeps its flat, spoon-shaped bill from side to side through cloudy water, held slightly open, and snaps it shut the instant it feels a shrimp brush between the halves, so it hunts by touch. A flamingo feeds with its head upside down, straining brine shrimp and algae through comb-like ridges called lamellae inside its curved bill, and pigments in that food turn its feathers pink, which is why the chicks hatch gray.

The crossbill, a stubby finch of northern conifer forests, has bill tips that cross like the blades of scissors, and when it jams them between two cone scales, the crossed tips give it the leverage to pry a scale apart so its tongue can lift out the seed. On a single spruce, two crossbill species feed side by side without competing, because bill size sorts them: the small-billed white-winged crossbill works tiny spruce and tamarack cones, while the heavier-billed red crossbill breaks into big pine cones. On the Galápagos Islands off Ecuador, Charles Darwin found closely related little finches whose beaks ranged from heavy nutcrackers to fine insect tweezers, and each bird's beak matches its diet; just six genes explain nearly half the variation in beak size.

Falcons such as the peregrine, which can top 200 miles an hour in a dive, carry an extra notch on the upper edge of the hooked beak, the tomial tooth, which hawks and eagles lack; a falcon fits its prey's neck into the notch and bites through the spinal cord, killing it at once. In the cloud forests of the Andes, the sword-billed hummingbird's bill, 8 to 12 centimeters long, is the only bird bill longer than the rest of the body, so it can drink from flowers no other hummingbird reaches, but it is too long to preen with, and the bird must groom its feathers with its feet. In 2009 the biologist Glenn Tattersall filmed a toucan with a heat-sensing camera and found that it pumps blood into its huge bill to shed body heat, working like a car's radiator, one of the largest heat windows in the animal kingdom, rivaling an elephant's ears. On the little Galápagos island of Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured finch beaks for decades, and when a drought in 1977 killed roughly 85 percent of its medium ground finches, the easy, soft seeds vanished first, so the survivors were the birds with the biggest, strongest beaks, able to crack the tough seeds left behind. Each crossbill is also handed, its lower tip crossing either leftward or rightward, fixed for life, so it attacks cones from one side, and the biologist Craig Benkman showed that red crossbills come in a near 50-50 mix because the rarer kind always has more cones that nobody has worked yet, so it does better and pulls the ratio back toward half and half.

When a second drought struck Daphne Major in 2004, the much bigger large ground finch had moved in and was hogging the big, hard seeds, so in this drought the medium ground finches with the smallest beaks survived, better at the small seeds left over: the opposite of 1977. digesting-grass-the-ruminants-four-stoma.context_blurb:
Grass covers much of the land, but it is one of the hardest foods to digest, because it is built from cellulose, a tough fiber. Cattle, sheep, goats, deer and giraffes live on it anyway. They are ruminants, and their secret is a four-chambered stomach and a giant partnership with microbes.

A cow standing quietly in a field, jaw working steadily with nothing new in her mouth, is chewing the cud: she swallowed her grass fast, her stomach softened it, and now a wad has come back up her throat to be chewed again and swallowed a second time. Animals that bring up and re-chew their food this way are called ruminants. The club includes deer, sheep, goats, antelope and cattle, and on the African savanna the towering giraffe is a cud-chewer too.

Eating fast and chewing later is a survival plan. Wildebeest and gazelles out on the open savanna, where lions lie hidden in the grass, gulp their mouthfuls quickly and then move off to somewhere safer to do the slow chewing, out of a hunter's reach. The four chambers of the stomach work like a food-processing line. The first three ferment, soak and squeeze the grass, and only the fourth, the abomasum, uses acid to digest, like our own stomach, so it is called the true stomach.

None of these animals can digest grass by itself, because none makes cellulase, the enzyme that cuts cellulose apart; instead each one carries trillions of gut microbes that make the enzyme and break the grass down for it, and the animal lives on what they produce. Most of that work happens in the first chamber, the giant fermenting vat called the rumen. Fermenting makes gas, and a single cow gives off between 150 and 500 liters of methane each day. More than 80 percent of that methane leaves through her mouth as burps, not out the other end. Cattle also swallow nails and bits of wire with their feed. The second chamber, lined with a honeycomb pattern, catches the metal, and a sharp piece can pierce its wall and cause a deadly "hardware disease." So farmers feed each calf a magnet, which settles in that honeycomb chamber for life and pins stray nails and wire safely in place.

Horses and rabbits found the other main answer. They have no four-chambered stomach and chew no cud; their microbes ferment the grass in a big pouch called the cecum, far past the stomach, toward the end of the intestine. That late placement has a cost, because vitamins and protein the microbes make there would pass out of the body before they could be absorbed. A rabbit's fix is to make special soft droppings, called cecotropes, and eat them straight from its bottom, digesting them a second time to capture the goodness.

filter-feeding-the-ocean.context_blurb:
Some of the biggest animals in the sea live on some of the smallest food. Blue whales, whale sharks, manta rays, flamingos and even one seal survive by sieving tiny creatures out of huge amounts of water. Each has its own strainer and its own trick for moving water through it.

No animal in Earth's history has been bigger than the blue whale, and it has no teeth. Its mouth is lined with hundreds of baleen plates, stiff fringed sheets hanging from its upper jaw, and they are made of keratin, the same protein as your fingernails and hair. This 30-meter, 150-ton giant lives almost entirely on krill, shrimp-like animals barely the size of your finger. The whale shark, the biggest fish in the sea, does much the same: it opens its huge mouth to gulp a whole cloud of plankton and strains the tiny food through comb-like gill rakers.

A flamingo's chicks hatch gray, and its adult pink comes from its food: carotenoid pigments, the kind that color carrots, in the brine shrimp and algae it eats. Take the pigment out of the diet and new feathers grow pale. To feed, a flamingo turns its head upside down in a shallow salty lake while its thick tongue pumps like a piston, driving water in and out over comb-like plates called lamellae inside its bent bill. A blue whale's baleen works as a one-way sieve: after a gulp, the whale forces the seawater back out between the plates, trapping krill as small as half a millimeter inside, then swallows what is left.

A blue whale feeds by lunging into a swarm of krill and unfolding the pleats along its throat like an expanding bag. One lunge takes in about 70,000 liters of seawater, a gulp heavier than the whale itself, holding about 10 kilograms of krill. Off Alaska, humpback whales hunt herring as a team: they circle upward beneath a school, blowing out bubbles that rise as a shimmering net and fence the fish into a ball, then lunge up through the middle together. A giant manta ray, with wings more than five meters across, curls the paddle-like fins beside its mouth, the cephalic lobes, into an O that funnels water and plankton into its open mouth, then strains the food through feathery gill plates.

The Antarctic crabeater seal, perhaps the most plentiful big wild mammal anywhere, lives on krill rather than crabs, and its strainer is its teeth, which are intricately lobed and interlock into a sieve like baleen in miniature. Right whales are slow, chunky whales of cold seas. Its baleen plates, over 2 meters tall, are the longest of any whale because it feeds by skimming, swimming steadily along with its mouth agape and straining plankton nonstop. Right whales and bowheads also have filters that never clog. Flume experiments showed that the water flows lengthwise along the inside of the baleen rack, front to back, rather than straight through it, sweeping the prey toward the back of the mouth to be swallowed while the filter cleans itself.

Baleen whales descend from toothed ancestors, and the blue whale's DNA still holds the instructions for making tooth enamel. But those genes have rotted into broken, non-working pseudogenes, leftovers of its toothed past, wrecked by mutations once teeth were no longer used.

lures-and-ambush.context_blurb:
Many predators never chase their food. They wait, hidden or perfectly still, and use a lure to bring their prey within reach: a fake worm, a glowing bait, a perfume, a false signal. Turtles, deep-sea fish, spiders, snakes and fireflies have all invented such tricks, and each one ends in a single lightning strike.

The alligator snapping turtle, a huge North American river turtle, lies still on the bottom with its jaws wide open and wiggles a pink, worm-shaped tip on its tongue, a fake worm that draws fish straight into its mouth. It is the only turtle with a body part built as a lure. A female deep-sea anglerfish hangs in the black water and dangles a glowing lure from her head, on a rod-like spine just in front of her mouth, and small fish drawn to the light swim into her jaws. The frogfish, disguised as a sponge-covered rock on a coral reef, waves a twitching lure on the end of a fin spine, and when prey comes close it strikes faster than any other backboned animal, its mouth ballooning to as much as 12 times its normal size to suck the victim in.

The bolas spider of American forests spins no web; at night she hangs a single sticky glue-ball on a short silk line and gives off a scent that copies the mating perfume of a female moth, so a male moth flies straight to her and she swings the ball to knock him down. In Iran's western mountains, a horned viper hides among the rocks and twitches its tail tip, which is shaped and moved exactly like a crawling spider, though it is made only of soft tissue and long scales. It mostly fools migrating warblers, and when one strikes, the snake strikes back in about 0.2 seconds. The anglerfish's fishing rod began as the first spine of the fin on its back: over millions of years that spine crept forward over the head and became a stalk with a shining bait at the end.

The anglerfish does not make the light itself: bacteria that live inside the lure glow for it, and the fish feeds them oxygen and nutrients through its blood in return. A female Photuris firefly flashes back the courtship code of a different firefly species, copying its timing perfectly, and when a hopeful male comes down beside her looking for a mate, she eats him. She hunts these Photinus males for more than a meal: their bodies carry defensive poisons called lucibufagins, like the heart poison of foxglove, which she cannot make herself, so she steals them to protect herself and passes them on to her eggs.

The spider-tailed viper's close cousins hunt mammals, but it is the only one that specializes in birds. In tests on chicken plasma, its venom sped up clotting by about 96 percent, while its cousins' venoms barely affected it. The bird-hunter's venom is chemically tuned to the clotting system of the very birds its tail lures in, so lure and venom evolved together.

remarkable-tongues.context_blurb:
Tongues do far more than taste. Across the animal world they have become sticky mops, spring-loaded harpoons, nectar pumps and probes long enough to reach deep inside a tree, a termite mound or a flower. Each design solves a feeding problem, and the strangest part is often where all that tongue is kept when it is not in use.

The giant anteater of South America has no teeth at all; its sticky tongue, about 60 centimeters long and anchored all the way down at the breastbone, darts in and out of a nest up to 150 times a minute, lapping up ants and termites whole. A frog's tongue snatches an insect in under 0.07 seconds, about five times faster than you can blink, and flings the bug back toward its mouth at up to 12 times the acceleration of gravity.

The tip of a chameleon's tongue is a sticky pad of muscle that turns into a suction cup on contact, gripping its prey with both glue and suction. Woodpeckers reach their food a different way. A woodpecker's tongue can stretch up to a third of the bird's whole body length; the northern flicker holds the North American record, poking its tongue two inches beyond the tip of its bill to reach ants. When the tongue is pulled in, most of its length is looped up and over the back of the skull: the supporting hyoid bone starts near the nostril, splits into a V between the eyes, and its two arms curl over the top and around the back of the head before rejoining.

Old nature books said the woodpecker spears grubs like a harpoon, but the tongue tip is armed with tiny backward-pointing barbs and coated in sticky saliva, so it snags a grub and wraps around it instead. Part of the frog's secret is the tongue itself, which has the softness of brain tissue, about ten times softer than a human tongue, so it moulds itself around the bug. Its spit helps too, watery when it hits the bug and then thickening to grip harder than honey as the tongue snaps back.

The pangolin, a toothless, scaly ant-eater of Africa and Asia that looks like a walking pinecone, cannot chew its ants, so it swallows small stones that grind up the food inside it. Its tongue can be over 40 centimeters long, longer than its head and body, and is rooted near its pelvis and last ribs. The tube-lipped nectar bat of Ecuador's cloud forests has the longest tongue for its size of any mammal, about 3.5 inches on a body of 2.5 inches, so there is no room for it in the mouth: its base is stowed down in the rib cage, between the heart and the breastbone.

A chameleon fires its tongue like a catapult: muscles stretch tight the sliding sheaths of springy collagen wrapped around the tongue's bony core, then let them go all at once, flinging the tongue out more than one and a half body lengths. Because the energy is stored first and released in one burst, the tongue reaches about 3,000 watts per kilogram, roughly five to ten times the muscle's own maximum power. Scientists once pictured a hummingbird's tongue as a tiny straw that sipped nectar by capillary action, but high-speed film showed it is an elastic pump: its forked, fringed tip, pressed flat while inside the beak, springs open the instant it touches nectar and snaps shut around droplets as it pulls back.

Woodpeckers face one more danger: each strike jolts the skull with more than 400 g, far past the roughly 135 g that can concuss a human, thousands of times every day. Van Wassenbergh's team filmed three woodpecker species and found that the head stops almost exactly as fast as the beak tip, so the skull does no cushioning at all; a stiff skull makes pecking efficient, and the old claim that the wrapped tongue bone protects the brain is a myth. The bird stays unharmed because its brain is tiny, only about 2 grams, the size of a pea, and each blow lasts a fraction of a millisecond, so the pressure inside the skull stays two to three times below the level that causes concussion.

squeezing-not-biting.context_blurb:
Boas, pythons and anacondas kill not with venom but by wrapping prey in their coils and squeezing. Then they swallow it whole, often an animal wider than their own heads. Modern experiments have overturned the old story of how constriction kills, and the way these snakes swallow and digest a giant meal is just as surprising.

The heaviest snake on Earth is the green anaconda of South American swamps, which can weigh about 250 kilograms (550 pounds), nearly twice a reticulated python, because its body is roughly a foot thick. The longest snake is the reticulated python of Southeast Asia's tropical forests, which can stretch past 6 meters, more than 20 feet.

A constrictor does not crush its prey in one big squeeze; it works with the prey's own breathing, taking up the slack each time the animal breathes out, so its coils cinch a notch tighter and the lungs can never refill. To swallow, a snake uses teeth that all curve backward like rows of fishhooks; they cannot chew, but they grip and ratchet the prey inward so it goes down whole and head-first, which folds its legs back out of the way.

For centuries people thought constrictors killed by crushing bones or by slow suffocation, but in 2015 the American biologist Scott Boback showed the real killer is faster: the coils cut off the blood flow, so the trapped animal blacks out and dies within seconds, long before it would run out of air. A snake does not really unhinge or dislocate its jaw: its lower jaw is two separate bones joined at the chin by a stretchy ligament, so the two halves spread apart and walk over the prey one side at a time.

In Boback's lab, within six seconds of a boa wrapping an anesthetized rat, the pressure in the rat's leg artery had fallen to half while the pressure in a nearby vein had jumped sixfold, so the blood almost stopped moving. A Burmese python that has fasted for months can gulp down a whole deer or pig, and within about three days its heart, liver, pancreas, kidneys and small intestine grow 40 to 100 percent bigger to digest the meal, then shrink back once the job is done.

teeth-built-for-the-job.context_blurb:
Teeth are tools, and their shapes tell you what an animal eats. Meat-eaters carry blades and plant-eaters carry grinders, and some animals have pushed teeth to extremes: endless replacement rows, teeth that never stop growing, fangs built for a single stab and grinders that sharpen themselves. Read the teeth, and you can read the life.

In a wolf's jaw the back teeth are narrow blades that close like scissors to slice meat, while in a cow's they are wide, flat, ridged slabs that grind tough plants, so the shape alone reveals the diet. A shark's teeth sit in rows stacked behind one another like a conveyor belt, so when a front tooth breaks off, the one waiting behind it rotates forward into place, sometimes within a day or two.

A great white shark keeps about 300 teeth in five or more rows and can shed and regrow more than 20,000 of them in its lifetime. A rat's front incisors never stop growing, a squirrel's by about half an inch a month, so a rodent must gnaw constantly to wear them down. A horse has a long toothless gap along the side of its jaw, the diastema, which its tongue uses to shuffle grass back to the grinders, and in a wolf or a lion that same spot holds long, dagger-like canines that grab and hold prey.

The carnassials at the back of a cat's jaw have no flat grinding surface; their blade edges slide past each other like a pair of scissors, shearing through hide, tendon and even bone. Wolves and hyenas have carnassials too. If a rodent cannot wear its incisors down, they keep curving: one woodchuck's upper incisor grew right up through the roof of its mouth and into its brain, killing it. An elephant carries only four huge grinding molars at a time, each up to a foot long and some eleven pounds, and they ride forward like a conveyor belt: worn ones crumble off the front in thin sheets as new ones push in from behind. The saber-toothed cat Smilodon had upper canines as long as eight inches, but they were fragile and not for crunching: they were built to deliver one precise stab to the throat of prey already pinned down.

An elephant gets only six sets of molars in its whole life, the last arriving in its early forties, and when that final set wears smooth it cannot chew its food anymore and gradually starves. Its own teeth are its life clock. A beaver's incisors sharpen themselves: the front face is hard enamel and the back softer dentine, so gnawing wears the back away faster and always leaves a chisel edge. That front face is rusty orange because its enamel has iron worked into it, making it hard and acid-resistant; 2024 research found that the iron supplies the strength, while the orange color probably comes from amino acids in the enamel. Smilodon's bite was only about a third as strong as a lion's, so after its forelimbs pinned the prey, powerful neck muscles hauled the skull downward to drive the blades home.

Duck-billed dinosaurs such as Edmontosaurus had the finest grinders ever evolved, with hundreds of teeth cemented into one grinding slab called a dental battery. Each tooth was built from six kinds of tissue, against four in a horse's molar, and because the tissues wore away at different rates, chewing constantly re-carved fresh ridges, so the teeth sharpened themselves as they wore.

venom-for-the-hunt.context_blurb: Many predators carry venom for subduing prey, not just for defense. Snakes, spiders, scorpions, cone snails, cephalopods, and even a handful of mammals use chemistry to kill or paralyze prey too dangerous to subdue any other way. Look closely at the different venom delivery systems different animal groups have evolved, how venoms work in the body of the prey, and why nature keeps re-inventing the same basic trick across lineages that are not even remotely related.

blue-whale.context_blurb:
No animal in the history of life has outgrown the blue whale, not even the biggest dinosaur. It swims in every ocean and feeds almost entirely on krill, shrimp-like creatures no longer than a finger. Its size, its voice and its habit of eating in giant gulps are all parts of a single strategy for living off some of the smallest prey in the sea.

The largest animal known ever to have lived is not extinct: it is the blue whale, alive in the oceans today, up to about 100 feet long and 200 tons in weight.

That makes it far heavier than any dinosaur, because Argentinosaurus, one of the biggest, weighed nearly a hundred tons, so a blue whale weighs more than twice as much, as much as about 33 elephants. Even its tongue can weigh about 3 tons, as heavy as a full-grown elephant. When it feeds, it lunges into a krill swarm at full speed with its pleated throat thrown wide and engulfs in one gulp a volume of water and prey bigger than its own body, about 140 percent of its weight, before straining the water out through its baleen. A big blue whale can eat up to 6 tons of krill in a day, millions of the tiny animals.

A blue whale heart preserved in Toronto's Royal Ontario Museum measures about six and a half feet in height with its aorta and weighs nearly 400 pounds, so big that staff joked a person could squeeze into it as if into a Smart car. Its aorta, the main artery leaving the heart, is about 9 inches across, about the width of a dinner plate, huge for a blood vessel but far too narrow for the storybook child to crawl through. Its low moans reach about 188 decibels, among the loudest sounds of any animal, and other whales can hear them as far as 1,000 miles away. A newborn calf, carried for nearly a year and born in warm tropical seas, is already 23 to 25 feet long and weighs up to 3 tons, more than a full-grown elephant on its first day.

Yet a swimmer beside a calling whale may hear nothing, because the calls, around 10 to 40 hertz, are pitched too low for human ears, and such low sounds fade little in water, which is why they carry so far. The calf grows at a staggering rate, gaining about 200 pounds a day, 8 to 10 pounds an hour, on milk that is 35 to 50 percent fat. Its baleen does not work like a kitchen sieve with water pushed straight through, because flow-tank studies showed that the water slides lengthwise along the inner face of the plates, sweeping the trapped krill to the back of the mouth for swallowing and keeping the fringe from clogging. Biologists call this cross-flow filtration.

Its giant body is surprisingly new: tracing whale fossils, Slater, Goldbogen and Pyenson found that the biggest baleen whales stayed about 10 meters long for most of their history, then leapt to today's 30 meters only in the last few million years, on several branches of the family tree at once. The jump came around 4.5 million years ago, when the first ice ages began packing krill into dense patches along the coasts, and suddenly it paid to be a colossal filter feeder.

dolphin.context_blurb:
Dolphins are small toothed whales, cousins of orcas and sperm whales, found in oceans and some rivers around the world. The best known is the bottlenose dolphin, the big gray dolphin of aquariums and tropical beaches. Dolphins hunt with sound, call one another by name and pass skills from mother to calf, which makes them some of the cleverest animals in the sea.

A dolphin is shaped like a fish but is not one: it is a warm-blooded mammal that breathes air, and it must rise to the surface for every breath it takes through the blowhole on top of its head.

In its first months, every bottlenose dolphin invents a signature whistle, which it keeps for life. No two dolphins share one, and others recognize who is calling, so the whistle works like a personal name; about half of all the whistles a dolphin makes are its own signature. In Shark Bay, on the coast of Western Australia, a few dolphins hunt fish that lurk among sharp, broken rocks on the bottom. To protect their tender beaks, these "spongers" rip a sponge shaped like a cone from the seabed and wear it over the beak like a glove while they dig.

Dolphins also hunt with sound. In dark or muddy water a dolphin fires clicks and reads the echoes, which is called echolocation. It makes the clicks without using its mouth, by forcing air under pressure through two flaps of tissue, nicknamed monkey lips, that sit just beneath the blowhole on top of its head. Then the melon, the fatty dome in its forehead, works like a lens for sound and bends the clicks into a narrow, aimed beam instead of letting them spread in every direction. Breathing air shapes how a dolphin sleeps, too. If its whole brain slept, it would stop swimming and breathing and drown. So only half its brain sleeps at a time while the other half stays awake to keep it surfacing, and the dolphin closes just one eye, the one opposite the sleeping half.

The echoes come back by an unexpected road: a dolphin has only pinhole ear openings, and the returning sound reaches its inner ear through a thin, fat-filled channel in its lower jawbone. The whistles are more than labels. Vincent Janik, who studies wild dolphins, discovered that one will pick up the whistle of a close companion and copy it, usually when the two are apart, as if calling the friend back; he described it as the first known case of animals besides humans addressing one another by name. Sponging is a family tradition, taught rather than inborn. Calves follow their mothers to "sponge school" from birth and wear little sponges of their own by age two or three, and nearly every sponger carries a DNA marker passed down only through mothers, so the skill runs down the mother line. Dolphins dive deep as well; in 1965 a Navy-trained bottlenose named Tuffy reached about 300 meters. On a deep dive its heart slows sharply, and one section of its lungs squeezes shut under the pressure while its blood is rerouted, so very little nitrogen dissolves into its blood, the danger that gives human divers the bends.

Dolphin sonar is astonishingly sharp: from 8 meters away a dolphin can tell apart two metal cylinders whose walls differ by just 0.23 millimeters, less than the thickness of a credit card. It can detect targets more than 100 meters away.

humpback-whale.context_blurb:
The humpback whale is a 40-ton baleen whale found in every ocean, up to 17 meters long, with a knobbly head and a habit of putting on a show at the surface. Each year it travels between cold feeding waters and warm breeding seas, and it is famous for its acrobatics, its clever hunting and its haunting songs.

A humpback's pale side flippers stretch nearly 5 meters, about a third of its body length, and no other animal on Earth has longer limbs. Its head is covered in knobs about the size of golf balls, and from each one sprouts a single hair, which scientists think helps the whale sense the water flowing past it. On its breeding grounds a humpback slaps its flippers and tail on the sea with loud booms, and then it breaches, flinging its entire body out of the water in a leap and crashing back down.

Its scientific name is Megaptera novaeangliae. Megaptera is Greek for great wing, a name earned by those enormous flippers, while novaeangliae means of New England, where scientists first described the whale in the 1780s. The flippers also make it nimble: a whale you would expect to steer like a ship can turn a full circle within its own length like a dolphin, and it can even swim backward. Each winter, on warm breeding grounds near Hawaii and in the Caribbean, only the males sing, and scientists think the song is a display for mates rather than a message with a set meaning.

Roger Payne and Scott McVay found that the song is built like music: short sounds called units link into phrases, phrases group into themes, and themes in a fixed order make up the whole song. A single song lasts several minutes, but a male sings it over and over for hours, and recordings off Hawaii caught sessions of up to seven hours. Humpbacks also hunt with bubbles. Diving beneath a school of fish, a group blows a spiral curtain of bubbles that the fish will not cross, packing the fish into a dense ball, and then the whole group surges up through the middle of it with mouths open wide.

The trick is not instinct: whales learn it from one another, so only some groups use it, and off Alaska one whale, the caller, trumpets a loud feeding call that tells the whole team to lunge at the same moment. Roger Payne's recordings of 1967 caused a sensation, and later work found something stranger: every male in a population sings the same song, and when the tune changes, all of them switch to the new version together. It is a culture, passed from whale to whale.

The knobs along the front edge of each flipper, called tubercles, are no decoration. In a 2004 wind-tunnel test, Miklosovic, Murray, Howle and Fish found that a bumpy model flipper held on to the flow until it was tilted about 40 percent steeper than the angle at which a smooth model stalled. The knobs divide the water rushing at the flipper and channel it into the valleys between them, so a 40-ton whale can bank into tight turns, and designers now borrow the idea for wind-turbine blades and fans.

New songs sweep across whole oceans like fashions: researchers tracked one tune that began off eastern Australia and passed from whale to whale across the islands of the South Pacific, traveling 14,000 kilometers east all the way to Ecuador. A lunging humpback gulps a volume of water as large as its own body, and in 2012 Pyenson and colleagues found the organ that runs the move: a grape-sized lump in the springy joint where the two halves of the lower jaw meet, found only in humpbacks and their rorqual relatives. Packed with nerve endings, it senses how far the jaw has swung open and how much the throat pouch has ballooned, and it feeds that to the brain to time each lunge, from the opening gape to the moment the mouth snaps shut.

narwhal.context_blurb:
The narwhal is a mottled, mid-sized whale that lives year-round among the sea ice of the Arctic, off Canada, Greenland and Russia. Its males carry the most famous tooth on Earth, a long spiral tusk, and only recently have scientists begun to learn what it is for.

The narwhal's long, straight, twisted tusk earned it the nickname the unicorn of the sea, after the horned horse of old legends.

The tusk is no horn but a single overgrown tooth, a left canine that grows straight out through the upper lip and can reach about 3 meters. Apart from the tusk, its mouth is nearly empty, with just two teeth in the upper jaw and none for chewing, so the narwhal swallows its fish whole.

The tusk always spirals counterclockwise, to the left, and in the rare male with two tusks both twist left, with one always longer. In 2017 drones over Tremblay Sound in Nunavut filmed narwhals tapping Arctic cod with quick, precise flicks of the tusk to stun them, then sucking up the dazed fish. It was the first time anyone had filmed the tusk in use. The name narwhal comes from the Old Norse nár-hvalr, corpse-whale, probably for its grey, mottled skin and its habit of floating motionless at the surface like a drifting body.

Harvard dental researcher Martin Nweeia found that the tusk lacks enamel and carries some 10 million microscopic channels that open onto the sea, so researchers think it may sense changes in the water's temperature and saltiness, though its exact job is still being studied. Narwhals dive about 1,800 meters, over a mile, after Greenland halibut, staying under for 25 minutes or longer on muscles rich in oxygen-storing myoglobin, and their rib cage folds and compresses to survive the crushing pressure.

orca-killer-whale.context_blurb:
The orca, or killer whale, is a sleek hunter in black and white, found from the Arctic to the Antarctic. It lives in tight family groups, and each group has its own calls, its own favorite prey and its own hunting tricks, passed from old to young. Some populations differ so much that scientists now argue over whether they are separate species.

Despite its nickname, the orca is not a whale in the usual sense but the largest dolphin, the biggest member of the dolphin family.

Orcas swim in all five of the world's oceans, from tropical waters to both polar seas, which makes them the most widespread of all whales and dolphins. A big male can reach 8 meters and more than 6 tonnes, and its jaws hold over 40 inward-curving teeth that interlock, each about 10 centimeters long, the length of a finger.

Each orca group specializes in its own prey, and the shy offshore orcas eat sharks, whose skin is as rough as sandpaper and grinds their teeth right down to the gums. In Antarctica, orcas line up four abreast and charge an ice floe where a Weddell seal is resting, raising a wave that washes the seal off the floe and into the water, a hunt called wave-washing.

Only about 100 Antarctic orcas know how to wave-wash, because the skill is not instinct: the pod's older females teach it to the young, generation after generation. On the Argentine coast at Península Valdés, orcas hurl themselves right up onto the beach to snatch sea lion pups from the shallows, then wriggle back to sea, and adults teach this risky move to their young. Off Norway, orcas herd herring into a tight ball near the surface with bubbles and flashes of their white bellies, and then a whale whips its tail into the ball, and the shockwave stuns up to about 15 herring at once, which it picks off one by one. This is called carousel feeding.

Orcas are among the few animals besides humans that go through menopause, living to 80 or more, and Lauren Brent's study found that in lean salmon years the old grandmothers lead from the front, guiding the pod to the salmon, when their memory matters most. Each pod keeps its own dialect of calls almost unchanged for decades, but in 1987 a K-pod orca of Puget Sound started wearing a dead salmon on its head like a hat, a fad that swept all three resident pods within months, vanished, and returned in 2024. In the North Pacific, the orcas that hunt mammals and those that eat fish never mix, and their lines parted many thousands of generations ago, and in 2024 Morin and colleagues proposed making them full species. The Society for Marine Mammalogy's committee fell just short of the votes needed, so it named them subspecies, Orcinus orca rectipinnus and Orcinus orca ater, within a single killer-whale species. Whether they are one species or several is still debated.

sea-otter.context_blurb:
The sea otter (Enhydra lutris) is a small marine mammal of the cold North Pacific coasts, from California to Alaska and across to Russia and Japan. A member of the weasel family, it lives almost entirely at sea, floating on its back among the kelp. It carries no blubber, so nearly everything about it is a strategy for staying warm.

The sea otter is the marine mammal that lies on its back in kelp beds, cracking a clam against a stone it holds on its belly, and it plunges into ice-cold water every day with no layer of blubber at all. Its only insulation is its fur, which traps a thin layer of air against the skin, so the icy water never touches its body.

That fur is the densest of any animal on Earth: up to a million hairs in one square inch of skin, compared with about 100,000 hairs on an entire human head. Matted or oily fur stops trapping air and lets the cold in, so a sea otter spends about a tenth of its day grooming, cleaning and fluffing its coat.

The otter also burns food for heat, so it must eat roughly one-fourth of its weight in food each day, like a 160-pound person eating 40 pounds. In 2021 Wright and colleagues found where much of that heat comes from: the otter's ordinary swimming muscles run a leaky metabolism, their mitochondria letting energy short-circuit into pure heat instead of movement. The leak reaches about 40 percent of the muscle cells' capacity and gives the otter a resting metabolism about three times higher than expected for its size. Pups make this heat at full adult strength before their muscles can even swim, so the trait evolved for warmth, not for moving.

Few mammals use tools, but this one does. It picks a favorite rock and keeps it from dive to dive, bashing shellfish against it as fast as 45 blows in 15 seconds on a tough abalone. Between dives it stows that rock, along with food it has gathered, in a roomy pouch of loose skin in its armpit, under the front leg, usually on the left side. Its flat, rounded molars are built for crushing shells, not slicing meat.

Sea otters sleep together in floating groups called rafts, and as they drift on the open sea they hold each other's paws so the current cannot scatter them in the night.

Sea otters eat huge numbers of sea urchins, which would otherwise devour the kelp, so the otters keep whole underwater forests of kelp alive; where otters vanish, the urchins strip the seafloor bare. That makes the sea otter the classic example of a keystone species, an animal whose loss topples a whole ecosystem.

sperm-whale.context_blurb:
The sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) is a giant toothed whale with a huge, square head, found in oceans around the world. It dives deeper than almost any other animal to hunt squid in total darkness, and it talks to its family in patterns of clicks. Whalers once hunted it nearly to extinction for the waxy oil in its head.

No predator with teeth is bigger than the sperm whale: a grown bull reaches about 16 meters and 45 tonnes, dwarfing any shark or big cat. No other mammal feeds so far down: a sperm whale dives to around 2,250 meters (7,380 feet) on a single breath and can stay under for well over an hour, hunting squid in cold, pitch-black water.

Down there it battles giant squid, and a surfacing whale often carries the proof: round white scars from squid suckers ringing its head and long scratches from squid arms along its sides.

With no light at all, it finds a single squid by echolocation, sending out clicks and reading the echoes that bounce back; underwater microphones can pick up those clicks from up to 100 miles away. Its blocky head holds as much as 1,900 liters of pale, waxy oil called spermaceti, which works as an acoustic lens, focusing the clicks into a narrow, powerful beam. Early whalers mistook the oil for the whale's sperm, which is how it got its name.

Its clicks are the loudest sounds made by any animal, around 230 decibels or more, far beyond a jet engine's roar of about 150, and researchers suspect that a click fired at close range may stun a squid. On the way down, its flexible ribcage folds in and its lungs collapse, which keeps the whale from absorbing dangerous amounts of nitrogen under the crushing pressure. Its diving muscles are crammed with myoglobin, an oxygen-gripping protein, far more densely than a land mammal's muscle could hold without the protein clumping into a useless mass. In 2013 Stephen Mirceta's team found that champion divers evolved myoglobin with a strong positive electric charge, so the molecules repel one another and stay separate.

Hal Whitehead and Shane Gero found that families sharing the same click rhythms, called codas, belong to the same vocal clan, and clans stretch across whole oceans; a calf picks up the family rhythm by listening to the grown whales, so what it inherits is a dialect handed down by culture, not by genes. Scientists have not decoded it as a language. About 9 to 10 million years ago a 15-meter relative, Livyatan melvillei, hunted the coast of Peru, and unlike today's sperm whale, which has working teeth only in its narrow lower jaw, it carried massive working teeth in both jaws, some about 36 centimeters long, for tearing apart baleen whales. Its name honors the biblical sea beast Leviathan and Herman Melville, who wrote Moby-Dick.

walrus.context_blurb: The walrus is a huge, tusked marine mammal that lives in cold shallow seas around the Arctic. Both males and females grow long ivory tusks. Walruses haul out on ice floes and beaches in large herds, feed on bottom-dwelling clams and sea invertebrates, and use their tusks and whiskers together as a specialized set of tools. Climate change is now rapidly reshaping the ice cover they depend on.

growing-by-molting-the-exoskeleton-probl.context_blurb:
Crabs, lobsters, insects and spiders wear their skeletons on the outside. That armor protects them, but it cannot grow, so every so often they must shed it and build a bigger one, a risky process called molting.

Crabs carry no internal bones: their skeleton is an exoskeleton, a stiff case of chitin and calcium that guards the soft body and anchors the muscles, doing from the outside what your bones do from within. Once hardened, that shell cannot stretch at all. So to grow, a crab sheds the whole thing: it forms a new, soft skeleton underneath, climbs out of the old one and swells to a bigger size before the new shell sets.

A cicada nymph spends 13 or 17 years underground, then climbs a tree and its skin splits down the back. For the first few hours the newly emerged adult is soft and pale as a ghost, usually white or pale green, until its body hardens and its true colors appear. The empty brown shell left clinging to the bark, a hollow replica of the insect right down to its legs, is called an exuvia. Molting also lets some animals repair themselves. A spider that loses a leg grows a new one at its next molt, but the new leg comes out smaller and paler and catches up to full size over the next few molts. A lobster's hard shell cannot stretch either, so a young lobster molts about 25 times in its first five to seven years.

Right after molting, a lobster's new shell is as thin as wet paper, and it is easy prey. Before hiding, it often eats the cast-off shell it has just left, because that shell is rich in calcium, which helps the new armor harden faster.

radial-vs-bilateral-why-a-jellyfish-has-.context_blurb:
Animals come in two great body plans. Most, from worms to people, are bilateral: a left side and a right side that mirror each other, with a head in front and a tail behind. A few, like jellyfish, sea anemones and sea stars, are radial, arranged around a central point like the spokes of a wheel. The plan decides how an animal moves, hunts and escapes.

A radial animal has a top and a bottom but no front end and no back end: cut it through the center in any direction and the pieces match, like slices of a pie. A wheel-shaped body meets food or danger from every side equally well, but with no leading end to steer by, a radial animal can never pick one direction and charge or flee along it.

About 99 percent of animal species, more than a million kinds, are bilateral: you, a fish, an insect and a worm all have a matching left and right, so the radial jellyfish is the rare exception. A bilateral body can taper to a pointed front, so a tuna or a shark slices through the water with far less drag, which is why nearly every fast hunter and fast escaper is bilateral. A jellyfish never needed a streamlined shape.

Having a front also lets an animal gather its senses and nerves into a head, which biologists call cephalization. A jellyfish or a sea star has its nerves spread in a net or a ring, with barely any head at all. At the other extreme, octopuses and squid, along with their cousins the cuttlefish, crowd big camera-style eyes, a large brain and a beak into the front of the body, making them the most head-centered animals in the sea.

A sea star looks perfectly radial, with five arms around a center, yet it begins life as a tiny swimming larva with mirror-image sides, like yours. As the larva transforms, its left side grows while the right side is absorbed and lost, and the left side then rebuilds the whole body in five parts around a center. That is why biologists count sea stars and their relatives, the echinoderms, as bilateral animals that turned radial later.
