the-big-invertebrate-groups.context_blurb:
Almost every animal on Earth lacks a backbone. Turn over the rocks of a single tide pool and you can meet most of the great invertebrate groups at once, from crabs and snails to starfish, anemones, worms and sponges. Biologists sort them by body plan, and each plan hides its own surprises.

A crab's legs bend at joints and its body is wrapped in a hard outer skeleton of chitin, the two traits that mark it as an arthropod, like insects, spiders, scorpions, lobsters, centipedes and millipedes. No group is bigger: about four in five of all known animal species are arthropods. Jellyfish, corals and sea anemones belong to the cnidarian group, armed with stinging cells that fire tiny harpoons into small fish that touch their tentacles. The starfish is an echinoderm, built like a wheel on five-fold symmetry with no front or back, a plan its sea urchin and sea cucumber relatives share as they creep on hundreds of tiny tube feet.

An earthworm's body is a long tube of repeating rings, or segments, most bearing tiny bristles, and that segmented plan makes it an annelid, like the leech. An earthworm has more than a hundred segments, while every leech, large or small, has exactly 34 segments and no bristles at all. A snail belongs to the mollusks, soft-bodied animals with a muscular foot, and it builds its shell without any skeleton: a fold of tissue called the mantle, draped over its body, lays the shell down one layer at a time. Simplest of all are the sponges, or Porifera, 'pore-bearers.' A sponge has no gut, nerves or muscles and lacks true tissues and organs altogether; collar cells inside it beat tiny whips to pump seawater through its pores and strain out food.

An octopus, big-brained and jet-propelled, looks nothing like a snail, yet both are mollusks: the muscular foot a snail creeps on is, in the octopus, divided into the arms that seize its prey. Arthropods pay a price for their armor. Because the outer skeleton cannot stretch, a crab must climb out of it to grow, a shedding called molting, and for hours afterward its fresh shell stays soft and pale, so the crab is almost helpless until it hardens. A starfish larva drifting in the plankton has bilateral symmetry, with a left and right, a front and back, and only reorganizes into the five-fold adult wheel when it settles.

The octopus has three hearts, and its blood carries oxygen on copper instead of iron, so it runs blue. Its central heart stops when it swims, which is why an octopus prefers to crawl. A starfish can eat a clam clamped shut too tightly for any claw to open: it pulls for hours, then pushes its own stomach out through its mouth and into the narrow gap between the shells, digests the clam outside its body, and slurps the liquid meal back in. In 1907 H. V. Wilson strained a living sponge through fine mesh, reducing it to loose cells, and the cells found one another again and reassembled into a working sponge, possible because they were never bound into true tissues. Even our own nerves were first understood through a mollusk: around 1950 Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley threaded wires into the giant nerve fiber of a squid, up to a thousand times wider than a human one, and showed how a nerve fires, with sodium rushing in and potassium flowing out.

In most animals the embryo's first opening becomes the mouth. In the deuterostomes it becomes the anus instead, with the mouth opening afterward, and that camp holds the echinoderm family, including the sea urchin, alongside fish, frogs and us. Arthropods, mollusks such as the octopus and mussel, and segmented worms all build the mouth first. So in how it develops, the brainless urchin in the tide pool is more like you than the clever octopus beside it, though a 2021 genomic study has questioned exactly how close the two camps' branches sit.

the-five-vertebrate-classes-the-recognit.context_blurb:
Animals with backbones, the vertebrates, are traditionally sorted into five living classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Each class has a tell, one or two features that settle the question at a glance. But modern family trees show that the neat lineup hides some surprises, including a dinosaur and a mammal cousin in disguise.

A fish breathes through gills, comb-like filaments behind the head that pull oxygen straight out of the water, and with its fins it lives its whole life underwater; lift a trout into the air and it suffocates. A reptile's tell is dry skin covered in keratin scales or scutes, worn by snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles alike, and a snake sheds its whole old skin at once, inside out, like a sock. Reptiles also lay their eggs on land. A bird's tell is feathers, whose tiny branches hook together into a light, smooth, warm covering strong enough for flight, which no other class grows. Birds also have toothless, beaked jaws and lay hard-shelled eggs. A mammal's double tell is hair or fur plus milk: mothers nurse their young from mammary glands, the mammae that give the class its name. A whale lives like a fish, yet it is a mammal: it breathes air through a blowhole, grows a scattering of hair, has warm blood and nurses its calf on rich milk.

Amphibians have thin, wet skin that they actually breathe through, and some, such as the lungless salamanders of damp Appalachian forests, have no lungs at all and take in all their oxygen through their skin. A newt may look like a small lizard, but it is an amphibian, a kind of salamander with damp skin that starts life as a gilled larva in the water before crawling out onto land. Feathers, not flight, define a bird, so flightless penguins and ostriches are still genuine birds. Almost all mammals give birth to live young, but five species in Australia and New Guinea, the platypus and the four spiny echidnas, are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. Several furry animals sail through the air on stretched flaps of skin, but they only glide downward; the bat is the only mammal that truly flies, flapping real wings with its own muscle power. The earliest known bat lived about 50 million years ago.

Frogs must return to ponds to lay soft eggs that would dry out on land, but a reptile's shelled egg holds the embryo in a sealed amniotic sac, a private water world whose membranes keep it moist, so reptiles can breed far from water, even in deserts. A feather is a made-over reptile scale: both are made of one tough protein, beta-keratin, shaped two different ways. That fits a bigger twist: birds evolved from little feathered theropods, the dinosaur family of Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor, and they are the only branch of the dinosaurs still alive, so the birds are living dinosaurs. On a family tree built from shared traits and DNA, crocodiles are more closely related to sparrows than to lizards, because crocodiles and birds share the archosaur branch, so birds are not a separate group at all but one twig growing from deep within the reptile branch.

Birds move air one way through their lungs in a continuous loop, long thought to be special equipment for flight, but in 2010 Colleen Farmer and Kent Sanders found the same one-way airflow in the American alligator, which has no air sacs at all. Since crocodilians and birds sit on opposite sides of the archosaur tree, the one-way lung probably goes back to their common ancestor, so the other dinosaurs likely breathed this way too.

Mammals never descended from reptiles. About 320 million years ago the egg-laying land vertebrates split into two sister branches: the synapsids, which led to mammals, and the sauropsids, which led to reptiles and birds. The sail-backed Dimetrodon, often shelved with the dinosaurs, carries the synapsid mark, one opening in the skull behind each eye, so it is a stem-mammal, closer kin to a cow than to any lizard.

the-rule-breakers-monotremes-and-marsupi.context_blurb:
Nearly all mammals carry their young inside the body and give birth to well-developed babies. Two groups break the rules. The monotremes of Australia and New Guinea still lay eggs, and the marsupials, such as kangaroos, wombats and opossums, give birth to tiny, unfinished young that complete their growth in a pouch.

The egg-laying mammals are called monotremes: they lay leathery eggs, yet they still nurse their hatchlings with milk. There are exactly five living kinds, the duck-billed platypus and four spiny, ant-eating echidnas: the short-beaked echidna and three long-beaked ones. A monotreme mother has no nipples, so her milk oozes out through pores in patches of her skin and the babies lap it from her fur. A diving platypus shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils and finds shrimp, insects and worms with about 40,000 electroreceptors in rows along its bill, which detect the faint electricity made when prey muscles move. The male platypus alone carries a venomous spur on each hind heel, and its venom will not kill a person but brings agonizing pain that may linger for months.

A newborn kangaroo is blind, hairless and no bigger than a jellybean, roughly 2 centimeters long and under a gram, and it crawls up through its mother's fur to the pouch on its own, pulling with strong, clawed forelimbs. A wombat digs long tunnels, kicking dirt and sticks behind it, so its pouch opens backward, toward the mother's rear, and the soil she throws up never falls in on her joey. North America's only native marsupial, the Virginia opossum, bears newborns the size of honeybees, but her pouch has just 13 teats, so a baby lives only if it reaches a teat and clamps on.

When a preserved platypus reached the British Museum in London in 1799, naturalists suspected a hoax, a duck's bill sewn onto a beaver-like body. Platypus fur glows cyan and green under ultraviolet light. The platypus has also lost the genes for a working stomach. The echidna senses electricity through its beak too, but its beak holds a mere 400 to 2,000 receptors. A mother echidna rolls her single leathery egg into a temporary pouch, and the hatchling, a hairless puggle, suckles there until its spines sprout and it gets too prickly to carry; then she moves it to a burrow, where it keeps suckling for about six months. Attenborough's long-beaked echidna went unrecorded by science for 62 years, until camera traps set in New Guinea's Cyclops Mountains in 2023 caught the animal alive on film, nosing through the forest.

No other animal makes cube-shaped droppings: a wombat's come out with flat faces because the last stretch of its intestine has alternating stiff and stretchy zones that mould them as they dry. The wombat stacks the cubes on rocks and logs to mark its ground, and their flat sides keep them from rolling off; the research won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize.

Today the egg-layers hang on as a handful of species. But about 100 million years ago, at Lightning Ridge, an opal field in New South Wales, at least six kinds of egg-laying mammal lived side by side, and some of their bones are preserved as gem opal. The 2024 star of that site, nicknamed the echidnapus, has a skull that blends platypus and echidna features.

what-makes-a-bird.context_blurb: Birds are the only living animals with feathers, and feathers are the single most useful feature for picking a bird out of a lineup. But birds also share a specific body plan: a toothless beak, hollow bones, a large keeled breastbone, and air-sac lungs. Look closely at the main features that make a bird a bird, which of them show up elsewhere in the animal kingdom, and how birds inherited their key traits from a specific group of dinosaurs.

what-makes-a-mammal.context_blurb: Mammals are a diverse group of animals that includes everything from mice to blue whales. All of them share a specific set of features: hair, milk-producing mammary glands, three middle-ear bones, and a four-chambered heart. Look closely at the key features that define a mammal, how biologists use them to tell mammals apart from the other vertebrate groups, and the handful of mammal species that break the usual rules in surprising ways.

what-makes-a-reptile-an-amphibian-dry-sc.context_blurb: Reptiles and amphibians are easy to confuse at first glance, but they are two very different animal groups. Reptiles, including snakes, lizards, turtles, and crocodilians, have dry scaly skin and lay shelled eggs on land. Amphibians, including frogs, salamanders, and caecilians, have soft moist skin and mostly lay unshelled eggs in water. Look closely at the key features that separate the two groups and why the differences are more than just skin-deep.

antifreeze-blood-and-freezing-solid.context_blurb:
Below freezing, ice is a killer, because sharp crystals that form inside a living cell burst it like a water balloon. Animals of the polar seas, the northern forests and the Arctic tundra have found two ways around the danger. Some keep their bodies liquid with natural antifreeze; others let themselves freeze solid and come back to life when spring arrives.

In the forests of Canada the wood frog spends the winter under the leaf litter frozen solid, with up to about two-thirds of its body water turned to ice, no heartbeat and no breath, then thaws in spring and simply hops away. In the waters around Antarctica the crocodile icefish is stranger still: no other vertebrate lacks red blood cells and hemoglobin entirely, and without that red pigment its blood runs clear and white.

Those seas sit near minus 1.9°C, cold enough to turn an ordinary fish's blood to slush, but the notothenioid fish carry antifreeze proteins that latch onto any tiny ice crystal that gets inside and hold it so it cannot grow. The wood frog guards its cells another way: before it freezes, the frog's liver floods its cells with glucose, blood sugar, which keeps the inside of each cell from freezing while ice forms only in the safe gaps between them.

When the April soil warms, the frozen frog's heart and brain restart on their own after months of silence, and within about 10 hours it is hopping and behaving normally again. Inside a knobby gall on a goldenrod plant, the larva of the goldenrod gall fly freezes on purpose: in autumn it fills itself with glycerol, and as the cold deepens it adds a second protectant, sorbitol, which lets it survive frozen at temperatures as low as minus 40°C, thawing and refreezing all winter. The Arctic ground squirrel of Alaska hibernates at a body temperature of minus 2.9°C, the lowest ever measured in a mammal, and its blood stays liquid because it supercools: the squirrel clears out the tiny specks that ice needs to start forming around.

Antifreeze has a cost. The notothenioid's proteins grip ice so tightly that trapped crystals refuse to melt even when summer water warms above their normal melting point, so the fish may carry ice inside its body all its life. The gene for that antifreeze was not invented from scratch: in 1997 biologists showed it had been rebuilt from the gene for trypsinogen, a gut enzyme from the pancreas that digests food, by keeping the old gene's ends and copying a tiny snippet over and over to grow the long backbone. The switch happened about 5 to 14 million years ago, around the time the Antarctic Ocean first froze. The icefish copes with thin, clear blood by pumping a great deal of it: its heart is oversized, moving four to five times more blood for its weight than a normal fish's, through extra-wide vessels. Why it lost its red cells at all is still argued, and a leading 2006 review by Sidell and O'Brien finds no measured benefit: the mutation probably survived only because cold, predator-poor Antarctic water relaxed the pressure of natural selection long enough for the giant heart and other fixes to evolve. Icefish live right beside red-blooded cousins, and their blood carries only about a tenth as much oxygen, so other biologists still debate whether the loss was ever useful.

coming-back-from-dry-death-cryptobiosis.context_blurb:
A few tiny animals can dry out until they seem dead, wait for years, and then wake up when water returns. Biologists call this power cryptobiosis, meaning "hidden life." The most famous champion is the tardigrade, a microscopic animal of damp moss, but brine shrimp, midge larvae and rotifers share the trick, and scientists are still working out how it is done.

Squeeze a clump of wet moss and the drop that falls may hold a tardigrade, a plump animal about half a millimeter long that clambers on eight stubby, clawed legs. Its rounded body and slow, lumbering walk have earned it the nickname water bear, and sometimes moss piglet. When the moss dries in the sun, the tardigrade tucks in its head and legs, loses over 95 percent of the water in its body, and shrivels into a little barrel called a tun. Hours after one drop of water lands on it, the tun swells, and the water bear walks away. Brine shrimp play the same game with their eggs, which can sit bone-dry for years. That is why old comic-book ads sold brine shrimp to American kids as "Sea-Monkeys": a packet of dried eggs poured into water becomes a bowl of swimmers a few days later.

The famous toughness has a catch. An active, water-filled tardigrade is soft and fragile; a hungry mite can eat it, and a careless finger can crush it. Only the dried, dormant tun can shrug off boiling heat, deep cold and crushing pressure. In September 2007 European scientists ran a test named Tardigrades in Space, fixing dried water bears to the outside of the Foton-M3 satellite. For about ten days the animals sat in the bare vacuum of space, beyond the air, and many revived back on Earth, making the tardigrade the first animal shown to survive it. The same shutdown guards against more than thirst: cryptobiosis is the umbrella word for going dormant to survive drought, freezing or a lack of oxygen.

How does a dried animal keep its cells from falling apart? As a tardigrade dries, special proteins called CAHS proteins team up with a little trehalose, a sugar, and set the fluid inside its cells into a solid glass. The glass locks each cell's parts in place until water returns. In that state the animal's metabolism falls below 0.01 percent of normal, so faint it is almost undetectable, and a tun can last for years with nothing to eat or drink, by some reports up to about thirty. The water bear has rivals. In seasonal pools of central Africa lives the larva of a midge, a small mosquito-like fly. When its pool dries up, the larva loses about 97 percent of its water and turns glassy too, and one dried larva has revived after about 17 years.

The deepest secrets lie in the tardigrade's own genes. In 2016 Japanese scientists reading the DNA of a tardigrade species, Ramazzottius varieornatus, found a protein never seen elsewhere in nature and named it Dsup, for "damage suppressor." Dsup binds to DNA and wraps it like a shield against radiation damage, and it still protects DNA when its gene is placed in human cells grown in a lab dish.

Cold survivors may last far longer. In 2021 Russian scientists thawed a bdelloid rotifer, a microscopic freshwater animal, out of Siberian permafrost. Radiocarbon dating of the frozen mud around it showed the rotifer had been dormant for about 24,000 years, and once warmed, it woke and began to reproduce.

Scientists long assumed every dry survivor leaned on trehalose, because brine shrimp pack their dried eggs with the sugar. Tardigrades break that rule. In 2008 Ralph Hengherr's team found that the common lab tardigrade Milnesium tardigradum dries and revives perfectly with no detectable trehalose at all, because its own CAHS proteins do the main work of turning the cell to glass. That glass also marks the water bear's true limit. Headlines say a tun survives 150 degrees Celsius, and it can take a quick scald, but when Hengherr heated nine dried species in 2009, revival stayed high up to roughly 80 degrees, then fell steeply. The drop matched the temperature at which each species' inner glass softens back toward a liquid, and once the glass melts, the protection is gone.

heat-exchange-plumbing-countercurrent.context_blurb:
Many animals save heat with a simple piece of plumbing: they run warm blood flowing one way right beside cold blood flowing the other. Heat crosses from the warm stream to the cold one before it can escape. This countercurrent exchange keeps penguins' feet from freezing, keeps fast fish warm, and can even be run in reverse.

A penguin can stand on bare Antarctic ice for hours. Warm feet would melt the ice beneath them, which would then refreeze into a trap, and they would waste precious heat. So the penguin keeps its feet just above freezing: cold, cheap to run, and losing almost no heat.

Inside each leg, the vessels taking warm blood down to the feet are wrapped around the vessels bringing chilled blood back up. As they pass in opposite directions, the warm blood hands its heat across to the returning blood, so the heat is recycled into the body instead of being lost at the feet. Herons and ducks standing in icy water use the same leg bundles. Fish use the trick too. Most fish are cold-blooded and turn sluggish in cold water, but a great white shark keeps its swimming muscles 6 to 10 degrees Celsius warmer than the sea, so it can hunt hard where its prey slows down.

In tuna and great whites, the net of blood vessels that does this is called the rete mirabile, Latin for "wonderful net": warm blood leaving the muscle passes cold blood coming in and hands its heat back before it can escape through the gills. The swordfish warms a different organ. Its heater organ, made from an altered eye muscle, keeps its eyes and brain 10 to 15 degrees above the icy sea, and a warm retina responds faster, so it can spot fast-darting squid and fish that a cold-eyed fish would miss. A reindeer breathes Arctic air at minus 40 degrees, yet scroll-like bones in its nose, wrapped in blood vessels, warm each breath to body temperature. When it breathes out, the same bones recapture warmth and water from the air leaving its body, so almost nothing is wasted. Tuna and sharks warm only certain patches, while their hearts pump cold blood. In 2015 scientists found that the opah, a round, silver deep-sea fish, is warm throughout its whole body, even its heart. It makes heat by constantly flapping its wing-like fins and holds it in with fat-wrapped vessel nets inside its gills.

Tuna and the great white's shark family are only distant relatives, yet each evolved this warm-muscle plumbing separately, and penguins and reindeer reached the same trick on their own too, a textbook case of convergent evolution. The plumbing can also run in reverse. A whale working hard builds up heat in its huge muscles, and its flippers and tail flukes are its only thin, bare-skinned parts. To cool down, it skips the heat-saving vein bundles and floods the flukes with warm blood, so the heat pours out into the sea. Fish gills use the same countercurrent idea for oxygen. Water streams across the gill filaments in one direction while blood runs the opposite way, so the blood keeps meeting fresher water and pulls out about 90 percent of the oxygen in it. The swim bladder of a deep-sea fish goes further, because its vessel net works as a multiplier. Oxygen leaving in the outgoing vein leaks across to the incoming artery, so each pass adds to the one before and the oxygen keeps building, until the fish can force gas into the bladder against pressures of hundreds of atmospheres.

living-without-water.context_blurb:
Deserts punish any animal that loses moisture, and some go a year or more without rain. Desert animals survive with a toolkit of tricks: they make water inside their bodies, refuse to waste it, store it, and drink in ways no other creature can. Camels, kangaroo rats, tortoises, frogs and a spiky lizard each have their own.

The camel's hump is no tank of water, whatever storybooks say: it is fat, up to about 80 pounds of it in a dromedary, an energy store the camel burns when food runs short. A kangaroo rat of the southwestern deserts never drinks at all: it gets nearly all its water from the dry seeds it eats, because burning their hydrogen for energy produces metabolic water inside its body. It also dodges the heat, sheltering from dawn to dusk below ground in a burrow that stays cool and humid, and coming out only at night.

Rather than sweat its water away, a camel lets its body temperature swing through the day, from about 34 C at dawn to about 40 C by late afternoon, a change that would leave a person feverish. When a parched camel finally reaches a well, it can gulp about 30 gallons, more than 100 liters, in around ten minutes, a flood that would be fatal to most large mammals, yet its cells are built to survive the sudden rush. The desert tortoise of the Mojave and Sonoran deserts keeps a reserve in an oversized bladder that can hold about two-fifths of its body weight, but when a predator frightens it, it voids that store, a loss that can prove deadlier than the attack.

The thorny devil, a thorn-covered lizard of Australia's dry interior, drinks without lowering its head: tiny grooves between its scales draw water along by capillary action, even uphill, and carry it to the corners of its mouth. In a long Australian drought, the water-holding frog soaks itself full, burrows underground and wraps itself in a cocoon made of its own shed skin, sleeping there for up to five years. Aboriginal peoples, and thirsty travellers after them, have long dug these frogs up and squeezed them for a drink, and that clean-tasting water is very dilute urine, held in an enormous bladder that can make up about 57 percent of the frog's body mass. The frog also recycles its nitrogen waste, so it never spends water flushing it out, and it cuts its oxygen use by about 70 percent while it sleeps.

When a camel goes days without drinking, the fluid in its vessels grows thick and sludgy. Its red cells are oval rather than round, a shape that keeps them flowing through even the narrowest capillaries, so a camel can survive losing about a quarter of its body water, while most mammals die after losing about 12 percent. The kangaroo rat's narrow, coiled nose works as a heat exchanger, cooling each outgoing breath and condensing its moisture, so the animal recovers as much as 83 percent of the water in every breath.

For years scientists assumed the thorny devil filled its grooves with morning dew. Philip Withers and colleagues found that neither dew nor a damp patch of ground ever filled the channels enough to make it swallow. Instead the lizard uses its legs to flick damp sand onto its own back, and the grooves draw that moisture down to its mouth. Rain and damp sand, not dew, are its real sources.

size-ears-and-heat-radiators-and-bergman.context_blurb:
A body makes heat throughout its bulk but can lose it only through its skin. That simple fact shapes animals all over the world: in hot places, big ears and long limbs work as radiators, while in the cold, compact bodies with small ears hold the heat in. Biologists sum up these patterns as Bergmann's rule and Allen's rule.

An African elephant has almost no sweat glands, so its huge ears are its cooling system: blood vessels run just beneath skin only 1 to 2 millimeters thick on the back of the ear, and as the elephant fans them, the blood dumps its heat into the air. In the Sahara, the fennec fox, the smallest fox alive at barely a kilogram, has ears up to 10 centimeters long, the biggest for its size in the dog family, and above all they serve as radiators, shedding the fox's body heat into the desert air. They double as listening dishes that pinpoint prey moving underground.

An elephant's entire blood supply passes through its ears about every 20 minutes, so heat from deep inside keeps reaching the thin ear skin, and flapping can lower its body temperature by as much as 9 degrees Celsius. Out in the deserts of the American West, the black-tailed jackrabbit cools off the same way: at about 30 degrees Celsius in the shade, blood vessels in its enormous ears open wide and its excess heat drains into the cooler air, so it never needs to pant or sweat away precious water. The Arctic fox is the fennec's mirror image: small round ears, a short snout, stubby legs and a ball-like body all hold its heat in, so it does not even begin to shiver until about minus 40 degrees Celsius.

The reason is geometry: spread the same volume of warm blood into a wide, thin shape and it exposes far more surface for its volume, so heat escapes much faster than from a rounded lump. Carl Bergmann, a German biologist writing in 1847, saw that within one animal group the members living where it is coldest usually grow biggest, because a bulky body has less surface for its volume and loses heat more slowly; among bears, the Arctic polar bear is the largest of all. The tropical sun bear, the smallest, weighs under a fifth as much.

Allen's rule is the partner pattern: animals of colder climates tend to have shorter ears, legs, tails and snouts, so while the desert jackrabbit's long ears work as radiators, the Arctic hare of northern Canada and Greenland has small, stubby ears that save its warmth.

sleeping-through-winter-hibernation-and-.context_blurb:
When winter leaves almost nothing to eat, some animals simply shut down. They slow their hearts, breathe less, let their bodies cool and live for months on stored fat. The record-holders seem to bend the rules of life.

That deep, energy-saving winter sleep is hibernation: by burning stored fat at a fraction of its normal pace, an animal rides out the months when food is gone. The groundhog, or woodchuck, a plump North American burrower, is a true deep hibernator: its heart drops from roughly 80 beats a minute to 4 or 5, and its body cools nearly to freezing.

Of all the primates, only one is known to hibernate deeply: the fat-tailed dwarf lemur of Madagascar, which sleeps about seven months a year in a tree hollow, living off fat stored in its tail. The common poorwill, a desert nightjar of western North America, is the only bird known to truly hibernate, tucked chilled and motionless into the rocks for weeks or months, so the Hopi named it holchoko, the sleeping one.

A denning bear sleeps far lighter than a groundhog: it cools only a few degrees and never fully powers down, so it can wake and defend itself if something disturbs its den. That warmth lets a mother bear do what no groundhog could: give birth in the dark den and nurse her cubs through the winter. A denning bear can go up to about eight months without eating, drinking, urinating or passing any waste. Its den stays clean because a plug of hardened feces, dead gut cells and hair builds up in its lower gut and seals it shut until the bear emerges in spring. Its muscles barely waste, because instead of urinating out its waste nitrogen, the bear recycles nearly all of it into brand-new muscle protein.

A hummingbird burns fuel so fast that a cold night could starve it, so every night it drops into torpor, a nightly mini-hibernation that cuts its metabolism by about 95 percent. White-nose syndrome, a fungus that thrives in cold caves, has wiped out millions of bats across North America since 2006 by rousing them from hibernation again and again, so they burn their winter fat too fast and starve before spring.

Its hot-weather twin is estivation: when its water hole dries up, an African lungfish digs down into the mud, seals itself in a cocoon of its own hardened mucus and can wait up to four years in the wild for rain. The North American wood frog spends winter frozen solid, with up to two-thirds of its body water turned to ice and no heartbeat or breathing, and then each spring it thaws out and revives. A painted turtle under pond ice for months makes energy without oxygen, and lactic acid builds up to levels that would kill most animals. To survive, it uses its own skeleton as a giant antacid: its bones and shell slowly dissolve, releasing carbonates that neutralize the acid.

The wood frog survives freezing because it packs its cells with sugar and urea, a natural antifreeze that keeps the fluid inside them liquid, so ice forms only in the spaces between cells. The arctic ground squirrel goes furthest of all: it lets its body core fall to about 27 degrees Fahrenheit, below the point where water freezes, without a single ice crystal forming, which no other warm-blooded animal is known to survive. Ice needs a speck or rough surface to start growing on, so before winter the squirrel cleans its blood of anything a crystal could form around; one crystal would burst its cells. In the 1980s Brian Barnes of the University of Alaska Fairbanks proved it by implanting tiny radio transmitters in the squirrels and letting them hibernate outdoors in natural conditions, where their cores dropped below freezing. During the long sleep its neurons wither, pruning back their branches, yet within about two hours of waking they regrow and end up with even more connections than a summer squirrel has.

Strangely, the cold sleep itself is cheap: a ground squirrel spends an estimated 60 to 80 percent of its saved winter fuel on the warm-ups it makes every week or so, rewarming to about 37 degrees Celsius for roughly 16 hours. Why is still debated: perhaps to reboot an immune system that shuts off in the cold, or because torpor is not true sleep and it warms up to sleep for real.

the-two-engines-warm-blooded-vs-cold-blo.context_blurb:
Animals run on two kinds of engine. Mammals and birds are warm-blooded: they burn food to make their own steady body heat, which keeps them active in the cold but costs a lot of fuel. Reptiles, amphibians, fish and insects are cold-blooded: they take their warmth from the world around them, which is cheap but leaves them at the mercy of the weather. Some animals blur the line.

A lizard gets its warmth from outside its body, basking on sun-warmed rock, and it shuttles between sun and shade to steer its temperature, a habit called behavioral thermoregulation. That is the fundamental split: a snake takes its warmth from outside, while a mouse burns food to make its own, so the mouse can move in the cold but must eat almost nonstop, while the snake is cheap to run.

Size for size, a mouse must eat far more than a lizard because so much of its food is burned just to keep its inner furnace burning at a steady temperature, which is why a lizard can rest for weeks without eating. Because it pays nothing to heat itself, a healthy adult ball python can go at least six months without a meal, and one ball python fasted for 21 months, the longest snake fast on record.

The Etruscan shrew, the smallest mammal by weight, loses heat so fast that it must eat 1.5 to 2 times its body weight every day, its heart races at up to about 1,500 beats a minute, and it can starve within just two or three hours. A hummingbird, which drinks nectar equal to about four-fifths of its weight each day, survives cold nights by dropping into torpor, cooling its body and slowing its engine about tenfold, then rewarming at dawn. Honeybees are insects, yet a winter cluster keeps its core near 85 degrees Fahrenheit, because the bees shiver their big flight muscles without moving their wings, making heat instead of motion, and take turns between the warm center and the chilly edge.

A bluefin tuna's rete mirabile, a net of vessels that runs warm outgoing blood beside cold incoming blood, captures its muscle heat up to 99 percent efficiently, holding its swimming muscles as much as about 20 degrees Celsius warmer than the water. Using the same kind of heat-trapping net, the great white shark can hold its body up to about 14 degrees Celsius (25 degrees Fahrenheit) above the sea, warmer than any other living shark, which powers its ambush attacks. The leatherback sea turtle has no furnace and does not shiver, yet in water of just 7.5 degrees Celsius it stays about 18 degrees warmer than its surroundings, through gigantothermy: its sheer enormous size, over 900 kilograms, holds the heat in, helped by insulating tissues and heat-exchanging flippers. A ground squirrel waking from hibernation rewarms without a shiver using brown fat, whose cells carry a protein, UCP1, that punches a hole in the energy-storing membrane of their mitochondria, so the fuel's energy leaks out as heat instead of being banked as usable power.

A Burmese python can fast for months at little cost, but a big meal sets off a violent burst: within days its metabolism runs 10 to 44 times faster than at rest while its organs swell, and everything shrinks back by about the tenth day. Whether giant dinosaurs ran warm or cold is still open: in 2014 John Grady's team argued from their growth rates that they were mesothermic, an in-between engine that could raise body heat without holding it steady, like a tuna, but other scientists soon challenged the statistics. In 2022 Ricardo Araújo's team measured the body heat of extinct mammal ancestors using the looping, fluid-filled balance canals of the inner ear: warm blood thins the fluid inside, so hot-running animals need narrower canals, and the change shows warm blood switching on in the Late Triassic, about 233 million years ago. Exactly when that warm engine first started is still being studied.

compound-eyes-and-the-insect-mosaic.context_blurb:
Insects and many of their relatives see through compound eyes: big domed eyes built from thousands of tiny units packed side by side, each pointing a slightly different way and catching its own scrap of the view. Such an eye is poor at fine detail, but it is superb at catching movement, exactly what fast hunters and fast escapers need.

A dragonfly's eyes wrap around most of its head, and each one holds up to 30,000 of those units, called ommatidia. Every ommatidium is a lens over a light catcher that registers a single dot of light, and the brain stitches the dots into a mosaic picture.

Motion is where this design shines. A housefly takes in about 250 flashes of light per second, where a human manages about 60, so a fly sees roughly four times faster than you do. To the fly, a swatting hand drifts down in slow motion, leaving plenty of time to escape.

The dragonfly turns its eyes into a weapon, snatching mosquitoes and midges out of the air about 95 percent of the time. High-speed films of its head, wings and eyes show why. Its brain does not simply chase the spot where the prey is now: sixteen special nerve cells track the target, and the brain forecasts where the prey is heading, then steers the wings to meet it there.

The mantis shrimp, a bright reef hunter of the Indo-Pacific, owns the oddest compound eyes on the planet. Each eye rides on its own movable stalk, worked by eight tiny muscles, so the two eyes can swivel independently and look in completely different directions at the same moment.

eyeshine-and-seeing-in-the-dark.context_blurb:
Many night-active animals, from cats and deer to raccoons and crocodiles, have eyes that blaze back at you in a beam of light. That glow is a side effect of a trick for seeing in near darkness. Other night hunters solve the same problem in completely different ways.

A deer's eyes flash greenish gold in headlights because of the tapetum lucidum, Latin for "bright tapestry," a mirror-like sheet behind the retina: light that slips past the light-sensing cells hits the mirror and bounces back through them, giving the eye a second chance to catch it.

Humans and most other primates have no tapetum, so our eyes never shine. In a flash photo, the light reaches the back of the eye and lights up the blood-rich retina, and the camera records that red as red-eye. A cat gives up color for night sight: its retina is packed with rod cells, six to eight times as many as ours, and holds very few cones. Rods catch dim light and movement superbly but not color, so a cat can spot a mouse in near blackness yet cannot tell red from green as we do. Eyeshine comes in different colors, green in cats, yellow in raccoons, blue in many dogs, because the mirror itself is built from different materials, such as crystals of zinc, riboflavin or collagen, and each reflects its own band of light.

The tarsier, a mouse-sized primate of Southeast Asian forests that hunts insects by moonlight, has no mirror at all, so instead each of its eyeballs grew enormous, about 16 millimeters across and as big as its whole brain, the largest eyes for body size of any mammal. Its daytime ancestors lost the tapetum, and its kind never regained it.

Arctic reindeer live through months of dim twilight. In 2013 Stokkan and colleagues found that the reindeer's mirror changes color with the seasons, from gold in summer to deep blue in winter, the first seasonal change of its kind seen in a mammal. Blue reflects less light straight back out and scatters more of it through the retina, making the eye more sensitive in the long Arctic dusk. In the near-black middle depths of the ocean, the barreleye fish hangs still and gazes upward through a see-through forehead. Its eyes are shaped like tubes, since a tube collects much more light than a round eye of equal width.

The colossal squid has the largest eye in the history of the animal kingdom, as wide as a dinner plate, about 27 centimeters, with a lens as big as an orange. According to the vision scientists Nilsson and Warrant, the giant eye is built to spot the faint glow a hunting sperm whale, the squid's chief predator, stirs up in the plankton as it dives, an early warning in the black deep.

focusing-light-underwater.context_blurb:
Seeing clearly underwater is a different problem from seeing in air, because light behaves differently once it enters water. Fish, octopuses and some deep-sea oddities have each solved it, with eyes that work very differently from ours.

On land, most of your focusing happens at the transparent bulge on the front of your eye, the cornea, because light bends sharply as it passes from thin air into the denser eye. Underwater there is no such jump: water bends light almost as much as the cornea does, so the cornea has little left to do, and the lens must do nearly all the work. To do that heavy bending, a fish's lens is a hard, nearly perfect sphere, clear as glass and bulging out through the pupil, nothing like the soft, flattened lens of a land animal.

A human focuses by squeezing a soft lens fatter or thinner. A fish cannot reshape its rigid ball, so it slides the whole lens back and forth inside the eye, the way you would slide a projector's lens to sharpen the picture.

The puller is a small muscle called the retractor lentis, anchored to the iris. At rest the fish eye is set for close-up viewing, so to focus on something far away, the muscle hauls the lens backward, toward the retina at the back of the eye. An octopus, a mollusk more closely related to snails and clams than to fish, has almost the same eye, with a round lens that it focuses by sliding. It did not inherit that eye from a shared ancestor: octopuses and fish split more than 500 million years ago, when their ancestors had only patches of light-sensing skin, and each line invented the same camera eye entirely on its own.

A plain glass ball focuses badly, because edge rays and center rays come to a focus in different places. A fish lens beats this blur because it is graded, watery at the surface and much denser at the core, and that change from rim to center bends every ray to a single point. The German scientist Ludwig Matthiessen compared the eyes of goldfish, tuna and sharks in the 1880s and found the same number in every one. The distance from the center of the lens to the retina is about 2.5 times the lens's radius, so measuring a fish's lens tells a biologist how far behind it the retina must sit.

In the barreleye Rhynchohyalus, a pouch bulges from the side of each tube-shaped eye and throws a clear picture of the deep water beneath it onto an extra retina. Partridge and colleagues showed that a curved mirror of stacked guanine crystals does the focusing there, reflecting the image instead of bending it, which makes this fish one of only two backboned animals known to see with a mirror.

predator-eyes-vs-prey-eyes.context_blurb:
Look at where an animal's eyes sit and you can often guess whether it hunts or is hunted. Hunters tend to have eyes that face forward, while hunted animals tend to have eyes set wide apart, a trade-off between judging distance and watching all around. The shape of the pupil tells a story too.

Wolves, owls, house cats and people are all hunters, and their eyes sit at the front of the head, both pointing the same way, so the overlapping views let them judge exactly how far away their prey is: eyes in front, the animal hunts. Rabbits, horses and deer have eyes set at the sides of the skull, giving up that overlap for a nearly all-around view, so even with their heads down grazing they can catch a lion or wolf creeping in from almost any direction: eyes on the side, the animal hides.

With eyes on the sides of its skull, a horse sees close to 340 degrees around, but it has two blind spots, one directly behind it and a wedge reaching a few feet straight out in front of its nose, which is why a grazing horse keeps lifting its head.

When a goat lowers its head to graze, its long, horizontal slit pupils roll by up to 50 degrees, in opposite directions, to keep each pupil level with the ground, so the whole sweep of land stays in focus for spotting predators. Biologists call this eye-roll cyclovergence.

Martin Banks's team studied 214 land animals and found that vertical slit pupils belong almost only to predators shorter than about 42 centimeters at the shoulder, such as house cats and geckos, which hunt as ambushers lying in wait for the pounce, while tall chasers like lions keep round pupils.

seeing-colors-we-cant-ultraviolet.context_blurb:
Human eyes see the colors of the rainbow from red to violet, but just beyond violet lies ultraviolet light, which we cannot see at all. Many animals can, and for them a plain bird or a dull wing may carry bold messages.

Most songbirds, even a robin or a starling that looks plain brown to us, have four kinds of color-sensing cone instead of our three, and the fourth is tuned to near-ultraviolet light, so their feathers can carry a whole extra layer of color signals we never see. The male orange sulphur butterfly looks almost identical to the clouded sulphur, but his wings flash an iridescent ultraviolet signal that a female uses to pick out a male of her own species, and a single gene, called bric a brac, switches that UV flash on or off.

Arctic reindeer see ultraviolet because their lens and cornea let it through instead of blocking it as ours do, and since wolf urine soaks up ultraviolet, it shows as dark stains on the UV-bright snow, marking a wolf's trail long after the wolf has gone. The mantis shrimp, a fist-sized reef hunter, has up to six separate ultraviolet receptors, each tuned by layers of natural sunscreen chemicals that act as colored filters, a setup biologists think lets it tell many shades of UV apart. That finer sense is inferred from the filters and has not yet been proven by experiment.

Across the bird family tree, eyes have switched between violet-tuned and true-ultraviolet on at least fourteen occasions, and each switch takes just one swapped amino acid, a single building block changed in the cone's light-catching protein, its opsin, which slides the cone's best sensitivity from violet into the ultraviolet. Because so big a change rides on one tiny swap, it is easy to reverse.

the-mantis-shrimp-color-myth.context_blurb:
The mantis shrimp, a fist-sized reef hunter, has some of the most complicated eyes on Earth, with about 16 kinds of light receptor. For years popular articles claimed it must see a dazzling rainbow of colors beyond human imagination. Careful experiments told a stranger and more interesting story about how this animal really sees.

Twelve of its roughly 16 kinds of light receptor are tuned to color, spanning deep ultraviolet to far red, against just the red, green and blue receptors of a human eye, and that gap launched the internet legend of super color vision.

At the University of Queensland, researchers rewarded mantis shrimp with food for choosing one color of light and found that they could no longer tell two colors apart once the hues were within about 12 to 25 nanometers of each other, while people can distinguish hues only 1 to 5 nanometers apart. The animal with twelve color channels is worse at telling similar hues apart than a human, the opposite of the legend.

The 2014 study, led by Hanne Thoen, proposed a new way of seeing: eye muscles sweep a stripe of color sensors across an object in one quick pass, and the brain recognizes its spectral signature like a barcode instead of finely comparing hues, trading precision for speed. It is still treated as a reinterpretation under study, not a closed case. No other animal is known to detect circularly polarized light, light whose wave spirals like a corkscrew; in each unit of the mantis shrimp's eye one cell, R8, acts like an optical quarter-wave plate, untwisting the spiral into flat light that the cells below it can read.

The eye splits ultraviolet into six channels using only two UV pigments, by stacking four colored filters in front of them, and those filters are made of mycosporine-like amino acids, the same sunscreen molecules many reef animals make to shield their bodies from the sun.

the-strangest-eyes-in-the-animal-kingdom.context_blurb:
Eyes have been invented again and again in the animal kingdom, and some designs are stranger than anything in a textbook. There are eyes that focus with mirrors instead of lenses, eyes that look out through a transparent head, eyes that see above and below the water at once, and eyes rebuilt every single night.

A scallop, a hinged shellfish related to clams and oysters, has up to 200 tiny blue eyes lining the fringed rim of its mantle, peering out between the halves of its shell. Instead of a lens, each scallop eye focuses light by bouncing it off a curved mirror behind the retina. The four-eyed fish, Anableps, of Central American rivers and lagoons, really has two eyes, but it floats with the waterline across the middle of each, and a band of tissue splits each eye so the top half sees in air while the bottom half sees underwater.

The scallop's mirror is built from 20 to 30 stacked layers of tiny guanine crystals, each a perfectly square, flat plate, fitted edge to edge like bathroom tiles so the reflected image stays sharp. In the cold, dark Pacific depths lives the barreleye, whose head is topped by a clear dome full of fluid, and through it you can see its two glowing green eyes, tucked within the skull. For 70 years scientists thought its tube-shaped eyes were fixed staring upward, but in 2008 scientists from MBARI, a California ocean research institute, filmed a live barreleye whose eyes swiveled forward to aim at food.

Each Anableps eye has two pupils and two retinas but only one lens, and the lens is egg-shaped, so its two directions bend light by different amounts, focusing light from both air and water. The brownsnout spookfish of the deep sea is the only backboned animal known to focus an image with a mirror: each eye is split in two, and while one half uses a lens, the other focuses with a curved mirror of stacked guanine crystals. The ogre-faced spider, a night hunter of warm forests, has two huge eyes about 2,000 times more sensitive to light than ours, and every night it builds a fresh light-catching membrane inside them, then chemically destroys it again at dawn.

anomalocaris.context_blurb:
Anomalocaris hunted the Cambrian seas more than 500 million years ago, ages before fish ruled the oceans. Its flattened fossils come from the Burgess Shale, a bed of dark stone in the Canadian Rockies of British Columbia. It was the top hunter of its world, and scientists needed nearly a century to piece its body together.

Reaching about a meter in length, Anomalocaris was the largest predator in the Burgess Shale, a giant in a world where most animals measured a few centimeters.

Its name means "odd shrimp," because in 1892 the paleontologist Joseph Whiteaves found a single detached grasping arm and took it for the curled tail of a shrimp, so the whole animal was named after a misread body part. Those two arms, jointed into about fourteen segments, reached forward from its head, and their inner edges carried rows of trident-like spikes that seized prey and swept it toward the mouth. The mouth itself was a ring of hard, overlapping plates edged with tooth-like points; seen head-on it looks like a pineapple slice, and it closed like a clamp on its victims. Anomalocaris swam by rippling sixteen flexible flaps down each side of its body in overlapping waves, steering sharp turns with a three-part tail fan.

It hunted by sight. A whole fossil eye found in 2011 in the shale of South Australia holds some 16,000 tiny lenses, giving Anomalocaris stalked compound eyes that rivaled those of a modern dragonfly. For decades nobody knew what the whole animal looked like. Before 1985 its body parts were catalogued as separate creatures: the arm as a shrimp, the body as a sponge or sea cucumber, and the round mouth, which Charles Walcott named Peytoia, as a jellyfish. Not until 1985 did Harry Whittington and Derek Briggs find the pieces joined and see a single animal. Anomalocaris shared some arthropod hallmarks, such as stalked compound eyes and segmented grasping arms, but it never grew jointed trunk limbs, the jointed legs every living crab and beetle walks or swims on, so it sits just outside the arthropods as an early side branch. Its body carried only soft swimming flaps.

For a century it was pictured prying open trilobites, and real clues pointed that way: trilobites with healed bite wounds, and fossil droppings full of crushed shell. But a 2023 computer test of the stress its arm could bear showed the slender gripping spines bending and breaking against hard shell, so scientists concluded the arms were built to catch soft-bodied prey. Whether some of its relatives tackled harder prey is still debated.

arthropleura.context_blurb:
Arthropleura was a giant millipede relative that crawled through the coal-swamp forests of what are now Europe and North America in the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago and long before the first dinosaurs. It is the largest land invertebrate known to have lived, and its size has puzzled scientists ever since.

The biggest reached about 2.6 to 2.7 meters, more than 8 feet, roughly the length of a small car, and weighed around 50 kilograms. A big adult had about 28 to 32 armored segments, and each carried two pairs of legs, the signature of the millipedes, while centipedes have only one pair per segment.

Most Arthropleura fossils are not bodies but cast-off skins, like the 75-centimeter piece that fell from a cliff and landed on Howick Bay's beach in Northumberland in 2018: a section of armor the animal had shed as it grew, later filled with sand and turned to stone. The geologist Neil Davies called it a complete fluke of a discovery. Despite its size it was no hunter: with no venom fangs or grasping claws, it is now thought to have eaten like a modern millipede, munching rotting wood, fallen leaves, nuts and seeds.

Textbooks long credited the oxygen-rich Carboniferous air for giants like Arthropleura and the huge dragonfly Meganeura, but Davies argued that oxygen alone cannot explain them and pointed instead to the rich, nutrient-packed food of those ancient forests.

hallucigenia.context_blurb:
Hallucigenia was a fingernail-sized ocean animal shaped like a worm, that lived over 500 million years ago, in the Cambrian, when strange new body plans burst onto the scene. It is known from flattened fossils in Canada's Burgess Shale, and it is famous for how badly scientists first pieced it together.

For decades it was drawn upside down, with its row of stiff spines mistaken for legs. Around 1991, researchers drilled away the rock covering better fossils and uncovered a second set of soft legs tipped with claws, so the spines really stood up along its back as armor.

It was back to front as well. Scientists had taken a dark smudge at one end for its head, but a 2015 study showed the blob was fluid from decay that had oozed out of the body as it fossilized. The real head, at the other end, had a pair of eyes and a mouth ringed with tiny needle-like teeth.

Its claws revealed its relatives. Each claw is made of three cones fitted inside each other like a stack of paper cups, a structure found today only in velvet worms, soft caterpillar-like animals.

meganeura.context_blurb:
Meganeura was a giant dragonfly-like insect that flew over the steaming coal-swamp forests of what is now Europe about 300 million years ago, during the Carboniferous period, long before the dinosaurs. It is one of the largest insects that ever lived, and its size raises a puzzle: how could an insect grow so big?

Its wingspan reached roughly 65 to 75 centimeters, over two feet from tip to tip, wider than a hawk's. A single fossil wing measures about 32 centimeters, some 13 inches, a foot long, and it is laced with so many veins that the animal's name, Meganeura, means large-veined.

It was a fast aerial hunter, using big compound eyes and spiny, grasping legs to grab other insects out of the air in flight, and it may even have caught small early amphibians. Meganeura was not a true dragonfly but an extinct cousin, and in 2005 David Grimaldi and Michael Engel named these giant look-alikes griffinflies, to end the confusion.

Its size was possible partly because the Carboniferous air held far more oxygen than today's, around 30 to 35 percent against about 21 percent now, enough to supply a much bigger insect body, though newer research argues that oxygen is not the whole story. When oxygen levels later fell, the giant insects vanished. Insects have no lungs; they breathe through a mesh of tiny air tubes. Alexander Kaiser and colleagues used X-rays in 2007 to compare small and large beetles, and found that the bigger the beetle, the bigger the share of its body those breathing tubes take up. Because oxygen spreads only short distances, that ever-growing plumbing caps how big an insect can get, and oxygen-rich air would have raised the cap.

opabinia.context_blurb:
Opabinia was a strange little sea animal, only a few centimeters long, that swam in the Cambrian seas of what is now British Columbia more than 500 million years ago. Soft-bodied, with no jaws and no legs, it has become one of the most famous animals of the Cambrian explosion.

On top of its head sat five eyes, a cluster of four on short stalks plus a large eye in the middle, an odd number that no living animal has.

When Harry Whittington presented his careful reconstruction to a room of scientists in the 1970s, the audience burst out laughing, sure that such an animal could not be real; it was. From the front of its head stuck a long, flexible hose, about four times the length of the head, like a vacuum-cleaner nozzle, and its tip ended in a spiny claw for grasping food.

Its mouth sat on the underside of the body, opening backward, so it used the claw to pluck food from the seafloor and pass it back and under to the mouth. Few animals have ever eaten in such a roundabout way.

trilobites.context_blurb:
Trilobites were hard-shelled sea animals that crawled, burrowed and swam across the ocean floor from the Cambrian period until the end of the Permian. More than 22,000 kinds have been named, and they are among the most common animal fossils on Earth. Their shells, their stone eyes and even their last meals have left extraordinary records in rock.

Trilobites were arthropods, members of the same great group as today's insects, crabs and spiders, with jointed armor over a soft body and many jointed legs, like a modern woodlouse. Many, especially in the Ordovician, grew long, sharp spines all over their shells, perhaps to keep predators from biting or to stop them sinking into soft mud, turning them into walking pincushions.

Their backs were armored but their bellies and legs were soft, so when threatened, many rolled up into a tight armored ball, tucking the tail under the head like a pillbug. They came in every size: the largest known, Isotelus rex, reached about 72 centimeters, while the smallest, Acanthopleurella stipulae, was just 1.5 millimeters long, smaller than a grain of rice.

Trilobites ruled the seas for almost 270 million years, from about 521 million years ago in the Cambrian to about 251 million years ago, against barely 2 million years so far for our own genus, Homo. Like all arthropods, a trilobite grew by molting, splitting its old shell along built-in weak lines and crawling out, so a single animal left behind many empty shells over its life, and many trilobite fossils are cast-offs, not dead animals. Trilobites had some of the first true compound eyes, mosaics of many lens units like a bee's, and their lenses were made of calcite, a clear mineral crystal, so each lens was a tiny piece of stone; no other animal has made its eyes from rock.

The Devonian trilobite Erbenochile had a tall tower of an eye with about 560 calcite lenses in 33 to 36 vertical rows, giving it a nearly all-round view, and a rim of shell jutted over the top like a visor, shading the eye from glare above. No one knew what trilobites ate until 2023, when a synchrotron scan of Bohemolichas, a trilobite fossil some 465 million years old, revealed a gut stuffed with crushed shells of clams, ostracods and other shelled seafloor prey, the first trilobite gut contents ever found. So that species was a shell-crusher and scavenger. Then, about 251 million years ago, every last trilobite died in the end-Permian Great Dying, the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, which wiped out more than 90 percent of all species.

The calcite lens of a phacopid trilobite was really two calcite pieces stacked together, joined along a curved boundary in the same blur-correcting shape that René Descartes and Christiaan Huygens worked out on paper in the 1600s, focusing every ray of light to one sharp point some 400 million years earlier.

growing-it-back-regeneration.context_blurb:
Many animals can regrow lost body parts, but how much varies enormously. Lizards regrow tails, deer regrow antlers every year, axolotls rebuild whole legs, and some flatworms and starfish can rebuild an entire body from a scrap. People can regrow only a few tissues, which is why scientists study these champions closely.

The axolotl, a Mexican salamander prized in biology labs, can lose a whole leg and grow it back in 40 to 50 days, including its bones, muscles, nerves and blood vessels, and the new leg is perfect, with no scar at all. Many lizards drop their tails to escape a predator, a trick called autotomy, and grow new ones within weeks. But X-rays show the replacement is a copy: the original tail had a chain of small bony vertebrae, while the new one is built around one unjointed tube of cartilage, with no bone. Male deer regrow a full set of antlers every year, and antler is the fastest-growing bone of any mammal. At peak summer growth, a wapiti or elk antler can lengthen by roughly an inch, about 27 millimeters, in a single day.

A sea cucumber, a soft, sausage-shaped relative of starfish, defends itself by blasting part of its own guts out of its back end to tangle or scare an attacker, and it grows the missing organs back within a few weeks. A lizard's new tail has a cost: one solid tube of cartilage cannot bend at joints the way a backbone does, so the spare is much less flexible all along its length. A deer's growing antlers are covered in velvet, a furry skin laced with nerves and blood vessels that feeds the fast-growing bone. Each late fall or winter, falling testosterone levels make the hardened antlers drop off, and the cycle starts again. Most starfish can rebuild a body only if some of the central disc remains, but a single arm of a Linckia starfish can rebuild a whole new animal. While it does, the new disc and tiny arms look like the bright head of a comet, with the old arm trailing behind like its tail, so these are called comet stars. The planarian, a freshwater flatworm no bigger than a rice grain, is the true champion: cut it into pieces, even more than a hundred, and each piece regrows into a complete worm, with a new head and brain.

The axolotl's powers go beyond limbs: it can also regrow its jaws, sections of its spinal cord, pieces of its brain and even parts of its heart, which is why labs study it in hope of repairing human spinal injuries. Scientists tie that gift to its strange life, because unlike other salamanders, which change into land animals, the axolotl never fully grows up, keeping its feathery gills and larval body for life. After it loses a leg, a bud of new cells called a blastema starts forming at the stump within the first week and goes on to rebuild the missing tissues. A planarian's secret is its neoblasts, adult stem cells that can become any body part and make up a fifth or more of its cells. Destroy them with radiation and the worm cannot regenerate and dies, yet transplanting a single neoblast back into it restores the power. A fragment as small as one 279th of a planarian can rebuild a complete worm, which is why nineteenth-century scientists described it as immortal under the knife's edge. Its regrowth is steered by a chemical signal called the Wnt pathway, which tells each cut end whether to become a head or a tail, and when scientists block that signal, a second head grows where the tail should be, making a two-headed worm. Starfish regrowth once backfired on people: in the 1960s, when crown-of-thorns starfish were killing vast stretches of Australia's Great Barrier Reef, fishermen chopped them into pieces and threw them back, which may have multiplied them rather than wiping them out.

Velvet antler grows so fast that its pattern of active genes looks more like bone cancer than normal bone, yet deer get cancer about five times less often than other mammals. Three defenses keep it in check: strengthened tumor-suppressor genes, mass cell suicide, in which up to about 64 percent of the cells in the antler's inner layer are programmed to die, and the yearly casting of the whole antler, which throws away any rogue cells.

living-fast-dying-young-the-mayflys-sing.context_blurb:
Mayflies are delicate insects famous for living as winged adults for only a day or less. Swarms rise from rivers together, whirl in mating clouds over the water and die soon after. But that short flight is only the final page of a much longer life, and every part of the adult is built for one quick task: breeding.

For a year, sometimes two or three, a mayfly lives as a nymph on the bottom of a river, crawling among the stones and breathing through feathery gills, and the winged adult is only the tiny tail end of its life. When it finally flies off as an adult, its mouthparts have shrunk and no longer work, so it never eats: it exists only to find a mate and reproduce before it dies.

The mayfly is the only insect that molts again after it already has working wings: the cloudy-winged dun, as fly fishermen call it, sheds its whole skin, wings included, and becomes the shiny final adult a few hours later. Mayfly hatches can be so huge that late on June 23, 2012, a weather radar near La Crosse, Wisconsin, picked up a gigantic swarm lifting off the Mississippi and showed it like a rainstorm, though there was no storm anywhere near. Under bridge lights the insects pile up so thick that crews plow them away like snow.

Inside the winged adult, the whole gut is sealed off and filled with air, no longer digesting anything but working like a balloon that lightens the weak-flying body so it can stay aloft long enough to mate. The antechinus, a small Australian marsupial about the size of a mouse, also spends itself on one season: for two or three weeks the males give up food and sleep to mate, and then their own stress hormone, cortisol, floods their bodies and causes fatal organ failure, so every male dies.

The briefest adult life of any insect belongs to Dolania americana, a mayfly of Florida's sandy rivers: after as long as two years as a nymph buried in sand, the female lives under five minutes, just long enough to emerge, mate and drop her eggs. Peters and Peters timed the dawn emergence on Florida's Blackwater River in 1977, and the whole population was dead within about 30 minutes.

not-dying-of-old-age-the-immortal-jellyf.context_blurb:
Most animals grow old: the longer they live, the more likely they are to die. A few creatures bend that rule. A tiny jellyfish can run its life backward, a pond animal shows no sign of aging, lobsters keep growing, and a burrowing rodent stays young for decades. None of them is truly unkillable, but each has a remarkable trick.

Turritopsis dohrnii, a jellyfish only about 4.5 millimeters across, about the size of a pinky fingernail, is called the immortal jellyfish because when an adult is stressed it can rewind into its own younger stage and start its life over. The freshwater Hydra, a tiny pond animal shaped like a green tube with tentacles, breaks the usual rule of aging: as it gets older, its yearly risk of death stays flat instead of rising, because stem cells keep rebuilding its whole body. Biologists call this negligible senescence.

When a Turritopsis medusa, the free-swimming adult, is starved or badly hurt, it sinks to the seabed, balls up into a blob and turns back into a young polyp, the stalk-like stage that lives fixed to the seabed and that jellyfish grow from. Immortal does not mean unkillable: in the wild most die before they ever rewind, because predators eat them or disease kills them while they are still adults. A naked mole-rat, a hairless East African rodent no bigger than a mouse, can live more than 30 years, about ten times as long as a mouse its size. Lobsters do not slow down with age, and the biggest, oldest females lay even more eggs, partly because they go on producing telomerase, an enzyme that rebuilds the tips of their chromosomes, which normally fray shorter each time a cell divides. Yet lobsters are not immortal either: the bigger they grow, the harder it is to shed their shell, and many old giants die of exhaustion or are eaten during a molt, left defenseless.

To rewind, Turritopsis does more than shrink: its finished adult cells turn into entirely different kinds of cell, a muscle cell becoming a nerve cell, for instance, a switch called transdifferentiation. Because a Hydra's death rate stays flat, one team calculated that, if nothing ate them, a few percent of a Hydra population would still be alive after more than 1,400 years. Vera Gorbunova and Andrei Seluanov, a husband-and-wife team at the University of Rochester, found that naked mole-rats pack a thick sugary molecule, hyaluronan, between their cells, and it keeps the cells from crowding together and overgrowing, so cancer almost never takes hold.

In 2022 Maria Pascual-Torner, Carlos Lopez-Otin and colleagues read the full DNA of Turritopsis dohrnii and of its mortal cousin Turritopsis rubra, and found that the immortal one carries duplicate copies of DNA-repair and DNA-protecting genes, roughly twice as many as its cousin. Its trick is not magic but an expanded toolkit for keeping its DNA clean. Naked mole-rat cells quit dividing while still loosely spaced, long before mouse cells would, because the giant hyaluronan around them trips the p16 brake, a tumor-suppressor switch that halts growth early, and when researchers digested the molecule away, the cells could form tumors.

the-great-migrations.context_blurb:
Every year some animals travel astonishing distances between feeding grounds and breeding grounds. Terns fly from pole to pole, caribou and wildebeest walk in vast herds, salmon swim home to the stream where they hatched, and monarch butterflies pass the journey down through their great-grandchildren. How they find their way is one of biology's great puzzles.

The Arctic tern, a small white seabird, nests in the Arctic summer and then flies south to spend another summer off Antarctica, the longest yearly journey of any animal: tracked terns averaged about 70,900 kilometers a year, and some topped 81,600. On land, the record belongs to the caribou of Alaska and northern Canada, whose herds loop about 3,000 miles a year across the tundra, crossing frozen rivers and mountains in search of lichen and fresh grass.

On the Serengeti, up to 1.5 million wildebeest, with almost a million zebras alongside, move as one vast herd, each animal walking 800 to 1,000 kilometers a year. They find fresh grass by tracking the rain: they spot storm clouds far away and walk toward them, because heavy rain means new grass will soon sprout there. The deadliest stretch is the crossing of the Mara River, on the Kenya-Tanzania border, where over 3,000 crocodiles lurk in the water and big cats wait on the far bank to pick off the weakest. A salmon hatched in a mountain stream swims to sea, spends years feeding out in the Pacific, then comes back to spawn in the very stream where it hatched, finding it by smell: as a youngster it imprinted on the unique odor of its home water, the mix of amino acids dissolved in it.

After fighting upstream past waterfalls and bears, Pacific salmon all die within days of spawning, spent by one single breeding effort, as a surge of hormones triggers rapid aging and organ failure. By chasing summer at both ends of the planet, the Arctic tern lives almost all year in polar daylight and sees more daylight than any other animal. In 2022 a young bar-tailed godwit tagged B6 flew from Alaska to Tasmania, about 13,560 kilometers, nonstop for 11 days and 1 hour, without eating, drinking or landing, the longest nonstop flight recorded for any animal. Among mammals, the longest migration belongs to the gray whale, which travels from icy feeding waters off Alaska down to the warm lagoons of Baja California, where calves are born, a round trip of roughly 16,000 to 20,000 kilometers. One tracked female, Varvara, logged about 22,500. No single monarch butterfly makes the round trip between Canada and Mexico; the journey passes down like a relay over three to five generations, so the butterflies that reach Mexico are the great-great-grandchildren of those that set out the spring before.

Yet the monarchs return to the exact oyamel fir groves in the mountains of central Mexico where their ancestors spent the winter, although none of them has ever been there before. Most monarchs live about a month, but the autumn super generation that flies south lives roughly eight times longer, because it delays making the hormone that ages the body, so it can survive the winter and start the trip north. A monarch's sun compass needs an accurate clock, and Steven Reppert's lab found that clock in the antennae: paint the antennae black and the butterfly can no longer hold its course. To make its crossing, a godwit fattens until fat is about 55 percent of its weight, and just before takeoff it shrinks its gut, liver, kidneys and gizzard, organs useless in the air, absorbing that tissue to save weight. A classic study of this was titled Guts Don't Fly.

Smell guides a salmon only near the coast, so how it crosses thousands of kilometers of open ocean is still debated. The leading explanation is a magnetic map: as a young smolt a salmon seems to memorize the strength and tilt of Earth's magnetic field where its river meets the sea, then seeks that same signature years later. In 2013 Putman and colleagues showed that as the field slowly drifted over 56 years, Fraser River sockeye shifted their route around Vancouver Island to follow it.

the-oldest-animals-alive.context_blurb:
Some animals live astonishingly long lives, from sharks and whales to clams and corals. Working out how old they are is detective work, because wild animals carry no birth certificates. Scientists count growth rings in shells and ear stones, read chemical clues locked inside eyes, and even use the leftovers of nuclear bomb tests.

The Greenland shark, a slow, sluggish shark of the freezing water under Arctic sea ice, is the longest-lived vertebrate known; no backboned animal is proven to outlive it. Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise on the South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, hatched around 1832, making him over 190 years old, the oldest known living land animal.

Greenland sharks are estimated to live about 250 to 400 years or more, and the two largest studied were put at about 335 and 392, so one alive today may have been born in the 1600s, before the United States existed. The shark grows so slowly that it does not become an adult able to breed until it is at least about 150 years old. In 2006 biologists dredged a small ocean quahog clam off Iceland that had been alive since about 1499, during China's Ming dynasty; they nicknamed it Ming, and at about 507 years it was the oldest single animal anyone had ever found. Ming's age was worked out by counting the yearly growth layers in its shell, the way you count the rings of a tree trunk. Sadly, opening the shell killed it.

To read a Greenland shark's age, scientists cut into the eye's lens, whose center forms before the shark is born and is never replaced, keeping a chemical record of its birth. The key clue was radioactive carbon from the nuclear bomb tests of the 1950s and 1960s: only the smallest, youngest sharks carried that bomb pulse, proving the big ones were born long before the atomic age. Bony fish are often aged by their otoliths, a pair of tiny ear stones inside the skull whose yearly growth layers can be counted like tree rings, and that is how a rougheye rockfish caught off Alaska was found to be 205 years old. Size can fool you: a huge rockfish pulled from Alaskan waters in 2013 looked about 200 years old, but its otoliths showed it was only 64. In 2007, Alaskan hunters found a fragment of an exploding harpoon made around 1879 in New Bedford, Massachusetts, lodged in the shoulder of a living bowhead whale, proof that the whale had swum for well over 100 years. A bowhead, which can live past 200 years, is made of thousands of times as many cells as a person, yet it almost never gets cancer; its genome, read in 2015, revealed unusually good DNA repair, with special versions of repair genes such as ERCC1 and PCNA.

The true record holder is a deep-sea black coral off Hawaii, a colony of tiny polyps building one shared skeleton, radiocarbon-dated to about 4,265 years, about eight times Ming's age, so it was already growing when the pyramids of Egypt were freshly built. Ming remains the oldest single, non-colony animal ever found.
