learning-a-voice-vocal-mimicry-and-learn.context_blurb:
Most animals are born knowing every call they will ever make, and they never change them. A few have to pick up their sounds by ear and imitate them, much as a toddler picks up words. Biologists call them vocal learners, and studying them has shown how a brain learns a voice, from the first weeks of listening to the moment a song locks in for life.

The vocal learners make a short list: songbirds and parrots, hummingbirds, whales and dolphins, seals, elephants, bats, and humans. The champion mimic is the superb lyrebird of southeastern Australia's wet forests: one male can imitate some twenty other bird species in a row, from a kookaburra's laugh to a whipbird's whistle, and add sounds he picked up from people, such as car alarms, chainsaws and the click of a camera.

A young songbird learns its song in a short critical period, before it can sing, by listening to an adult tutor, and a white-crowned sparrow raised in silence, with no tune to copy, grows up singing a broken, simplified version of its song. A lyrebird named Chook, kept at Adelaide Zoo, copied the drills and saws of builders working on the panda enclosure next door, and he greeted his keepers in a clear human voice: Hello, Chook! Alex, an African grey parrot, spent three decades in the lab of Irene Pepperberg, learning to name colors and shapes and to count. Each night as she left, he called out the same farewell: he told her to be good, said he loved her and promised he would see her tomorrow. On September 6, 2007, the morning after one such goodbye, keepers found him dead, aged 31. In 1984, a diver in a San Diego tank heard someone order him out of the water, and the voice belonged to Noc, a beluga whale who had learned to drop his voice several octaves and mimic human speech by altering the pressure inside his nasal passages.

A sparrow that memorizes its tutor's song and is then deafened before it has practiced still holds the memory, yet its song never comes out right, because it has lost the ability to check its own voice against that memory. Humpback whales pass learned songs along too: scientists tracked one song type moving from population to population about 14,000 kilometers across the Pacific, from eastern Australia all the way to Ecuador. In a juvenile zebra finch, song learning runs through a brain region called Area X, where the FoxP2 gene, which also helps shape speech in people, is most active precisely during copying. When Sebastian Haesler's team turned FoxP2 down in Area X, the young finches' copies of their tutor's song dropped from about 68 percent alike to about 40 percent.

After a few months a young zebra finch's song crystallizes and never changes again, because perineuronal nets, rigid lattices of material, build up around neurons in the song-control center and cage them so that no new connections can form. In males the nets begin to thicken about 50 to 60 days after hatching and level off near 90 days, just when the song locks in, and males grow denser nets than females.

teaches.5bc11607cf: A lyrebird named Chook, kept at Adelaide Zoo, copied the drills and saws of builders working on the panda enclosure next door, and he greeted his keepers in a clear human voice: Hello, Chook!
teaches.48bc643b17: Each night as she left, he called out the same farewell: he told her to be good, said he loved her and promised he would see her tomorrow.
teaches.5199254596: In 1984, a diver in a San Diego tank heard someone order him out of the water, and the voice belonged to Noc, a beluga whale who had learned to drop his voice several octaves and mimic human speech by altering the pressure inside his nasal passages.
teaches.c3d42c80c2: A sparrow that memorizes its tutor's song and is then deafened before it has practiced still holds the memory, yet its song never comes out right, because it has lost the ability to check its own voice against that memory.
teaches.b935ae49b8: Humpback whales pass learned songs along too: scientists tracked one song type moving from population to population about 14,000 kilometers across the Pacific, from eastern Australia all the way to Ecuador.
teaches.a129d2dad5: In a juvenile zebra finch, song learning runs through a brain region called Area X, where the FoxP2 gene, which also helps shape speech in people, is most active precisely during copying.
teaches.fe6bf33394: After a few months a young zebra finch's song crystallizes and never changes again, because perineuronal nets, rigid lattices of material, build up around neurons in the song-control center and cage them so that no new connections can form.

making-light-bioluminescence.context_blurb:
Many living things make their own light, a gift biologists call bioluminescence. Beetles blink in summer meadows, plankton sparkle in breaking waves, and deep-sea fish dangle shining lures in water that has never seen the sun. The light is cold, made by chemistry rather than heat, and animals use it to court, to hunt, to hide and to scare.

In a summer meadow at dusk, the blinking yellow-green lights in the grass are the work of the firefly, a beetle that glows by a chemical reaction in its abdomen that gives off almost no heat, a cold light among the most efficient ever measured. On some beaches a breaking wave flashes cold blue, and every kick of a swimmer leaves a glowing swirl, because dinoflagellate plankton, tiny single-celled drifters, flash for about a tenth of a second whenever the water around them is disturbed. The flash may work as a burglar alarm, startling an attacker and drawing in a bigger predator to eat it. In the black depths a mile down, the deep-sea anglerfish dangles a little living lantern on a thin stalk over its toothy mouth, and fish that come to inspect the glow are snapped up.

A male firefly blinks his own species' code, a set pattern of flashes and pauses, so that a female of the same species answers it back after a precise delay, a back-and-forth called a photic dialog. The Big Dipper firefly even draws a glowing J in the air as it swoops. A Photuris female copies the answering flash of a different species' female, and when the fooled male lands beside her, she grabs him and eats his soft insides. In the ocean's twilight zone, hunters stare up at the faint light from above, watching for dark silhouettes, so many deep-sea animals glow on their undersides to match that light and cancel their shadow, a trick called counterillumination.

The anglerfish does not make its own light: living bacteria lodged inside its lure do the shining, in a partnership in which the fish feeds and shelters them. A baby anglerfish hatches with a dark, empty lure and must catch its glowing bacteria from the surrounding seawater; once inside, the bacteria shrink their genomes by about half, throwing away genes they no longer need. The thumb-sized Hawaiian bobtail squid hides from predators below by aiming the glow of the bacteria in its light organ downward, dimming or brightening it to match the moonlight above, so it casts no shadow. By eating Photinus males, the Photuris femme fatale gains their defensive steroids, the lucibufagins, poisons she cannot make herself, and those stolen toxins make her taste so foul that a jumping spider that grabs her spits her back out.

The record for the most ancient animal light used to belong to ostracod crustaceans, about 267 million years ago, but a 2024 study by DeLeo and colleagues traced the glow of octocorals, the soft corals and sea pens, back at least 540 million years. Light has evolved over and over: living things have invented it separately at least 94 times, and ray-finned fishes alone at least 27 times.

recognizing-yourself-the-mirror-test.context_blurb:
The mirror test asks whether an animal knows that the face in a mirror is its own. A researcher puts a mark where the animal can see it only in a reflection, then watches: does it treat the image as a stranger, or investigate the mark on its own body? Scientists still argue over what passing proves.

Most animals take a mirror image for another animal. A robin battering a window for days is fighting its own reflection, and a betta fish flares its fins at the glass for the same reason: neither realizes the intruder is itself.

In 1970 the psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr. left chimpanzees with a mirror for several days. They began by threatening the reflection as if it were a rival. Then they started using the mirror as a tool, grooming and inspecting places on their own bodies they could never see directly, such as the insides of their mouths. Next Gallup put the chimps under anesthesia and painted red dye on an eyebrow and an ear, and when they woke and looked in the mirror, they reached up to touch the marks on their own faces, not the glass, proof they knew who was in the glass.

At the New York Aquarium, the bottlenose dolphins Presley and Tab were the first non-primates to pass. Lacking hands, they twisted and contorted their bodies to swing the marked spot into view in the mirror and examine it. Happy, an Asian elephant at New York's Bronx Zoo, was given a white X above one eye and an invisible sham mark above the other. Again and again she lifted her trunk to the X she could see in the mirror while ignoring the sham mark, evidence that she knew the elephant in the glass was herself.

In 2008 Eurasian magpies joined the club, the first animals outside the mammals to pass, even though birds lack a neocortex. The researchers stuck a small colored sticker on each bird's throat, and magpies that could see it in the mirror scratched at their own throats to get it off. Most gorillas fail, not from a lack of brains but because among gorillas a long, hard stare is a threat, so they avoid gazing into a mirror long enough to notice a mark. Koko, the signing gorilla, and others raised by people passed easily.

In 2019 a small reef fish, the cleaner wrasse, scraped at a colored mark on its throat after spotting it in a mirror. The primatologist Frans de Waal and other skeptics argued that scraping at an itchy mark falls short of true self-recognition; de Waal called it an in-between level, closer to a monkey's than an ape's. In a 2024 follow-up, wrasse that had passed were shown photographs of strange rivals, one made a tenth bigger than the viewer and one a tenth smaller, and they backed off from the bigger rival while still attacking the smaller one. Mirror-naive fish attacked both; the researchers argue the wrasse carries a mental picture of its own size.

Gallup, the test's inventor, holds that only chimpanzees and, to a lesser degree, orangutans truly pass, and his strongest evidence is a crab-eating macaque that spent about 2,400 hours before a mirror and never once used it to examine a mark it had no other way of seeing. For Gallup that failure shows a real divide in the mind, against de Waal's view that self-awareness comes in degrees.

the-waggle-dance-how-a-bee-maps-the-flow.context_blurb:
A honeybee colony sends scouts out to find flowers, and a scout that strikes it rich must tell thousands of sisters where to go, inside a hive that is pitch dark. She does it with a dance. Karl von Frisch, an Austrian biologist, decoded that dance in the mid-twentieth century and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for the work.

A scout that finds a rich flower patch flies home into the dark hive and dances across the vertical comb in a coded pattern, the waggle dance, that tells the others where to fly. The dance traces a figure eight, but only the straight dash through its middle, the waggle run, in which she shakes her body from side to side, carries the message; the curved loops just bring her back to start it again.

The angle of the waggle run encodes direction: a run straight up the comb means fly straight toward the sun, and a run tilted to the left or right means fly that same angle to the left or right of the sun. The length of the run encodes distance: the longer she waggles, the farther away the food, with roughly one second of waggling meaning about one kilometer. For flowers closer than about 50 meters she skips the waggle code and does a simple round dance, running in a little circle one way, then turning to circle back the other way.

In the dark hive she cannot see the sun, so she uses straight up on the vertical comb, which she feels through gravity, to stand in for the sun's direction. The sun keeps moving across the sky while she dances, so an internal body clock slowly shifts her dance angle to keep it pointing true. To follow single bees through a crowd of thousands, von Frisch dabbed small spots of red paint on each forager's thorax and watched them in a glass-walled observation hive.

To prove the dance was a map, von Frisch put out sugar water in a dish whose position he knew, allowed one painted bee to discover it, and then watched the bees that had followed her dance fly straight out to that exact dish. They were reading directions, not just catching her excitement. No follower can see the dance in the dark, so each one crowds close and keeps touching the dancer with her antennae, reading the run by touch.

tool-users.context_blurb:
Using an object as a tool was once thought to be uniquely human. Then field biologists found chimpanzees, crows, otters, vultures, dolphins, octopuses and finches doing it in the wild, and some of them even make their tools. Each discovery forced scientists to rethink what really sets people apart from other animals.

A sea otter floating on its back smashes clams on a flat rock it keeps from earlier dives, laid on its chest as an anvil and carried between dives in a pouch of loose skin under its forearm. An Egyptian vulture cannot crack an ostrich egg with its beak, so it grabs a stone with its bill and flings it at the shell again and again until the shell breaks.

Jane Goodall, studying wild chimpanzees at Gombe in Tanzania in 1960, saw one she called David Greybeard strip the leaves from a grass stem and use it to fish termites from a mound, the first recorded case of an animal making a tool, not just using one. In Ivory Coast's Tai Forest, chimpanzees crack rock-hard Panda nuts on tree-root anvils with stone hammers weighing from 3 up to 15 kilograms. Otters are picky: a keeper rock has a flat side to work as an anvil and weighs about half a pound to a pound. On the Galapagos, where no true woodpeckers live, the woodpecker finch pries grubs out of bark with a cactus spine held in its beak, even snapping the spine shorter to handle it better. Off Indonesia, divers filmed a veined octopus carrying the two halves of a discarded coconut shell across open sand, walking stiffly on her arms for up to 20 meters, to fit them back together later as a hideout. Carrying a tool for later use is a rare sign of planning. A New Caledonian crow snaps off a twig fork and whittles the joint into a hooked tool to snag prey, genuine manufacture rather than grabbing a stick. One crow, named 007, solved an eight-stage puzzle in which each tool unlocked the next in just two and a half minutes.

When Goodall reported her sighting, her mentor Louis Leakey wrote that science would now have to change its definition of a tool, change its definition of a human, or welcome chimpanzees as humans. Digging under a modern nut-cracking site in the Tai Forest, archaeologists found chimpanzee stone hammers about 4,300 years old, a chimpanzee Stone Age. With no arm to throw, the Egyptian vulture gets its force by whipping its entire neck downward to hurl the stone; the behavior was famously filmed near Olduvai Gorge in 1966. Apart from humans and great apes, the New Caledonian crow is the only animal known to craft hooked tools in the wild, and it guards its favorite hooks between uses, keeping them safe about 95 percent of the time. It also rips blade-like tools from the spiny edges of Pandanus leaves, in wide, narrow and stepped shapes, and most crows across the species tear from the left edge of the leaf, a population-wide handedness. In one test, six of seven crows given a stick too short to reach food used it to fish out a longer stick and then reached the food, most on the first try. In Shark Bay, Australia, some bottlenose dolphins wear a cone-shaped sponge over the beak to dig in the rocky seafloor for fish that have no swim bladder, so the dolphins' sonar cannot spot them, while the sponge guards the beak from sharp rocks. A 2005 DNA study showed the skill passes from mother to daughter, a learned tradition.

At Serra da Capivara in Brazil, wild bearded capuchins pound quartzite cobbles and knock off sharp flakes almost identical to early human cutting tools, yet they never use the edges; they want to lick the powdery quartz dust from the broken rock. That 2016 discovery complicates how archaeologists read the earliest human stone tools.

air-breathers-in-water-lungs-where-youd-.context_blurb:
Gills pull oxygen out of water, so a creature that lives in water should need nothing more. Yet whales, lungfish, bettas, beetles and even a spider all breathe air, and many of them drown if they cannot reach it. In warm, stagnant ponds, gills alone cannot gather enough oxygen, and the mammals that went back to the sea never had gills at all.

Whales descend from land mammals that walked on four legs, and they still breathe with lungs. Over millions of years a whale's nostrils drifted to the top of its head and became the blowhole, so it can breathe while the rest of its body stays underwater. The spout even tells the two great families apart: a baleen whale such as the blue whale has two blowholes side by side, while a toothed whale such as a dolphin has just a single opening. Fish found the same answer. The African lungfish, an eel-shaped fish of muddy swamps, owns a true lung and gulps air at the surface, so a lungfish kept away from the air actually drowns. The betta, or Siamese fighting fish, thrives in warm rice-paddy puddles thanks to a labyrinth organ in its head, a maze of folded, blood-rich tissue that does the job of a lung.

Breathing air brings its own puzzles. A whale breathes only by choice, opening its blowhole on purpose each time, so it can never fall fully asleep; instead it rests half its brain at a time while the other half stays awake and remembers to surface. The Amazon's electric eel has gills so feeble that it takes about 80 percent of its oxygen from air gulped into its mouth, and it must rise for a breath about every ten minutes. The great diving beetle carries its own scuba tank: as it dives it traps a bubble of air beneath its hard wing covers, held there by water-repellent hairs, and the bubble glints like liquid silver. The Galapagos marine iguana, the only lizard that grazes in the sea, dives about 15 meters to eat algae, but the cold water drains its heat, so afterward it hauls out and bakes in the sun on the black volcanic rocks until it can move well again. The diving-bell spider of Europe's ponds spins a silk dome among the water plants and fills it with air it ferries down from the surface, a shimmering bell where it spends its whole life.

Some air-breathers push the trick to extremes. When drought bakes its pool into a crust, the African lungfish digs into the mud, curls up and seals itself in a cocoon of hardened slime. In that sleep, called aestivation, it slows almost to a stop, and some lungfish have survived buried and dried out for up to four years, then swum away when the rains returned. The diving beetle's bubble is also a physical gill: as the beetle burns its oxygen, fresh oxygen diffuses into the bubble from the surrounding water, so the pond keeps topping up the tank. It cannot last forever, because nitrogen builds up in the bubble while oxygen is spent faster than the water replaces it, so the beetle must let the old bubble go and rise for a fresh supply. Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal diving records: it has stayed under for 3 hours and 42 minutes on a single breath, and on another dive it reached 2,992 meters, nearly 3 kilometers down.

The deepest divers store their breath somewhere surprising, because a sperm whale's lungs fill only about 3 percent of its body cavity and squeeze nearly empty under pressure. Instead the whale banks its oxygen inside its muscle, which holds about ten times as much myoglobin as human muscle; myoglobin is the oxygen-binding protein that makes red meat red, and it stains the whale's flesh almost black. In deep divers each myoglobin molecule carries a strong positive charge, so the crowded copies push apart like matching magnet poles instead of clumping. Air-breathing fish also hold a secret about our own past. For a century scientists argued whether the coelacanth, the "living fossil" rediscovered in 1938, or the lungfish was the closest living fish kin of the backboned animals on land, until whole-genome studies settled it for the lungfish. Our deepest fishy cousin is the air-gulper that sleeps out droughts in the mud.

breathing-water-how-gills-pull-oxygen-fr.context_blurb:
Fish and many other water animals breathe with gills, and water makes breathing hard. It holds far less oxygen than air, so a gill has to be a remarkable piece of plumbing: a huge, thin, blood-filled surface across which oxygen slips from water into blood. The details of that design explain how a fish lives, from a resting goldfish to a tuna that can never stop.

Beneath the stiff gill cover, or operculum, on either side of a fish's head lie neat rows of soft, red, feather-like filaments: the gills, the organs a fish uses to breathe underwater. They are vivid red because each filament is crammed with tiny blood vessels, so what you see is blood lying just beneath a wafer-thin surface, where it picks up oxygen. Even a resting fish keeps water moving: a goldfish that has stopped swimming still opens its mouth and flares its gill covers in a steady flutter, driving new water over the gills without a single stroke.

Water travels in at the mouth and out under the gill covers, and unlike lungs, where fresh and used air share the same pipe, this one-way flow means the gills never bathe in water they have already stripped of oxygen. That matters because air holds roughly thirty times more oxygen than the same volume of water, so a fish must pass an enormous amount of water over its gills just to get by. Bony fish have four pairs of gill arches lined with comb-like filaments, and the more active the fish, the richer those combs, so a tuna that swims nonstop packs far denser filaments than a bottom-dweller resting on the seafloor, because its hard-working muscles need far more surface to feed them.

Freshwater is especially poor, holding about 8 cubic centimeters of oxygen per liter against about 210 in air, so above all gills need enormous surface area, vast thin sheets where plenty of oxygen can cross into the blood at once. Inside each thin plate, or lamella, the blood runs against the flow of water outside, a design called countercurrent exchange, so at every point the blood faces water that holds a little more oxygen than it does and keeps loading along the whole plate.

If blood and water ran the same way, they would soon level out at about half the oxygen, but running them against each other lets a fish harvest about 80 to 90 percent of the oxygen in the water. A tuna swims too fast to pump with its gill covers, so it rams water through by swimming with its mouth open, and that ram ventilation binds it for life: if it stops swimming, the flow stops and it suffocates. Great white, mako and whale sharks live by the same rule. The nurse shark rests on the seafloor for hours by pumping water over its gills with its cheek muscles, and when its mouth is buried in sand, it draws water in through spiracles, small openings behind its eyes. Most amphibians trade gills for lungs as they grow, the way a tadpole becomes a frog, but Mexico's axolotl and North America's mudpuppy keep feathery external gills on their heads for life and never leave the water. Gills have a second job too: wedged among the breathing tissue are cells called ionocytes that hold the blood at the right saltiness, pumping salt out in seawater, which is saltier than a fish's blood, and pulling scarce salts in for a freshwater fish. The same gills also dump the fish's nitrogen waste as ammonia.

The African lungfish faces the opposite danger from the tuna, because its shrunken gills can no longer pull enough oxygen from water and nearly all its oxygen comes through a true lung, so if it is held below the surface, even in clean, oxygen-rich water, it suffocates. A tuna that halts will drown, and so will a lungfish that cannot reach the top.

extraordinary-hearts-and-blood.context_blurb:
Hearts and blood come in surprising forms. The octopus has three hearts and blue blood, the giraffe must push blood up a neck 2 meters long, the horseshoe crab's blue blood is prized by medicine, and the Antarctic icefish has blood as clear as water. Each odd design solves a physical problem its owner faces.

An octopus has three hearts: a pair of branchial hearts pump blood through the gills to pick up oxygen, and a third, the systemic heart, drives that fresh blood around the rest of the body. Its blood is blue, not red, because it carries oxygen with a protein built around copper instead of iron. On the African savanna the giraffe, the tallest animal alive, has the hardest pumping job of all: its heart must drive blood up a neck about 2 meters long to the brain high overhead. On Atlantic beaches a helmet-shaped living fossil with a spiked tail, a design that predates the dinosaurs, crawls ashore each spring to breed. That creature is the horseshoe crab, and medical labs collect its pale blue blood because it turns solid at once on contact with bacteria, keeping vaccines free of contamination.

Why does an octopus need separate hearts just for its gills? Loading oxygen at the gills takes a high pressure of its own, while the systemic heart supplies a different push to the body, so the gill job gets its own pumps. The metal explains the color: our hemoglobin carries oxygen on iron, which turns blood red, but the octopus's hemocyanin carries it on copper, which turns blue when it holds oxygen. Copper blood carries oxygen more weakly than ours, and the octopus pays for it in speed. When it jets through open water, its systemic heart actually stops beating, which exhausts it, so an octopus usually crawls instead.

A giraffe's blood pressure reaches about 280 over 180, roughly double a human's, enough to force blood all the way up the neck. Lowering that head to drink should send blood rushing into its skull. But valves in the veins of its neck let blood flow only one way and block the backflow, so the giraffe does not black out. The horseshoe crab's blood is worth roughly 60,000 dollars a gallon. When bacteria taint a vaccine or medicine under test, the blood clots into a gel around them and traps the contamination.

No other backboned animal lacks red blood cells and hemoglobin, the iron-based pigment that carries oxygen in our blood, the way the Antarctic icefish does. With colorless blood, it has to move enormous volumes using an outsized heart, about five times the output of a normal fish, helped by the cold, oxygen-rich water. The earthworm has no single heart at all: five pairs of muscular tubes called aortic arches encircle the forward part of its gut and squeeze in turn to push its blood along. Inside horseshoe crab blood, cells called amebocytes are packed with granules of a protein named coagulogen, and when they meet bacterial toxins, a chain reaction turns the coagulogen into the clot.

Biologists once assumed the icefish had simply switched off its hemoglobin in the cold. Reading its genome showed something more final: in 15 of the 16 species the beta-globin gene is gone entirely and the alpha-globin gene is partly deleted, so the DNA itself is missing, not merely silenced. Even with its huge heart and wide blood vessels, the icefish's blood carries less than a fifth of the oxygen that its red-blooded relatives' blood holds.

why-insects-cant-be-giant-the-tracheae-p.context_blurb: Insects breathe through a network of tiny tubes called tracheae that run from pores in the body wall directly to the tissues. The system is efficient at small sizes, but it does not scale up: the tubes have to get wider as an insect gets bigger, and at some point they take up so much room that there is nothing left for muscle. Look closely at the physics and anatomy of why no modern insect gets as big as the giant Carboniferous ones ever did.

archaeopteryx-dinosaur-becomes-bird.context_blurb:
Birds are living dinosaurs, and Archaeopteryx shows the road between the two better than almost any other fossil. This raven-sized animal lived about 150 million years ago where southern Germany now lies, and the fine Solnhofen limestone kept its bones and feathers in startling detail.

It had a wishbone and true feathers like a bird, but also a dinosaur's teeth, finger claws and a long tail of bone, a blend that marks it as a fossil caught partway through the change from one group into another over deep time. When one specimen was dug up with feathers that had left only faint traces in the stone, the first scientists to study it missed them and filed it as Compsognathus, a little two-legged dinosaur.

Because it kept its old teeth, claws and tail after gaining feathers and a wishbone, Archaeopteryx shows that the change came piece by piece, with evolution swapping one body system at a time rather than remaking the whole animal in a single leap. One superb specimen was feathered from head to foot, its legs wrapped in feathery "trousers," and since the animal flew poorly at best, the researchers concluded that feathers first evolved for warmth or showing off rather than for flight. They summed up the order of events as "first show off, then take-off."

Modern birds need a deep keel on the breastbone to hold their flight muscles, but Archaeopteryx had a flat breastbone with no keel, so the paleontologist Mark Norell judged that it probably did not fly like a bird at all and, if it really tried, might have managed about as well as a turkey. Feathers are older than flight: along the forearm of Velociraptor, a ground hunter that never flew, six bumps sit in an even row, quill knobs like the anchor points where living birds fix the shafts of their long wing feathers. Its growth was still a dinosaur's: thin slices of its bone show dense tissue with few blood vessels, the slow-growing kind seen in cold-blooded reptiles, and it took years, roughly 970 days by one estimate, to reach adult size.

In 2018 Dennis Voeten imaged the inside of its wing bones with a synchrotron X-ray beam and found thin walls threaded with blood-vessel channels like those of birds that actively flap, and the closest match was the pheasant, which flies in short powered bursts to hop over obstacles or escape danger. Yet its shoulder could not raise the wing high above its back for the modern flight stroke, so Archaeopteryx flew, but not the way any bird flies today.

our-hominin-cousins-neanderthal-and-deni.context_blurb:
For most of human history, our species, Homo sapiens, had company. During the last ice age, other humans walked the Earth beside our ancestors. Both are long gone, but fossils and ancient DNA reveal who they were, and pieces of them live on in us.

The Neanderthals, people of Europe and western Asia, were a genuine, distinct human species living alongside our forebears in the ice-age world, and so were the mysterious Denisovans of Asia. Neanderthals were short and powerfully built for the cold, and their noses were strikingly big and wide, probably to warm and moisten the freezing air they breathed.

Old cartoons showed Neanderthals as dim, slouching ape-men, but their braincases were just as large as ours, and often a little larger, set in a long, low skull with a heavy brow ridge. Neanderthals were skilled toolmakers who hunted mammoths, bison and cave bears by thrusting spears into them at close range, and their skeletons carry broken bones much like the injuries of today's rodeo riders. The Denisovans were discovered not from a skeleton but from a lone, tiny bone from a finger, found in 2008 in Denisova Cave in the mountains of Siberia, and when Svante Paabo's team read its DNA in 2010, it showed that a previously unknown human group had lived there.

Our ancestors met and interbred with these cousins, so most people alive today whose roots lie outside Africa carry about 1 to 4 percent of their DNA from Neanderthals. Tibetans thrive in the thin air of their high plateau partly thanks to an EPAS1 gene variant that came from the Denisovans. Denisovan DNA is spread very unevenly: Melanesians such as Papuans, along with Aboriginal Australians, carry about 4 to 6 percent, far more than most people, who carry little or none. A 2021 study found that the Aeta Magbukon of the Philippines carry even more.

In 2018 Paabo's team read the DNA of a bone fragment from Denisova Cave that belonged to a girl of about 13, nicknamed Denny, who lived some 90,000 years ago. Her mitochondrial DNA, passed down only from mothers, was Neanderthal, and the rest of her genome was split almost evenly between Neanderthal and Denisovan. That made her the first-generation daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father, the only such direct hybrid of two human groups ever found.

tiktaalik.context_blurb:
Tiktaalik was a big freshwater animal of the warm, swampy shallows of what is now Arctic Canada, some 375 million years back, in the Late Devonian. It was a fish, but a fish partway to becoming a four-legged land animal, and its fossil is one of the clearest snapshots of life leaving the water.

Neil Shubin's team predicted where it should be before a single bone had turned up: reasoning about when fish first moved onto land, they searched rocks of the right age in the Canadian High Arctic, and after five expeditions they found it on Ellesmere Island in 2004. The tetrapod expert Jennifer Clack hailed it as a prediction come true, a rare case of paleontology calling its shot. Because it mixes fish and four-legged traits in one body, Shubin nicknamed it the fishapod, fish plus tetrapod. Inuit elders of Nunavut, where it was found, chose its name: Tiktaalik is an Inuktitut word meaning large freshwater fish. It grew about 1.25 to 2.75 meters (4 to 9 feet) long, and its body was still covered in diamond-shaped fish scales.

Its head was flat like a crocodile's, with the eyes up on top, perfect for peering above the water while the body stayed hidden below. The head of an ordinary fish is fastened to its shoulders by bony gill plates, but Tiktaalik had lost them and gained a neck, so it was the first fish able to turn its head to snap at prey. Besides gills it had lungs to gulp air, so it could breathe both water and air in swamp water that held little oxygen.

Its front fins still had thin fin-rays on the outside, but inside lay the bones of a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist, the same bones that bend our own arms and hands. Two enlarged holes on top of its skull, spiracles left over from a gill slit, probably helped it gulp air in warm water, and in the land animals that came after it, that same passage was rebuilt into the middle ear.

In 2014 Shubin's team described Tiktaalik's back half and found a huge pelvis, nearly as big as its shoulder girdle, with a true ball-and-socket hip and a hind fin every bit as long and intricate as its front fin. So powerful hind limbs began evolving while the animal was still a fish, before anything walked on land.

whale-evolution-pakicetus-to-modern.context_blurb: Whales descend from four-legged land mammals that walked into shallow water around 50 million years ago. The fossil record now includes a long sequence of transitional forms, from Pakicetus, which still had legs and lived on land, through Ambulocetus and other walking whales, to animals that could no longer walk out of the water at all. Look closely at the stepping stones in that transition and what each fossil adds to the picture of how a land animal became a whale.

champion-jumpers.context_blurb:
Some animals are built around the jump. Tiny sap-sucking bugs, grasshoppers, ants and kangaroos all push off with forces enormous for their size. The secret, again and again, is a spring: tendons and bows of rubbery shell that store energy and give it back, because muscle on its own cannot do the job, and physics sets hard limits on how a leg can launch a body.

The flea is famous as a high-jumper, but the true insect champion is the froghopper, or spittlebug, a 6-millimeter garden bug that springs 70 centimeters into the air, over double a flea's best. Its young hide in blobs of froth on plant stems, which explains the second name. Measured in body lengths, that leap tops 100 of them, like a six-foot person clearing a stack of tall buildings.

Its jumping legs are only about half its body length and 2 percent of its mass, nowhere near enough muscle to throw it so high, so muscle first slowly bends springs inside its body, and the springs then release the energy all at once. To fire, it locks its cocked hind legs with microscopic grippy teeth, then trips the latch, and the leap goes off with an audible click. A kangaroo uses springs differently, treating its huge hind-leg tendons as pogo-stick springs that store and return energy on every bound, so its hopping gets more efficient as it speeds up: at 6 meters per second the tendons can save a red kangaroo up to about 70 percent of its energy. Dawson and Taylor found in 1973 that its oxygen use barely rises with speed. Moving slowly, a kangaroo plants its thick tail like a fifth leg, and in 2014 O'Connor and colleagues measured that the tail supplies as much forward push as the front and hind legs together.

The froghopper's spring is a curved bow of hard cuticle lined with resilin, a rubbery protein that glows bright blue under ultraviolet light, tracing exactly where the spring sits. Its launch lasts less than a thousandth of a second and accelerates it at about 5,400 meters per second squared, a jolt of roughly 400 to 550 times the pull of gravity, while a fighter pilot starts to black out near 9. In a grasshopper, two crescent-shaped struts at the knee, made of cuticle and resilin, flex and store about half the jump energy, with the big thigh muscle supplying the rest. Tiny jumpers need springs because muscle cannot contract fast enough to deliver its power in an instant, so small animals load a spring slowly and trip a latch to release it at once, a system biologists call latch-mediated spring actuation. Trap-jaw ants latch their jaws open under spring tension and can slam them against the ground to fling themselves away, and when Larabee and Suarez glued some ants' jaws shut and set them against antlions, only about a quarter of those ants escaped, 26 percent, against 60 to 79 percent for ants that could jump.

moving-without-legs.context_blurb:
Snakes, legless lizards and other limbless animals cross ground, sand, trees and even air with no legs at all. They move by pressing parts of their bodies against the world around them in carefully timed patterns, and biologists recognize several distinct styles, each suited to a different surface.

A snake's everyday S-shaped slither, lateral undulation, works by pushing sideways against bumps, pebbles and edges: the rear edges of its belly scales catch on them and shove the body forward, so on smooth glass, with nothing to push against, a snake just slides in place. A big python stalking a deer moves in a dead-straight line instead: it pulls its loose belly skin forward in slow waves, anchors the belly scales against the ground and lets its body glide over them, a silent creep called rectilinear locomotion.

The sidewinder rattlesnake of the American Southwest throws sideways loops of its body so that only two short segments touch the burning, loose sand at any moment, while the rest is lifted into the air. Each loop leaves a separate J-shaped print, and the hook of every J points in the snake's direction of travel, so even empty tracks reveal its heading. Above each eye the sidewinder has a raised, horn-like scale, which is why it is also called the horned rattlesnake, and these horns fold down to shade its eyes and keep sand from drifting over them while it lies half-buried, waiting for prey. On a smooth vertical pole with nothing to push against, a snake climbs by concertina motion: it jams parts of its body into tight bends to wedge itself still, pushes its front end up, re-anchors, then drags the rest after, folding and unfolding like a squeezebox. A legless animal that blinks at you, or shows a small ear opening behind its eye, is no snake but a lizard without legs, like the glass lizard: snakes have no eyelids, only a clear scale over each eye, and no outer ears.

All these moves rely on the belly scales, called scutes, which slide forward easily but catch when dragged backward or sideways, like the treads on a tire, so each muscle push becomes forward travel. Filming corn snakes, Marvi, Hu and colleagues found that this grip is not fixed: the snake contracts its belly muscles to tilt each scale up on edge so its rear rim digs into the ground, and an awake, gripping snake has about double the friction of an unconscious one. Engineers copied the trick in a climbing robot called Scalybot. The paradise flying snake of Southeast Asia has no limbs to spread, so when it leaps from a treetop it splays its ribs to flatten its round body into a wide, hollowed ribbon that catches the air, and it keeps slithering in S-waves as it glides. For nearly a century biologists counted four ways of slithering, but in 2021 researchers on Guam filmed invasive brown tree snakes climbing smooth baffles a fifth way, lasso locomotion: the snake wraps into a single loop around the pole and shifts small bends within that loop to inch upward. The snakes, brought to Guam by accident around 1950, had already wiped out most of the island's forest birds.

A python embryo starts to build tiny hind legs, then gives up, so an adult python keeps nothing but two small spurs near its hips. The limb gene SHH still exists in snakes, but the DNA switch that should activate it where a leg begins, called the ZRS, is broken. Because the leg program was only switched off, never erased, Leal and Cohn argued that snake legs were lost, then partly regrown, then lost again over deep time, more than once. Fossils such as four-limbed Tetrapodophis and Najash, which had only hind legs, trace the changes, but the idea is still debated.

sticking-to-walls.context_blurb:
Geckos, tree frogs, flies, octopuses and limpets can all cling where we would slip and fall. Each has solved the problem its own way: some grip with dry hairs, some with a film of water, some with glue and some with suction. And every method also has to let go again on command, or the animal would be stuck for good.

A gecko uses no glue: the underside of each toe is packed with millions of tiny hairs called setae, and each one grips by van der Waals force, the faint pull between any two molecules that touch, so the countless tiny pulls add up to hold the whole lizard. A red-eyed tree frog does the reverse and sticks with water: its damp, round toe pads hold a super-thin film of fluid that grips the leaf by surface tension, the same pull that makes a wet glass stick to a coaster. An octopus grips smooth rock by pure suction: muscles in each sucker pull the middle of the cup back, lowering the water pressure trapped inside, so the higher pressure of the sea around it presses the sucker onto the stone.

A Tokay gecko of Southeast Asia carries about 500,000 setae on each toe, so many that its two front feet can hold some 40 times its body weight, enough to let it hang from a pane of glass by one toe. Under a microscope, a tree frog's toe pad is tiled with flat six-sided cells split by deep grooves, which drain extra water away to the edges of the pad so it can press close to the leaf instead of skidding on a puddle. A housefly walks upside down on a ceiling with two soft pads, the pulvilli, at the end of each leg, covered in fine hairs; each hair releases a tiny drop of gluey fluid less than a millionth of a millimeter thick, so the fly clings by the gecko's molecular pull plus the fluid's stickiness.

Van der Waals attraction has no off switch, so to let go the gecko changes the angle of its hairs: tilted to about 30 degrees from the surface, the tips peel free and the grip releases instantly, which is how it runs up glass without getting stuck. Inspired by the gecko, Al Crosby and Duncan Irschick built Geckskin from cheap nylon and bathroom caulk, and a patch no bigger than an index card can hold up to 700 pounds on glass, then peel off cleanly with a flick. The cone-shelled limpet clamps to wave-swept rocks and scrapes algae with teeth stiffened by fibers of the iron mineral goethite, and researchers at the University of Portsmouth found those teeth to be the strongest natural material ever tested, stronger even than spider silk. Its goethite fibers are ten thousand times thinner than a human hair.

the-fastest-runners.context_blurb:
Some animals are built for raw speed on land. Cheetahs, greyhounds, ostriches and pronghorns all run faster than almost anything else alive, and each owes its speed to particular features: long legs, a springy spine, stretchy tendons or a balancing tail. Some of that speed was shaped by predators that vanished long ago.

No land animal outruns the cheetah of the African savanna, which reaches about 100 to 120 kilometers an hour (roughly 70 to 75 miles an hour) in a flat-out sprint. No two-legged animal runs faster than the ostrich of the African plains, a flightless bird taller than a man that cruises near 55 kilometers an hour and sprints to about 70, with strides up to 5 meters. Each ostrich foot has just two toes, the big one tipped with a hoof-like claw for grip.

The cheetah's long, flexible spine coils like a drawn bow and springs open on every stride, throwing the shoulders so far forward that a single bound covers 6 to 7 meters, about the length of a car and a half. In its double-suspension gallop, all four feet are off the ground together twice in every stride, once with the legs stretched fully out and once with them bunched under the body. The greyhound, the fastest dog breed, has been clocked near 45 miles an hour, and it runs the same double-suspension gallop as the cheetah, powered by a flexible spine and an unusually large heart.

A cheetah goes from a standstill to about 70 miles an hour in around three seconds, out-accelerating most supercars. Sarah, an 11-year-old cheetah at the Cincinnati Zoo, sprinted 100 meters in 5.95 seconds in 2012, the fastest time ever recorded by anything, more than three and a half seconds quicker than Usain Bolt's human record of 9.58. To carve sharp corners at full speed, a cheetah counter-swings its long, heavy tail like a rudder, throwing its weight the other way so it does not flip over.

Jonas Rubenson's studies found that an ostrich doubles a human's running speed while spending half the energy because long tendons down its legs stretch as each foot lands and recoil like springs on push-off, returning about twice the elastic energy a human leg does. On the plains of the western United States, the pronghorn easily outruns every predator alive today, and the biologist John Byers argues that its speed was shaped by the American cheetah, a sprinting hunter that vanished some 10,000 years back; he calls it a ghost, the ghost of a predator long past.

That American cheetah, Miracinonyx, had a cheetah's long legs and short face, but a 2005 study of ancient DNA from its fossils placed it in the puma line, closer to today's mountain lion than to the Old World cheetah. The two cats evolved the same sprinter's body separately, a case of convergent evolution, so the pronghorn's ghost was really a sprinting cousin of the cougar.

deep-diving-bodies.context_blurb:
A human diver without gear is in trouble a few dozen meters down. Sperm whales, elephant seals, Weddell seals and beaked whales go hundreds or even thousands of meters deeper on one breath. To manage it, a deep diver's body has to beat crushing pressure, ration its oxygen for a very long time, and store that oxygen somewhere other than its lungs.

The sperm whale, biggest of all toothed hunters, plunges over a mile into total darkness to hunt the giant squid. The squid fights back, and whales come up with round wounds the size of saucers ringed across their skin, the marks of the giant squid's suckers. The southern elephant seal, the largest seal on Earth, hunts squid off Antarctica, can reach depths of 2,000 meters, and may stay under for as long as two hours on a single breath.

Instead of gulping a huge breath, a sperm whale empties roughly nine-tenths of the air from its lungs just before it dives, because the less gas it carries, the less there is for the pressure to squeeze or force dangerously into its body. A mile down, the water pushes down with some 200 times the surface pressure. Its flexible rib cage simply folds inward, the ribs hinging back toward the tail, and its lungs collapse flat on purpose instead of breaking.

So where does a diver keep its oxygen? Not in its lungs, as a human holding a breath does, but in its blood and in its muscles. Its muscle is packed so densely with myoglobin, a protein that grabs and stores oxygen, that the meat looks almost black instead of red. The Weddell seal of Antarctica shows how that store is rationed. It takes a last breath at a hole in the sea ice and may stay down for over an hour. As soon as it dives, its heart drops from a normal mammal's pace to just 16 beats per minute at its slowest, a slowdown called bradycardia. It also starves its skin, flippers and gut of blood, letting them go cold, and sends the oxygen-rich blood to its brain, heart and lungs, the organs that cannot do without it. When its oxygen runs low partway through the dive, the seal squeezes its spleen like a sponge, pouring a fresh supply of stored red blood cells into its bloodstream.

The deepest diver of all is Cuvier's beaked whale: in 2014 researchers off southern California followed a tagged one down to nearly 3,000 meters, about 2,992, the deepest dive ever measured for any mammal. Scuba divers who breathe compressed air can suffer the bends, when nitrogen dissolved in the blood under pressure fizzes out as bubbles. A whale's collapsed lungs stop that nitrogen from being forced into its blood in the first place. Diving muscle hides a chemical secret too. In a land mammal, myoglobin packed too tightly clumps into a toxic solid. In 2013 Mirceta and colleagues found that divers' myoglobin carries an unusually strong positive electric charge on its surface, and because like charges repel, the molecules push one another apart instead of sticking. Yet the protection is not perfect. In 2003 Jepson and colleagues examined beaked whales that had stranded in groups during naval sonar exercises and found gas bubbles spread through the soft tissues of their whole bodies, damage that experts had thought impossible in a whale. A leading idea is that the loud sonar panics the whales into surfacing too fast, and scientists still debate it.

jet-propulsion.context_blurb:
Some sea animals swim the way a rocket flies. They fill a chamber in their bodies with water and squeeze it out hard through a narrow opening, and the push sends them shooting the other way. Squid, octopuses, jellyfish, scallops and the nautilus all travel by jet, a trick that suits soft-bodied animals that need a sudden burst of speed.

When a squid needs speed, it fills its muscular mantle with water and fires it out through a narrow tube, rocketing off in the opposite direction: this is jet propulsion, the same principle that drives a rocket. Most clams and oysters stay cemented down or buried, but the scallop swims: it opens its two fan-shaped shells to take in water, then claps them shut to squirt the water out behind, hopping away from a hungry starfish.

Every jet swimmer obeys Newton's third law, which Isaac Newton set down in 1687: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, so water pushed hard one way pushes the animal the other way. The squid steers with that same nozzle, called the funnel or siphon: aimed forward, it sends the squid shooting backward, and swiveled to the side, it turns the animal, so one organ supplies both thrust and steering. An octopus usually crawls along the seafloor on its eight arms, but when a shark or moray eel closes in, it fires a jet of water from its funnel and shoots backward, and it can squirt a cloud of ink through the same funnel to cover its escape.

The neon flying squid of the Pacific, chased by dolphins or tuna, can blast itself right out of the sea, then spreads its fins and arms like little wings and glides about 30 meters, the length of a swimming pool, before splashing down. A jellyfish contracts its bell in pulses and glides a long way between them, and when scientists measured the energy burned per meter traveled, no animal they tested swam more efficiently, not any fish, bird or mammal. The nautilus of the deep Indo-Pacific also jets through a funnel, but it alone among living cephalopods carries a coiled outer shell split into sealed chambers, and by shifting the balance of gas and liquid inside them it controls its buoyancy, so it can rise or sink like a submarine. A dragonfly nymph, the fierce larva that hunts on pond bottoms, is the only insect known to swim by jet: it breathes through gills lining its rectum, and by firing that water out of its rear end it shoots forward to catch prey or flee.

Each time the jellyfish's bell springs back into shape, the recoil leaves behind a whirling ring of water that sucks the animal forward for free, a second push it pays no muscle energy for, and that carries it about 30 percent farther on each pulse.

A squid's escape jet is triggered by its giant axon, the thickest nerve fiber in the animal kingdom, up to about a millimeter across, which makes the whole mantle clench almost at once. That huge fiber let Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley slide electrodes inside a living nerve and measure how an electrical signal races along a cell, work that won the 1963 Nobel Prize and founded modern neuroscience. Jet propulsion is also ancient: the shelled nautiloids were already jetting through a funnel in the Late Cambrian and diversified through the Ordovician, well over 450 million years ago, ages before fish ruled the oceans, while the other jetting cephalopod groups arrived far later.

staying-up-or-sinking.context_blurb:
Left to itself, an animal's body is usually a little denser than seawater, so it sinks. Every creature of open water must solve that problem, and the sea is full of different answers: gas, oil, chalk chambers and even chemistry.

A perch can hang motionless in mid-lake because most bony fish have a swim bladder, a gas pocket inside the body that the fish inflates to rise or shrinks to sink, so that, set just right, it neither rises nor falls. Sharks lack this organ entirely, so their dense bodies ought to drop to the seabed. A shark's lift comes from an enormous liver packed with oil lighter than seawater.

Most of that oil is squalene, a light molecule the body makes on the way to building cholesterol, and in some deep-sea sharks it fills 80 percent or more of the liver. Even so, most sharks remain slightly heavier than water and get extra lift from water flowing over their fins, the way an airplane's wings work only while it moves. A shortfin mako would slowly sink if it ever stopped swimming. The cuttlefish chose a stiff solution. Its buoyancy tank, the flat white cuttlebone that washes up on beaches, is almost all chalk, about 95 to 97 percent aragonite, divided into hundreds of tiny chambers that the animal floods with fluid to sink or fills with gas to rise. Even fish eggs need help. About 70 percent of ocean fish release floating eggs, and many of those eggs carry a droplet of oil that keeps them riding near the sunlit surface, where the young will find food.

Gas has a weakness: it swells and shrinks with pressure. When an angler reels a rockfish up too fast from 300 or 400 feet down, the falling pressure lets its swim bladder balloon from the size of a thumb to the size of a party balloon, pushing the fish's stomach into its mouth. Herring, carp and eels have a safety valve, a duct running from the bladder to the gut. These fish can burp gas out through it and climb quickly without bursting the bladder, while a perch or bass, its bladder sealed, would rupture if it rose too fast. Thousands of meters down, gas fails entirely, so deep-sea fish such as the orange roughy and the coelacanth fill their bladders with oil or wax. Oil is almost impossible to compress, so it keeps the same volume under crushing pressure and gives steady lift where a gas bladder would be squeezed flat. The sperm whale's blocky head holds up to 1,900 liters of waxy spermaceti, and one leading idea says chilling the wax would make the whale sink and warming it would help it rise. Many researchers doubt this, noting that the temperature change would barely shift its buoyancy, and they see the head mainly as an echolocation organ, a kind of sonar. The debate is not settled. In the dim middle depths, the see-through glass squid fills one huge body chamber with a watery solution of ammonium chloride, lighter than seawater, which can make up half or more of its body mass and holds it up with no gas and no swimming.

The nautilus carries the oldest design of all: a coiled shell divided by inner walls into sealed chambers of gas, the same rig the extinct ammonites used for hundreds of millions of years. To rise, it does not add gas; it slowly pumps liquid out of a chamber through the siphuncle, a living tube that threads through every chamber, and gas expands into the space left behind.

the-tuna-body-plan-thunniform-swimming.context_blurb:
Bluefin tuna, mako sharks, dolphins and the extinct ichthyosaurs are barely related, yet they share one body: a stiff torpedo with a narrow tail-base and a crescent-shaped tail. Biologists call it the thunniform, or tuna-like, body plan. Fast swimmers of the open ocean keep reinventing it, inside and out, because the water itself demands it.

A bluefin tuna, a bony fish; a mako shark, a cartilage fish; and a dolphin, an air-breathing mammal, evolved separately yet ended up with the same stiff, streamlined torpedo body that slices through the water. A cruising tuna's body barely bends: the stiff front knifes through the water while almost all the swimming motion is packed into the slim stalk before the tail and the crescent tail itself. A tuna's or a shark's tail sweeps side to side, but a dolphin's tail beats up and down, which instantly gives the dolphin away as a mammal. When a bluefin sprints at over 40 miles an hour, its first dorsal fin folds flat into a groove along its back and its pectoral fins tuck into slots on its sides, leaving a smooth torpedo; it pops them back up for tight turns.

A tuna's tail is tall, narrow and stiff, and sliced across it has the curved cross-section of an airplane wing, an airfoil, so it makes thrust the way a wing makes lift and wastes little effort in swirl. A big Pacific bluefin holds its deep red swimming muscle about 11 degrees Celsius warmer than the water, and warm muscle fires faster and harder, part of why tuna are so fast. Because only some regions are warmed, this is called regional endothermy. The mako and the great white, both lamnid sharks, arrived at that streamlined body and moon-shaped tail on their own, and a few lamnids copied another tuna trick too: their muscles run warmer than the surrounding sea, by about 7 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit. The shortfin mako, the fastest shark, bursts to about 74 kilometers an hour.

A fish's warm blood should lose its heat at the gills, but the tuna has a rete mirabile, a wonderful net of intertwined arteries and veins that works as a countercurrent heat exchanger, trapping the muscle's heat before it can escape. The red muscle lies deep beside the spine in the middle of the body and does not bend the flank next to it; instead it hauls on long tendons that thread backward to the tail-base, driving the tail from a distance. The copying runs deeper than skin: tuna, makos, ichthyosaurs and dolphins all evolved an unusually thick, strengthened backbone and a stiff tail-stem, the hidden engineering that focuses the motion at the back of the body. The reason is the water itself: seawater is dense and sticky, so moving through it fast is so demanding that there is one best shape, and every fast cruiser is pushed toward it no matter where its ancestors started. Long before dolphins, in the age of dinosaurs, the ichthyosaurs, sea reptiles that first appeared about 248 million years ago, already had the tuna body plan, though as reptiles they beat their crescent tails side to side like fish, not up and down like dolphins.

In 2018 Lindgren and colleagues analyzed a superbly preserved Early Jurassic ichthyosaur, Stenopterygius, and found its skin still in place over a thick, smooth layer of blubber, which they read as direct evidence that the animal was warm-bodied. Warm-bloodedness is still an inference from that blubber, but its pigment cells also showed countershading, dark above and pale below, just like a dolphin's.

ears-at-the-extremes.context_blurb:
Animal ears can do things no human ear can. Some pick up sounds far too high for us to hear, some find a mouse in total darkness, and some are so tiny they seem impossible. For owls, moths, bats and one small fly, a single faint sound can mean dinner or death.

In a pitch-black barn a barn owl can drop from the rafters and pin a mouse on the first try without ever seeing it, because it hunts by hearing alone, homing in on the faint rustle of the mouse.

Its flat, saucer-shaped face is a working instrument. The ring of stiff feathers around it, the facial ruff, works like a satellite dish, collecting faint sounds and reflecting them toward the owl's ear openings.

In 1971 Roger Payne tested a trained barn owl in a totally dark room. It struck not only live mice but a mouse-sized wad of paper dragged across dry leaves. The paper gave off no body heat and could not be seen, so its rustle was the only clue, which ruled out sight and heat sensing and left sound alone. The owl's strikes landed within one degree of the target, the most precise sound-finding ever measured in a land animal. In the northern forests lives the great gray owl, which has the largest face disc of all owls, and in winter it listens for voles tunneling beneath the snow, then punches down through as much as 18 inches of snow to seize prey it never sees.

Hunters are listened for, too. Many night-flying moths have the simplest ears in nature: a thin patch of skin connected to as few as one to four nerve cells. Those ears are tuned to one sound, the ultrasonic sonar calls of a hunting bat, and when the calls arrive, the moth swerves or tumbles out of the sky. The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona goes further and fights back, firing about 4,500 ultrasonic clicks a second. The clicks drown the bat's returning echoes in static, the first proven case of sonar jamming in nature, and attacking bats often break off.

Snow refracts sound as a lens bends light, so to a great gray owl a vole can seem up to 5 degrees away from where it really is, an acoustic mirage. Just before it dives, the owl hovers in place on beating wings, probably to fix the vole's true position from the angle where the error is smallest. Some moths beat sonar with their coats. Their microscopic wing scales act as a natural sound-absorbing material, soaking up as much as 72 percent of the ultrasound that strikes them, so almost no echo returns and the bat sweeps past. The highest bat calls reach about 212 kilohertz, yet in one study the ear of the greater wax moth still responded at about 300 kilohertz, far beyond any bat.

The parasitic fly Ormia ochracea finds crickets by their chirps so it can lay its eggs on them, but its two eardrums sit only about half a millimeter apart, so the chirp arrives at the nearer one only about one or two microseconds sooner. In 1995 Miles, Robert and Hoy found the fix: a stiff bridge joins the two eardrums and pivots in the middle like a see-saw, magnifying that tiny difference into a movement the nerves can read. The fly can point to a chirp about as accurately as a human can.

echolocation-built-twice.context_blurb:
Echolocation means hunting and finding your way by sound: an animal calls out and reads the echoes that bounce back. Bats, toothed whales such as dolphins and sperm whales, and a few cave birds all do it. Bats and whales sit on distant branches of the mammal tree, yet each invented this sonar separately, one of nature's best examples of convergent evolution.

A bat hunting on a moonless night cannot see the moth in front of it. Instead it gives out high-pitched cries, mostly too high for human ears, and builds a picture of the moth from the shape of the echoes that return. The oilbird of northern South America does something similar in the black caves where it lives, clicking with its tongue. Its clicks are around 2,000 cycles per second, low enough for people to hear, and that lower pitch gives a blurrier picture than a bat's ultrasound, missing fine detail.

Dolphins echolocate in murky water where their eyes are nearly useless. They send out rapid clicks, and the melon, a lens of fatty tissue in the forehead, focuses them forward in a narrow beam, the way a flashlight aims its light. The echoes come back by another route: fat inside the lower jaw carries them through a thin plate of bone, the pan bone, to the inner ear.

A searching bat clicks slowly and steadily. In the last split second before it grabs a moth, the clicks speed up into a feeding buzz of up to 200 a second, giving rapid updates that fix the prey's exact position for the catch. When biologists compared the gene for prestin, a protein that powers the sound-sensing hair cells of the inner ear, they found it had changed in the same direction in echolocating bats and in toothed whales: the same molecular answer, reached twice, independently.

The match goes all the way down: at a single spot in that protein, both echolocating bats and toothed whales carry the identical swap of one building block for another, asparagine replaced by threonine, which is tied to sharper hearing of high notes. The sperm whale takes echolocation to extremes. Hunting squid a kilometer down, it makes clicks of nearly 230 decibels, the loudest sound of any animal. Those clicks are produced by the spermaceti organ, a huge structure that fills the whale's blocky head. In 1998 Simmons, Ferragamo and Moss found that a big brown bat can tell apart two echoes arriving only about 2 microseconds apart, so it can sense two surfaces just 0.3 millimeters apart as separate, a gap shorter than a single wavelength of its call.

Inside the sperm whale's head, the sound begins at two lip-shaped flaps near the front of the skull, nicknamed monkey lips, as air is pushed past them. That first pulse then bounces back and forth between two air sacs inside the head, and with each pass a slice of its energy escapes forward as a click. The horseshoe bat, named for the horseshoe-shaped flap of skin around its nose, works differently. It holds its call on one steady tone, and its ears are tuned to exactly that note. As it flies toward a target, its own speed raises the pitch of the echo. So the bat lowers the pitch of the call it sends out, keeping the echo on the note its ears expect. That steady tone lets it find a moth hidden in a bush, because the moth's beating wings put a quick, rhythmic flicker, or glint, on the returning echo, a sign of living prey. Some moths fight back. A desert tiger moth, Bertholdia trigona, answers with up to 4,500 clicks a second of its own, which jams the bat's sonar and spoils the attack, cutting the bat's success about tenfold.

When did bats start echolocating? Onychonycteris finneyi, the earliest bat known from a good fossil, lived 52 million years ago and already had full wings, yet its cochlea, the coiled hearing organ, was small as in a fruit bat, not enlarged like an echolocator's. In 2008 Nancy Simmons and her colleagues argued that this shows bats flew first and evolved echolocation later. The debate is not closed: a 2010 look at the same skull suggested it may have echolocated after all.

infrasound-and-hearing-through-the-feet.context_blurb:
Some animals talk in sounds too deep for people to hear. Below about 20 hertz lies infrasound, whose long, low waves carry far through air, water and even solid ground. Elephants, whales, giraffes and a blind desert mole all send or catch these hidden signals.

On the African savanna, African elephants keep in touch across miles of open plain with rumbles mostly between 14 and 35 hertz, largely below the bottom of human hearing.

Every rumble sets the ground trembling too, and the vibration races through the soil for miles; a distant elephant picks it up with its feet, and the shaking travels up its leg bones to the inner ear, bypassing the eardrum, so it can catch a call that has already faded in the air. The lowest calls of any animal belong to the blue whale, the biggest animal of all time: its calls, pitched around 10 to 40 hertz, rank among the loudest natural sounds in the sea and may carry across an entire ocean basin to another whale.

When an elephant senses a far-off tremor, she freezes, leans forward and raises one forefoot, toe aimed at the ground. As she presses it down, the foot spreads, widening its contact with the soil by up to about 20 percent so that it can feel the vibration better. The Namib Desert golden mole, a mouse-sized mammal of the dunes of southwest Africa, has no working eyes, yet it sand-swims through the dunes, dips its head against the sand and finds termites under clumps of grass purely by reading the vibrations in the ground. Giraffes seemed almost mute, but a study of 947 hours of zoo recordings made after dark caught 65 low, steady hums around 92 hertz: the giraffes were humming to one another in low tones, and the keepers had never noticed.

The blue whale's voice is even getting deeper. One Northeast Pacific song type dropped by about 31 percent from 1963 to 2008, and 7 of the world's 10 song types are sliding down too. Mark McDonald, John Hildebrand and Sarah Mesnick offer a surprising, still-debated reason. As blue whales recover from whaling and potential mates live closer together, a male no longer needs a loud, high call to reach far, so he can afford to sing lower. The steady, worldwide drop argues against ship noise as the cause.

The golden mole's trick lies in one huge ear bone. Of 117 mammals measured, golden moles have the heaviest middle-ear bones for their size, and the Namib mole's malleus weighs about 18 milligrams, closer to a human's than to a mouse's. Matthew Mason proposed that when a ground tremor shakes the skull, the heavy bone lags behind it, and that slight slip between bone and skull drives the inner ear, greatly boosting its sense of low sounds.

the-lateral-line-feeling-the-water-move.context_blurb:
Fish have a sense we lack: a kind of touch at a distance. Along each side of the body runs the lateral line, a row of tiny sensors that feel the water move. With it a fish can sense a wall, a hunter or a neighbor without seeing it, and the same sensor, moved inside the head, gave every backboned animal its ears.

The faint dotted line along each side of a goldfish is not a stripe of color but the lateral line, a row of sense organs opening through tiny pores, and it lets the fish feel the water moving around and against its body. The lateral line is tuned to slow, large water movements, such as currents, ripples and the push of something gliding past, below about 100 cycles a second; faster pressure wiggles are picked up by the ear instead.

Each of its thousands of sensors, called neuromasts, is a cluster of hair-like bristles set in a blob of clear jelly, the cupula; moving water shoves the jelly, the jelly bends the hairs, and the bent hairs send a signal along a nerve to the brain. A predatory fish that has been blinded still hits its prey accurately in darkness, but once scientists switch off the lateral line with cobalt ions they cannot find a thing, proof that they were tracking the water their prey disturbed. When Tony Pitcher and Brian Partridge covered the eyes of saithe, the fish still kept their places in the school, because every fish senses the pressure waves its neighbors push against its flank; only when the lateral line nerve was also cut did the school fall apart.

The blind Mexican cave fish, which never sees daylight in its caves, evolved more and larger neuromasts, even crowding the empty sockets where its eyes shrank away, so it swims straight to a faint food vibration in total darkness. The same bending hair cells power your ears: evolution sealed those bending hair cells inside the head to build the inner ear of every backboned animal, so both your hearing and your balance descend from a fish's lateral line. Scientists group the two together as the octavolateralis system.

Sharks and rays have an electric twin of the lateral line, the ampullae of Lorenzini, built from the same patch of embryo tissue, which lets them feel the faint electric fields of prey buried in sand. Ancestral jawed fish had both senses, but the fossil-and-gene trail shows the electric sense was lost in the bony-fish line that led to gars, bowfin and most modern fish, and then re-evolved at least twice, probably by retuning ordinary lateral-line hair cells.

endurance-aloft.context_blurb:
Some birds practically live in the sky. Albatrosses, swifts, frigatebirds, terns and godwits fly for days, months or even years with hardly a rest, and some of them sleep on the wing. Each of these long-haul fliers has found its own way to cross huge distances that would kill an ordinary bird.

A wandering albatross of the Southern Ocean has the broadest wingspan of all living birds, up to about 3.5 meters from tip to tip, wide enough to span a car. A common swift, a small dark bird of European skies, eats, drinks, mates and sleeps in the air, and once a youngster flies from its rooftop nest, it can stay aloft for about 10 months straight, never once touching down. The Arctic tern follows summer from one end of the Earth to the other: it raises its chicks in the Arctic, flies to Antarctica for the southern summer and back again, and covers about 70,900 kilometers a year, farther than any other animal.

An albatross can glide for hours or days without a flap because a tendon in each shoulder locks its outstretched wing in place, holding it open with no muscle effort. While fetching food for its chick, a parent can travel 10,000 to 15,000 kilometers in 10 to 20 days. Some albatrosses go so far that they fly right around the entire Southern Ocean, circling the bottom of the world. The tern's polar commute earns it another record: chasing summer from pole to pole, it spends about two-thirds of its life in continuous daylight and sees more sunlight in a year than any other animal. In October 2022 a five-month-old bar-tailed godwit, a long-billed shorebird, left Alaska wearing a satellite tag. It flew nonstop for eleven days and one hour, with no food, water or rest, all the way to Tasmania, about 13,560 kilometers away, the longest nonstop flight ever recorded for a bird.

What would ground an ordinary bird on such journeys is the energy it burns by flapping without a break, and each of these fliers dodges that cost with a wind-riding trick. Textbooks explain the albatross's trick, dynamic soaring, by the wind gradient: the wind moves slower close to the water and faster higher up, so the bird rises into the wind along a wave front, turns, and swoops downwind through the hollow between waves, gaining speed from the difference. Godwits prepare for their ocean crossing by rebuilding their bodies, shrinking the liver, kidneys and gut by up to a quarter to make room for fat and to enlarge the heart and flight muscles, because guts do not fly.

Great frigatebirds, black seabirds of the tropics with forked tails and seven-foot wings, cannot rest on the sea, because their feathers are not waterproof and would soak through. Henri Weimerskirch's team tracked them and found that they fly straight into towering cumulus clouds and ride the updrafts nearly 4,000 meters up, then glide long distances back down without flapping. They can stay aloft for up to two months. They even sleep on the wing, one half of the brain at a time. When a frigatebird circles on rising air, the waking half is the one linked to the eye facing into the turn, so it keeps watching where it is going. Niels Rattenborg's team fitted nesting frigatebirds with tiny brainwave recorders and found they slept in flight, mostly around sunset, but only about 42 minutes a day, a small fraction of what they sleep on land.

The textbook story of the albatross is now disputed. In 2013 Gottfried Sachs reconstructed real albatross flights from GPS and motion sensors and found that the wind gradient contributes almost nothing. In his data most of the free energy comes in the upper turn of each loop, at the moment the bird wheels from flying into the wind to flying with it. Each loop stayed within 15 meters of the sea and lasted about 10 seconds, and scientists still argue over where in the cycle the gain really happens.
