flight-evolved-four-separate-times.context_blurb:
True flight means flapping your way off the ground and staying aloft under your own power, and it is rare. Flying squirrels, colugos, gliding lizards and flying fish only glide, falling in style. In the whole history of life, unrelated animals invented powered flight from scratch only a handful of times, each building its wings in a different way.

Among mammals, only bats truly fly: a colugo of Southeast Asian rainforests can leap and coast a long way on a flap of skin, but it cannot climb through the air as a bat does. Insects built flight in a way nothing else has, because their wings are outgrowths of the body wall, sprouting straight out of the back rather than rebuilt from legs, which is why a dragonfly keeps all six legs and still flies.

Powered flight evolved four times, in insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats, and none of them inherited it from a flying ancestor. Insects came first: winged insects were already flying about 325 million years ago, long before any animal with a backbone took to the air. In the Late Triassic, more than 220 million years ago, the pterosaurs, long-jawed reptiles with leathery wings, became the first vertebrates ever to truly fly, beating the earliest birds by more than 60 million years.

Each flier built its wing differently. A bat's wing is a web of skin spread between its fingers, so its order name, Chiroptera, is Greek for "hand-wing." A pterosaur's skin wing hung from a single, enormously long fourth finger, longer than its whole forearm, reaching down to its legs. The biggest of them, Quetzalcoatlus, cruised over North America about 70 million years ago, as tall as a giraffe with wings 33 to 36 feet across, the biggest creature ever to fly. A bird spreads feathers over its whole arm, powered by huge chest muscles. Those muscles are anchored to the keel, a deep blade of bone jutting from the breastbone, so a strong flier like a pigeon has a big keel, while a flightless ostrich has almost none.

Oddly, both of a bird's big flight muscles sit low on its chest. The pectoralis pulls the wing down for the power stroke. The supracoracoideus raises it again for the recovery stroke: its tendon runs up through a tunnel of bone over the shoulder, like a rope over a pulley, so a chest muscle can pull the wing upward. These three groups are only distant relatives, yet all of them rebuilt the same starting part, the forelimb they all got from a common four-footed ancestor, and each stretched different bones of it. Pterosaurs stretched a single finger and birds the whole arm. A bat stretched four of its finger bones, and if you hold its wing up to the light you can see the four long bones spreading through the skin like umbrella ribs.

How did a giant pterosaur as tall as a giraffe get off the ground? Birds take off by leaping from their legs, but Michael Habib saw that in pterosaurs the upper arm bone is much tougher than the thigh bone, the opposite of the pattern in birds. In 2008 he proposed that the giant pole-vaulted off all four limbs, crouching and hurling itself upward on its folded, powerful arms before its wings snapped open. Others still argue that the very largest pterosaurs could barely fly. Insects faced their own limit. A housefly's wings flap roughly 200 times each second, too fast for a nerve to send one signal per stroke. Its secret is a pair of opposing muscle sheets in the thorax: when one contracts it stretches the other, which fires back after a tiny delay, so the thorax rings like a struck bell and a single nerve pulse keeps dozens of wingbeats going.

gliding-not-flying.context_blurb:
Many animals sail between trees without true flight. Flying squirrels, colugos, Draco lizards, flying frogs, flying snakes and flying fish all glide: they cannot climb through the air by flapping, but they turn a fall into a long, steered journey. Each of them evolved its gliding gear separately, out of a different part of the body.

A flying squirrel launches from a tree at night and opens the furry membrane that joins its front and back legs. With no wings to beat, it steers and brakes with its flattened, bushy tail, which works as a rudder, and it can also bank by lowering one arm. In Southeast Asian rainforests, a lizard about as long as a pencil, nicknamed the flying dragon, glides between tree trunks on bright, fan-like wings: it is the Draco, and it usually glides about 10 meters, sometimes as far as 60. The paradise tree snake has no limbs at all, yet it glides 10 meters or more by flaring its ribs to flatten its round body into a wide, slightly hollow ribbon.

The Draco's wings are spread by four to seven greatly elongated ribs, which fan outward like umbrella ribs and are worked by muscles that other lizards use only for breathing. In the forests of Borneo, a bright green frog named after the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace escapes danger by leaping into the air and sailing more than 15 meters on the huge webbing between its fingers and toes, four orange-and-black parachutes at once. The champion glider among mammals is the colugo of Southeast Asia, whose gliding membrane is the most complete of any animal, stretching from the neck out to every fingertip and toe tip and back along the whole tail. One colugo covered about 150 meters in a single glide.

Jake Socha of Virginia Tech spent more than twenty years on flying snakes and created the first realistic computer model of a snake gliding, and his virtual experiments showed that its S-shaped wriggling in midair keeps it from tumbling and stretches its glide. Line the gliders up and a pattern appears: every one of them built its wing from a different part of the body, a skin flap in the squirrel and colugo, giant fins in the flying fish, ribs in the Draco, a flattened body in the snake and webbed feet in the frog, yet they all reach the same result. Gliding has evolved again and again, a case of convergent evolution. People nickname the colugo the flying lemur, but it neither flies nor is a lemur: DNA shows its closest living relatives are the primates, the group that includes monkeys and people, not the bats some scientists had guessed. A flying squirrel has its own refinement. A rod of cartilage at its wrist swings out to stretch its membrane beyond the reach of its arm bones, and the tips curl upward. Wind studies showed that those upturned tips cut the drag of air swirling off the wingtips, just like the winglets on an airliner.

Gliding is ancient. In 2017 scientists described Maiopatagium and Vilevolodon, small furred creatures from Jurassic forests near Beijing, when dinosaurs still ruled. They were not true mammals but early relatives on the line that led to mammals. Their fossils preserve gliding membranes, proof that mammal ancestors were gliding roughly 100 million years before the first modern gliding mammals.

hovering-in-place.context_blurb:
Hanging still in the air is one of the hardest jobs in nature. A hawk riding the wind borrows moving air, but a true hoverer must make all of its own lift while going nowhere, and that burns fuel at a furious rate. Hummingbirds, hawkmoths, hoverflies and dragonflies have each found their own way to do it.

Among birds, only the hummingbirds of the Americas can truly hover on the spot, and they alone can also fly backward, even upside down for a moment. In ordinary hovering a hummingbird's wings beat about 50 times a second, so fast that they blur and hum, which is how the bird got its name. To power them, its heart pounds about 1,200 times a minute, against about 80 for a resting person.

Other birds get lift only on the downstroke, but a hovering hummingbird turns its wing over at the shoulder and sweeps the tip through a flat figure-8, so the wing presses air downward on both the forward and the backward stroke. Its breast muscles, the engine for all this, make up almost one third of its weight, about twice the share in an ordinary bird. Gardeners who spot a tiny hummingbird working the flowers on a summer afternoon are often looking at a moth: the hummingbird hawkmoth hovers the same way, wings beating about 85 times a second, faster than the bird's, as its long tongue dips into one flower after another.

The hoverfly, which hangs dead still over summer gardens, wears a wasp's black-and-yellow stripes as pure bluff: it is a true fly with no sting at all, but a predator that has been stung once by a wasp steers clear of anything striped like one. Biologists call this trick Batesian mimicry. The kestrel, a small falcon, only seems to hover: it faces into a headwind and flaps just hard enough to cancel the wind's push, so it stays put over the field while its head holds still to watch for voles. That is why its old English name is the windhover.

A hummingbird's upstroke is powered by a large muscle called the supracoracoideus, so its upbeat does real work and supplies about one quarter of its lift, while other birds get almost nothing from theirs. Hovering costs so much that a hummingbird cannot carry enough fuel to last the night, so after dark it sinks into torpor: its body goes cold and its heart slows from about 1,200 beats a minute to as few as 50, until dawn.

Hawkmoths and hummingbirds, an insect and a bird, beat out nearly the same figure-8 stroke, each lineage inventing it on its own, and among nectar feeders true hovering has evolved only about four times: in hummingbirds, some bats, hoverflies and hawkmoths. Biologists call such matching, separate inventions convergent evolution. A dragonfly hovers on four wings, each under its own control, and it saves flapping power by beating its front and back pairs out of phase, so they cross near the middle of each stroke.

For 180 years, books claimed that a hummingbird's grooved tongue soaks up nectar like a paper towel soaking up a spill. In 2015 Alejandro Rico-Guevara and his colleagues filmed the tongues of 18 species at high speed and proved the books wrong. The tongue is squeezed flat as it shoots out, and the instant its tips touch nectar, the flattened grooves spring back open and suck a column of nectar inside. That elastic pump works far faster than wicking, and it lets a hummingbird lick a flower up to 20 times a second.

Every one of the 360 living hummingbird species lives in the Americas, yet in 2004 Gerald Mayr named Eurotrochilus from fossils about 32 million years old, dug from a clay pit in southern Germany, and the bird was already built for hovering and sipping nectar. More have since turned up in France and Poland, so hummingbirds once hovered at Old World flowers before vanishing from that half of the globe.

animals-that-generate-electricity.context_blurb:
A handful of fish carry living batteries inside their bodies. In the murky Amazon the electric eel can knock a horse off its feet, and in the sea the torpedo ray stuns its prey with a jolt of its own making. These animals make power from muscle, and they use it to hunt and to defend themselves.

Despite its name, the electric eel belongs to the knifefish family rather than the eels, and its closest familiar cousins are catfish and carp, far nearer kin than the moray. Its power comes from electrocytes, flat cells made from the kind of cell that in other animals merely twitches a muscle, and roughly 6,000 of them sit end to end in each stack like batteries wired in series, with about 35 stacks side by side down each flank.

For two centuries scientists recognized only a single electric eel, until a 2019 study of 107 specimens divided it into three species, and the new Volta's electric eel fired 860 volts, the most powerful jolt yet recorded from a living creature and well past the old record of 650. It also fights smart. The biologist Kenneth Catania filmed eels with high-speed cameras and saw that an eel curls its body around struggling prey, bringing its positive head and negative tail together, which at least doubles the shock in an "electric embrace" that drives the prey's muscles to exhaustion.

In 1800 the explorer Alexander von Humboldt described eels leaping from a pool to attack horses, a tale mocked for two centuries until Catania filmed it in 2016: out of the water, an eel presses its chin against the threat so the full jolt drives straight into the body instead of spreading out and weakening through the water. The torpedo ray, a flat fish of the sea, keeps its two kidney-shaped electric organs inside its broad pectoral fins, the wide "wings" of its body, and the great torpedo can deliver about 220 volts, enough to knock down a person. Strangely, the eel's current is small. Its blast is high voltage but low current, peaking near 1 ampere, about one tenth of what a household socket carries; the danger is that high voltage pushing current across a body in rapid volleys of up to 500 pulses a second, each lasting about two thousandths of a second.

Evolution invented this weapon more than once. Electric organs arose separately at least six times in fishes, from the eel to the torpedo ray to the elephantnose fish, and a 2014 genome study found that each unrelated lineage reached into the same genetic toolbox, switching on the same genes and developmental pathways to turn muscle cells into electrocytes.

electroreception-reading-the-body-electr.context_blurb:
Every living animal leaks a faint electric field: each heartbeat and muscle twitch sends a tiny current into the water around it. Sharks, rays, the platypus and certain fish can feel those fields, a sense called electroreception. It lets them find prey hidden from eyes, nose and ears, and some animals even make electric fields of their own.

A flounder buried in the sand is invisible and gives off no scent a shark can follow, but its beating heart and twitching muscles still leak faint electricity into the seawater, and the shark homes in on that and digs the fish out. Adrianus Kalmijn proved it by burying electrodes in sand: sharks dug up the wires and ignored a dead fish nearby.

Cameras fixed to great whites caught something that looks reckless: in the final instant before biting a thrashing seal, the shark shuts its eyes to protect them and completes the strike blind, steering by its electric sense alone. The platypus goes further: diving for food on a dark river bottom, it seals its eyes, ears and nostrils shut and hunts with about 40,000 electroreceptors scattered over its rubbery bill, which pick up the muscle signals of hidden prey.

The platypus bill also carries push-rod sensors that feel pressure. When a shrimp flicks its tail, the electric signal races through the water faster than the pressure wave and reaches the bill a split second earlier, and the platypus times the gap between the two to judge how far away the shrimp is. In muddy, pitch-dark rivers, the elephantnose fish and the knifefish cannot count on prey leaking much electricity. Instead each one makes its own weak electric field with an organ in its tail and feels how nearby objects bend that field, a kind of living radar. When two knifefish meet with fields at nearly the same frequency, the signals interfere, so within milliseconds each fish shifts its own frequency away from the other's, a reflex called the jamming avoidance response. Insects have the sense too: a 2013 study by Clarke's team showed that bumblebees detect the weak static charge carried by flowers through their body hairs, which bend in the charge's presence.

A shark's electric sense lives in the ampullae of Lorenzini, pores packed with a see-through jelly that conducts the signal inward. In 2016 Josberger and colleagues found that this jelly, about 97 percent water, conducts protons better than any other biological material ever tested, coming within about 40 times of Nafion, the best proton-conducting plastic engineers have made for fuel cells. Sharks and skates, which are flat relatives of rays shaped like kites, build their electric sense from the same kind of cell, and both start each signal through the same calcium channel. In 2018 Bellono, Leitch and Julius found that the difference lies in a second channel: sharks add one that makes the cell fire sharp, repeated spikes, ideal for catching a prey's twitch, while skates use one that produces soft, finely graded ripples, better for reading the weak signals of another skate seeking a mate.

navigating-by-earths-magnetic-field.context_blurb:
Earth is wrapped in a magnetic field that changes in a regular pattern from the equator to the poles. Robins, sea turtles, butterflies and many other travelers read it to find their way, and how they sense it is one of the deepest mysteries in biology, one that may involve quantum physics.

European robins migrate even on cloudy, moonless nights, and when the Wiltschkos changed the magnetic field around caged robins, the birds turned to match it, proof that they steer by an internal magnetic compass.

A robin's compass does not point north like a hiker's needle: it reads the angle at which the field lines dip into the ground, shallow near the equator and steep near the poles, so it can tell equatorward from poleward without knowing which pole is which. Each stretch of coastline carries a unique magnetic signature, a pairing of the field's angle and strength. Loggerhead hatchlings read those signatures like latitude and longitude: exposed to the magnetic fields of three widely separated points along their Atlantic route, they swam three different headings, each right for that spot, because they were reading their own position on the globe. Decades later, at around 35, a female loggerhead comes back to lay her eggs within a few kilometers of the beach where she hatched, finding it by the magnetic address she learned as a hatchling. A monarch butterfly holds its southward heading under heavy clouds by reading the magnetic field, and its compass sits in its antennae: paint over them and the sense is gone, though it can still fly.

No one has proven how a bird's compass works. The leading idea is that light striking a protein called cryptochrome in the retina creates two molecules with linked, quantum-mechanical electron spins that Earth's weak field can tip, so a robin may see the field as a pattern over its vision.

Kenneth Lohmann's team fed young loggerheads for two months in just one artificial magnetic location, and later, placed in that field with no food in the tank, the turtles tilted upright and dogpaddled with their mouths open, the excited feeding display researchers call the turtle dance. The same 2025 study showed the turtles have two separate magnetic senses, a learned map and a compass that seem to run on different physics. Thorsten Ritz and the Wiltschkos found that a radio field under a thousandth the strength of Earth's own wrecked robins' sense of direction only when tuned near 1.3 megahertz, the rate at which a lone unpaired electron's spin flips in Earth's field, so the sensor is most likely such an electron. Iron magnets cannot respond to so faint a signal, so this supports the quantum idea, though it is still not proven inside a living bird.

dunkleosteus.context_blurb:
Dunkleosteus was a giant armored fish the length of a bus that ruled the seas of the Late Devonian period, roughly 380 to 360 million years ago, a time called the Age of Fishes. It belonged to the placoderms, an extinct group of "plate-skinned" fish, and it was the top predator of its world.

Its head and shoulders were cased in thick, interlocking plates of bone, fitted together like tank armor. Every placoderm died out in the extinction that ended the Devonian, about 359 million years ago. For a fish that bit harder than a great white shark, it had a strange mouth. Dunkleosteus had no teeth at all; instead, the front edges of its jaw bones grew into self-sharpening bony blades.

A great white bites with about 4,000 newtons. When Anderson and Westneat built a model of Dunkleosteus jaws in 2007, they found it focused about 5,300 newtons right at the tip of the blade, enough to cut through armor and bone. It used that bite even on its own kind. In 2016 Hall and colleagues described punctures and scrapes on Dunkleosteus head plates that match the bladed jaws of another Dunkleosteus, evidence that it attacked and ate members of its own kind. Its fossils also turn up beside tight masses of fish bone and half-broken prey, some of them containing teeth of Orodus, a relative of sharks. Paleontologists read these clumps, called boluses, as material Dunkleosteus vomited back up because it could not digest bone and other hard parts. They give a rare look at the menu of an animal 360 million years dead.

For years artists showed it feeding by suction, its jaws snapping open in about 20 milliseconds to suck in prey. In 2025 Engelman and colleagues argued that the real skull was built with much more cartilage than the old model allowed, and that its cleaver-like blades look like those of predators that bite with a wide gape and tear their prey into pieces. How it really fed is still debated.

helicoprion.context_blurb:
Helicoprion was a shark-like predator of the Permian seas, roughly 290 to 270 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs. For over a century it was known almost entirely from one strange fossil, a tightly coiled spiral, and nobody could agree where on the animal that spiral belonged.

The spiral is made of teeth, a whorl of them set like the blade of a saw and wound like a clock spring, which is why the name Helicoprion means "spiral saw" in Greek.

For a hundred years scientists argued over where it went. In 2013 Leif Tapanila's team CT-scanned a well-preserved fossil and found the whorl coiled inside the lower jaw, at the back of the mouth near the jaw joint. Why had no one found the rest of the animal? Like sharks, Helicoprion had a skeleton of cartilage, which rots away instead of fossilizing, so the hard tooth whorl was almost the only part that survived.

The whorl held every tooth the animal ever grew, because it never shed one. New teeth sprouted at the front, and the older, worn teeth rolled inward toward the center of the coil, so the tiny innermost teeth are the ones it grew as a baby. The scan of the skull brought another surprise: apart from its teeth, Helicoprion was built like the ratfishes and chimaeras, not like a shark. A 2015 study by Ramsay and colleagues showed that the jaw worked like a circular saw. As the lower jaw rotated shut, the foremost teeth of the whorl hooked prey and dragged it inward, the middle teeth pierced and cut, and the rear teeth pushed the food toward the throat. It probably sliced through soft prey such as squid.

megalodon.context_blurb:
Megalodon, the biggest shark of all time, hunted in oceans around the world from about 23 million years ago until it vanished. It was the largest shark that ever lived, a predator of whales, and it is known almost entirely from its enormous teeth. Movies love it, but the real animal is strange enough.

Scientists estimate megalodon grew to about 15 to 18 meters, around 50 to 60 feet, longer than a school bus, while a great white tops out near 20 feet. Despite the movies, megalodon is completely extinct: no hidden survivors lurk in deep trenches, and the last of them vanished millions of years before the first people.

Almost every megalodon fossil is a tooth, because like all sharks it had a skeleton of cartilage, which rots quickly and almost never turns to stone, so only its teeth and a few hardened vertebrae survive. The largest megalodon tooth ever found is close to 18 centimeters, about 7 inches, as big as a man's hand, while a great white's teeth are only about 5 centimeters, roughly 2 inches, less than a third the size.

Fossil whale bones from megalodon's time often carry huge saw-edged bite marks, and some still have a snapped-off megalodon tooth stuck fast in the bone, since a shark sheds thousands of teeth in its life.

A fossil rib of a whale, dug from a mine in North Carolina and some three or four million years old, shows three megalodon tooth marks, but new woven bone had grown over the wounds, so the whale escaped the bite alive and lived several more weeks before dying of infection. As the paleontologist Stephen Godfrey put it, the shark went away with a mouthful but did not kill the whale. A 2023 study of the chemistry in its tooth enamel found that megalodon kept some of its body roughly 7 C, or 13 F, warmer than the sea around it, and that warmth powered a huge, active hunting body. It may also have doomed the shark when the oceans cooled. Some 3.6 million years ago a perfect storm ended its 20-million-year reign: the oceans cooled, its warm coastal waters shrank, the whales it hunted shifted toward colder seas, and a smaller, more efficient rival, the great white shark, competed for the same prey.

Scientists long treated megalodon as an oversized great white, but the much finer serrations on its teeth and other traits showed that the two belong to separate lineages that only look alike because they evolved to hunt the same prey, so it was renamed Otodus megalodon. Their likeness is convergent evolution, though a minority of researchers still argue the differences are minor.

ichthyosaur.context_blurb:
Ichthyosaurs were sea reptiles that hunted the oceans through most of the age of dinosaurs, from about 250 to 90 million years ago. They looked like dolphins or tuna, with sleek bodies, a fin on top, paddle-like flippers and a half-moon tail, yet they were reptiles, and their fossils have kept surprising scientists for two centuries.

An ichthyosaur was a reptile, not a fish, so it had no gills: it breathed air and had to rise to the surface for every breath, just as a dolphin does, though dolphins would not appear for another 200 million years. Its eyes were the biggest of any animal that has ever lived, and eyes that big collect every scrap of light, which let it hunt in the black depths of the deep ocean, or near the surface at night.

In the giant Temnodontosaurus platyodon the eye socket is about 25 centimeters wide, as wide as a dinner plate, and the only living animal with an eye that comes close is the colossal squid. Temnodontosaurus was a 9-meter top predator with teeth like knives. One fossil found in Britain still holds its last meal: three juvenile ichthyosaurs, younger members of its own kind, along with the hooks from the arms of squid relatives. With long flippers and no true feet, an ichthyosaur could never crawl ashore to bury eggs like a turtle, and fossils of mothers caught in the act of giving birth, a baby half out of her body, prove that it bore live young out in the open sea.

The first whole ichthyosaur skeleton that London's scientists ever saw came out of the crumbling sea cliffs at Lyme Regis in Dorset: in 1811 Joseph Anning spotted the skull, and months later his sister Mary, a local girl of just twelve, dug out the rest of the 17-foot animal. Science had no name yet for an air-breathing reptile shaped like a dolphin, so when the skeleton came free that November, the local newspaper reported it as a crocodile. Two centuries later, in 2021, workers draining the Rutland Water reservoir in the English Midlands found the biggest ichthyosaur ever dug up in Britain, the Rutland Sea Dragon: about 10 meters from snout to tail, as long as a bus, with a skull that weighs about a tonne. It had lain in the mud for some 180 million years.

In China, a fossil of the early ichthyosaur Chaohusaurus preserves a mother with three young: one born, one still inside her and one caught halfway out. That baby was emerging head-first, not tail-first like a dolphin. Head-first birth suggests that ichthyosaurs inherited live birth from ancestors that already bore live young on land, rather than inventing it in the sea. Later ichthyosaurs gave birth tail-first, as dolphins do.

Ichthyosaurs are a textbook case of convergent evolution. A reptile like the ichthyosaur, a mammal like the dolphin, a bony fish like the tuna and the speedy lamnid sharks all evolved the same streamlined torpedo with a crescent tail, because that is the best body for fast, long-distance swimming in open water.

A Stenopterygius fossil from the shale of Germany kept traces of real skin, and even a layer of blubber. Its skin was dark on the back and pale on the belly, the pattern called countershading that sharks and dolphins still wear. It was camouflage: a predator looking down saw a dark back against the dark depths, and one looking up saw a pale belly against the bright surface.

Early collectors kept finding ichthyosaur tails bent sharply downward near the tip, and, sure the bend was crushing damage, they snapped the bones straight. Then superb fossils from Holzmaden in Germany, which kept the outline of the whole body, revealed a tail with two lobes. The bend was real: the tail vertebrae turn sharply down and run inside the lower lobe of the crescent fin, so the collectors had been destroying the bony support of the tail fin.

mosasaur.context_blurb:
Mosasaurs were giant sea reptiles that ruled the oceans in the last stretch of the dinosaur era, from about 100 to 66 million years ago. The biggest reached about 50 feet, with paddle limbs and jaws full of sharp teeth, and they hunted fish, squid, birds and one another across shallow inland seas such as the one that once covered Kansas.

Despite its name, a mosasaur was no dinosaur but a lizard that took to the sea: it belonged to the group that holds monitor lizards, such as the Komodo dragon, and snakes, its closest living relatives. Its ancestors ran on land on four clawed feet, but in the mosasaur each of the four limbs became a paddle for swimming, while a powerful tail drove it forward.

To stop slippery fish and squid from thrashing free, a mosasaur had a second row of teeth on its palate, the roof of the mouth, which gripped the prey and ratcheted it down the throat, a trait it shares with snakes. The old picture of a slow, eel-like mosasaur with a pointed tail fell apart when a Prognathodon skeleton from Jordan, described in 2013, preserved the outline of its tail: it ended in a crescent-shaped fluke like a shark's tail flipped upside down, the mark of a fast open-ocean swimmer.

Fossils of newborn Clidastes mosasaurs, with jaws barely 2 centimeters long, turn up in rock laid down far out over deep water, alongside open-ocean fish and squid, showing that mosasaurs gave birth to live young far out in open water and never came ashore. A Tylosaurus from the chalk of Kansas, a 40-foot mosasaur, still held its final meals inside its ribs: a seabird, a fish and another, smaller mosasaur about 2 meters long, proof that it ate even its own kind. Another Tylosaurus was found with a half-digested plesiosaur inside it. Mosasaurs vanished about 66 million years ago in the same catastrophe that killed the last non-bird dinosaurs: the asteroid strike that ended the Cretaceous period.

In 1987 Rothschild and Martin found patches of dead bone in up to 66 percent of the vertebrae of Platecarpus and Tylosaurus, which dived deep, killed by nitrogen bubbles that formed as they rose too fast: these mosasaurs suffered decompression sickness, the bends. The shallow-water Clidastes shows none, so the scars track diving depth, proof that these hunters dived deep and often but were not perfectly built for it.

plesiosaur.context_blurb:
Plesiosaurs were large sea reptiles that ruled the oceans through much of the dinosaur era, from about 200 million years ago until the end of the Cretaceous. Most carried a little head at the end of a lengthy neck, with a broad body and four big flippers, while their cousins the pliosaurs had short necks and huge heads. They were not dinosaurs, and they have puzzled scientists since the first skeleton was found.

The long-necked, small-headed silhouette in stories of the Loch Ness monster is borrowed from an actual reptile of the Mesozoic oceans, the plesiosaur, with a tiny head on a very long neck and a wide body with four paddle-like flippers. To cross open sea, a plesiosaur flapped all four flippers like underwater wings, flying through the water like a penguin; simulations and a swimming robot show that it drove mostly with the front pair and added a timed push with the back pair. Though it spent its whole life at sea, it had lungs and breathed air, so like a whale it surfaced again and again for every breath.

Nearly every mammal, even the giraffe, has seven neck bones, but Elasmosaurus stacked up some 72 short vertebrae, a count few animals have ever matched, and its cousin Albertonectes had at least 75. In the 34-foot Elasmosaurus, which swam the shallow sea that once covered Kansas, about 23 feet, nearly two-thirds of the animal, was neck, tipped with a tiny triangular head that gulped small fish and squid. Mary Anning's 1823 plesiosaur from Lyme Regis, the first almost whole skeleton, had a neck so long that Baron Georges Cuvier called it a fake, until a special meeting of the Geological Society proved it real and Cuvier admitted his mistake.

One leading idea is that the long neck let an elasmosaur ease its tiny head into a school of fish and snatch one before its bulky body came close enough to scare the whole school away, though this is not proven. The short-necked pliosaurs went the other way, and Pliosaurus funkei, a 40-to-50-foot giant with foot-long teeth known as Predator X, may have had a bite even more powerful than a T. rex's, though the exact figure is debated because the skull is incomplete. Scientists long wondered how plesiosaurs bred, until a fossil Polycotylus, 78 million years old, showed a mother with a single large baby inside her: they gave birth to live young at sea instead of laying eggs on land. A single big baby hints that plesiosaurs may have cared for their young, as whales do.

In 2010 Bernard and colleagues measured the oxygen chemistry in plesiosaur tooth enamel, and later studies of their bone growth told the same story. Plesiosaurs generated their own body heat, at a bird-like metabolic rate, rather than borrowing it from the water, though a 2024 study suggests their temperature, about 27 to 34 C, still varied somewhat. One Styxosaurus held 253 swallowed stones, long explained as ballast, but such stones never weigh more than about 0.2 percent of the animal, far too little to sink a huge reptile. Most researchers now think the stones ground up tough, shelled prey such as squid relatives in the gut, the way a bird's gizzard does, though the debate is not closed.

teaches.0a6a3121c5: Plesiosaurs generated their own body heat, at a bird-like metabolic rate, rather than borrowing it from the water, though a 2024 study suggests their temperature, about 27 to 34 C, still varied somewhat.

scent-trails-and-the-moth-that-smells-a-.context_blurb:
Many animals talk in smells. A pheromone is a chemical message that one animal releases for others of its kind to read, and it can mark a path, prove membership in a family or summon a mate from far away. Ants run whole colonies on scent, and a male moth can follow a whiff of perfume through the dark.

A female silk moth releases a scent called bombykol into the breeze, and a male who never sees her flies upwind, following that smell alone all the way to her. Bombykol was the first pheromone ever chemically identified, by Adolf Butenandt in 1959. The male's huge, feathery antennae carry over 20 million microscopic pores, and a single molecule of bombykol can set one of his scent-detecting nerve cells firing; a few molecules landing each second are enough to send him off to find her.

A scout ant that finds food lays a scent trail on its way home. Ants on the shortest route finish the round trip fastest, so that trail gets walked more often and its scent builds up first. Because ants follow the strongest smell, the whole colony settles on the best path with no leader at all.

The ant that found the food may be long gone, but it never needs to meet the others: it changes the ground itself with a dab of scent, and every later ant simply reacts to the trail the last one left, a kind of communication through marks in the world called stigmergy. Marco Dorigo turned the trick into a real computer routing method, Ant Colony Optimization.

Every colony carries its own chemical badge, a blend of waxy hydrocarbons coating the body, so guards wave in an ant that smells right and attack one that smells wrong. The Alcon blue caterpillar cheats that system: it coats itself in chemicals that copy the colony's own scent so closely that Myrmica ants carry it into their nest and feed it before their own grubs. The better it copies the smell, the more completely it fools them.

super-smellers.context_blurb:
Many animals live in a world of smell far richer than ours. A dog, a shark or an elephant can pick up odors we would never notice, follow them to their source and sort them in fine detail. Scientists measure that power by counting scent receptors and smell genes, and by testing how faint a trail an animal can follow.

We have about 6 million scent receptors in our noses, but a dog can have up to 300 million, and the bloodhound, a tracking dog bred for centuries to follow the faintest trail, sits at that top end. A dog also devotes far more of its brain to smell than we do, with roughly 40 times more scent-sensing tissue, so a bloodhound gets teased as basically a giant nose with a dog tacked on behind it.

A dog smells in stereo: its two nostrils sample the air separately, so it can tell which side an odor is coming from and use its nose like a compass. As a sniffing dog exhales, the used air leaves through the slits at the sides of its nose instead of straight out the front, so the outgoing breath does not blow away the scent it is still drawing in.

The dog-cognition researcher Alexandra Horowitz explains that a trained scent dog can detect an odor as faint as one teaspoon of sugar dissolved in two Olympic-sized swimming pools of water. A shark steers toward prey by comparing when a smell reaches each nostril and turning toward whichever side the odor hits first, even if the other nostril senses a stronger smell. Gardiner and Atema showed this in 2010 by piping squid odor through separate tubes to each nostril of smooth dogfish; a head start of a tenth of a second was enough.

No animal is known to have more genes for smell receptors than the African elephant: nearly 2,000, more than twice a dog's and about five times a human's, so its trunk can sort scents in astonishing detail.

tasting-with-the-whole-body.context_blurb:
Taste usually lives on the tongue, but many animals have spread it across their bodies. Catfish taste with their skin, butterflies and flies with their feet and octopuses with their suckers, while snakes gather scents with a flicking tongue. Each design lets an animal read the chemistry of its world exactly where it needs to.

The channel catfish of muddy American rivers is essentially a swimming tongue: its whole skin, and especially its long whiskers, the barbels, is packed with taste buds, so it tastes food the moment it brushes any part of its body. We have roughly 10,000 taste buds, all on the tongue, while a big catfish can carry as many as 175,000, spread over its whole body.

A female butterfly tastes with her feet: before laying eggs she drums on a leaf with her forelegs, letting taste sensors on her feet read its chemistry to make sure it is the right, safe food plant for her caterpillars. Vincent Dethier, an American biologist of the 1950s, got curious when a blowfly kept visiting his sandwich, and by touching sugar water to flies' feet he found that the instant a hungry fly's foot meets sugar, it reflexively unrolls its tongue to drink. In 2020 Van Giesen and colleagues found that octopus suckers carry a new family of chemotactile receptors tuned to chemicals leaking from prey, so an arm reaching into a dark crevice can taste a hidden crab by touch.

A snake's flicking tongue catches scent particles from the air and carries them not to its nose but to a paired sense organ in the roof of its mouth, the vomeronasal or Jacobson's organ. In 1994 Kurt Schwenk showed in the journal Science why the tongue is forked: each tip samples a slightly different spot, so the snake can tell which side a scent trail is stronger on and steer to follow it, smelling in stereo.

feeling-in-the-dark-the-touch-specialist.context_blurb:
Where eyes are useless, in black soil or murky water, some animals read the world by touch. Moles, seals, manatees and naked mole-rats carry touch organs so sensitive that they work almost like eyes, and some of these animals can feel, decide and act faster than you can blink.

In the wet, dark soil of eastern North American wetlands digs a small mammal with the strangest face on Earth. It is the star-nosed mole: around its nostrils sits a ring of 22 pink, fleshy tentacles, and despite its looks the star is not for smelling at all but is the most sensitive touch organ known in any mammal.

Packed with more than 25,000 tiny touch sensors, the star lets the mole identify a worm and swallow it in about 120 milliseconds, roughly a quarter of a second, a world record for a feeding mammal. Harbor seals hunt in murky coastal water by feel. In Georg Dehnhardt's 2001 experiment, a blindfolded seal followed the invisible wake a fish had left, its swirling trail of disturbed water, sensing it with its whiskers alone. With its whiskers masked, the seal would not even begin to search. A manatee sorts water plants in cloudy water with about 600 stiff bristles on its face, which it works like fingers. Researchers judge that touch to be at least as fine as an elephant feeling with the tip of its trunk.

A naked mole-rat, a wrinkled, nearly hairless rodent of East African desert tunnels, has rows of stiff sensory hairs along its sides and tail that work as feelers. Thanks to them it can run backward through its tunnels as fast and as surely as it runs forward, useful where there is no room to turn around. When Kenneth Catania studied high-speed film of the mole at work, he saw that the star never glides smoothly across the soil. It dabs 10 to 15 spots every second, jumping from point to point the way our eyes flick across a scene in quick darts called saccades, so Catania called the star a "tactile eye."

seeing-heat-the-pit-vipers-infrared-eye.context_blurb:
Pit vipers, such as rattlesnakes, copperheads and the fer-de-lance, can hunt in total darkness because they sense the heat of their prey. A small pit on each side of the face works like a crude infrared camera, building a heat picture of the world that guides a deadly strike. Some boas and pythons have a heat sense of their own.

Between each eye and nostril a pit viper carries a heat-detecting pit that senses the infrared glow of a warm animal's body, so a rattlesnake in a pitch-black burrow can find a mouse it cannot see. Even blindfolded, a rattlesnake strikes a mouse dead-on in total darkness, hitting the chest, the warmest-glowing part of the body, about 99 percent of the time.

There is no eye or lens in the pit, only a little air pocket with a membrane, thinner than paper, slung across it, and the membrane physically warms wherever a warm animal's infrared glow falls on it. Heat-sensing nerve endings then fire, building a rough heat picture rather than a sharp image. Those nerves respond to temperature changes smaller than 0.001 degrees Celsius, a mere thousandth of a degree, making the pit one of the most sensitive heat detectors in any animal. With a pit on each side of the head, the two overlapping heat images give the snake stereo heat vision, so it can judge how far away its prey is and aim a strike its eyes cannot guide.

In 2010 Elena Gracheva's team identified the heat trigger in the pit, the protein that converts warmth into nerve firing: TRPA1, the same channel that in people produces the fiery sting of wasabi or mustard up the nose. In the viper it has been retuned to fire on heat. Pit vipers, pythons and boas sit far apart on the snake family tree, with many heat-blind snakes between them, so each group evolved its heat sense separately, a case of convergent evolution. The anatomy differs too: vipers have one big pit on each side, while boas and pythons have rows of smaller pits along their lips.

pterosaur-quetzalcoatlus.context_blurb:
Pterosaurs were winged reptiles that ruled the skies from the Late Triassic, about 230 million years ago, until the dinosaurs' world ended, 66 million years ago. Quetzalcoatlus, which soared over Texas some 68 million years ago, was one of the largest of them and one of the biggest animals ever to fly. Its head alone was longer than a tall man, and its name honors Quetzalcoatl, the feathered-serpent sky god of the Aztecs.

Cartoons call pterosaurs flying dinosaurs, but that is a mistake: a pterosaur was neither a dinosaur nor a bird but a flying reptile on a branch of its own, a close cousin of the dinosaurs. The first pterosaurs were bird-sized, and they made history as the first animals with backbones to fly by flapping their own wings, long before any bird took to the air.

Each wing was a membrane of skin running from the body out to the tip of one hugely lengthened fourth finger, so nearly the whole wing hung from a single giant finger. Quetzalcoatlus northropi measured about 10 to 11 meters (33 to 36 feet) from wingtip to wingtip, as wide as a small airplane.

A flier that big could stay light enough to leave the ground because its bones were hollow and filled with air, just like a bird's. After landing, it folded its wings up and walked on all fours, its limbs held straight beneath its body like a walking animal's rather than sprawled out to the sides.

Weighing about as much as a giraffe, Quetzalcoatlus could not take a running start and flap into the sky as a bird does. In 2008 Michael Habib proposed that it vaulted into the air off its powerful front limbs like a pole-vaulter, planting all four limbs and springing upward in a move called the quad-launch. He read it from the bones: its upper arm bone is very strong and its thigh bone comparatively weak, the reverse of a runner's, so the arms did the launching.

Paleontologists argued for decades about its meals. The best fossil evidence today says Quetzalcoatlus hunted on foot, striding over open ground and snapping up small animals the way a stork or a ground hornbill does, rather than fishing from the air.

A bare skin wing should have fluttered uselessly at speed, like a loose sail. But the pterosaur wing was stiffened from inside by thousands of thin rods called actinofibrils, each about a tenth of a millimeter thick, packed four to seven to the millimeter in crisscrossing layers that fanned out toward the wing finger. They worked like the battens in a sail, holding the wing taut against the air yet letting it fold up neatly on landing. Their material is still uncertain, most likely collagen.

Pterosaurs were covered in fuzz called pycnofibers, long thought to be simple hair-like insulation. In 2019 scientists examined an exquisitely preserved little anurognathid pterosaur and found that some filaments split into branches, a feather-like structure once credited only to feathered dinosaurs. That raised a striking possibility: true feathers, or the genetic recipe for them, may have first appeared in a shared ancestor of pterosaurs and dinosaurs, tens of millions of years before birds. If so, pterosaur fuzz and dinosaur feathers were not two separate inventions. The idea is still debated.
